knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is a pure binary linear optimization problem because every decision variable belongs to \(\{0,1\}\) and every objective and constraint function is affine.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical minimization form; equalities and maximization objectives are equivalent variants.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.1 Linear integer program p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A pure 0-1 linear model has the form
\[
\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}.
\]
All decision variables are binary; continuous or general-integer decision variables are absent. Linear equalities may be represented by paired inequalities, and a maximization objective may be converted to minimization by negating its coefficient vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pure 0-1 linear model optimizes a linear objective over linear constraints using only binary decision variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Pure 0-1 Linear Models

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.1 Linear integer program p. 29

children.title: Binary Control Models
children.top_down_role: Binary variables governing discrete operational or structural choices.

assumptions_latex: The alternatives are indexed by the finite set \(J=\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
Exactly one alternative must be selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vector \(z\) uniquely records the selected alternative through its sole component equal to one.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-hot binary controls for mutually exclusive alternatives.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A binary control model for mutually exclusive alternatives introduces \(z\in\{0,1\}^m\) and imposes
\[
\sum_{j\in J}z_j=1.
\]
The interpretation is that alternative \(j\) is selected exactly when \(z_j=1\). If selection is optional rather than mandatory, the equality is replaced by \(\sum_{j\in J}z_j\le 1\). Additional constraints may condition operational decisions on the selected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary control vector selects one alternative by imposing a one-hot constraint, or at most one alternative when selection is optional.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Control Models

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

children.title: Activation Models
children.top_down_role: Binary variables governing whether modeled activities, resources, or constraints are active.

assumptions_latex: Finite valid bounds \(L\le x\le U\) are known, with \(L\le0\le U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities force \(x=0\) when \(y=0\) and permit every \(x\in[L,U]\) when \(y=1\).

notation.meaning: valid lower and upper activity bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded scalar on-off activity; the vector case applies componentwise.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A bounded activation model links an activity \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) to a binary variable \(y\in\{0,1\}\) by
\[
Ly\le x\le Uy.
\]
Thus \(y=0\) deactivates the activity by requiring \(x=0\), whereas \(y=1\) restores the original interval \([L,U]\). For a nonnegative activity with \(0\le x\le U\), the coupling reduces to \(0\le x\le Uy\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An activation variable switches a bounded activity off at zero or on within its valid bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Activation Models

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Bound Requirement for Linear Activation Links
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a finite big-M activation inequality without a valid activity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the active state permits arbitrarily large nonnegative values, \(D_\infty=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,1):x\ge0\}\), then no finite \(M\) makes \(0\le x\le My\) an exact representation of \(D_\infty\), because every active point with \(x>M\) is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite big-M activation link is exact only when M is a valid finite activity bound.
assumptions_latex: The active set is unbounded above.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists M<\infty:\ D_\infty=\{(x,y):y\in\{0,1\},\ 0\le x\le My\}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Bound Requirement for Linear Activation Links

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ideal Convex Hull of a Bounded Scalar Activation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous relaxation of the exact two-term on-off activity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\le U\) be finite and \(D=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,1):L\le x\le U\}\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}(D)=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R\times[0,1]:Ly\le x\le Uy\}.\] Thus the bounded scalar activation inequalities form an ideal formulation in the \((x,y)\)-space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing the activation binary to the unit interval gives exactly the convex hull of the off point and active interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(D)=\{(x,y):0\le y\le1,\ Ly\le x\le Uy\}.\)

notation.meaning: union of the inactive point and active bounded interval

knowledge_statements.title: Ideal Convex Hull of a Bounded Scalar Activation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Activation model whose on state requires a positive minimum activity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\ell\le U<\infty\), the constraints \[\ell y\le x\le Uy,\qquad y\in\{0,1\},\] represent exactly \((x,y)=(0,0)\) or \(y=1\) with \(x\in[\ell,U]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive lower activation bound models an activity that is either zero or above a minimum operating level.

notation.meaning: minimum activity in the active state

knowledge_statements.title: Semicontinuous Minimum-Activity Variant

children.title: Control–Activation Couplings
children.top_down_role: Structural links between binary controls and the entities they activate.

assumptions_latex: The inactive state is prescribed as \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Over the stated domain, \(y=0\Rightarrow x=0\) holds if and only if \(Ly\le x\le Uy\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bounded linear representation of zero-inactive control coupling.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in[L,U]\) and \(y\in\{0,1\}\), the control implication
\[
y=0\ \Longrightarrow\ x=0
\]
is represented exactly by
\[
Ly\le x\le Uy.
\]
When \(y=0\), both inequalities imply \(x=0\); when \(y=1\), they reproduce precisely the original bounds. Finite valid bounds are essential to this linear coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite bounds convert the implication that an inactive control forces zero activity into two exact linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Control–Activation Couplings

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

children.title: Indicator Models
children.top_down_role: Constraint interfaces governed directly by binary indicators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) whenever \(y=1\), while the indicator imposes no such restriction when \(y=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic indicator constraint, independent of a particular big-M reformulation.

source_refs.locator: 4.6 Disjunctive Programs with Trigger Variables p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An indicator model contains a conditional constraint of the form
\[
y=1\ \Longrightarrow\ a^{\mathsf T}x\le b,
\]
where \(y\in\{0,1\}\). Its feasible set is
\[
\{(x,0):x\in X\}\mathbin{\cup}\{(x,1):x\in X,\ a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\}.
\]
The reverse implication is not part of the definition unless it is imposed separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator constraint enforces a specified inequality when its binary indicator equals one and otherwise leaves that inequality inactive.
knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Models

source_witnesses.locator: 4.6 Disjunctive Programs with Trigger Variables p. 67

children.title: Trigger Models
children.top_down_role: Conditional model components controlled by binary trigger states.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonempty finite index set, \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(i\in S\), and \(t\in\{0,1\}\).
For the optional triggered inequality, \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(x\in X\), \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities make \(t=1\) exactly when \(y_i=1\) for every \(i\in S\), so \(t\) may serve as the indicator of the conditional constraint \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjunctive binary trigger followed by an optional indicated linear constraint.

source_refs.locator: 4.6 Disjunctive Programs with Trigger Variables p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be a nonempty finite set, let \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(i\in S\), and let \(t\in\{0,1\}\). A conjunctive trigger is represented by
\[
t\le y_i\quad(i\in S),\qquad t\ge\sum_{i\in S}y_i-|S|+1.
\]
These constraints give \(t=1\) if and only if \(y_i=1\) for every \(i\in S\). Given \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(x\in X\), \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}\), a triggered model may then include
\[
t=1\ \Longrightarrow\ a^{\mathsf T}x\le b.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary trigger can represent the conjunction of finitely many binary controls and can activate a specified linear constraint exactly when all controls are true.
knowledge_statements.title: Trigger Models

source_witnesses.locator: 4.6 Disjunctive Programs with Trigger Variables p. 67

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear representation of a trigger true when at least one antecedent is true.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be nonempty and finite, with \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) and \(t\in\{0,1\}\). The constraints
\[
t\ge y_i\quad(i\in S),\qquad t\le\sum_{i\in S}y_i
\]
are equivalent to \(t=1\Longleftrightarrow\bigvee_{i\in S}(y_i=1)\). Thus \(t\) can activate a subsequent indicator constraint exactly when at least one antecedent is true.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary OR trigger is represented by a lower bound from every antecedent and an upper bound by their sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities hold exactly when \(t=\max_{i\in S}y_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Binary Trigger

children.title: Disjunctive Models
children.top_down_role: Binary representations of alternatives drawn from distinct feasible regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb{N}\) is positive, and for each \(k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), \(r_k\in\mathbb{N}\), \(A^k\in\mathbb{R}^{r_k\times n}\), and \(b^k\in\mathbb{R}^{r_k}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is feasible exactly when it belongs to at least one set \(P_k\); one-hot variables \(z_k\in\{0,1\}\) may record a selected disjunct.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite union of polyhedra with optional one-hot selectors.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.2 Disjunctive constraints p. 10
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

source_refs.locator: Generalized disjunctive programming: A framework for formulation and alternative algorithms for MINLP optimization p. 93

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive. For every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), let \(r_k\in\mathbb{N}\), \(A^k\in\mathbb{R}^{r_k\times n}\), \(b^k\in\mathbb{R}^{r_k}\), and
\[
P_k=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A^kx\le b^k\}.
\]
A finite disjunctive model requires
\[
x\in\bigcup_{k=1}^K P_k.
\]
Binary selectors \(z_k\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(\sum_{k=1}^Kz_k=1\) may identify one selected disjunct, with \(z_k=1\) requiring \(x\in P_k\). If the disjuncts overlap, more than one selector assignment may correspond to the same feasible vector \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite disjunctive model restricts a decision vector to a finite union of explicitly defined polyhedra, and one-hot binary variables may identify a selected member of that union.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Models

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.2 Disjunctive constraints p. 10
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

source_witnesses.locator: Generalized disjunctive programming: A framework for formulation and alternative algorithms for MINLP optimization p. 93

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Hull Extended Formulation for a Finite Union of Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disaggregated exact formulation and ideal continuous relaxation for a finite union of nonempty polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_k=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A^kx\le b^k\}\) be a nonempty polytope for \(k=1,\ldots,K\). Define
\[
Q=\left\{(x,(x^k),z):x=\sum_{k=1}^Kx^k,\ A^kx^k\le b^kz_k\ (k=1,\ldots,K),\ z\ge0,\ \sum_{k=1}^Kz_k=1\right\}.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{k=1}^KP_k)\). Requiring \(z\in\{0,1\}^K\) instead gives projection \(\bigcup_{k=1}^KP_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disaggregation yields an exact binary formulation of a finite union of nonempty polytopes and its convex hull when selectors are relaxed.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P_k=\{x:A^kx\le b^k\}\) is nonempty and bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuous formulation projects to \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_kP_k)\), while one-hot binary selectors project to \(\bigcup_kP_k\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Hull Extended Formulation for a Finite Union of Polytopes

children.title: Conditional-Structure Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Representational correspondences among indicator, trigger, and disjunctive structures.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The indicator system is exactly the union, over binary assignments, of the sets enforcing the constraints whose assigned indicators equal one.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic correspondence between indicator implications and binary-indexed disjunctions.

source_refs.locator: Generalized disjunctive programming: A framework for formulation and alternative algorithms for MINLP optimization p. 93

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the indicator implications \(y_j=1\Rightarrow g_j(x)\le0\), define
\[
P_s=\{x\in X:g_j(x)\le0\text{ for every }j\text{ with }s_j=1\},
\qquad s\in\{0,1\}^m.
\]
Then their feasible set satisfies
\[
\{(x,y):x\in X,\ y_j=1\Rightarrow g_j(x)\le0\}
=
\bigcup_{s\in\{0,1\}^m}(P_s\times\{s\}).
\]
Thus conditional binary structure and a binary-indexed disjunction are equivalent descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Indicator implications partition by binary assignments into a finite disjunction of assignment-specific feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional-Structure Correspondences

source_witnesses.locator: Generalized disjunctive programming: A framework for formulation and alternative algorithms for MINLP optimization p. 93

children.title: Clausal Constraint Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces expressing binary restrictions through clauses.

assumptions_latex: \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) represents Boolean truth for each variable.
A literal is either \(x_i\) or its complement \(1-x_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linear inequality is satisfied exactly by the binary assignments that satisfy the clause.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard binary encoding of a Boolean clause
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct linear interface for one nonempty Boolean clause.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a nonempty clause contain positive literals indexed by \(P\) and negated literals indexed by \(N\), where \(P\cap N=\varnothing\). Under the truth encoding \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\), the clause
\[
\bigvee_{i\in P}x_i\ \vee\ \bigvee_{i\in N}\neg x_i
\]
is represented exactly by
\[
\sum_{i\in P}x_i+\sum_{i\in N}(1-x_i)\ge1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Boolean clause becomes one linear inequality requiring at least one positive or complemented binary literal to equal one.
knowledge_statements.title: Clausal Constraint Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate cases outside the seed's nonempty, disjoint-literal clause form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under binary truth encoding, an empty clause is false for every assignment and has the infeasible linear form \(0\ge1\). A clause containing both \(x_i\) and \(\neg x_i\) for some \(i\) is true for every assignment because \(x_i+(1-x_i)=1\), and may be deleted without changing feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty clause makes the model infeasible, while a clause containing a variable and its negation is tautological.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Empty clauses certify infeasibility, while tautological clauses impose no restriction.
knowledge_statements.title: Empty and Tautological Clause Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact direct 0-1 linear interface for a finite conjunction of clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal C\) be a finite family of clauses, with \(P_C\) and \(N_C\) indexing the positive and negated literals of clause \(C\). A binary assignment satisfies \(\bigwedge_{C\in\mathcal C}C\) if and only if
\[
\sum_{i\in P_C}x_i+\sum_{i\in N_C}(1-x_i)\ge1\qquad(C\in\mathcal C).
\]
Thus a CNF formula requires no auxiliary variables when its truth variables are already present.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CNF formula is represented exactly by imposing the direct clause inequality for every clause.
assumptions_latex: After removing tautologies, every clause is nonempty and has disjoint positive and negative literal sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The binary solutions are exactly the satisfying assignments of the CNF formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjunctive-Normal-Form Constraint System

children.title: Cardinality Constraint Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces organized by bounds on selected literals or variables.

assumptions_latex: \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(i\) in a finite set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint holds exactly when between \(\ell\) and \(u\) of the indexed Boolean variables are true.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cardinality equals the sum of binary truth values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided cardinality interface, including at-most, at-least, and exactly constraints.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cardinality constraint on binary variables \((x_i)_{i\in S}\) has the linear form
\[
\ell\le\sum_{i\in S}x_i\le u.
\]
Because the sum counts the components equal to one, it restricts the number of true variables to \([\ell,u]\). Setting \(\ell=u=k\) gives an exactly-\(k\) constraint; omitting either side gives an at-most or at-least constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cardinality interface bounds the number of true binary variables through lower and upper bounds on their sum.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality Constraint Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality interface for arbitrary positive and negated literals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P,N\) be disjoint finite index sets and \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\). The number of true literals in \(\{x_i:i\in P\}\cup\{\neg x_i:i\in N\}\) is
\[
\sum_{i\in P}x_i+\sum_{i\in N}(1-x_i).
\]
Hence the literal-cardinality restriction is represented exactly by
\[
\ell\le\sum_{i\in P}x_i+\sum_{i\in N}(1-x_i)\le u.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cardinality bounds on positive and negated literals are linear bounds on the sum of their binary truth values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities hold exactly when between \(\ell\) and \(u\) listed literals are true.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality Constraints on Boolean Literals

children.title: Pseudo-Boolean Constraint Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces exposing weighted Boolean constraints to optimization systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed integer-weighted relation defines a pseudo-Boolean constraint and exposes it directly as a 0-1 linear constraint.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard linear pseudo-Boolean constraint syntax
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear pseudo-Boolean constraints with integer coefficients.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.1 Linear integer program p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A linear pseudo-Boolean constraint is a relation
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\ \bowtie\ b,
\]
where \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\), \(a_i,b\in\mathbb{Z}\), and \(\bowtie\) is one of \(\le\), \(=\), or \(\ge\). Negative coefficients are permitted; complemented literals may be eliminated using \(\neg x_i=1-x_i\). Cardinality constraints are the special case in which the relevant coefficients are all one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear pseudo-Boolean constraint compares an integer-weighted sum of binary truth values with an integer threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Boolean Constraint Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.1 Linear integer program p. 29

children.title: Logical Interface Translations
children.top_down_role: Translations among clausal, cardinality, and pseudo-Boolean constraint forms.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite propositional formula built from Boolean variables using \(\neg\), \(\wedge\), and \(\vee\).
A binary variable \(z_G\in\{0,1\}\) is assigned to every subformula \(G\) of \(F\), with leaf variables identified with their original binary truth variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After imposing the gate constraints for every internal subformula and fixing \(z_F=1\), the resulting 0-1 linear system projects exactly onto the satisfying assignments of \(F\).

notation.meaning: binary truth value assigned to subformula G
binary truth values of two child subformulas
binary truth value of the root formula

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard exact binary linearizations of Boolean connectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact auxiliary-variable translation of finite propositional formulas into 0-1 linear constraints.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a finite propositional formula, and assign a variable \(z_G\in\{0,1\}\) to every subformula \(G\) of \(F\), identifying each leaf variable with its original binary truth variable. For binary child values \(p,q\in\{0,1\}\) and parent value \(z\in\{0,1\}\), encode \(z=\neg p\) by \(z=1-p\). Encode \(z=p\wedge q\) by
\[
z\le p,\quad z\le q,\quad z\ge p+q-1.
\]
Encode \(z=p\vee q\) by
\[
z\ge p,\quad z\ge q,\quad z\le p+q.
\]
Imposing the applicable encoding at every internal subformula and fixing the root variable by \(z_F=1\) yields a 0-1 linear system whose projection onto the original variables is precisely the set of satisfying assignments of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning a binary variable to every subformula and imposing exact linear encodings of NOT, AND, and OR produces a 0-1 linear system whose original-variable solutions are exactly the satisfying assignments of the formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Logical Interface Translations

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary-variable and constraint count for the exact gate-by-gate translation of a Boolean syntax tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) have \(t\) internal occurrences of the connectives \(\neg,\wedge,\vee\). The gate translation introduces at most one auxiliary binary variable per internal occurrence and at most three linear constraints per occurrence. Hence it uses at most \(t\) auxiliary variables and \(3t+1\) constraints, including \(z_F=1\), and its construction time and output size are \(O(t)\), apart from coefficient-encoding storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gate-by-gate linear translation has size and construction time linear in the Boolean formula's syntax-tree size.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is represented as a finite syntax tree using \(\neg,\wedge,\vee\).
Each internal occurrence is encoded independently by the gate constraints in the immutable seed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The translation introduces \(O(t)\) auxiliary variables and constraints and can be constructed in \(O(t)\) time.

notation.meaning: number of internal connective occurrences in the syntax tree

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Size of Syntax-Tree Translation

children.title: Multilinear Polynomial Views
children.top_down_role: Pseudo-Boolean objectives or constraints viewed through multilinear polynomial structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Multilinear Polynomial Views
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique multilinear representation of a real-valued pseudo-Boolean function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), there is a unique family \((a_S)_{S\subseteq[n]}\) such that
\[
f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}a_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i\qquad\text{for every }x\in\{0,1\}^n.
\]
The representing polynomial is multilinear and has degree \(\max\{|S|:a_S\ne0\}\), with the zero function assigned degree \(-\infty\) by convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real pseudo-Boolean function has a unique multilinear expansion in square-free binary monomials. Its degree is the largest size of a subset indexing a nonzero coefficient, with the zero function assigned degree minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has a unique multilinear polynomial representation on \(\{0,1\}^n\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic characterization of the unique multilinear representative on the binary cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I=\langle x_1^2-x_1,\ldots,x_n^2-x_n\rangle\subseteq\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). Every polynomial \(p\) is congruent modulo \(I\) to a unique multilinear polynomial \(\operatorname{ml}(p)\), obtained by replacing every positive power \(x_i^k\) by \(x_i\). For polynomials \(p,q\),
\[
p(x)=q(x)\ \text{for every }x\in\{0,1\}^n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p-q\in I
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{ml}(p)=\operatorname{ml}(q).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduction modulo the Boolean equations gives the unique multilinear normal form; two polynomials agree on the binary cube exactly when their difference lies in the Boolean ideal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multilinear reduction is the unique normal form for polynomial functions on \(\{0,1\}^n\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-vector identification between binary vectors and subsets.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set-function view of \(f\) is the function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by
\[
F(S)=f(\mathbf{1}_S),\qquad (\mathbf{1}_S)_i=\begin{cases}1,&i\in S,\\0,&i\notin S.\end{cases}
\]
Conversely, any \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb{R}\) defines a pseudo-Boolean function by \(f(x)=F(\{i:x_i=1\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary vector is identified with its support, turning a pseudo-Boolean function into a set function and vice versa.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Function Views

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order and lattice operations transported by the incidence-vector identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^n\), let \(S_x=\{i:x_i=1\}\). Then
\[
x\le y\ \text{componentwise}\iff S_x\subseteq S_y,
\]
\[
S_{\min(x,y)}=S_x\cap S_y,\qquad S_{\max(x,y)}=S_x\cup S_y,
\]
and
\[
S_{\mathbf 1-x}=[n]\setminus S_x.
\]
Thus the support map is an isomorphism from the binary cube with componentwise order, meet, join, and complementation to the Boolean subset lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking supports identifies binary order and operations with subset inclusion, intersection, union, and complement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The support map is an isomorphism between the binary cube and the Boolean subset lattice.
knowledge_statements.title: Boolean-Lattice Structure of Supports

children.title: Polynomial–Set Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between multilinear coefficients and set-function values.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial–Set Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean-lattice Möbius inversion for polynomial and set-function data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) have the multilinear representation \(f(x)=\sum_{T\subseteq[n]}a_T\prod_{i\in T}x_i\), and define \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(F(S)=f(\mathbf{1}_S)\). Then
\[
F(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}a_T\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq[n].
\]
The inverse correspondence is
\[
a_T=\sum_{U\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|U|}F(U)
\qquad\text{for every }T\subseteq[n].
\]
Thus evaluation on incidence vectors and Möbius inversion are mutually inverse transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed finite binary dimension, set-function values are subset sums of multilinear coefficients, and Boolean-lattice Möbius inversion recovers every coefficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed transforms give a bijection between set-function values \(F(S)\) and multilinear coefficients \(a_T\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fast Boolean-Lattice Zeta and Möbius Transforms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic complexity of converting a complete value table to or from its multilinear coefficient table.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given all \(2^n\) entries of either \((a_T)_{T\subseteq[n]}\) or \((F(S))_{S\subseteq[n]}\), the relations
\[
F(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}a_T,
\qquad
a_T=\sum_{U\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|U|}F(U)
\]
can be evaluated for every subset by the in-place fast zeta or Möbius transform. Each transform uses \(n2^{n-1}\) pair updates, hence \(O(n2^n)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(2^n)\) storage, including the input/output table.

Arithmetic operations over \(\mathbb{R}\) have unit cost

children.title: Literal Views
children.top_down_role: Representations organized around positive or complemented binary literals.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-assignment literal products as indicator functions and a basis for functions on the binary cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(u\in\{0,1\}^n\), define
\[
\delta_u(x)=\prod_{i:u_i=1}x_i\prod_{i:u_i=0}(1-x_i).
\]
Then \(\delta_u(x)=1\) exactly when \(x=u\), and \(0\) otherwise, while \(\sum_u\delta_u(x)=1\). Consequently every \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) has the unique expansion
\[
f(x)=\sum_{u\in\{0,1\}^n}f(u)\delta_u(x).
\]
The basis contains exactly \(2^n\) monomials, and functions with \(f(u)\ne0\) for every assignment use all \(2^n\) terms in this basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete literal products are assignment indicators forming a unique basis of size 2^n for all real functions on the binary cube.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\delta_u:u\in\{0,1\}^n\}\) is the \(2^n\)-element assignment-indicator basis.

notation.meaning: Complete literal monomial indicating assignment u

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Literal Monomial Basis

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each literal is binary and satisfies \(x_i+\bar{x}_i=1\).

notation.meaning: Positive literal associated with variable i
Negative or complemented literal associated with variable i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary literals and the conjunction semantics of their products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each index \(i\in[n]\), the two literals are the positive literal \(x_i\) and the negative literal \(\bar{x}_i=1-x_i\). A consistent literal monomial has the form
\[
L_{P,N}(x)=\prod_{i\in P}x_i\prod_{j\in N}(1-x_j),
\]
where \(P,N\subseteq[n]\) and \(P\cap N=\varnothing\). It equals \(1\) exactly when all specified positive literals and negative literals are satisfied, and equals \(0\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary literal is either a variable or its complement; a consistent literal product indicates simultaneous satisfaction of its literals.
knowledge_statements.title: Literal Views

children.title: Posiform Views
children.top_down_role: Pseudo-Boolean expressions organized as nonnegative literal products.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Posiform Constant Lower Bound and Exactness Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound and exact equality test for a fixed posiform expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
p(x)=c_0+\sum_{k=1}^m c_kL_k(x),\qquad c_k>0,
\]
be a posiform on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Then \(p(x)\ge c_0\) for every binary vector, and
\[
p(x^*)=c_0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L_k(x^*)=0\ \text{for every }k.
\]
Thus an assignment annihilating every positive-coefficient monomial certifies that \(c_0\) is the minimum and that the assignment is globally minimizing. If no such assignment exists, \(c_0\) remains a valid but nonexact lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A posiform's constant is a global lower bound, attained exactly when every positive monomial vanishes.
assumptions_latex: Each \(L_k\) is a consistent literal monomial
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\ge c_0\), with equality exactly when all nonconstant terms vanish.

notation.meaning: Constant term and posiform lower bound

knowledge_statements.title: Posiform Constant Lower Bound and Exactness Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of uniqueness for positive-coefficient consistent-literal representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\ge2\), the function \(f(x)=x_1\) has the distinct posiform representations
\[
f(x)=x_1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
f(x)=x_1x_2+x_1(1-x_2).
\]
Hence posiform coefficients and monomial supports are not uniquely determined by the represented function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posiform representations are generally nonunique; a term can be split across the two polarities of another variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The same pseudo-Boolean function can have different posiform coefficient and monomial families.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness of Posiform Representations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a posiform representation for every real pseudo-Boolean function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) admits a representation
\[
f(x)=c_0+\sum_{k=1}^m c_kL_k(x),
\]
where \(c_0\in\mathbb{R}\), every \(c_k>0\), and every \(L_k\) is a nonempty consistent literal monomial. In particular, with \(c_0=\min_u f(u)\),
\[
f(x)=c_0+\sum_{u:f(u)>c_0}\bigl(f(u)-c_0\bigr)\delta_u(x).
\]
This construction uses at most \(2^n-1\) nonconstant terms and can require exponentially many terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every pseudo-Boolean function is a constant plus a nonnegative combination of consistent literal products; the complete-assignment construction may be exponential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has a posiform representation with an unrestricted constant and positive nonconstant coefficients.

notation.meaning: Complete literal monomial indicating assignment u

knowledge_statements.title: Universal Posiform Representation

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A posiform is a constant plus a nonnegative linear combination of literal monomials.

notation.meaning: A positive or negative binary literal
Nonnegative coefficient of a literal monomial

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard posiform convention with an unrestricted additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A posiform on \(\{0,1\}^n\) is an expression
\[
p(x)=c_0+\sum_{k=1}^{m}c_k\prod_{i\in I_k}\ell_{ki}(x),
\]
where \(c_0\in\mathbb{R}\), \(c_k\ge0\), \(I_k\subseteq[n]\), and each \(\ell_{ki}(x)\) is either \(x_i\) or \(1-x_i\). No product contains both literals of the same variable; the empty product, when present, equals \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A posiform is an arbitrary constant plus nonnegative weighted products of consistent positive and complemented binary literals.
knowledge_statements.title: Posiform Views

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise complementation as a bijective change of binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(C\subseteq[n]\) and define
\[
y_i=\begin{cases}1-x_i,&i\in C,\\x_i,&i\notin C.\end{cases}
\]
This transformation is an involution on \(\{0,1\}^n\). For any pseudo-Boolean function \(f\), define \(g(y)=f(x(y))\), where \(x_i(y)=1-y_i\) for \(i\in C\) and \(x_i(y)=y_i\) otherwise. Then \(g(y)=f(x)\) at corresponding vectors, so minimizers and minimum values correspond bijectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing any chosen coordinates is an involutive relabeling of the binary cube that preserves objective values and minimizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Complemented-Variable Views

children.title: Literal Complementation Equivalences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient conversion induced by complementing a prescribed subset of binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}a_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i\), fix \(C\subseteq[n]\), and substitute \(x_i=1-y_i\) for \(i\in C\) and \(x_i=y_i\) otherwise. If \(g(y)=\sum_{T\subseteq[n]}b_T\prod_{i\in T}y_i\), then
\[
b_T=(-1)^{|T\cap C|}\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq[n]:\ S\setminus C=T\setminus C,\\S\cap C\supseteq T\cap C}}a_S.
\]
This coefficient transformation is an involution and preserves degree. Processing the complemented coordinates successively computes all coefficients in \(O(|C|2^n)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(2^n)\) storage when dense coefficient tables are used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial complementation induces an explicit involutive, degree-preserving transformation of multilinear coefficients, computable by successive pair updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed transform is involutive, preserves degree, and has dense-table arithmetic cost \(O(|C|2^n)\).

notation.meaning: Equality of expressions at every binary vector

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional equivalence after expansion and Boolean reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On the binary cube, the identities
\[
\bar{x}_i=1-x_i,
\qquad x_i^k=x_i\ \text{ for }k\ge1,
\qquad x_i(1-x_i)=0
\]
hold pointwise. Consequently, expanding every complemented literal and reducing powers converts any polynomial in literals into a multilinear polynomial with the same values on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Conversely, replacing selected occurrences of \(1-x_i\) by \(\bar{x}_i\) yields an equivalent literal expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding complements and applying binary identities converts literal expressions to equivalent multilinear polynomials; introducing complemented literals reverses the representation change.
knowledge_statements.title: Literal Complementation Equivalences

knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Structured Pseudo-Boolean Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by degree of the unique multilinear representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(d\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), and let
\[
f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}a_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i
\]
be the unique multilinear representation of \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). Its degree is \(\deg(f)=\max\{|S|:a_S\ne0\}\), with \(\deg(0)=-\infty\). A degree-at-most-\(d\) pseudo-Boolean model is one whose objective and every pseudo-Boolean constraint function have no nonzero monomial indexed by a set larger than \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a specified degree bound d, a degree-structured pseudo-Boolean model has no objective or constraint monomial involving more than d distinct binary variables; the zero function has degree minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degree bound \(\deg(f)\le d\) is equivalent to \(a_S=0\) whenever \(|S|>d\).

Then \(\deg(f)\le d\) if and only if \[\Delta_{i_1}\cdots\Delta_{i_{d+1}}f\equiv0\] for every \(d+1\) distinct indices. Moreover, \(\deg(f)=d\) exactly when all order-\(d+1\) differences vanish and at least one order-\(d\) difference is nonzero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constant, Linear, and Quadratic Degree Tiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical low-degree subclasses in the degree hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonzero pseudo-Boolean function has degree zero exactly when it is constant. It has degree at most one exactly when it is affine, \(a_\varnothing+\sum_i a_ix_i\), and degree at most two exactly when it is quadratic, \(a_\varnothing+\sum_i a_ix_i+\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}x_ix_j\). The zero function belongs to every degree-at-most class because \(\deg(0)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The degree-zero, degree-at-most-one, and degree-at-most-two tiers are constant, affine, and quadratic functions, with zero in every bounded-degree tier.
assumptions_latex: Functions use their unique multilinear representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degree bounds \(0,1,2\) coincide with constant, affine, and quadratic multilinear forms, respectively.
knowledge_statements.title: Constant, Linear, and Quadratic Degree Tiers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure and monotonicity laws for multilinear degree under arithmetic and variable restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f,g:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb R\), with products multilinearized using \(x_i^2=x_i\), \[\deg(f+g)\le\max\{\deg(f),\deg(g)\},\qquad \deg(fg)\le\min\{n,\deg(f)+\deg(g)\}.\] Either inequality may be strict through cancellation or overlapping variables. Substitution of constants from \(\{0,1\}\) for any variables cannot increase degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudo-Boolean degree is submaximal under addition, subadditive under multiplication, and nonincreasing under binary restrictions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) use their unique multilinear representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degree obeys the stated addition, multiplication, and restriction bounds.

children.title: Constrained Pseudo-Boolean Models
children.top_down_role: Pseudo-Boolean models with explicit feasibility restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Pseudo-Boolean Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite constrained minimization with pseudo-Boolean equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(m,r\in\mathbb{N}_0\), a constrained pseudo-Boolean model has the form
\[
\min\{f(x):x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ g_j(x)\le0\ (j=1,\ldots,m),\ h_k(x)=0\ (k=1,\ldots,r)\},
\]
where \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m,h_1,\ldots,h_r:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). Its feasible set is
\[
X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:g_j(x)\le0\ \text{for every }j,\ h_k(x)=0\ \text{for every }k\},
\]
and the model is feasible precisely when \(X\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For specified finite numbers of binary variables, inequalities, and equalities, a constrained pseudo-Boolean model minimizes a pseudo-Boolean objective over the binary vectors satisfying all pseudo-Boolean constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is \(X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:g_j(x)\le0\ \forall j,\ h_k(x)=0\ \forall k\}\).

source_refs.locator: Computation with polynomial equations and inequalities arising in combinatorial optimization p. 447

source_witnesses.locator: Computation with polynomial equations and inequalities arising in combinatorial optimization p. 447

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and global-optimality characterization for feasible constrained pseudo-Boolean models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:g_j(x)\le0\ (j=1,\ldots,m),\ h_k(x)=0\ (k=1,\ldots,r)\}.
\]
If \(X\ne\varnothing\), then \(X\) is finite and there exists \(x^*\in X\) with
\[
f(x^*)=\min_{x\in X}f(x).
\]
A vector \(x^*\) is globally optimal exactly when \(x^*\in X\) and \(f(x^*)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). If \(X=\varnothing\), no feasible optimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every feasible constrained pseudo-Boolean model attains its minimum; global optimality is feasibility plus objective dominance over the finite feasible set.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many displayed constraints
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A global minimizer exists exactly when \(X\ne\varnothing\), and it satisfies the displayed dominance condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Pseudo-Boolean Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained minimization over the complete binary cube.

For \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), an unconstrained pseudo-Boolean model is
\[
\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}f(x),

where \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). Because the domain is finite and nonempty, the minimum is attained. The word unconstrained means that no feasibility conditions other than \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) are imposed; interactions may still occur through arbitrary multilinear terms in \(f\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimization problem is \(\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}f(x)\), with no restrictions beyond binarity.

children.title: Constraint-Absorption Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Reformulations moving explicit restrictions into unconstrained representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Absorption Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain exact penalty using a positive violation function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(\varnothing\ne X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), let \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(V:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}_+\) satisfy \(V(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\in X\). If \(X\ne\{0,1\}^n\), define
\[
\delta=\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n\setminus X}V(x)>0,
\qquad
R=\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}f(x)-\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}f(x).
\]
For every \(\rho>R/\delta\), the unconstrained problem
\[
\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\bigl(f(x)+\rho V(x)\bigr)
\]
has exactly the global minimizers of \(f\) over \(X\). If \(X=\{0,1\}^n\), taking \(V\equiv0\) makes every \(\rho\ge0\) yield the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite binary cube, if a nonnegative violation function vanishes exactly on a nonempty feasible set, then any penalty weight strictly larger than the objective range divided by the smallest positive violation gives exactly the constrained global minimizers; the full-cube case needs no penalty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(X\ne\{0,1\}^n\), then for \(\rho>R/\delta\), the global minimizers of \(f+\rho V\) are exactly the global minimizers of \(f\) over \(X\).

notation.meaning: Objective range over the binary cube

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-exact violation function for finite pseudo-Boolean equality and inequality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{0,1\}^n\) and \[X=\{x\in D:g_j(x)\le0\ (j\in J),\ h_k(x)=0\ (k\in K)\}.\] For finite \(J,K\) and weights \(a_j,b_k>0\), \[V(x)=\sum_{j\in J}a_j[g_j(x)]_++\sum_{k\in K}b_k|h_k(x)|\] is nonnegative and satisfies \(V(x)=0\iff x\in X\). If \(X\ne\varnothing\), sufficiently large \(\rho\) makes \(\min_{x\in D}(f(x)+\rho V(x))\) exactly equivalent in global minimizers to \(\min\{f(x):x\in X\}\). As a function on \(D\), the absorbed objective has a multilinear pseudo-Boolean representation, although its degree or representation size may increase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-part and absolute-value penalties combine into a violation function vanishing exactly on the feasible binary vectors, permitting exact absorption into an unconstrained pseudo-Boolean objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V^{-1}(0)=X\), and sufficiently large \(\rho\) preserves exactly the constrained global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Wise Violation Absorption

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scalar threshold for absorbing a nonempty proper feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{0,1\}^n\), \(\varnothing\ne X\subsetneq D\), \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and let \(V:D\to\mathbb R_+\) vanish exactly on \(X\). Define \[f_X^*=\min_{x\in X}f(x),\qquad \rho_*=\max_{x\in D\setminus X}\frac{f_X^*-f(x)}{V(x)}.\] Then \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}(f(x)+\rho V(x))=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\] if and only if \(\rho>\rho_*\). At \(\rho=\rho_*\), an infeasible maximizer in the definition of \(\rho_*\) ties the feasible optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sharp transition equals the largest objective advantage of an infeasible point per unit violation; every larger weight is exact, while equality creates an infeasible tie.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{D}(f+\rho V)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{X}f\iff\rho>\rho_*\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Finite-Domain Exact-Penalty Threshold

children.title: Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Models
children.top_down_role: Binary quadratic objectives without explicit feasibility constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard unconstrained binary quadratic minimization form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), an unconstrained binary quadratic model is
\[
\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\;x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha,
\]
where \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\). Only the symmetric part \((Q+Q^{\mathsf T})/2\) affects the quadratic form. Since \(x_i^2=x_i\) on the binary domain, diagonal entries of \(Q\) may equivalently be absorbed into the linear coefficient vector. The constant \(\alpha\) changes the optimal value but not the minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive finite binary dimension, an unconstrained binary quadratic model minimizes a quadratic polynomial over all binary vectors; only the symmetric part of the quadratic matrix matters, diagonal quadratic terms can be folded into linear terms, and a constant does not change the minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model minimizes a polynomial of degree at most two over the full binary cube.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Baseline exact algorithm for an explicitly evaluable unconstrained binary quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Evaluate \(f(x)\) for all \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and return a vector attaining the least value. This uses exactly \(2^n\) objective evaluations. Direct evaluation of a dense explicitly stored quadratic requires \(O(n^2 2^n)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(n^2)\) coefficient storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exhaustive enumeration is exact, uses 2^n objective evaluations, and takes quadratic work per vector for a dense direct evaluation.
assumptions_latex: Objective values can be compared exactly under the chosen arithmetic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}f(x),\qquad N_{\mathrm{eval}}=2^n.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Enumeration Algorithm

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coordinatewise local-optimality test for a multilinear binary quadratic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\kappa+\sum_i a_ix_i+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}x_ix_j\). If \(x^{(i)}\) is obtained by flipping coordinate \(i\), then \[f(x^{(i)})-f(x)=(1-2x_i)\left(a_i+\sum_{j\ne i}b_{ij}x_j\right).\] Therefore \(x\) is a one-flip local minimizer exactly when these quantities are nonnegative for every \(i\); every global minimizer satisfies them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The explicit change from flipping one bit exactly characterizes one-flip local minima and gives necessary conditions for global optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is one-flip locally optimal}\iff(1-2x_i)\left(a_i+\sum_{j\ne i}b_{ij}x_j\right)\ge0\quad\forall i.

notation.meaning: Vector obtained by flipping coordinate i

knowledge_statements.title: One-Flip Local Optimality Conditions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Flip Optimality Is Not Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of coordinatewise optimality to imply global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1+x_2-3x_1x_2\), \(f(0,0)=0\) and \(f(1,0)=f(0,1)=1\), so \((0,0)\) is a strict one-flip local minimizer. But \(f(1,1)=-1\), so it is not globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point can beat every one-bit neighbor while being worse than a point reached by two simultaneous flips.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{One-flip local optimality does not imply global optimality for general QUBO.}
knowledge_statements.title: One-Flip Optimality Is Not Global Optimality

children.title: Constrained Binary Quadratic Models
children.top_down_role: Binary quadratic objectives over explicitly restricted feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) is optimized under quadratic inequality constraints.

notation.meaning: quadratic coefficient matrix for the objective or constraint k
linear coefficient vector for the objective or constraint k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional binary quadratically constrained model.

source_refs.locator: Linear programming relaxations of quadratically constrained quadratic programs p. 407

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constrained binary quadratic model has decision vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and the form \[\min\left\{x^{\mathsf T}Q_0x+c_0^{\mathsf T}x+\gamma_0: x^{\mathsf T}Q_kx+c_k^{\mathsf T}x\le b_k\ \text{for }k=1,\ldots,m\right\}.\] Each matrix may be taken symmetric because \(x^{\mathsf T}Q_kx=x^{\mathsf T}((Q_k+Q_k^{\mathsf T})/2)x\). Binary identities \(x_i^2=x_i\) permit diagonal quadratic terms to be absorbed into the corresponding linear coefficients without changing feasible objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained binary quadratic model minimizes a quadratic function of binary variables subject to finitely many quadratic inequalities; symmetry and binary square identities provide equivalent coefficient conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Binary Quadratic Models

source_witnesses.locator: Linear programming relaxations of quadratically constrained quadratic programs p. 407

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hardness of Constrained Binary Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity inherited from zero-one linear feasibility and optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under rational finite encoding, feasibility of constrained binary quadratic models is NP-complete even when \(Q_k=0\) for every objective and constraint, because zero-one linear feasibility is a special case and a proposed binary vector is verifiable in polynomial time. Optimization is NP-hard under the same restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The class is already NP-hard in its zero-one linear special case, and its feasibility problem is NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: All coefficients are rational and finitely encoded
The number of binary variables is part of the input
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: General feasibility is NP-complete and optimization is NP-hard, even when every \(Q_k=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Hardness of Constrained Binary Quadratic Models

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact normalization of finite binary quadratic constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Over \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quadratic equality \(q(x)=b\) is equivalent to \(q(x)\le b\) and \(-q(x)\le-b\), while \(q(x)\ge b\) is equivalent to \(-q(x)\le-b\). Thus finite systems containing quadratic equalities and either inequality direction can be written in the seed's all-\(\le\) convention without changing the feasible binary set or objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic equalities and reversed inequalities normalize exactly into finitely many less-than-or-equal quadratic constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) is quadratic on the binary cube
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The all-\(\le\) convention represents finite binary quadratic equality-and-inequality systems without loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Equality and Inequality Conventions

children.title: Constraint-Penalty Transitions
children.top_down_role: Transitions between explicit quadratic constraints and penalized unconstrained forms.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(f(x)+\rho V(x))=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\) for every \(\rho>(f_F-f_{\min})/\delta\).
review_flags: quadratic closure requires constraint-specific expansion check
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite penalty transition from constrained binary optimization to an unconstrained objective.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Penalty Function Approach p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{0,1\}^n\), let \(F=\{x\in X:g_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) be nonempty, assume \(X\setminus F\ne\varnothing\), and define \(V(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m g_j(x)^2\). If \(V(x)>0\) on \(X\setminus F\), then \(\delta=\min_{x\in X\setminus F}V(x)>0\). For \(f_{\min}=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(f_F=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\), every \(\rho>(f_F-f_{\min})/\delta\) satisfies \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\{f(x)+\rho V(x)\}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x).\] Thus a sufficiently large quadratic penalty gives an exact transition when its expansion remains within the desired model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite binary domain with at least one feasible and one infeasible point, a positive constraint-violation penalty becomes exact once its weight exceeds the objective advantage any infeasible point can obtain per unit violation.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Penalty Transitions

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5 Penalty Function Approach p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degree-Growth Boundary for Squared Quadratic Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of direct QUBO closure for genuinely quadratic residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Squaring a genuinely quadratic binary residual need not remain quadratic after multilinear reduction. For \[g(x)=x_1x_2+x_3x_4,\] one has on \(\{0,1\}^4\) \[g(x)^2=x_1x_2+x_3x_4+2x_1x_2x_3x_4.\] Thus \(f+\rho g^2\) is generally a higher-degree pseudo-Boolean objective rather than a QUBO. A transition from general quadratic constraints to an unconstrained quadratic model therefore requires another quadratic violation construction or an exact quadratization with auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared genuinely quadratic residuals can create quartic terms, so exact penalization does not automatically remain a QUBO.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Squared quadratic residual penalties are not closed within the QUBO class.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Growth Boundary for Squared Quadratic Residuals

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Closure for Affine Equality Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct exact QUBO transition for affine binary equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be quadratic on \(\{0,1\}^n\), and let the constraints be feasible affine equalities \(a_j^{\mathsf T}x=b_j\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\). Then \[P_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho\sum_{j=1}^m(a_j^{\mathsf T}x-b_j)^2\] is quadratic after replacing \(x_i^2\) by \(x_i\). For every sufficiently large \(\rho\), its global minimizers are exactly the constrained minimizers of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared affine equality residuals preserve quadratic degree on binary variables and, with sufficient weight, give a direct exact QUBO reformulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_\rho\) is a QUBO and is exact for all sufficiently large \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Closure for Affine Equality Penalties

children.title: QUBO Representations
children.top_down_role: Quadratic unconstrained representations over binary variables.

knowledge_statements.title: QUBO Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical unconstrained quadratic representation over zero-one variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic unconstrained binary optimization representation is \[\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\kappa,\] where \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) may be assumed symmetric. Every polynomial \(a+\sum_i b_ix_i+\sum_{i<j}c_{ij}x_ix_j\) of degree at most two on \(\{0,1\}^n\) has this form: choose \(Q_{ii}=b_i\), \(Q_{ij}=Q_{ji}=c_{ij}/2\), and \(\kappa=a\). Conversely, expanding the matrix expression yields a degree-at-most-two pseudo-Boolean function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: QUBO represents every quadratic pseudo-Boolean objective as a matrix quadratic form over zero-one vectors, with diagonal entries encoding linear terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\kappa\) and degree-at-most-two pseudo-Boolean polynomials are equivalent representations.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of the Normalized QUBO Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient uniqueness after imposing symmetry and separating the constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose symmetric \(Q,R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and constants \(\kappa,\lambda\) satisfy \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\kappa=x^{\mathsf T}Rx+\lambda\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Then \(Q=R\) and \(\kappa=\lambda\). Thus the symmetric QUBO representation with a separately written constant is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once symmetry and a separate constant are required, equality on the binary cube forces every QUBO coefficient to agree.
assumptions_latex: The expressions agree on every binary vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=R\quad\text{and}\quad\kappa=\lambda.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness of the Normalized QUBO Matrix

children.title: Ising Representations
children.top_down_role: Quadratic spin representations over signed states.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic symmetry and its field-dependent boundary for a pairwise Ising representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(E(s)=\kappa+\sum_i h_is_i+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}s_is_j\), \[E(-s)=\kappa-\sum_i h_is_i+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}s_is_j.\] Hence \(h=0\) implies \(E(-s)=E(s)\) for every configuration, and every minimizer has a globally reversed minimizer. Nonzero local fields generally break this symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-field Ising energy is invariant under simultaneous reversal of all spins; local fields generally break that invariance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h=0\implies E(-s)=E(s)\quad\forall s.

notation.meaning: Configuration obtained by reversing every spin

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Field Global Spin-Flip Symmetry
Ising Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise Ising energy representation using spins in \(\{-1,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An Ising representation of a quadratic binary energy is \[\min_{s\in\{-1,1\}^n}\left(\kappa+\sum_{i=1}^n h_is_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}J_{ij}s_is_j\right).\] The vector \(h\) contains local fields, while \(J_{ij}\) contains pairwise couplings. Because \(s_i^2=1\), diagonal quadratic terms contribute only to \(\kappa\). Consequently every degree-at-most-two function on the spin hypercube has such a representation, and the representation is unique after restricting interaction terms to distinct unordered pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An Ising model expresses a quadratic spin energy through a constant, local fields, and pairwise couplings on variables taking values minus one or one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every quadratic function on \(\{-1,1\}^n\) has the displayed constant-field-coupling form.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical finite pairwise Ising definition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The canonical finite Ising representation is mathematically precise and the content kind fits, but no inspectable source and locator are supplied for the representation and uniqueness claim.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise-interaction energy of a spin configuration on a graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E), assign each vertex i a spin \sigma_i\in\{-1,+1\}, and assign each edge ij an interaction coefficient J_{ij}. For S=\{i\in V:\sigma_i=1\}, the Ising Hamiltonian is H(S)=-\sum_{ij\in E}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j. Thus an edge contributes -J_{ij} when its endpoint spins agree and +J_{ij} when they differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each graph vertex has spin −1 or +1 and each edge has an interaction coefficient. The Hamiltonian is the negative sum of each coefficient times the product of its endpoint spins; agreeing spins contribute −J and differing spins contribute +J.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an undirected interaction graph}
J_{ij}\text{ is assigned to every }ij\in E
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(S)=-\sum_{ij\in E}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the signed-spin configuration space and energy function. The inverse temperature is an instance parameter but does not appear in the displayed Hamiltonian; interaction locality is a common physical specialization rather than a general requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An Ising-model instance specifies $n$ sites, interaction energies $V_{ij}$ for unordered pairs $\{i,j\}$, magnetic-field intensity $B$, and inverse temperature $\beta$. A configuration is $\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}^n$, and its energy is given by the Hamiltonian
\[
H(\sigma)=-\sum_{\{i,j\}}V_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j-B\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma_k.
\]
In common spatial models, $V_{ij}=0$ for nonadjacent sites, but this locality condition is not part of the general definition stated here.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An Ising instance specifies sites, pairwise interaction energies, a magnetic field, and an inverse temperature. A configuration assigns either minus one or plus one to every site. Its energy is the negative sum of the pairwise interaction terms and magnetic-field terms. Physical lattice models commonly allow nonzero interactions only between adjacent sites, but the general definition does not require locality.
assumptions_latex: V_{ij}\text{ is specified for every unordered site pair }\{i,j\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(\sigma)=-\sum_{\{i,j\}}V_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j-B\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma_k.

children.title: Cut Representations
children.top_down_role: Graph-cut interpretations of quadratic binary interactions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic labeling symmetry of an undirected cut representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\), let \(\bar x=\mathbf1-x\). Then \(|\bar x_i-\bar x_j|=|x_i-x_j|\) for every edge, so \[\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}|\bar x_i-\bar x_j|=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}|x_i-x_j|.\] Thus complementary shores define the same cut and the same weighted cut value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing every binary label exchanges the two shores without changing the cut or its value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w(\delta(S))=w(\delta(V\setminus S)).
knowledge_statements.title: Complementary-Shore Invariance
Cut Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted cut encoding of pairwise binary disagreement terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a binary labeling \(x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\) defines the cut \(S=\{i\in V:x_i=1\}\). Its weighted cut value is \[w(\delta(S))=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}|x_i-x_j|=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(x_i+x_j-2x_ix_j).\] Hence every weighted cut objective is a quadratic pseudo-Boolean function. Conversely, a pair term \(c_{ij}x_ix_j\) can be rewritten as \((c_{ij}/2)(x_i+x_j-|x_i-x_j|)\), leaving unary terms plus a weighted disagreement term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph cut equals a sum of weighted binary disagreements, each of which is quadratic; pairwise binary products can likewise be converted into disagreement plus unary terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(\delta(S))=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(x_i+x_j-2x_ix_j)\).

notation.meaning: edges with exactly one endpoint in S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut identities are correct and fit the representation leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation supporting the bidirectional cut-product representation.

children.title: QUBO–Ising Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural translation between binary-variable and spin-variable representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse affine coefficient transformation under the single-count Ising convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E(s)=C+\sum_i h_is_i+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}s_is_j\) and set \(s=2x-\mathbf1\). Then \[E(2x-\mathbf1)=\kappa+\sum_i a_ix_i+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}x_ix_j,\] where \[b_{ij}=4J_{ij},\qquad a_i=2h_i-2\sum_{j\ne i}J_{ij},\qquad \kappa=C-\sum_i h_i+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}.\] This is inverse to \(x=(\mathbf1+s)/2\) and preserves all objective values and minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing each spin by twice its binary variable minus one gives the inverse coefficient map from Ising form to QUBO.
assumptions_latex: Each pair \(J_{ij}\) is counted once with \(i<j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E(s)=E(2x-\mathbf1)\text{ with the displayed QUBO coefficients.}
review_flags: Normalization is tied to the displayed single-count pair convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Ising-to-QUBO Coefficient Map
QUBO–Ising Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine bijection between zero-one QUBO variables and Ising spins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\) and set \(x=(\mathbf 1+s)/2\), which bijects \(\{-1,1\}^n\) with \(\{0,1\}^n\). Then \[x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\kappa=\kappa+\tfrac14\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}Q\mathbf 1+\tfrac12(Q\mathbf 1)^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac14s^{\mathsf T}Qs.\] After using \(s_i^2=1\), this becomes an Ising energy with \(J_{ij}=Q_{ij}/2\) for \(i<j\), \(h_i=(Q\mathbf 1)_i/2\), and constant \(\kappa+\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}Q\mathbf 1/4+\operatorname{tr}(Q)/4\). The bijection preserves objective values and maps minimizers exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine substitution x=(1+s)/2 converts any symmetric QUBO into an equivalent Ising model, preserving every objective value and all minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\kappa)\) corresponds bijectively to the minimizers of the stated Ising energy.
review_flags: coefficient convention should be checked against selected Ising normalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine substitution and coefficients are internally correct for the displayed Ising convention, but an authoritative locator is required to support and disambiguate that normalization.

children.title: Quadratic–Cut Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural translation between quadratic interactions and weighted cut models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegative-Weight Boundary of the Fixed-Reference Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition under which every edge in the seed's fixed-reference cut construction has nonnegative weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the fixed-reference construction, \(w_{ij}=-b_{ij}/2\) and \(w_{0i}=a_i+\tfrac12\sum_{j\ne i}b_{ij}\). Therefore all constructed edge weights are nonnegative exactly when \[b_{ij}\le0\quad(i<j),\qquad a_i+\tfrac12\sum_{j\ne i}b_{ij}\ge0\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).\] Arbitrary coefficients still give an exact signed-cut identity, but violation of either condition prevents this particular construction from being a nonnegative-capacity cut instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed-reference signed-cut construction has only nonnegative weights exactly when every pair coefficient is nonpositive and every constructed reference-edge weight is nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: The fixed-reference convention of the deferred correspondence seed is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall e,\ w_e\ge0)\iff\left[(\forall i<j,\ b_{ij}\le0)\land(\forall i,\ a_i+\tfrac12\sum_{j\ne i}b_{ij}\ge0)\right].

notation.meaning: Weight on an ordinary variable-pair edge

review_flags: Boundary is specific to the displayed one-reference-vertex construction; standard two-terminal graph-cut encodings may normalize unary terms differently.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative-Weight Boundary of the Fixed-Reference Construction
Quadratic–Cut Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of a quadratic binary objective to a cut objective with one auxiliary fixed vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\kappa+\sum_i a_ix_i+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}x_ix_j\). Introduce a vertex \(0\) fixed at label \(x_0=0\), give edge \(\{i,j\}\) weight \(w_{ij}=-b_{ij}/2\), and give edge \(\{0,i\}\) weight \(w_{0i}=a_i+\tfrac12\sum_{j\ne i}b_{ij}\). Then \[f(x)=\kappa+\sum_i w_{0i}|x_i-x_0|+\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}|x_i-x_j|.\] Thus minimizing a quadratic pseudo-Boolean function is exactly a weighted-cut minimization with possibly signed weights; negating all weights gives an equivalent maximum-cut objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every quadratic binary objective is a constant plus a signed cut value after adding one fixed reference vertex; sign reversal converts minimization to maximum cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\) equals the displayed signed cut expression for every binary labeling.

notation.meaning: fixed reference label equal to zero

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constructed weights give the stated identity, including the signed-weight qualification, but no inspectable source supports the exact quadratic-to-cut correspondence.

children.title: Binary Energy Models
children.top_down_role: Binary optimization models expressed through energy objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Energy Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite binary energy functions with unary and quadratic interaction terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary energy model assigns each configuration \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) the value \[E(x)=\kappa+\sum_{i=1}^n\theta_ix_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}\theta_{ij}x_ix_j.\] Optimization seeks a ground state \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}E(x)\), and the minimum is the ground-state energy. The coefficient \(\theta_i\) is unary, while a nonzero \(\theta_{ij}\) couples variables \(i\) and \(j\). This model is precisely a quadratic pseudo-Boolean objective under energy terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary energy model assigns unary and pairwise quadratic costs to each zero-one configuration; its minimizing configurations are ground states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}E(x)\) is a ground state.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine equivalence between zero-one quadratic energies and Ising spin energies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\), set \(s_i=2x_i-1\in\{-1,1\}\). Every energy \[E(x)=\kappa+\sum_i\theta_i x_i+\sum_{i<j}\theta_{ij}x_ix_j\] then has the Ising form \[\widetilde E(s)=C+\sum_i h_i s_i+\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}s_is_j,\] where \[J_{ij}=\frac{\theta_{ij}}4,\quad h_i=\frac{\theta_i}{2}+\frac14\sum_{j\ne i}\theta_{\min\{i,j\},\max\{i,j\}},\quad C=\kappa+\frac12\sum_i\theta_i+\frac14\sum_{i<j}\theta_{ij}.\] The inverse substitution \(x_i=(1+s_i)/2\) preserves every energy value and bijectively preserves ground states and their multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine zero-one/spin encoding converts every binary quadratic energy exactly into an Ising energy while preserving all ground states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(x)=\widetilde E(2x-\mathbf1)\), with a bijection of ground-state sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-One and Ising Energy Equivalence

children.title: Pairwise-Interaction Models
children.top_down_role: Models organized around interactions between pairs of binary states.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise-Interaction Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General pairwise energy on finite binary state spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pairwise-interaction model on binary variables has energy \[E(x)=\kappa+\sum_{i\in V}\phi_i(x_i)+\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}\phi_{ij}(x_i,x_j),\qquad x\in\{0,1\}^{V},\] where each unary potential \(\phi_i:\{0,1\}\to\mathbb R\) and pair potential \(\phi_{ij}:\{0,1\}^2\to\mathbb R\) is finite-valued. Every pair potential admits a unique multilinear expansion \(\alpha_{ij}+\beta_{ij}x_i+\gamma_{ij}x_j+\delta_{ij}x_ix_j\); after collecting constants and unary terms, the model is a quadratic pseudo-Boolean energy supported on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pairwise model sums unary potentials and edge potentials. For binary states, collecting each potential's multilinear expansion yields an equivalent quadratic pseudo-Boolean energy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite binary pairwise-interaction model is representable as a quadratic pseudo-Boolean energy.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unique multilinear expansion on the binary square

children.title: Interaction Graph Structure
children.top_down_role: Graph structure induced by nonzero pairwise interactions.

knowledge_statements.title: Interaction Graph Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph encoding the nonzero pairwise support of a quadratic binary energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(E(x)=\kappa+\sum_i\theta_ix_i+\sum_{i<j}\theta_{ij}x_ix_j\), its interaction graph is the undirected graph \(G_E=(V,E_E)\) with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \[E_E=\bigl\{\{i,j\}:i<j,\ \theta_{ij}\ne0\bigr\}.\] Thus an edge records direct pairwise dependence, while unary coefficients do not create edges. The connected-component decomposition \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_r\) yields \(E(x)=\kappa+\sum_{k=1}^rE_k(x_{V_k})\), so a global minimizer can be assembled from independent componentwise minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interaction graph joins exactly those binary variables with a nonzero pairwise coefficient. Its connected components identify independently optimizable energy blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite quadratic binary energy
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Connected components of \(G_E\) induce an additive decomposition of \(E\).
