knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a quadratic binary energy with interaction graph \(G=(V,E_G)\). If the components of \(G-S\) have vertex sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_r\), then for each fixed \(z\in\{0,1\}^{S}\) there are functions \(E_S\) and \(E_k\) such that \[E(x_{V\setminus S},z)=E_S(z)+\sum_{k=1}^rE_k(x_{C_k};z).\] Hence, conditional on \(x_S=z\), the component minimizations are independent.

children.title: Energy–Interaction Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between aggregate energy representations and their pairwise components.

knowledge_statements.title: Energy–Interaction Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient correspondence between quadratic binary energies and graph-supported interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph \(G=(V,E)\), unary coefficients \(\theta_i\), edge coefficients \(\theta_{ij}\), and a constant \(\kappa\), the interaction data determine \[E(x)=\kappa+\sum_{i\in V}\theta_ix_i+\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}\theta_{ij}x_ix_j.\] Conversely, the unique multilinear representation of any quadratic binary energy determines these coefficients and its minimal interaction graph by retaining precisely the pairs with \(\theta_{ij}\ne0\). Therefore binary quadratic energies and weighted pairwise-interaction systems correspond up to adding zero-weight edges; after removing such edges, the supporting graph is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic energy coefficients define weighted unary and pairwise interactions, while the unique multilinear expansion recovers the minimal interaction graph and all weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quadratic binary energies correspond bijectively to weighted interaction data on their minimal support graphs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic recovery of quadratic energy coefficients and interaction support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E:\{0,1\}^{V}\to\mathbb R\) be quadratic, let \(\mathbf0\) be the all-zero configuration, and let \(e_i\) select only \(i\). In the unique multilinear expansion \[E(x)=\kappa+\sum_i\theta_i x_i+\sum_{i<j}\theta_{ij}x_ix_j,\] \[\kappa=E(\mathbf0),\qquad \theta_i=E(e_i)-E(\mathbf0),\qquad \theta_{ij}=E(e_i+e_j)-E(e_i)-E(e_j)+E(\mathbf0).\] Thus \(\{i,j\}\) is an interaction edge exactly when the displayed mixed discrete difference is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First and mixed second discrete differences recover all unary and pairwise interaction weights and the minimal edge support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_{ij}=\Delta_i\Delta_jE(\mathbf0)\), so the minimal interaction support is intrinsic to \(E\).

children.title: Fortet Linearizations

knowledge_statements.title: Fortet Linearizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear formulation of the product of two binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary variables \(x_i,x_j\), introduce \(y_{ij}\) and impose \[y_{ij}\le x_i,\qquad y_{ij}\le x_j,\qquad y_{ij}\ge x_i+x_j-1,\qquad y_{ij}\ge0.\] For every \((x_i,x_j)\in\{0,1\}^2\), these inequalities force \(y_{ij}=x_ix_j\). Moreover, their continuous feasible region with \(0\le x_i,x_j\le1\) is \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x_i,x_j,y_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^3:y_{ij}=x_ix_j\}\). Replacing every quadratic product by its corresponding \(y_{ij}\) therefore gives an exact mixed-integer linear reformulation, and the displayed subsystem is ideal for a single product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fortet inequalities replace a binary product with one auxiliary variable. They are exact for binary factors and describe the convex hull for a single product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities force \(y_{ij}=x_ix_j\) and give the single-product convex hull.

notation.meaning: auxiliary variable representing the binary product

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\{0,1\}\) and \(L\le y\le U\), introduce \(w\in\mathbb R\) and impose \[w\ge Lx,\qquad w\le Ux,\qquad w\ge y-U(1-x),\qquad w\le y-L(1-x).\] These inequalities are equivalent to \(w=xy\) on the stated mixed-binary domain. If integrality is relaxed to \(0\le x\le1\), they describe the convex hull of \(\{(x,y,w):x\in\{0,1\},\ L\le y\le U,\ w=xy\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four bound-based inequalities exactly represent the product of a binary variable and a bounded continuous variable, and give its convex hull after relaxing integrality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Formulation \(F_1\) is at least as strong as formulation \(F_2\) when \[\operatorname{proj}_x(F_1)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(F_2).\] For every minimization objective \(c^\top x\) bounded below on both projected relaxations, this inclusion implies \[\min\{c^\top x:x\in\operatorname{proj}_x(F_1)\}\ge \min\{c^\top x:x\in\operatorname{proj}_x(F_2)\}.\] Strict inclusion means that \(F_1\) can yield a strictly stronger relaxation bound for some linear objective, although not necessarily for every objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One formulation is stronger when its projected relaxation is contained in the other's, producing no weaker lower bounds for minimization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention-explicit binary RLT construction indexed by the maximum degree of literal multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in[0,1]^n:Ax\ge b\}\). For an explicitly fixed degree \(d\), multiply every defining inequality by each nonnegative literal product \[m_{I,J}(x)=\prod_{i\in I}x_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x_j),\qquad I\cap J=\varnothing,\quad |I|+|J|\le d.\] Expand the products, reduce powers using \(x_i^2=x_i\), and replace every occurrence of the same square-free monomial \(\prod_{i\in S}x_i\) by one common variable \(y_S\), with \(y_\varnothing=1\) and \(y_{\{i\}}=x_i\). Include the corresponding products of the bound inequalities so that the lifted monomial variables satisfy the same linearized consistency system. The projection of the resulting linear system is the degree-\(d\) binary RLT relaxation under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary RLT multiplies model and bound inequalities by all selected bounded-degree literal products, reduces binary powers, and consistently linearizes common monomials.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in[0,1]^n:Ax\ge b\}\) is a relaxation of a binary linear feasible set.
The multiplier-degree convention \(d\) and the complete family of literal products are fixed explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated lifted linear system projects to the degree-\(d\) binary RLT relaxation.

notation.meaning: Product of positive and complemented binary literals.
Common lifted variable for a square-free monomial.
Maximum degree of literal multipliers under the stated convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nesting, Full-Degree Exactness, and Size Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hierarchy properties for the complete degree-indexed binary RLT construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_d\) denote the projection of the complete degree-\(d\) construction above. Then \[P=R_0\supseteq R_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq R_n=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(P\cap\{0,1\}^n\bigr).\] Proper intermediate levels need not equal the binary hull. The construction uses square-free monomial variables indexed by subsets of size at most \(\min\{n,d+1\}\), hence at most \(\sum_{k=0}^{\min\{n,d+1\}}\binom nk\) such variables. Before removal of duplicate or redundant rows, the number of literal multipliers through degree \(d\) is \(\sum_{k=0}^{d}2^k\binom nk\), so the explicit row count is of that order per multiplied base inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete binary RLT levels are nested, reach the binary convex hull at full degree, and have combinatorial size in the chosen degree.
assumptions_latex: \(R_d\) uses every admissible literal multiplier through degree \(d\).
Common monomials are identified consistently and all bound-generated constraints are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq R_n=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\{0,1\}^n)\), with combinatorial lifted-variable and row growth.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-level RLT for zero–one linear models using products of constraints and binary literals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(P\) and level \(t\). Initialize with all inequalities defining \(P\) and the identities \(x_i^2=x_i\). For every defining inequality \(a^\top x-\beta\ge0\) and disjoint sets \(I,J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying \(|I|+|J|\le t\), form \[m_{I,J}(x)(a^\top x-\beta)\ge0.\] Expand, reduce powers using \(x_i^2=x_i\), and replace every common monomial \(\prod_{i\in S}x_i\) by one variable \(y_S\), with \(y_\varnothing=1\) and \(y_{\{i\}}=x_i\). Stop after all selected products are linearized; output their joint linear system as the level-\(t\) RLT relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: RLT multiplies model inequalities by bounded-degree products of binary literals, reduces binary powers, and replaces each shared monomial by one linearization variable.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a formulation \(F\), let \(s(F)\) count its auxiliary variables and inequalities, and let \(R(F)\) be its projected continuous relaxation. Size and strength induce different orders: \(s(F_1)<s(F_2)\) does not by itself imply either \(R(F_1)\subseteq R(F_2)\) or \(R(F_2)\subseteq R(F_1)\). Conversely, \(R(F_1)\subsetneq R(F_2)\) does not imply \(s(F_1)\le s(F_2)\). Hence formulation selection may trade a larger lifted system for a tighter relaxation or a smaller direct system for cheaper processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Formulation size and relaxation strength are independent: extra variables may strengthen projection, while a smaller model need not be tighter.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected Dominance and the Size–Strength Pareto Order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of equivalent product formulations by projected relaxation containment and explicit formulation size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For exact product formulations \(F_1,F_2\) in a common retained space, define \(F_1\) to be at least as strong as \(F_2\) when \(R(F_1)\subseteq R(F_2)\). Then every retained-variable minimization objective has a relaxation bound under \(F_1\) at least as large as under \(F_2\). For a fixed size measure \(s\), \(F_1\) Pareto-dominates \(F_2\) when \(R(F_1)\subseteq R(F_2)\), \(s(F_1)\le s(F_2)\), and at least one relation is strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected containment orders relaxation strength, while simultaneous nonworsening of containment and size defines Pareto dominance.
assumptions_latex: \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) represent the same integer-feasible product set.
\(R(F_1)\) and \(R(F_2)\) are projected into the same retained-variable space.
A single size convention \(s\) is used for both formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(F_1)\subseteq R(F_2)\) implies no weaker minimization bounds, while adding \(s(F_1)\le s(F_2)\) defines two-criterion Pareto dominance.

notation.meaning: Projected continuous relaxation of formulation F.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Dominance and the Size–Strength Pareto Order

children.title: Monomial Quadratizations
children.top_down_role: Quadratic reductions organized around individual high-degree monomials.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Auxiliary Quadratization of a Negative Monomial
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimization quadratization of one negative multilinear monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ge3\), \(x\in\{0,1\}^d\), and \(a>0\), \[-a\prod_{i=1}^d x_i=\min_{y\in\{0,1\}}a y\left(d-1-\sum_{i=1}^d x_i\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative binary monomial of arbitrary degree has an exact one-auxiliary quadratic representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-a\prod_{i=1}^d x_i=\min_{y\in\{0,1\}}a y(d-1-\sum_i x_i)\).

notation.meaning: Auxiliary binary variable activating the negative contribution when all factors equal one.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Auxiliary Quadratization of a Negative Monomial

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Chain Quadratization of a Signed Monomial
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Penalty-calibrated pair-product chain for a single monomial of either sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c\in\mathbb R\), \(d\ge3\), and \(p(u,v,w)=uv-2uw-2vw+3w\). Introduce \(y_1,\ldots,y_{d-2}\in\{0,1\}\), put \(z_1=x_1\), and for \(k=1,\ldots,d-2\) interpret the chain equality as \(y_k=z_kx_{k+1}\), where \(z_1=x_1\) and \(z_k=y_{k-1}\) for \(k\ge2\). If \(M>|c|\), then \[c\prod_{i=1}^d x_i=\min_{y\in\{0,1\}^{d-2}}\left[c\,y_{d-2}x_d+M\sum_{k=1}^{d-2}p(z_k,x_{k+1},y_k)\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signed degree-d monomial can be quadratized by a chain of d−2 product auxiliaries using a penalty larger than the coefficient magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed quadratic function minimizes to \(c\prod_{i=1}^d x_i\) for every fixed binary \(x\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative binary product penalty that vanishes exactly when \(w=uv\).
Auxiliary representing the prefix product through factor \(k+1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Chain Quadratization of a Signed Monomial

assumptions_latex: A minimization model contains the monomial \(\prod_{i=1}^d x_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Iterated local substitutions yield an exact quadratic representation after minimizing over the introduced binary auxiliaries.

notation.meaning: New binary variable replacing a selected factor product uv.
Quadratic penalty vanishing exactly when y=uv.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative Rosenberg-type reduction of a positive-degree binary monomial to quadratic degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary \(u,v,y\), define \[p(u,v,y)=uv-2uy-2vy+3y.\] Then \(p(u,v,y)\ge0\), and \(p(u,v,y)=0\) exactly when \(y=uv\). Select two factors of \(\prod_{i=1}^d x_i\), replace their product by \(y\), and add \(M p(u,v,y)\) to the minimization objective. Repeat until every resulting term has degree at most two. If each penalty weight \(M\) exceeds the largest possible objective improvement obtainable by violating its substitution, minimizing over all auxiliaries enforces every substitution and preserves the original monomial objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-degree binary monomial is reduced iteratively by replacing factor pairs with auxiliaries and adding sufficiently large exact quadratic penalties.
knowledge_statements.title: Monomial Quadratizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Rosenberg penalty identity is correct and the representation kind fits, but the sequential exactness claim depends on a sufficiently precise penalty-weight rule. A quadratization source is needed to validate that rule and its interaction across substitutions.

children.title: Termwise Quadratizations
children.top_down_role: Quadratic reductions applied separately across expression terms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of separable minimization when independently designed term quadratizations share an auxiliary without compatibility analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The identity \(\min_y\sum_Tq_T(y^T)=\sum_T\min_{y^T}q_T(y^T)\) is guaranteed for disjoint blocks \(y^T\), but not for shared blocks. For \(y\in\{0,1\}\), let \(q_1(y)=y\) and \(q_2(y)=1-y\). Then \(\min q_1=\min q_2=0\), whereas \(\min_y(q_1(y)+q_2(y))=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unqualified auxiliary sharing can destroy the separability identity used by termwise quadratization.
assumptions_latex: The components are intended to be minimized independently.
A shared auxiliary is introduced without compatibility conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Independent component exactness does not imply exactness of their sum when auxiliary blocks overlap.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjointness Boundary for Termwise Minimization
Termwise Quadratizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent quadratization of each high-degree term, without sharing auxiliaries between terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=c_0+\sum_{\varnothing\ne T\subseteq[n]}c_T\prod_{i\in T}x_i\) for \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Suppose that, for every \(T\) with \(|T|>2\), a quadratic function \(q_T\) satisfies \[c_T\prod_{i\in T}x_i=\min_{y^T\in\{0,1\}^{r_T}}q_T(x_T,y^T).\] If the auxiliary blocks \(y^T\) are pairwise disjoint, then \[q(x,y)=c_0+\sum_{1\le |T|\le2}c_T\prod_{i\in T}x_i+\sum_{|T|>2}q_T(x_T,y^T)\] satisfies \(f(x)=\min_y q(x,y)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independently exact quadratic replacements can be summed when their auxiliary blocks are disjoint, yielding an exact quadratization of the full pseudo-Boolean function without double-counting its constant term.
assumptions_latex: Each term with \(|T|>2\) is assigned an auxiliary block disjoint from the blocks of all other terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\min_y q(x,y)\) for the sum of the independently exact term quadratizations.

notation.meaning: Auxiliary block used only for the monomial indexed by T.
Quadratic replacement of the term indexed by T.

children.title: Local Auxiliary Structures
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary-variable structures localized to monomials or terms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Penalty-Weight Boundary for a Single Local Product Gate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient exactness scale and failure under an underweighted objective penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q:\{0,1\}^3\to\mathbb R\), let \(P(u,v,y)=uv-2uy-2vy+3y\), and define \[\Delta=\max_{u,v\in\{0,1\}}|q(u,v,1)-q(u,v,0)|.\] If \(\lambda>\Delta\), every minimizer of \(q+\lambda P\) satisfies \(y=uv\). Positivity alone is insufficient: for fixed \((u,v)=(1,0)\) and \(q(1,0,y)=-\lambda y\), the valid value \(y=0\) and invalid value \(y=1\) tie because the latter incurs penalty \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The product penalty must outweigh any objective gain from choosing an incorrect auxiliary value; a merely positive weight can permit an invalid optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda>\Delta\Longrightarrow\arg\min(q+\lambda P)\subseteq\{(u,v,y):y=uv\}

notation.meaning: Largest unpenalized objective change caused by flipping the auxiliary at fixed children.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Weight Boundary for a Single Local Product Gate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear and quadratic local encodings of one auxiliary parent as the product of two binary children.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u,v,y\in\{0,1\}\), \(y=uv\) is equivalent to \[y\le u,\qquad y\le v,\qquad y\ge u+v-1.\] It is also the zero set of \[P(u,v,y)=uv-2uy-2vy+3y,\] for which \(P=0\) exactly when \(y=uv\) and \(P\ge1\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local binary product auxiliary has an exact three-inequality encoding and an exact nonnegative quadratic penalty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y=uv\iff[y\le u,\ y\le v,\ y\ge u+v-1]\iff P(u,v,y)=0

notation.meaning: Quadratic penalty for one binary product gate.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Local Binary Product Gate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Size and Depth Bounds for Binary Product Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial resources for local pairwise-product trees without shared subproducts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A full rooted binary tree with \(m\ge2\) leaves has exactly \(m-1\) internal product gates. Its height satisfies \[\lceil\log_2m\rceil\le h\le m-1.\] A balanced tree attains the lower bound, while a fully chained tree attains the upper bound. Balancing changes dependency depth but not gate count when no internal subproduct is shared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product tree uses m−1 pairwise gates; balancing reduces depth from linear to logarithmic without changing that count.
assumptions_latex: Each internal node has exactly two children.
No internal subproduct is shared outside the tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{gate}}=m-1,\qquad\lceil\log_2m\rceil\le h\le m-1.

notation.meaning: Height of the rooted binary product tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Size and Depth Bounds for Binary Product Trees

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Exact-Penalty Condition for a Finite Local-Gate System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient global penalty scale for simultaneous enforcement of finitely many product gates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\) be real-valued on a finite binary domain, and let \(P_1,\ldots,P_g\) be integer-valued nonnegative gate penalties with \(P_k=0\) exactly when gate \(k\) is valid. Assume a jointly valid assignment exists. If \[\lambda>\max q-\min q,\] then every minimizer of \(q+\lambda\sum_{k=1}^gP_k\) satisfies every gate simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A penalty weight larger than the entire unpenalized objective range excludes every gate-violating minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(P_k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and vanishes exactly on valid gate assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda>\max q-\min q\Rightarrow\arg\min\left(q+\lambda\sum_kP_k\right)\subseteq\bigcap_k\{P_k=0\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Exact-Penalty Condition for a Finite Local-Gate System

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ideality of the Local Binary Product Gate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull strength of the three-inequality local product formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polytope \[Q=\{(u,v,y)\in[0,1]^3:y\le u,\ y\le v,\ y\ge u+v-1\}\] is exactly \[\operatorname{conv}\{(u,v,y)\in\{0,1\}^3:y=uv\}.\] Thus the standard local product-gate linearization is ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard three inequalities describe the convex hull of one binary product gate, so the local linearization is ideal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\operatorname{conv}\{(u,v,y)\in\{0,1\}^3:y=uv\}

notation.meaning: Continuous relaxation of the three-inequality binary product gate.

knowledge_statements.title: Ideality of the Local Binary Product Gate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composition of Exact Product Gates on a Rooted Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact composition of local parent–child product relations representing one multilinear monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a rooted binary tree have leaves indexed by \(T\). Assign \(y_i=x_i\) at leaf \(i\), and for every internal node \(v\) with children \(a,b\) impose \(y_v=y_ay_b\). If \(L(v)\) denotes the descendant leaves of \(v\), every binary assignment satisfying all gate relations obeys \[y_v=\prod_{i\in L(v)}x_i\quad\text{for every node }v.\] In particular, at the root \(r\), \(y_r=\prod_{i\in T}x_i\). The same conclusion holds for every minimizer of a penalized formulation whose penalty scale guarantees satisfaction of all gates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact pairwise-product gates compose through a rooted tree, making every node equal its descendant-leaf product and the root equal the target monomial.
assumptions_latex: Every internal product relation is imposed exactly, or is satisfied by every minimizer under an exact penalty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall v,\ y_v=\prod_{i\in L(v)}x_i;\qquad y_r=\prod_{i\in T}x_i

notation.meaning: Root of the local product tree.

review_flags: Shared product DAGs additionally require consistent definitions at every reused node.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Exact Product Gates on a Rooted Tree

assumptions_latex: A rooted binary tree has leaves indexed by \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local parent–child product relations make the root variable equal \(m(x)\).

notation.meaning: Binary variable associated with tree node v.
Root of the auxiliary product tree.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-structured auxiliaries encode a monomial through local pairwise product relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign \(y_i=x_i\) to each leaf \(i\in T\). For every internal node \(v\) with children \(a,b\), introduce \(y_v\in\{0,1\}\) and impose the local relation \(y_v=y_a y_b\), either through pairwise product inequalities or an exact quadratic penalty. Induction over the tree gives \[y_v=\prod_{i\in L(v)}x_i,\] where \(L(v)\) is the leaf set below \(v\). Consequently, at the root \(r\), \[y_r=\prod_{i\in T}x_i=m(x).\] The structure uses \(|T|-1\) local product nodes, with possible reuse when several monomials share subtrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary tree of local pairwise-product auxiliaries represents a monomial exactly; shared subtrees can serve several monomials.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Auxiliary Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tree construction correctly represents one monomial through local product relations and fits the representation kind, but no source supports the construction, node count, or extension to shared-subtree reuse.

children.title: Aggregative Quadratizations
children.top_down_role: Quadratic reductions combining multiple high-degree components.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An aggregative quadratization satisfies \(f(x)=\min_y q(x,y)\) while auxiliaries encode joint aggregate information from multiple original terms.

notation.meaning: Quadratic function in original and auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact quadratization whose auxiliaries jointly encode aggregates used by multiple pseudo-Boolean terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An aggregative quadratization of \(f\) is a quadratic function \(q:\{0,1\}^{n+m}\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[f(x)=\min_{y\in\{0,1\}^m}q(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\{0,1\}^n,\] in which at least one auxiliary variable participates in the quadratic replacements of multiple original monomials through a shared aggregate, rather than belonging to one term alone. Exactness requires both inequalities \(q(x,y)\ge f(x)\) for every \((x,y)\) and, for each \(x\), existence of an auxiliary assignment \(y\) attaining equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An aggregative quadratization is an exact quadratic extension whose auxiliaries encode joint information used by multiple original monomials.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregative Quadratizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimization identity is a valid general quadratization definition, but the added notion of an aggregative quadratization and a shared aggregate is not defined with enough structural precision or tied to an authoritative terminology source.

children.title: Shared-Auxiliary Quadratizations
children.top_down_role: Quadratic reductions reusing auxiliary variables across multiple components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact quadratization of a specified pseudo-Boolean component decomposition using common auxiliary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a decomposition \(f=\sum_{r=1}^m f_r\). A shared-auxiliary quadratization relative to this decomposition is a quadratic function \[Q(x,y)=\sum_{r=1}^m Q_r(x,y),\qquad x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ y\in\{0,1\}^k,\] satisfying \[f(x)=\min_{y\in\{0,1\}^k}Q(x,y)\quad\text{for every }x.\] It is genuinely shared when some coordinate \(y_j\) occurs nontrivially in at least two specified summands \(Q_r\). Exactness is required for the aggregate \(Q\); it does not by itself imply \(f_r(x)=\min_yQ_r(x,y)\) for each component. Because decompositions of \(Q\) are not unique, the sharing claim is always relative to the specified component decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared-auxiliary quadratization is an aggregate-exact quadratic extension in which a common auxiliary bit occurs in multiple specified component terms.
assumptions_latex: A component decomposition \(f=\sum_{r=1}^m f_r\) is fixed.
\(Q\) has total degree at most two in the original and auxiliary binary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\min_yQ(x,y)\) for every original assignment, with genuine sharing defined relative to the specified summands.
review_flags: The definition is mathematically explicit, but the family name is not asserted to be universal terminology.
Sharing is decomposition-dependent and must not be inferred from an arbitrary algebraic regrouping.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Auxiliary Quadratizations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aggregate Exactness Does Not Imply Componentwise Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between shared aggregate quadratization and separately exact component quadratizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The identity \[\sum_{r=1}^m f_r(x)=\min_y\sum_{r=1}^mQ_r(x,y)\] constrains only the sum. Without the additional inequalities \(Q_r(x,y)\ge f_r(x)\) and attainment conditions for every component, it does not imply \(f_r(x)=\min_yQ_r(x,y)\) separately. Conversely, separate component exactness does not ensure aggregate exactness under a common auxiliary vector unless the component minimizer sets are compatible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregate exactness neither requires nor follows from separate component exactness without additional lower-bound and common-minimizer conditions.
assumptions_latex: The component decomposition and common auxiliary vector are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aggregate exactness and componentwise exactness are distinct conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Exactness Does Not Imply Componentwise Exactness

children.title: Auxiliary Reuse Patterns
children.top_down_role: Structural patterns governing auxiliary-variable sharing.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary Reuse Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-based representation of reusable product auxiliaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sum_{T\subseteq[n]}c_T\prod_{i\in T}x_i\), where \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Choose a family \(\mathcal S\) of subsets of \([n]\), introduce \(y_S\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(S\in\mathcal S\), and associate it with the relation \(y_S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\). A reuse pattern assigns each monomial support \(T\) a product of factors from \(\{x_i:i\in[n]\}\cup\{y_S:S\in\mathcal S\}\) that equals \(\prod_{i\in T}x_i\) whenever all associated relations hold. Reuse occurs when the same \(y_S\) appears in the assigned representations of at least two distinct monomials. The monomial factorization is quadratic-compatible when every assigned product contains at most two factors; relations with \(|S|>2\) still require a separate quadratic encoding or recursive factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reuse pattern represents repeated subproducts by common auxiliary bits. Its represented monomials are quadratic-compatible when each uses at most two factors, although higher-degree auxiliary defining relations must also be quadratized separately.
assumptions_latex: Each auxiliary is associated with \(y_S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each monomial is represented exactly on the auxiliary defining relations, and reuse occurs when one \(y_S\) serves at least two monomials.

notation.meaning: binary variable representing the subproduct indexed by S

source_refs.locator: Using expression graphs in optimization algorithms p. 247

review_flags: The source supports expression reuse indirectly; the pseudo-Boolean specialization remains provisional.

source_witnesses.locator: Using expression graphs in optimization algorithms p. 247

children.title: Aggregation Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where common aggregation remains available.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion for aggregating individually exact component quadratizations over one common auxiliary vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r=1,\ldots,m\), suppose \(Q_r(x,y)\ge f_r(x)\) for every binary \((x,y)\) and \(f_r(x)=\min_y Q_r(x,y)\). For each fixed \(x\), \[\min_y\sum_{r=1}^m Q_r(x,y)=\sum_{r=1}^m f_r(x)\] if and only if \[\bigcap_{r=1}^m\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\{0,1\}^k}Q_r(x,y)\ne\varnothing.\] Thus the shared aggregate is exact for every original assignment precisely when these intersections are nonempty for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Individually exact, componentwise lower-bounding quadratizations can be summed over common auxiliaries exactly when their auxiliary argmin sets have a common member for every original assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(f_r(x)=\min_y Q_r(x,y)\) for every component and original assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_y\sum_rQ_r(x,y)=\sum_rf_r(x)\) exactly when the component argmin sets intersect.

notation.meaning: Component quadratization using the common auxiliary vector.

review_flags: Corrects the deferred candidate's erroneous use of 'nonnegative' in place of componentwise lower-bounding.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Minimizer Compatibility Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp one-bit counterexample to exact aggregation without a common component minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let one shared auxiliary satisfy \(y\in\{0,1\}\), and set \(f_1=f_2=0\), \(Q_1(y)=y\), and \(Q_2(y)=1-y\). Each component is a lower-bounding exact quadratization because \(\min_yQ_1=\min_yQ_2=0\). Their argmin sets are \(\{0\}\) and \(\{1\}\), however, and \[\min_{y\in\{0,1\}}\bigl(Q_1(y)+Q_2(y)\bigr)=1>0=f_1+f_2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two exact components with incompatible minimizing auxiliary values can produce an inexact shared aggregate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separate exactness does not imply exactness after sharing auxiliaries when the component argmin sets are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint-Argmin Aggregation Failure
Aggregation Compatibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact compatibility criterion for aggregating component quadratizations over common auxiliaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(r=1,\ldots,m\), suppose \(Q_r(x,y)\ge f_r(x)\) for every binary \((x,y)\) and \(f_r(x)=\min_y Q_r(x,y)\). Then the aggregate \(Q=\sum_r Q_r\) satisfies
\[
\min_y Q(x,y)=\sum_{r=1}^m f_r(x)
\]
for a fixed \(x\) if and only if
\[
\bigcap_{r=1}^m\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\{0,1\}^k}Q_r(x,y)\ne\varnothing.
\]
Thus global aggregation compatibility holds precisely when this intersection is nonempty for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative component quadratizations may share auxiliaries exactly when, for every original assignment, all components possess a common minimizing auxiliary assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_y\sum_r Q_r(x,y)=\sum_r f_r(x)\) exactly when the component argmin sets intersect.

notation.meaning: component quadratization using the common auxiliary vector

review_flags: The equivalence is elementary but no supplied locator directly supports this aggregation criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The argmin-intersection equivalence is correct under the stated component lower bounds and fits a compatibility-condition leaf. No source is supplied, however, and the plain statement incorrectly calls the components nonnegative rather than lower-bounded by their respective f_r values.

children.title: Quadratization Size Regimes
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary-variable and constraint-growth regimes for quadratizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratization Size Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size classification by auxiliary variables and quadratic interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a quadratization \(Q(x,y)\) of a pseudo-Boolean function in \(n\) original variables, define its auxiliary size by \(s_{m aux}(Q)=\dim(y)\) and its interaction size by \(s_{m int}(Q)=|\{\{u,v\}:u\ne v,\;[uv]Q\ne0\}|\), where \([uv]Q\) is the coefficient of \(uv\). For a family \(\{Q_n\}\), a size regime is the asymptotic pair \((s_{m aux}(Q_n),s_{m int}(Q_n))\), classified, for example, as constant, logarithmic, linear, polynomial, or exponential in the encoded input size. Coefficient bit length is a separate encoding-size component and must be reported when coefficients vary with \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratization size is classified by auxiliary-bit count, nonzero pairwise interactions, and—when variable—coefficient bit length as functions of encoded input size.
assumptions_latex: Each \(Q_n\) is an exact quadratic representation after minimizing its auxiliary variables.
Input size is measured under a fixed binary encoding convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The size regime is determined by \(s_{m aux}(Q_n)\), \(s_{m int}(Q_n)\), and any nonconstant coefficient bit length.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

review_flags: The locator supports encoding-size conventions; the quadratization-specific metrics are a local specialization.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited encoding-size section may support general bit-complexity conventions, but it does not directly support the proposed quadratization-specific regime based on auxiliary count and interaction count. A quadratization source or explicit standard-field rationale is required.

children.title: Quadratization Strength Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relaxation-strength regimes across quadratic reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratization Strength Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength ordering through projected epigraph relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two exact formulations of the same binary minimization problem. For formulation \(i\), let \(R_i\) be its continuous epigraph relaxation in variables \((x,y_i,\eta)\), where minimizing \(\eta\) is the relaxed objective, and define \(E_i=\operatorname{proj}_{x,\eta}(R_i)\). Formulation \(1\) is at least as strong as formulation \(2\) under this convention when \(E_1\subseteq E_2\). This inclusion implies that formulation \(1\) gives a relaxation bound at least as strong for every additional restriction expressed in the common original variables. A strength regime records equality, strict dominance, or incomparability of these projected epigraph relaxations, optionally relative to a fixed ideal benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strength is compared using projected epigraph relaxations: the smaller projected epigraph is stronger, and families may be equivalent, strictly ordered, or incomparable.
assumptions_latex: Both formulations represent the same binary minimization problem.
Both relaxations use a common epigraph variable \(\eta\) and the same projection convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_1\subseteq E_2\) makes formulation \(1\) at least as strong as formulation \(2\) under the stated epigraph convention.

notation.meaning: continuous epigraph relaxation of formulation i
projection of the relaxation onto the common original and epigraph variables

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal-Value Tests for Weak and Strong Persistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact restricted-optimum certificates for original-variable fixings in a finite quadratized problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v=\min_{x,y}Q(x,y)\) and \(v_{i,b}=\min\{Q(x,y):x_i=b\}\), with an empty minimum equal to \(+\infty\). Then \(x_i=b\) is weakly persistent if and only if \(v_{i,b}=v\), and strongly persistent if and only if \(v_{i,1-b}>v\). More generally, simultaneous fixings \(x_I=b_I\) are weakly persistent exactly when their jointly restricted optimum equals \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak persistency is certified by equality of a restricted and global optimum; strong persistency by a strict gap after imposing the opposite value.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is minimized over a finite binary feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i=b\) is weakly persistent iff \(v_{i,b}=v\), and strongly persistent iff \(v_{i,1-b}>v\).

notation.meaning: Simultaneous assignment on original-variable index set \(I\).

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Value Tests for Weak and Strong Persistency
Quadratization Persistency Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak and strong persistency of original-variable fixings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an exact quadratization \(Q(x,y)\) and a proposed fixing \(x_i=b\), where \(b\in\{0,1\}\). The fixing is weakly persistent if some global minimizer \((x^*,y^*)\) of \(Q\) satisfies \(x_i^*=b\); it is strongly persistent if every global minimizer satisfies \(x_i^*=b\). For a set \(I\) of indices, simultaneous weak persistency requires one common global minimizer satisfying all proposed fixings, whereas strong persistency requires every global minimizer to satisfy them. A persistency regime records which original variables admit certified weak or strong fixings under the chosen relaxation or reduction rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak persistency means at least one optimum respects the proposed fixings; strong persistency means every optimum does, with simultaneous weak fixings requiring one common optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is an exact quadratization on a finite binary domain.
Persistency is stated only for original variables \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak persistency is existential over global minimizers; strong persistency is universal over global minimizers.

notation.meaning: proposed binary fixing of original variable \(i\)
set of simultaneously fixed original-variable indices

review_flags: No supplied locator directly treats weak and strong persistency for quadratizations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The existential and universal definitions are internally consistent and appropriately distinguish simultaneous weak fixings, but no source supports the weak/strong persistency terminology in this quadratization setting.

children.title: Size–Strength Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Boundaries where smaller reductions sacrifice relaxation strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Size–Strength Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No unconditional monotone relation between formulation size and relaxation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Formulation size alone does not order relaxation strength. Given any exact quadratization with relaxation \(R\), adjoining \(t\) unused auxiliary variables \(z\in[0,1]^t\) produces \(R'=R\times[0,1]^t\); its size increases, but \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R')=\operatorname{proj}_x(R)\), so strength is unchanged. Conversely, adding valid inequalities or auxiliary constraints may strictly shrink the projected relaxation while increasing description size. Therefore a claimed size–strength tradeoff is meaningful only after fixing the formulation class, size measure, relaxation convention, and permitted redundant variables and constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger quadratizations need not be stronger: unused auxiliaries increase size without changing projection, although additional valid structure can sometimes strengthen a relaxation.
assumptions_latex: Strength is measured by projection of a specified continuous relaxation.
Size counts auxiliary variables or formulation constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither larger nor smaller size implies stronger relaxation without additional restrictions on the formulation family.

children.title: Strength–Persistency Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Boundaries where relaxation strength and persistency behavior diverge.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strength Alone Does Not Order Relaxation-Face Fixings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested nonexact epigraph relaxations showing that containment alone does not transfer optimal-face fixings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{0:x\in\{0,1\}\}\), with integer epigraph \(I=\{(x,\eta):x\in\{0,1\},\eta\ge0\}\). Let \[E_2=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(I\cup\{(0,-2),(1,-1)\}\bigr)+\{(0,t):t\ge0\}\] and \[E_1=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(I\cup\{(1,-1)\}\bigr)+\{(0,t):t\ge0\}.\] Then \(E_1\subset E_2\), but the optimal face of \(E_2\) fixes \(x=0\), while that of \(E_1\) fixes \(x=1\). Neither relaxation has the integer optimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger nonexact relaxation can yield an opposite optimal-face fixing, so strength alone does not certify integer persistency.
assumptions_latex: Strength is measured by projected epigraph containment.
Fixings are inferred from relaxation optimal faces without exactness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_1\subset E_2\) does not imply monotone transfer of optimal-face fixings for nonexact relaxations.

notation.meaning: Integer epigraph of the zero-objective binary problem.
Stronger and weaker valid epigraph relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Strength Alone Does Not Order Relaxation-Face Fixings
Strength–Persistency Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional transfer of persistency certificates under nested exact relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_1\subseteq R_2\) be two relaxations of the same minimization problem, with the same objective on original variables, and suppose both relaxation optimal values equal the integer optimum. Then every integer optimum belongs to each relaxation optimal face. If the optimal face of \(R_2\) fixes \(x_i=b\), that fixing is strongly persistent and remains fixed on the smaller optimal face of \(R_1\). The converse need not hold: \(R_1\) may fix additional coordinates. Without exact relaxation values, projection dominance alone certifies bounds but does not by itself certify persistency for the integer optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under exact nested relaxations, fixings obtained from the weaker optimal face persist in the stronger one; without exactness, strength alone does not certify integer persistency.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1\subseteq R_2\) are valid relaxations with a common objective.
Both relaxation optimal values equal the integer optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A coordinate fixed throughout the optimal face of \(R_2\) is strongly persistent and is also fixed throughout the optimal face of \(R_1\).

notation.meaning: stronger and weaker nested relaxations, respectively

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the stated relaxation-to-persistency transfer.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional transfer claim is mathematically plausible under nested valid relaxations with exact optimal values, and property is an appropriate kind for the leaf. No locator supports the stated connection between relaxation optimal faces and strong persistency.

children.title: Exact-Penalty Encodings
children.top_down_role: Penalty encodings intended to preserve the relevant optimal solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Penalty Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain threshold for an exact additive constraint penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be nonempty, let \(c:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(g:X\to\mathbb R\), and suppose \(F=\{x\in X:g(x)=0\}\) is nonempty. Let \(p:X\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfy \(p(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in F\), and define \(\Delta=\max_{x\in X}c(x)-\min_{x\in X}c(x)\). If \(X\setminus F\ne\varnothing\), define \(\delta=\min_{x\in X\setminus F}p(x)>0\). For every \(\rho>\Delta/\delta\), each minimizer of \(c(x)+\rho p(x)\) over \(X\) belongs to \(F\) and minimizes \(c\) over \(F\). If \(X=F\), the same conclusion holds for every \(\rho\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite binary domain with infeasible points, a penalty weight exceeding the objective range divided by the smallest positive violation makes every penalized optimum feasible and constrained-optimal; if every point is feasible, no positive threshold is needed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(c(x)+\rho p(x))\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}c(x)\) under the stated threshold, with the specified trivial case when \(X=F\).

notation.meaning: constraint-feasible subset of the binary domain
smallest positive penalty value when infeasible points exist
objective range on the ambient binary domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient weight condition for preserving exactly the constrained global minimizers on a finite domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be finite, let \(F\subseteq X\) be nonempty, let \(c:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(p:X\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfy \(p(x)=0\) exactly for \(x\in F\). Write \(f^*=\min_{x\in F}c(x)\). If \(X\setminus F\ne\varnothing\), define
\[
\rho_* = \max_{x\in X\setminus F}\frac{f^*-c(x)}{p(x)}.
\]
For \(\rho\ge0\), the minimizers of \(c+\rho p\) over \(X\) are exactly the minimizers of \(c\) over \(F\) if and only if \(\rho>\rho_*\). When \(\rho_*=0\), equality admits an infeasible tie; more generally, whenever the admissible boundary \(\rho=\rho_*\ge0\) is used, an infeasible maximizer in the definition of \(\rho_*\) ties the feasible optimum. If \(X=F\), exactness holds for every \(\rho\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sharp finite-domain penalty threshold is the largest objective advantage per unit violation among infeasible points, and it must be strictly exceeded whenever that boundary is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(c(x)+\rho p(x))=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}c(x)\iff\rho>\rho_* when \(X\setminus F\ne\varnothing\), with the stated all-feasible exception.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Finite-Domain Exact-Penalty Threshold

children.title: Slack Encodings
children.top_down_role: Encodings using auxiliary slack representations for constrained relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Slack Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary slack representation of a bounded integer inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a\in\mathbb Z^n\), \(b\in\mathbb Z\), and \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Assume a known integer bound \(0\le b-a^\top x\le U\) whenever \(a^\top x\le b\). With \(k=\lceil\log_2(U+1)\rceil\), introduce \(z\in\{0,1\}^k\) and \(s(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}2^jz_j\), together with \(s(z)\le U\). Then
\[
a^\top x\le b
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z:\ a^\top x+s(z)=b,\quad s(z)\le U.
\]
For \(U=0\), no slack bit is required and the inequality reduces to equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded integer inequality is equivalent to an equality with a nonnegative binary-encoded slack, using the range constraint to exclude unused binary codes.
assumptions_latex: \(a\) and \(b\) are integral and \(x\) is binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^\top x\le b\) is equivalent to existence of a bounded binary-encoded slack satisfying \(a^\top x+s=b\).

source_refs.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

review_flags: Locator supports binary encoding size provisionally but may not state this slack equivalence explicitly.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation of every integer slack from zero through U using a truncated final positional weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\in\mathbb Z_+\). For \(U=0\), set \(s=0\) without auxiliary bits. For \(U\ge1\), let \(k=\lceil\log_2(U+1)\rceil\), define
\[
w_j=2^j\quad(0\le j\le k-2),\qquad w_{k-1}=U-(2^{k-1}-1),
\]
and set \(s(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}w_jz_j\) for \(z\in\{0,1\}^k\). Then
\[
\{s(z):z\in\{0,1\}^k\}=\{0,1,\ldots,U\}.
\]
Thus an integral inequality \(a^\top x\le b\) whose slack is bounded by \(U\) is equivalent to \(a^\top x+s(z)=b\) without a separate unused-code restriction. The decoding need not be one-to-one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A truncated final positional weight represents exactly all slack values from zero through U without a separate unused-code constraint, although encodings may be nonunique.
assumptions_latex: The original inequality has integral slack in \(\{0,1,\ldots,U\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}w_jz_j:z\in\{0,1\}^k\}=\{0,1,\ldots,U\}, so the bounded inequality admits the stated equality encoding.
knowledge_statements.title: Range-Constraint-Free Truncated Binary Slack

children.title: Ancilla Encodings
children.top_down_role: Encodings introducing auxiliary binary states for structural reduction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ancilla-specific failure of global equivalence when the product-consistency penalty is underweighted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(\rho\ge0\) and choose \(B>3\rho\). Minimize
\[
c(u,v,z)=B(u+v-z)
\]
subject to \(u,v,z\in\{0,1\}\) and \(z=uv\). The constrained optimum is \(0\), attained at \((0,0,0)\). After deleting \(z=uv\) and adding \(\rho P(u,v,z)\), the inconsistent point \((0,0,1)\) has value \(-B+3\rho<0\). Hence the penalized problem has a strictly better inconsistent point and is not equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every fixed ancilla-penalty weight, scaling the original objective can make an inconsistent product assignment beat every constrained optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The penalized unconstrained problem need not preserve the constrained optimum when the product-consistency penalty is too small relative to the objective scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient Ancilla-Penalty Weight

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic ancilla encoding and recursive degree reduction for binary products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u,v,z\in\{0,1\}\), define
\[
P(u,v,z)=uv-2uz-2vz+3z.
\]
Then \(P(u,v,z)\ge0\) and \(P(u,v,z)=0\) if and only if \(z=uv\). Thus a selected occurrence of \(uv\) in a higher-degree binary expression may be replaced by the ancilla \(z\) and product consistency enforced by adding \(\rho P\). Repeating such substitutions reduces degree, while preservation of global minimizers additionally requires an adequate exact-penalty weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary ancilla can replace a product using a nonnegative quadratic penalty that vanishes exactly when the ancilla equals that product.
assumptions_latex: Global optimizer equivalence is asserted only when the aggregate penalty weight is sufficiently large.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(u,v,z)=0\Longleftrightarrow z=uv, and repeated product substitutions permit recursive degree reduction.
review_flags: The previously deferred seed was not regenerated; this corrected record separates local product consistency from the sibling exact-penalty condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Product-Consistency Ancilla
Ancilla Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic ancilla encoding of a binary product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For binary variables \(u,v,z\), the quadratic penalty
\[
P(u,v,z)=uv-2uz-2vz+3z
\]
is nonnegative and satisfies \(P(u,v,z)=0\) if and only if \(z=uv\). Hence an occurrence of the product \(uv\) inside a higher-degree binary expression may be replaced by the ancilla \(z\), while adding \(\rho P(u,v,z)\) with a sufficiently large exact-penalty weight \(\rho>0\). Repeated substitutions yield a quadratic expression; global equivalence requires \(\rho\) to dominate every possible objective improvement obtained by violating the product relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ancilla bit can represent a binary product using a nonnegative quadratic penalty that vanishes exactly when the ancilla equals that product.
assumptions_latex: The penalty weight is large enough to make violations globally unattractive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(u,v,z)=0\Longleftrightarrow z=uv\), enabling exact degree reduction under an adequate penalty weight.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the displayed binary-product penalty.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed quadratic product penalty is correct on the binary domain and the representation kind fits the leaf, but no source or locator supports the formula or the global exact-penalty qualification.

children.title: Auxiliary-State Overhead
children.top_down_role: Variable-growth consequences of slack and ancilla representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-State Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit overhead for independent bounded slacks and product ancillas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose an encoding introduces bounded integer slacks \(s_j\in\{0,\ldots,U_j\}\), where \(U_j\in\mathbb Z_+\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\), and \(r\in\mathbb Z_+\) distinct binary product states, each represented by one ancilla. Standard binary slack encoding uses
\[
K=\sum_{j=1}^m\left\lceil\log_2(U_j+1)\right\rceil+r
\]
auxiliary bits, with a range restriction for each slack when \(U_j+1\) is not a power of two. Consequently, the auxiliary-state overhead is \(O\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^m\log(U_j+1)+r\right)\). This count excludes variables introduced solely to quadratize resulting equality penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent binary slacks and product ancillas use the sum of the binary digit counts of the slacks plus one bit per distinct product state, excluding any further variables needed to quadratize equality penalties.
assumptions_latex: Each \(U_j\) is a nonnegative integer and \(s_j\in\{0,\ldots,U_j\}\).
Each distinct product state uses exactly one ancilla.
Coefficient and constraint storage are excluded from the auxiliary-bit count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\sum_{j=1}^m\lceil\log_2(U_j+1)\rceil+r=O\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^m\log(U_j+1)+r\right)\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative integer upper bound on slack j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum binary dimension needed to represent every value of one bounded integer slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let an exact encoding represent every integer in \(\{0,1,\ldots,U\}\) using \(q\) binary auxiliary variables. Because \(q\) bits have at most \(2^q\) assignments,
\[
2^q\ge U+1,
\qquad q\ge\left\lceil\log_2(U+1)\right\rceil.
\]
Consequently, standard binary slack encoding has minimum binary dimension for an independently decoded slack that can attain all \(U+1\) values, although other encodings may differ in coefficients, redundancy, and relaxation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Representing all U+1 slack values requires at least ceiling log2(U+1) binary variables, matching standard binary encoding.
assumptions_latex: The slack can attain all \(U+1\) values and is decoded solely from \(q\) binary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\ge\lceil\log_2(U+1)\rceil.

notation.meaning: upper bound on the integer slack

children.title: Big-M Formulations
children.top_down_role: Conditional formulations controlled through finite bounding constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Big-M Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear encoding of a binary-triggered inequality using one valid deactivation constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), and \(y\in\{0,1\}\). Consider \(y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\leq\beta\). If \(M\in\mathbb R\) satisfies \(M\geq\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta)\), then \[a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\] enforces the implication and defines the same feasible pairs over \(X\times\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid upper bound on constraint violation converts a binary implication into one linear big-M inequality with the same integer feasible pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\}=\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\leq\beta\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Big-M Encoding of a Triggered Equality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided Big-M formulation for one equality activated at binary value one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\), and suppose \(M^+\geq\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta)\) and \(M^-\geq\sup_{x\in X}(\beta-a^\top x)\), with both constants finite. Then \[a^\top x\leq\beta+M^+(1-y),\qquad a^\top x\geq\beta-M^-(1-y)\] exactly represents \(y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x=\beta\) over \(X\times\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A triggered equality is represented by two Big-M inequalities using valid upper- and lower-side deactivation bounds.
assumptions_latex: Both one-sided violation suprema over \(X\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:a^\top x\leq\beta+M^+(1-y),\ a^\top x\geq\beta-M^-(1-y)\}=\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x=\beta\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Big-M representation of a finite disjunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent binary encoding of a finite disjunction over a bounded domain using componentwise upper bounds and exactly one selected alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be bounded and, for \(j=1,\ldots,p\), let \(f_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{m_j}\) be smooth, \(G_j=\{x\in X:f_j(x)\le 0\}\), and \(\bar f_j\in\mathbb{R}^{m_j}\) satisfy \(f_j(x)\le \bar f_j\) componentwise for every \(x\in X\). Then \(\bigvee_{j=1}^p(x\in G_j)\) holds if and only if there exists \(y\in\{0,1\}^p\) such that \(\sum_{j=1}^p y_j=1\) and \(f_j(x)\le \bar f_j(1-y_j)\) componentwise for every \(j\), with \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded domain, valid componentwise upper bounds yield a big-M encoding of membership in at least one of the sets defined by f_j(x) ≤ 0. Exactly one binary variable is selected; its alternative is enforced, while every unselected alternative is relaxed by its valid upper bound.
assumptions_latex: f_j(x)\le \bar f_j\text{ componentwise for all }x\in X\text{ and }j=1,\ldots,p
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigvee_{j=1}^p(x\in G_j)\iff \exists y\in\{0,1\}^p:\ \sum_{j=1}^p y_j=1,\quad f_j(x)\le \bar f_j(1-y_j)\ \forall j,\quad x\in X

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Native logical formulation of a binary-triggered constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(g:X\to\mathbb R\), and \(y\in\{0,1\}\). The indicator constraint \[y=1\Rightarrow g(x)\leq0\] defines \(S=\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:y=0\text{ or }g(x)\leq0\}\). It adds no restriction beyond \(x\in X\) when \(y=0\), and imposes \(g(x)\leq0\) when \(y=1\). Its solver implementation may use reformulation, branching, or separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator constraint activates a specified constraint at one binary value and otherwise leaves the base domain unrestricted.

knowledge_statements.title: Big-M Calibration Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and relaxation strength among nonnegative deactivation constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), and define \(M^*=\max\{0,\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta)\}\). Among nonnegative constants, every \(M\geq M^*\) is valid, whereas every \(M\) satisfying \(0\leq M<M^*\) excludes some pair \((x,0)\) allowed by the implication. If \(M^*\leq M_1\leq M_2\), then \(R(M_1)\subseteq R(M_2)\), where \(R(M)=\{(x,y)\in X\times[0,1]:a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among nonnegative big-M constants, the smallest valid deactivation bound is strongest; smaller values are invalid, while larger values monotonically weaken the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The base domain \(X\) is fixed across calibrations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq M<M^*\) is invalid, and \(M^*\leq M_1\leq M_2\Rightarrow R(M_1)\subseteq R(M_2)\).

notation.meaning: Smallest nonnegative valid scalar big-M constant.
Continuous big-M relaxation at calibration M.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact calibration of one linear implication over an independent finite box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\ell_i\le x_i\le u_i\ (i=1,\ldots,n)\}\), where all bounds are finite. For \(y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\le\beta\), the smallest nonnegative valid constant is
\[
M^*=\max\left\{0,\sum_{i:a_i\ge0}a_i u_i+\sum_{i:a_i<0}a_i\ell_i-\beta\right\}.
\]
It is computed by choosing the upper endpoint for every nonnegative coefficient and the lower endpoint for every negative coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over a finite independent box, the tight big-M is computed by maximizing each linear term at the appropriate variable bound.
assumptions_latex: The inactive-state domain is exactly the stated independent box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M^*=\max\{0,\sum_{a_i\ge0}a_i u_i+\sum_{a_i<0}a_i\ell_i-\beta\}.

notation.meaning: lower and upper bounds for variable i

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Form Box-Domain Big-M Calibration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp existence condition for finite nonnegative scalar calibration of one indicator implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\le\beta\) over a nonempty inactive-state domain \(X\), a finite nonnegative \(M\) in
\[
a^\top x\le\beta+M(1-y)
\]
is valid if and only if
\[
\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta)<+\infty.
\]
If the supremum is infinite, every finite \(M\) excludes an allowed inactive pair \((x,0)\); increasing a finite numerical constant cannot restore validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite big-M exists exactly when inactive-state violation is bounded above; otherwise every finite choice is invalid.
assumptions_latex: The formulation must preserve every inactive pair \((x,0)\) with \(x\in X\).
Only nonnegative finite constants are considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M\in\mathbb R_+\text{ finite and valid}\iff\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta)<+\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Big-M Existence Boundary

children.title: Indicator–Big-M Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Representational relationships between indicator constraints and Big-M forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator–Big-M Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence over binary triggers under a finite valid violation bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), and \(y\in\{0,1\}\). Suppose the finite constant \(M\in\mathbb R\) satisfies \(M\geq\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta)\). Then \(y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\leq\beta\) and \(a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\) have identical feasible sets in \(X\times\{0,1\}\). This equivalence concerns binary feasible pairs and does not assert equivalence of continuous relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite valid big-M constant makes the linear inequality exactly equivalent to the indicator for binary triggers, but not necessarily after relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\leq\beta\}=\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Necessary and Sufficient Finite-M Equivalence Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp condition for one Big-M row to equal its indicator semantics over binary triggers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\), and \(M\in\mathbb R\). The inequality \(a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\) is equivalent over \(X\times\{0,1\}\) to \(y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\leq\beta\) if and only if \[M\geq\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta).\] Hence a finite equivalent Big-M row exists exactly when this supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Big-M row equals its binary indicator precisely when M bounds every inactive-state violation; an unbounded violation precludes finite-M equivalence.
assumptions_latex: Equivalence is evaluated relative to the fixed base domain \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\leq\beta\}=\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\}\iff M\geq\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta)\).

notation.meaning: Base domain used to test inactive-state validity.

knowledge_statements.title: Necessary and Sufficient Finite-M Equivalence Condition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Equivalence Does Not Imply a Hull Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar separation between exact binary equivalence and continuous-relaxation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[0,2]\) and consider \(y=1\Rightarrow x\leq0\). The valid constant \(M=3\) gives the binary-equivalent row \(x\leq3(1-y)\). After relaxing \(y\in[0,1]\), \((x,y)=(3/2,1/2)\) satisfies this row. The labeled disjunction's convex hull instead satisfies \(x\leq2(1-y)\), so that point lies outside the hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid but loose M preserves binary equivalence while admitting fractional points outside the labeled disjunction's convex hull.
assumptions_latex: The trigger is relaxed to \(0\leq y\leq1\) only for the relaxation comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((3/2,1/2)\in\{(x,y)\in[0,2]\times[0,1]:x\leq3(1-y)\}\setminus\operatorname{conv}(([0,2]\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\{1\}))\).
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Equivalence Does Not Imply a Hull Relaxation

children.title: Convex-Hull Trigger Formulations
children.top_down_role: Trigger formulations emphasizing hull-level relaxation strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Hull Trigger Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disaggregated ideal formulation for a two-term bounded polyhedral disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), and for \(i\in\{0,1\}\) let \(m_i\in\mathbb N\), \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times n}\), \(b_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i}\), and \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\leq b_i\}\) be nonempty bounded polyhedra. Define \(H\) by \[x=x^0+x^1,\quad A_i x^i\leq b_i\lambda_i\ (i=0,1),\quad \lambda_0+[1;1H\lambda_1=1,\quad \lambda_i\geq0,\quad y=\lambda_1.\] Then \(\operatorname{proj}_x(H)=\operatorname{conv}(P_0\cup P_1)\). Requiring \(y\in\{0,1\}\) selects exactly one disjunct, while allowing \(y\in[0,1]\) yields the convex hull under projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disaggregating variables by disjunct yields an extended trigger formulation whose continuous relaxation projects exactly to the union's convex hull.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P_i\) is a nonempty bounded polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(H)=\operatorname{conv}(P_0\cup P_1)\), and \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(H\cap\{y\in\{0,1\}\})=(P_0\times\{0\})\cup(P_1\times\{1\})\).

notation.meaning: Polyhedron selected by trigger value i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full labeled-hull and extended-space trigger-integrality property of the bounded two-term disaggregated formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the assumptions of the seeded formulation, let \(H\) be its continuous extended system with \(y=\lambda_1\). Then \[\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(H)=\operatorname{conv}\big((P_0\times\{0\})\cup(P_1\times\{1\})\big).\] Moreover, every vertex of \(H\) has \((\lambda_0,\lambda_1)\in\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\), and hence \(y\in\{0,1\}\). Thus the disaggregated formulation is ideal in its trigger variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The continuous disaggregated system gives the labeled disjunction's convex hull, and every extended-system vertex has an integral trigger.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is the seeded disaggregated convex-combination system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(H)=\operatorname{conv}((P_0\times\{0\})\cup(P_1\times\{1\}))\), and every vertex of \(H\) satisfies \(y\in\{0,1\}\).

children.title: Parsimonious Trigger Formulations
children.top_down_role: Trigger formulations emphasizing limited auxiliary structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Parsimonious Trigger Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact single-copy formulation for a linear binary trigger.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), and let the finite constant \(M\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(M\geq\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta)\). Define \(F_M=\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\}\) and \(R(M)=\{(x,y)\in X\times[0,1]:a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\}\). The formulation uses the original vector, one binary trigger, and one additional inequality; it is exact for binary \(y\), and \(\operatorname{conv}(F_M)\subseteq R(M)\). Validity alone does not imply equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A big-M trigger is compact and integer-exact, but validity alone does not guarantee a convex-hull continuous relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite valid deactivation bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_M=\{(x,y)\in X\times\{0,1\}:y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\leq\beta\}\) and \(\operatorname{conv}(F_M)\subseteq R(M)\).

notation.meaning: Integer feasible set of the compact formulation.
Relaxation obtained by replacing the binary domain with the unit interval.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absence of a Finite Deactivation Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence boundary for the scalar compact big-M trigger on the stated domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta)=+\infty\), no finite \(M\) makes \(a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\) valid for every \((x,0)\in X\times\{0\}\). Consequently, every finite choice excludes a pair allowed by the implication \(y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\leq\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If possible constraint violation is unbounded, no finite scalar big-M exactly encodes the trigger on the given domain.
assumptions_latex: The triggered row imposes no restriction when \(y=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists M\in\mathbb R:\ a^\top x\leq\beta+M\quad\forall x\in X.
knowledge_statements.title: Absence of a Finite Deactivation Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smallest Valid Big-M Gives the Strongest Scalar Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and monotonicity within the compact single-row big-M family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M^*=\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-\beta)<+\infty\) and \(R(M)=\{(x,y)\in X\times[0,1]:a^\top x\leq\beta+M(1-y)\}\). A finite \(M\) is valid at \(y=0\) if and only if \(M\geq M^*\). If \(M^*\leq M_1\leq M_2\), then \(R(M_1)\subseteq R(M_2)\); hence \(M^*\) gives the strongest member of this scalar family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The supremum of possible violation is the smallest valid big-M, and increasing it can only weaken the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ valid}\iff M\geq M^*,\qquad M^*\leq M_1\leq M_2\Rightarrow R(M_1)\subseteq R(M_2).

notation.meaning: Continuous relaxation using deactivation constant M.

knowledge_statements.title: Smallest Valid Big-M Gives the Strongest Scalar Relaxation

children.title: Hull–Parsimony Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between formulation strength and representational economy.

knowledge_statements.title: Hull–Parsimony Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal comparison of ideal extended and compact trigger formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\{0,1\}\) be a triggered disjunctive set. Suppose an extended formulation \(H\) and a compact formulation \(C\) both project to \(S\) when their triggers are binary. If \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(H_{\mathrm{LP}})=\operatorname{conv}(S)\) and \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq C_{\mathrm{LP}}\), then the extended formulation is at least as strong as the compact formulation under projection. Strict containment gives a strictly stronger relaxation, while equality means compactness was achieved without losing projected relaxation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare trigger formulations after projection: a hull formulation dominates a compact relaxation, with equality precisely when the compact formulation is also ideal.
assumptions_latex: Both formulations represent the same binary feasible set \(S\).
Relaxations are compared in the common \((x,y)\)-space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(H_{\mathrm{LP}})=\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq C_{\mathrm{LP}}\); equality holds if and only if \(C\) is ideal in the common space.

notation.meaning: Continuous relaxation of the extended hull formulation.
Continuous relaxation of the compact formulation.

children.title: Projection-Based Trigger Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Projected relationships among alternative trigger formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Based Trigger Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength ordering for extended formulations in a shared original-variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) be nonempty continuous relaxations of formulations of the same triggered set, possibly with different auxiliary variables, and define \(P_i=\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(E_i)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\). Formulation \(E_1\) is at least as strong as \(E_2\) in the original space exactly when \(P_1\subseteq P_2\). For every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(d\in\mathbb R\), this containment implies \[\inf_{(x,y)\in P_1}(c^\top x+d y)\geq\inf_{(x,y)\in P_2}(c^\top x+d y).\] Equal projections make the formulations relaxation-equivalent in the original space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended trigger formulations are compared through their projections; containment determines relaxation dominance and equality determines projected equivalence.
assumptions_latex: The same original variables \((x,y)\) and minimization convention are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_1\subseteq P_2\Rightarrow\inf_{(x,y)\in P_1}(c^\top x+d y)\geq\inf_{(x,y)\in P_2}(c^\top x+d y)\) for every \((c,d)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Relaxation in an extended variable space.
Projection of the relaxation onto original variables.
