children.title: Penalty Calibration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Penalty-magnitude regimes affecting representational fidelity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient pointwise certificate that a specified additive penalty has exactly the constrained global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a set, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), let \(v:X\to\mathbb R_+\), and suppose \(S=\{x\in X:v(x)=0\}\neq\varnothing\) and \(f^*=\min_{x\in S}f(x)\) is attained. For \(\rho\geq0\), \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\{f(x)+\rho v(x)\}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x)\] if and only if \[f(x)+\rho v(x)>f^*\qquad\text{for every }x\in X\setminus S.\] Equality at any infeasible point or a strict violation of this inequality prevents exact equality of the minimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed penalty is exact precisely when every infeasible point has penalized value strictly above the constrained optimum.
assumptions_latex: The constrained optimum \(f^*\) is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{X}(f+\rho v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{S}f\iff (\forall x\notin S)\ f(x)+\rho v(x)>f^*\).
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Weight Exact-Penalty Certificate
Penalty Calibration Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness threshold for a nonnegative additive feasibility penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be compact, let \(f,v:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, let \(v(x)\geq0\), and define \(S=\{x\in X:v(x)=0\}\neq\varnothing\) and \(f^*=\min_{x\in S}f(x)\). Set \[\rho^*=\sup_{x\in X\setminus S}\frac{f^*-f(x)}{v(x)}.\] If \(\rho^*<+\infty\), every global minimizer of \(f(x)+\rho v(x)\) is feasible and solves the constrained problem whenever \(\rho>\max\{0,\rho^*\}\). At \(\rho=\rho^*\), infeasible minimizers may tie; below the threshold, exactness is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additive penalty is globally exact above the worst objective-improvement-to-violation ratio; equality can permit ties, and smaller penalties may fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho>\max\{0,\rho^*\}\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\{f(x)+\rho v(x)\}\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold statement is mathematically plausible and fits the condition leaf, but this nontrivial exact-penalty theorem has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Under-Penalization Failure
children.top_down_role: Failure caused by penalties too weak to enforce the intended structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General certificate that a specified infeasible point defeats every feasible point at a given penalty weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v\geq0\), let \(S=\{x:v(x)=0\}\neq\varnothing\), and let \(f^*=\min_{x\in S}f(x)\). If an infeasible point \(\bar x\notin S\) satisfies \[f(\bar x)+\rho v(\bar x)<f^*,\] then no feasible point minimizes \(f+\rho v\); consequently every attained penalized minimizer is infeasible. If equality holds, \(\bar x\) has the feasible-optimum value, so exactness is not certified and an infeasible minimizer occurs whenever no point has smaller penalized value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible point whose weighted violation is smaller than its objective advantage certifies under-penalization; equality marks the possible-tie boundary.
assumptions_latex: The constrained optimum \(f^*\) is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x)+\rho v(\bar x)<f^*\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{x}(f(x)+\rho v(x))\cap S=\varnothing\), whenever the penalized minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Under-Penalization Witness
Under-Penalization Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-binary-variable example below the exact-penalty threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the constrained binary problem \[\min\{-x:x\in\{0,1\},\ x=0\}.\] Its unique feasible and optimal point is \(x=0\), with value \(0\). Penalizing violation by \(\rho x\) produces the unconstrained binary objective \((-1+\rho)x\). For every \(0\leq\rho<1\), its unique minimizer is \(x=1\), which violates \(x=0\). At \(\rho=1\), both binary points minimize and an infeasible minimizer remains; only \(\rho>1\) makes every minimizer feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a one-bit problem, any penalty below the objective gain selects the infeasible point; equality still permits an infeasible tie.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq\rho<1\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\{0,1\}}(-x+\rho x)=\{1\}\), although the constrained feasible set is \(\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Violation of the constraint x equals zero.

children.title: Over-Penalization Failure
children.top_down_role: Numerical or relaxation degradation caused by excessively large penalties.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Penalty-Dependent Evaluation Error Can Reverse a Fixed Feasible Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite counterexample in which exact minimizers remain unchanged while a penalty-dependent error bound destroys reliable objective discrimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{0,1,2\}\), \(v(0)=v(1)=0\), \(v(2)=1\), \(f(0)=f(2)=0\), and \(f(1)=\delta>0\). For every \(\rho>0\), \(F_\rho=f+\rho v\) has the unique minimizer \(0\). Suppose computed values satisfy \(|\widehat F_\rho(x)-F_\rho(x)|\leq u\rho\), where \(u>0\). If \(2u\rho>\delta\), admissible errors \(e(0)=u\rho\) and \(e(1)=-u\rho\) make \(\widehat F_\rho(1)<\widehat F_\rho(0)\), although the exact minimizer is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With an explicitly penalty-dependent error bound, a sufficiently large penalty can reverse a fixed exact ordering between feasible points without changing the mathematical optimum.
assumptions_latex: Computed objective errors are uniformly bounded by \(u\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(2u\rho>\delta\Rightarrow\) admissible errors exist for which \(\widehat F_\rho(1)<\widehat F_\rho(0)\), while \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F_\rho(x)=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Exact objective gap between the two feasible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Dependent Evaluation Error Can Reverse a Fixed Feasible Ordering

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical ordering boundary under an explicit penalty-dependent uniform evaluation-error model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho v(x)\), let \(F_\rho^*=\min_{x\in X}F_\rho(x)\), and suppose every computed value satisfies \(|\widehat F_\rho(x)-F_\rho(x)|\leq\varepsilon(\rho)\). If the exact separation between minimizers and nonminimizers is \[\Delta(\rho)=\inf\{F_\rho(x)-F_\rho^*:F_\rho(x)>F_\rho^*\}>0,\] then \(\Delta(\rho)>2\varepsilon(\rho)\) guarantees correct ordering of every minimizer against every nonminimizer. If \(\Delta(\rho)<2\varepsilon(\rho)\), admissible evaluation errors can reverse such an ordering. Thus increasing an already exact penalty causes numerical failure only through a specified error bound that grows enough to overwhelm the relevant exact objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An excessive penalty is numerically dangerous only when its induced evaluation error reaches at least half the exact penalized-objective gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta(\rho)>2\varepsilon(\rho)\) guarantees minimizer-versus-nonminimizer ordering, whereas \(\Delta(\rho)<2\varepsilon(\rho)\) permits reversal under admissible errors.

notation.meaning: Uniform absolute evaluation-error bound at penalty weight rho.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Gap Boundary for Excessive Penalties
Over-Penalization Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact-arithmetic validity and numerical degradation from excessive penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an exact penalty \(f(x)+\rho v(x)\) with \(v(x)\geq0\), increasing \(\rho\) above an exactness threshold does not destroy global exactness in exact arithmetic. The failure boundary is numerical: if nonzero objective coefficients have characteristic magnitude \(C>0\), then the coefficient spread contributed by the penalty is at least \(\rho/C\). As \(\rho/C\to\infty\), the scaled objective increasingly suppresses distinctions in \(f\); consequently, finite-precision or tolerance-based implementations may lose reliable objective discrimination even though the mathematical minimizers remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excessive penalties do not break exact-arithmetic exactness, but unbounded coefficient spread can erase objective distinctions in finite-precision implementations.
assumptions_latex: \(v(x)\geq0\) and \(\rho\) already exceeds an exactness threshold.
Computation uses finite precision or nonzero solver tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho/C\to\infty\) marks numerical ill-scaling, not loss of exact-penalty validity in exact arithmetic.

notation.meaning: Characteristic magnitude of the original objective coefficients.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative warning is plausible, but C and coefficient spread are not rigorously defined, and no finite-precision or solver-tolerance model supports the quantitative claim.

children.title: Scaling-Induced Instability
children.top_down_role: Numerical instability arising from poorly scaled penalty coefficients.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact covariance rule distinguishing inconsistent objective scaling from harmless common scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\alpha>0\), \(\rho\geq0\), and nonnegative violation function \(v\), \[\alpha f(x)+\rho v(x)=\alpha\left(f(x)+\frac{\rho}{\alpha}v(x)\right).\] Hence scaling only the original objective by \(\alpha\) changes the effective penalty coefficient from \(\rho\) to \(\rho/\alpha\). Scaling both \(f\) and \(\rho\) by the same positive factor preserves all penalized minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-only scaling divides the effective penalty weight by the scaling factor, while common positive scaling of objective and penalty leaves minimizers unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{\alpha f(x)+\rho v(x)\}=\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{f(x)+(\rho/\alpha)v(x)\}\), and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{\alpha f(x)+\alpha\rho v(x)\}=\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{f(x)+\rho v(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Effective penalty coefficient after objective-only scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty Calibration Under Objective Scaling
Scaling-Induced Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective rescaling invalidates any fixed penalty calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha>0\), consider \[\min\{-\alpha x:x\in\{0,1\},\ x=0\}.\] Penalization with a fixed coefficient \(\rho>0\) gives \((-\alpha+\rho)x\). If \(\alpha>ho\), the unique penalized minimizer is the infeasible point \(x=1\); if \(\alpha=\rho\), it ties with the feasible point. Thus multiplying the original objective by \(\alpha\) multiplies the strict exactness threshold from \(1\) to \(\alpha\), and no fixed penalty remains exact under arbitrary positive objective rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescaling the objective rescales the required penalty threshold, so a formerly exact fixed penalty can become under-calibrated.
assumptions_latex: The penalty coefficient \(\rho>0\) is held fixed while \(\alpha\) varies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha>\rho\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\{0,1\}}\{-\alpha x+\rho x\}=\{1\}\), whereas feasibility requires \(x=0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical single-resource binary linear knapsack formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given $a,c\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ and $\beta\in\mathbb{Q}$, the $0$-$1$ knapsack problem is
\[
\max\{c^\top x\mid a^\top x\leq\beta,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical 0-1 Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Profit-maximization form with one capacity constraint and indivisible items.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given items indexed by \(I=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the classical 0-1 knapsack problem is
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le B\right\}.
\]
Here \(x_i=1\) means that item \(i\) is selected. The feasible family consists of all subsets whose total weight does not exceed the capacity, and the objective selects a feasible subset of maximum total profit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select an indivisible subset of items maximizing total profit while its total weight does not exceed one capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal solution belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmax}\{p^{\mathsf T}x:w^{\mathsf T}x\le B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) and a nonnegative integer target \(T\), SUBSET SUM asks whether there exists \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfying

children.title: Subset-Sum Specialization
children.top_down_role: Structural specialization linking subset-sum instances to the classical knapsack family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary of the exact-target correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(p_i=w_i=a_i\), the inequalities \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq B\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}x\geq P\) force an exact sum only when \(P=B\). If \(P<B\), every attainable sum in \([P,B]\) is accepted. For \(a=(2)\), \(P=1\), and \(B=2\), knapsack decision is affirmative although no subset sums to \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal weights and profits alone do not encode exact subset sum; capacity and profit threshold must also coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=B\Rightarrow(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq B\land a^{\mathsf T}x\geq P\iff a^{\mathsf T}x=P),\text{ while }P<B\text{ need not}.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality of Thresholds Is Essential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequence of the direct subset-sum-to-knapsack mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(a_i\mapsto(p_i,w_i)=(a_i,a_i)\) and \(T\mapsto(P,B)=(T,T)\) is computable in polynomial time and preserves affirmative instances. Therefore NP-hardness of SUBSET SUM implies NP-hardness of 0-1 KNAPSACK decision even on instances satisfying \(p_i=w_i\) and \(P=B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The equal-profit, equal-weight specialization transfers subset-sum hardness directly to knapsack decision.
assumptions_latex: All integers are encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{SUBSET SUM}\leq_p\text{KNAPSACK-DECISION}|_{p=w,\,P=B}.
knowledge_statements.title: Complexity Transfer Through the Specialization
Subset-Sum Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction to the decision form of 0-1 knapsack using identical weights and profits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a SUBSET SUM instance with \(n\) values \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) and target \(T\), define a 0-1 knapsack decision instance by
\[
p_i=w_i=a_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),\qquad B=P=T.
\]
The resulting instance asks whether some \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfies \(w^{\mathsf T}x\le B\) and \(p^{\mathsf T}x\ge P\). Under the displayed identification,
\[
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^n:a^{\mathsf T}x=T
\iff
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^n:w^{\mathsf T}x\le B,\ p^{\mathsf T}x\ge P.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subset sum is represented as knapsack decision by setting every profit and weight equal to the corresponding input value and setting both thresholds equal to the target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x\in\{0,1\}^n:a^{\mathsf T}x=T\iff\exists x\in\{0,1\}^n:w^{\mathsf T}x\le B,\ p^{\mathsf T}x\ge P\).

children.title: Capacity-Regime Contrasts
children.top_down_role: Contrasts between capacity-limited optimization and target-total feasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-set and optimal-value changes under the single capacity parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(B)=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:w^{\mathsf T}x\leq B\}\), \(B_1\leq B_2\) implies \(F(B_1)\subseteq F(B_2)\). Hence \(v(B)=\max_{x\in F(B)}p^{\mathsf T}x\) is nondecreasing. It is a right-continuous step function whose changes can occur only at attainable subset weights \(w^{\mathsf T}x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing capacity only adds feasible subsets, so optimal profit cannot decrease and changes only at attainable subset weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B_1\leq B_2\Rightarrow F(B_1)\subseteq F(B_2)\text{ and }v(B_1)\leq v(B_2).

notation.meaning: optimal knapsack profit at capacity B

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Monotonicity and Breakpoints
Capacity-Regime Contrasts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility simplifications at the two extreme capacity regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive weights \(w_i\) and capacity \(B\), let \(F(B)=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:w^{\mathsf T}x\le B\}\). If \(0\le B<\min_i w_i\), then \(F(B)=\{0\}\). If \(B\ge\sum_i w_i\), then \(F(B)=\{0,1\}^n\); with nonnegative profits, selecting every item is optimal. In the intermediate regime \(\min_i w_i\le B<\sum_i w_i\), at least one nonempty subset is feasible and at least one subset is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Very small capacity permits only the empty set; capacity at least total weight permits every subset; intermediate capacity admits a nonempty subset but excludes at least one subset.
assumptions_latex: For the all-items optimality conclusion, \(p_i\ge0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B<\min_iw_i\Rightarrow F(B)=\{0\}\), while \(B\ge\sum_iw_i\Rightarrow F(B)=\{0,1\}^n\).

notation.meaning: binary subsets feasible at capacity B

knowledge_statements.title: Multidimensional Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One knapsack with several resource capacities shared by every selected item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(m\) resource types, multidimensional 0-1 knapsack is
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ri}x_i\le b_r\text{ for every }r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\right\}.
\]
Each selected item simultaneously consumes \(a_{ri}\) units of every resource \(r\); there is one selection vector and no assignment of items to distinct containers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose one item subset maximizing profit while satisfying several resource-capacity inequalities simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimum maximizes \(p^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\le b\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudo-polynomial fixed-dimension regime versus variable-dimension hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative integral consumptions and capacities, the capacity-vector dynamic program uses \(O\!\left(n\prod_{r=1}^m(b_r+1)\right)\) state transitions and \(O\!\left(\prod_{r=1}^m(b_r+1)\right)\) storage with rolling item layers. This is pseudo-polynomial for fixed \(m\). When \(m\) is part of the input, multidimensional 0-1 knapsack is strongly NP-hard, including restricted instances with bounded integral coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral multidimensional knapsack is pseudo-polynomial for a fixed number of resources but strongly NP-hard when the dimension varies.
assumptions_latex: For the hardness statement, \(m\) is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m\text{ fixed}:T=O\!\left(n\prod_r(b_r+1)\right);\qquad m\text{ variable}:\text{strong NP-hardness}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Packing structure of multidimensional knapsack.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pseudo-polynomial algorithm when the number of knapsacks is fixed and capacities are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For knapsacks j=1,\ldots,m with integral capacities B_j, process items sequentially and store D_i(b_1,\ldots,b_m), the maximum profit obtainable from the first i items using at most b_j capacity in knapsack j. Each item is either skipped or assigned to one knapsack having sufficient residual capacity. The table has \prod_{j=1}^m(B_j+1) capacity states and can be updated in O\!\left(nm\prod_{j=1}^m(B_j+1)\right) time and O\!\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(B_j+1)\right) working memory.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment form with several containers and at most one placement per item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For items \(i\in I\) and knapsacks \(j\in J\), the multiple-knapsack problem is
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{I\times J}}\left\{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}p_i x_{ij}:\sum_{i\in I}w_i x_{ij}\le B_j\ \forall j,\quad \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}\le1\ \forall i\right\}.
\]
Thus an item may be assigned to at most one knapsack, and each knapsack has its own capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign each item to at most one of several capacity-limited knapsacks to maximize total profit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal assignment maximizes total profit subject to every capacity constraint and every at-most-one-assignment constraint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pseudo-polynomial algorithm for integral shared capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For exact-one classes G_1,\ldots,G_q, let D_k(b) be the maximum profit from choosing one alternative from each of the first k classes with total weight at most b. Set D_0(b)=0 and D_k(b)=\max\{D_{k-1}(b-w_i)+p_i:i\in G_k,\ w_i\le b\}, treating unreachable states as -\infty. Then D_q(B) is optimal, with O(B|I|) time and O(B) working memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process choice classes one at a time and update a capacity table by selecting one feasible alternative from the current class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_q(B)=\operatorname{OPT},\qquad T=O(B|I|),\quad S=O(B).

notation.meaning: best profit for the first k classes within capacity b

knowledge_statements.title: Class-Indexed Capacity Dynamic Program

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Hardness, Pseudo-Polynomial Solvability, and FPTAS
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and approximation complexity of multiple-choice knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Ordinary 0-1 knapsack reduces to exact-one multiple-choice knapsack by giving each item a two-alternative class consisting of the item and a zero-weight, zero-profit dummy. With integral capacity, the class-indexed dynamic program is pseudo-polynomial. For nonnegative rational input data, profit scaling yields a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple-choice knapsack is weakly NP-hard, has a capacity-indexed pseudo-polynomial algorithm, and admits an FPTAS.
assumptions_latex: Weights and capacity are nonnegative integers for the pseudo-polynomial statement.
Profits are nonnegative for the multiplicative approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \textsc{Multiple-Choice-Knapsack}\text{ is weakly NP-hard and admits an FPTAS.}
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Hardness, Pseudo-Polynomial Solvability, and FPTAS

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence between optional and exact-one choice classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every at-most-one class G_k, add a unique dummy d_k with w_{d_k}=p_{d_k}=0 and impose \sum_{i\in G_k\cup\{d_k\}}x_i=1. Projection deleting dummy coordinates is a bijection onto the original optional-choice solutions and preserves weight and profit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-weight, zero-profit dummy converts each optional class into an exact-one class without changing attainable objective values.
assumptions_latex: The classes are finite and pairwise disjoint.
Each dummy belongs to exactly one class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_I(F_{=1}^{\mathrm{dummy}})=F_{\le1},\qquad p^{\mathsf T}x\text{ and }w^{\mathsf T}x\text{ are preserved.}
knowledge_statements.title: Dummy-Alternative Equivalence
Multiple-Choice Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-one version with items partitioned into mutually exclusive choice classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), and let \(G_1,\ldots,G_q\) partition the finite item set \(I\). The exact-one multiple-choice knapsack problem is
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{I}}\left\{\sum_{i\in I}p_i x_i:\sum_{i\in I}w_i x_i\le B,\quad \sum_{i\in G_k}x_i=1\text{ for every }k\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\right\}.
\]
Exactly one alternative is selected from each class while all selected alternatives share one capacity. Under the at-most-one convention, each class equality is replaced by \(\sum_{i\in G_k}x_i\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose exactly one alternative from each of finitely many item classes while respecting a shared capacity and maximizing profit; the at-most-one convention uses class inequalities instead.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), and \(G_1,\ldots,G_q\) are nonempty, pairwise disjoint finite sets with union \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible vector satisfies \(w^{\mathsf T}x\le B\) and \(\sum_{i\in G_k}x_i=1\) for all \(k\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\).

notation.meaning: indicator that alternative i is chosen

children.title: Resource–Choice Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes combining multiple resources, containers, or choice classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource–Choice Interaction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural distinctions among multiple resources, multiple containers, and partitioned choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The three extensions impose different constraint structures. Multidimensional knapsack uses one selection vector \(x\) and several shared-resource rows \(Ax\le b\). Multiple knapsack uses assignment variables \(x_{ij}\), container capacities, and coupling constraints \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}\le1\). Exact-one multiple-choice knapsack uses one shared capacity and class constraints \(\sum_{i\in G_k}x_i=1\). Multidimensional knapsack reduces to classical knapsack when \(m=1\), and multiple knapsack reduces to classical knapsack when \(|J|=1\). Multiple-choice knapsack becomes the classical formulation only after its class constraints are removed; this is a constraint deletion rather than a parameter-degenerate multiple-choice instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple resources constrain one subset, multiple knapsacks assign items to containers, and multiple-choice knapsack enforces one selection per class. The first two reduce to classical knapsack with one resource or one container, whereas multiple-choice requires removal of its class constraints.
assumptions_latex: All item, resource, container, and class index sets are finite, and the relevant item and container sets are nonempty.
Variables have the binary domains stated in the corresponding formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three model families have distinct resource-row, assignment-coupling, and partition-row structures and are not interchangeable in general.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct structural comparison of the three canonical formulations

children.title: Cardinality Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Knapsack variants with explicit limits on the number of selected items.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pseudo-polynomial algorithm for upper- and exact-cardinality variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integer weights and capacity B, let D_i(b,r) be the maximum profit from items 1,\ldots,i with weight at most b and exactly r selected items. Initialize D_0(b,0)=0 and D_0(b,r)=-\infty for r>0, and use D_i(b,r)=\max\{D_{i-1}(b,r),D_{i-1}(b-w_i,r-1)+p_i\} when w_i\le b. The at-most-k optimum is \max_{0\le r\le k}D_n(B,r), and the exact-k optimum is D_n(B,k).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add selected-item count as a second state coordinate in the ordinary capacity dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T=O(nBk),\qquad S=O(Bk),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_{=k}=D_n(B,k).

notation.meaning: best prefix profit within capacity b using exactly r items

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-and-Cardinality Dynamic Program

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and approximation complexity of cardinality-constrained knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Setting k=n makes the upper-cardinality row redundant, so ordinary 0-1 knapsack is a special case. Hence upper-cardinality knapsack is weakly NP-hard. For integral capacity it has the O(nBk) pseudo-polynomial dynamic program, and for nonnegative profits it admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme; the same state structure handles the feasible exact-k variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cardinality knapsack inherits weak NP-hardness, retains a pseudo-polynomial exact algorithm, and admits an FPTAS for nonnegative profits.
assumptions_latex: Weights and capacity are nonnegative integers for the pseudo-polynomial statement.
Profits are nonnegative for the multiplicative approximation guarantee.
The exact-k instance is feasible when that variant is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \textsc{Cardinality-Knapsack}\text{ is weakly NP-hard and admits an FPTAS.}
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Hardness and Approximation Boundary
Cardinality Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical knapsack augmented by an upper bound on the number of selected items.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a cardinality limit \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), cardinality-constrained 0-1 knapsack is
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le B,\quad \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\le k\right\}.
\]
The additional inequality restricts every feasible subset to contain at most \(k\) items. The exact-cardinality variant replaces this inequality by \(\sum_i x_i=k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize knapsack profit subject to both the weight capacity and a limit on how many items may be chosen.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible solution satisfies \(w^{\mathsf T}x\le B\) and \(\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}x\le k\).

notation.meaning: maximum permitted number of selected items

children.title: Quadratic Knapsack
children.top_down_role: Knapsack variants with pairwise terms in the objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary knapsack with pairwise interactions represented by a quadratic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), a linear-profit vector \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), positive weights \(w\), and capacity \(B\), quadratic 0-1 knapsack is
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\left\{x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:w^{\mathsf T}x\le B\right\}.
\]
Without loss of objective value, \(Q\) may be replaced by its symmetric part. Off-diagonal coefficients encode pairwise gains or penalties incurred when both corresponding items are selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a capacity-feasible subset whose value includes linear item profits and pairwise interaction terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimum maximizes \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:w^{\mathsf T}x\le B\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity for rationally encoded instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Quadratic 0-1 knapsack is NP-hard even under the restriction \(Q=0\). Its rationally encoded threshold decision problem is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic knapsack remains NP-hard when all interaction coefficients vanish, and its rational decision form is NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: All numerical data and the decision threshold are rational and encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{QKP}\text{ is NP-hard, and its threshold decision problem is NP-complete}.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Knapsack NP-Completeness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact MILP representation of the quadratic objective on the binary domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each represented product introduce \(y_{ij}\) and impose \(0\le y_{ij}\le x_i\), \(y_{ij}\le x_j\), and \(y_{ij}\ge x_i+x_j-1\). If \(x_i,x_j\in\{0,1\}\), these inequalities force \(y_{ij}=x_ix_j\); replacing every product by \(y_{ij}\) therefore yields an exact mixed-integer linear formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each binary pair product has an exact auxiliary-variable linearization.
assumptions_latex: One auxiliary variable is introduced for each represented product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y_{ij}=x_ix_j\quad\text{at every feasible binary point}.

notation.meaning: auxiliary variable representing the binary product

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Binary-Product Linearization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small failure of the standard product linearization after relaxing binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\max y_{12}\) subject to \(x_1+x_2\le1\), \(0\le y_{12}\le x_1\), \(y_{12}\le x_2\), \(y_{12}\ge x_1+x_2-1\), and \(0\le x_1,x_2\le1\). Every binary feasible point has \(y_{12}=x_1x_2=0\), but \(x_1=x_2=y_{12}=1/2\) is relaxation-feasible with value \(1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact binary product formulation can have a positive LP value even when capacity prevents every interacting pair from being selected.
assumptions_latex: The product-variable formulation is relaxed to continuous variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z_{LP}\ge\tfrac12>0=z_{IP}.

notation.meaning: linearized product of the two item variables

knowledge_statements.title: McCormick-Relaxation Gap Under Exclusive Capacity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diagonal Absorption and Interaction Normal Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical coefficient normalization for a binary quadratic-knapsack objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary \(x\), \(x_i^2=x_i\). Hence diagonal terms are absorbed into the linear coefficients, and \(Q_{ij}x_ix_j+Q_{ji}x_jx_i\) is represented by one unordered-pair coefficient \(q_{ij}=Q_{ij}+Q_{ji}\). Therefore \[x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x=\sum_i(c_i+Q_{ii})x_i+\sum_{i<j}(Q_{ij}+Q_{ji})x_ix_j.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary idempotence absorbs diagonal terms into item profits and combines matrix entries into one coefficient per unordered pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x=\sum_i p_ix_i+\sum_{i<j}q_{ij}x_ix_j.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Absorption and Interaction Normal Form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign boundary for monotonicity of the normalized quadratic-knapsack objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two unit-weight items with capacity \(B=2\), normalized profits \(p_1=p_2=1\), and interaction \(q_{12}=-3\), the feasible selections satisfy \(f(1,0)=1\) and \(f(1,1)=-1\). Thus nonnegative individual profits alone do not make the objective monotone under item inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative pair interaction can make adding a feasible positive-profit item reduce the objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative Interactions Destroy Objective Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity consequence of nonnegative normalized individual and pair profits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sum_i p_i x_i+\sum_{i<j}q_{ij}x_ix_j\). If \(p_i\ge0\) and \(q_{ij}\ge0\), then \(x\le x'\) componentwise implies \(f(x)\le f(x')\). With positive item weights, an optimal capacity-feasible solution can therefore be chosen inclusion-maximal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonnegative individual and pair profits, selecting additional items never decreases value, and an optimum can be chosen inclusion-maximal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\le x'\Longrightarrow f(x)\le f(x'),\qquad \exists x^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}f\text{ inclusion-maximal}.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity in the Nonnegative-Interaction Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal exact baseline for a finite quadratic-knapsack instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the normalized objective as \(f(S)=\sum_{i\in S}p_i+\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq S}q_{ij}\). Enumerate every subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), discard it when \(\sum_{i\in S}w_i>B\), evaluate \(f(S)\) for every remaining subset, and return one of maximum value. With an explicit nonzero-interaction edge set \(E\), direct evaluation takes \(O(n+|E|)\) time per subset, giving \(O(2^n(n+|E|))\) time and polynomial working space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerating all subsets and retaining the best capacity-feasible one is an exact exponential-time quadratic-knapsack algorithm.
assumptions_latex: The instance has finitely encoded coefficients.
Objective additions and comparisons are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{time}=O(2^n(n+|E|)),\qquad\operatorname{space}=\operatorname{poly}(n+|E|)

notation.meaning: Set of unordered pairs with represented nonzero interactions.
Normalized profit of selected subset S.

review_flags: This is an exact baseline, not a polynomial approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Subset-Enumeration Algorithm

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality test using a feasible selection and a verified global upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\hat x\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfies \(w^{\mathsf T}\hat x\le B\), and \(U\) is verified to satisfy \(f(x)\le U\) for every capacity-feasible binary \(x\), then \(f(\hat x)=U\) certifies global optimality of \(\hat x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible quadratic-knapsack selection is optimal when its value matches a verified global upper bound.
assumptions_latex: f(x)\le U\text{ for every capacity-feasible binary }x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\hat x)=U\Longrightarrow\hat x\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{f(x):x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ w^{\mathsf T}x\le B\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Bound Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian relaxation of the capacity constraint in maximization form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) and \(\lambda\ge0\), let \(g(\lambda)=\lambda B+\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\{f(x)-\lambda w^{\mathsf T}x\}\). Then every capacity-feasible \(x\) satisfies \(f(x)\le g(\lambda)\), so \(\inf_{\lambda\ge0}g(\lambda)\) is an upper bound on the quadratic-knapsack optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing capacity with a nonnegative multiplier yields a Lagrangian upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(w^{\mathsf T}x\le B\) is the relaxed constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z^*\le\inf_{\lambda\ge0}g(\lambda).
knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Lagrangian Upper Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation boundary already present in the nonnegative-interaction regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(k\), use one unit-weight item per vertex, capacity \(B=k\), zero individual profits, and \(q_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(\{i,j\}\in E\). The objective counts edges induced by the selected vertices. Because all interactions are nonnegative, an optimum can be extended to exactly \(k\) vertices, making this restriction densest \(k\)-subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative quadratic knapsack contains densest k-subgraph, so its general approximation theory cannot be inferred from ordinary linear knapsack.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{|S|\le k}\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq S}q_{ij}=\max_{|S|=k}|E(S)|.

notation.meaning: edges induced by vertex set S

review_flags: The containment alone asserts no particular approximation or inapproximability ratio.
knowledge_statements.title: Densest-k-Subgraph Containment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper plane for a quadratic 0-1 knapsack objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a linear majorant on the feasible binary knapsack set and records the upper bound obtained by maximizing it over a containing set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:a^Tx\le b\}$. A linear function $l$ is an upper plane of $Q$ on $S$ if $l(x)\ge Q(x)$ for every $x\in S$. If $f^*=\max_{x\in S}Q(x)$ and $\widetilde S\supseteq S$, then $f^*\le\max\{l(x):x\in\widetilde S\}$. For $\widetilde S=S$ the bounding problem is a 0-1 linear knapsack problem; for $\widetilde S=\{x\in[0,1]^n:a^Tx\le b\}$ it is a continuous linear knapsack problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper plane is a linear function that majorizes the quadratic objective at every feasible binary knapsack point. Maximizing it over a superset of the feasible set gives an upper bound on the quadratic-knapsack optimum. The binary and continuous knapsack sets yield 0-1 and continuous linear-knapsack bounding problems, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*\le\max_{x\in\widetilde S}l(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best Linear L2 Approximation of the Quadratic Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The approximation domain and L2 criterion are those assigned to Q in the surrounding quadratic-knapsack development.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The best linear \(L_2\)-approximation of \(Q(x)\) is
\[
l_Q(x)=c_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i x_i,
\]
where
\[
c_0=-\frac14\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}q_{ij},\qquad
c_i=q_{ii}+\frac12\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij},\quad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the stated L2 approximation setting, the best linear approximation of Q has intercept minus one quarter of the indicated off-diagonal sum and coefficient i equal to q_ii plus one half of the other coefficients indexed with i.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(x)\), its coefficients \(q_{ij}\), the approximation domain, and the \(L_2\) criterion are as defined in the surrounding setting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle l_Q(x)=c_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i x_i\), where \(\displaystyle c_0=-\frac14\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}q_{ij}\) and \(\displaystyle c_i=q_{ii}+\frac12\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Breakpoint and Parametric-Solution Bounds for SKP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded bounds for the parametric function and subproblems associated with problem (SKP).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For problem \((SKP)\):
(i) the number of breakpoints of \(d(\lambda)\) is at most \(n\); and
(ii) there exist at most \(n+1\) solutions
\[
0=x^0<x^1<\cdots<x^p
\]
such that, for every \(\lambda\ge 0\), one of \(x^k\), \(k=0,\ldots,p\), solves \((L_\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function d(lambda) has at most n breakpoints. Moreover, an ordered collection of at most n+1 solutions contains a solution of L_lambda for every nonnegative lambda.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(\lambda)\) has at most \(n\) breakpoints, and there exist \(p+1\le n+1\) solutions \(0=x^0<\cdots<x^p\) such that \(\forall\lambda\ge0\,\exists k\in\{0,\ldots,p\}\) for which \(x^k\) solves \((L_\lambda)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Knapsack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary knapsack generalized to nonlinear value and resource functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A binary nonlinear knapsack problem has the form
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\left\{f(x):g_r(x)\le b_r\text{ for every }r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\right\},
\]
where \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is a nonlinear value function and each \(g_r:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) measures nonlinear resource consumption. The classical 0-1 knapsack is recovered by taking \(m=1\), \(f(x)=p^{\mathsf T}x\), and \(g_1(x)=w^{\mathsf T}x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximize a nonlinear value of a selected subset subject to one or more nonlinear resource-capacity constraints.
assumptions_latex: The functions \(f\) and \(g_r\) are finite on \(\{0,1\}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:g_r(x)\le b_r\ \forall r\}\), and the objective is to maximize \(f\) on this set.

children.top_down_role: Regimes distinguished by separable, pairwise, or higher-order item interactions.

knowledge_statements.title: Interaction-Structure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic interactions classified through the support graph of off-diagonal coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For quadratic knapsack with objective \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\), replace \(Q\) by \((Q+Q^{\mathsf T})/2\) and define the interaction graph \(G_Q\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with edge \(\{i,j\}\) exactly when \(i\ne j\) and \(Q_{ij}\ne0\). If \(G_Q\) has no edges, then the binary identities \(x_i^2=x_i\) give
\[
x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x=\sum_{i=1}^n(Q_{ii}+c_i)x_i,
\]
which is a linear knapsack objective. If \(G_Q\) is disconnected, the quadratic objective is additive across the connected components of \(G_Q\), although the capacity constraint may still couple those components. A complete interaction graph permits a nonzero interaction for every item pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No interaction edges yield a linear knapsack objective; disconnected interaction graphs separate the objective by components while the shared capacity may still couple them; a complete graph permits every pairwise interaction.
assumptions_latex: The knapsack constraint is \(w^{\mathsf T}x\le B\), with \(w_i>0\) for every \(i\) and \(B\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(G_Q)=\varnothing\Rightarrow x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x=\sum_{i=1}^n(Q_{ii}+c_i)x_i\); disconnected \(G_Q\) gives componentwise objective additivity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Interaction Does Not Imply Polynomial Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary for graph sparsity in quadratic knapsack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An empty interaction graph does not make quadratic knapsack polynomial-time solvable: when all off-diagonal coefficients vanish, binary idempotence converts the objective to a linear profit vector, leaving ordinary 0-1 knapsack, which is NP-hard. Therefore bounded degree, forest structure, or bounded treewidth of the objective-interaction graph alone cannot guarantee polynomial time while the knapsack capacity is binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even no pairwise interactions leaves ordinary NP-hard knapsack, so sparse objective structure alone is not a tractability certificate.
assumptions_latex: Weights and capacity are binary encoded.
The number of items is variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E(G_Q)=\varnothing\not\Rightarrow\text{ polynomial-time solvability unless }\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(V_0(c)=0\) for every \(c\in\{0,\ldots,W\}\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), compute
\[
V_i(c)=\begin{cases}V_{i-1}(c),&c<w_i,\\ \max\{V_{i-1}(c),\,p_i+V_{i-1}(c-w_i)\},&c\ge w_i,
\end{cases}
\]
for every \(c\in\{0,\ldots,W\}\). Output \(V_n(W)\); an optimal binary vector is recovered by tracing whether each maximizing transition includes item \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute the best profit for every prefix of items and integer capacity, choosing at each state whether to exclude or include the current item.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-function recurrence, bottom-up table construction, backtracking recovery, and pseudopolynomial running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(P_m(z)=\max\{\sum_{j=1}^{m}p_jw_j:\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_jw_j\le z,\ (w_1,\ldots,w_m)\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). Then \[P_m(z)=\begin{cases}P_{m-1}(z),&0\le z<a_m,\\\max\{P_{m-1}(z),P_{m-1}(z-a_m)+p_m\},&a_m\le z\le b,\end{cases}\] with \[P_1(z)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le z<a_1,\\p_1,&a_1\le z\le b.\end{cases}\] When the weights \(a_j\) are positive integers, the entries for \(m=1,\ldots,N\) and \(z=0,\ldots,b\) can be computed bottom-up in \(O(Nb)\) time; \(P_N(b)\) is the optimal value and backtracking recovers an optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: P_m(z) is the maximum profit obtainable from the first m items with capacity z. The recurrence chooses between excluding item m and including it when it fits. With positive integer weights, a bottom-up table computes the optimum in O(Nb) time, and backtracking recovers an optimal selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}=P_N(b),\qquad T(N,b)=O(Nb),\qquad\text{and an optimal solution is recoverable by backtracking.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) and \(c\in\{0,\ldots,W\}\), define
\[
V_i(c)=\max\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{i}p_jx_j:\sum_{j=1}^{i}w_jx_j\le c,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{i}\right\}.
\]
Then \(V_0(c)=0\), and the state transition is \(V_i(c)=V_{i-1}(c)\) when \(c<w_i\), while for \(c\ge w_i\) it is \(V_i(c)=\max\{V_{i-1}(c),p_i+V_{i-1}(c-w_i)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) and \(s\in\{0,\ldots,W\}\), define \[E_i(s)=\max\left\{\sum_{j=1}^ip_jx_j:\sum_{j=1}^iw_jx_j=s,\ x\in\{0,1\}^i\right\},\] with \(\max\varnothing=-\infty\). Then \(E_0(0)=0\), \(E_0(s)=-\infty\) for \(s>0\), and \(E_i(s)=\max\{E_{i-1}(s),p_i+E_{i-1}(s-w_i)\}\), treating invalid indices as \(-\infty\). The knapsack optimum is \(\max_{0\le s\le W}E_n(s)\).
