children.title: Generalized Set Covering
children.top_down_role: Covering systems with generalized requirements, capacities, or multiplicities.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite sets, \(A\in\{0,1\}^{I\times J}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^I\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized set-covering problem is \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax\ge b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^J\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary generalized covering with integral row demands.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Generalized Set Covering: The Satisfiability Problem p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite row and column sets \(I\) and \(J\), an incidence matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{I\times J}\), coverage requirements \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^I\), and costs \(c\in\mathbb R^J\), the generalized set-covering problem is \[\min\left\{c^Tx:Ax\ge b,\quad x\in\{0,1\}^J\right\}.\] Thus row \(i\) must be covered by at least \(b_i\) selected columns. Ordinary set covering is the special case \(b_i=1\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized set covering chooses binary columns at minimum cost while meeting an integer coverage requirement for every row.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Set Covering

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility test and elementary forcing rule for the pure covering system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax\ge b\), \(x\in\{0,1\}^J\), with \(A\in\{0,1\}^{I\times J}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_+^I\), feasibility holds if and only if\[b_i\le\sum_{j\in J}A_{ij}\qquad(i\in I),\]because \(x=\mathbf1\) is feasible whenever these inequalities hold. If \(b_i=\sum_jA_{ij}\), every feasible solution has \(x_j=1\) for each incident column \(j\). A row violating the displayed inequality certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pure covering system is feasible exactly when no row demands more incident columns than exist; full-demand rows force every incident column.
assumptions_latex: There are no constraints besides \(Ax\ge b\) and the binary bounds.
\(A\) is binary and \(b\) is nonnegative integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Row capacities decide feasibility and full-demand rows identify forced columns.

notation.meaning: Number of available columns incident to row i.

knowledge_statements.title: Row-Capacity Feasibility and Forcing Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case optimization complexity inherited from ordinary weighted set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax\ge b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^J\}\) is NP-hard even when \(b=\mathbf1\), since that restriction is ordinary minimum-weight set cover. For finitely encoded rational costs and threshold \(K\), deciding whether a feasible solution of cost at most \(K\) exists is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized set covering is NP-hard already in the ordinary unit-demand special case.
assumptions_latex: The row and column sets are part of the input.
Costs and the decision threshold are finitely encoded rationals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Generalized set-cover optimization is NP-hard and its threshold decision form is NP-complete.

children.title: Satisfiability Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Logical feasibility structures exposed through binary constraint interfaces.

assumptions_latex: \(F=\bigwedge_{i=1}^m C_i\) is a CNF formula over Boolean variables \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is satisfiable if and only if the associated binary system has a feasible solution.

notation.meaning: Indicator that variable j is true.
Indicator that variable j is false.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility encoding of CNF satisfiability as binary covering plus consistency equations.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each variable introduce \(t_j,f_j\in\{0,1\}\) and impose \(t_j+f_j=1\). Let \(a_{ij}^+=1\) when literal \(z_j\) occurs in clause \(C_i\), and let \(a_{ij}^-=1\) when \(\neg z_j\) occurs. Then \(F\) is satisfiable exactly when \[\sum_{j=1}^n\left(a_{ij}^+t_j+a_{ij}^-f_j\right)\ge1\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad t_j+f_j=1\quad(j=1,\ldots,n)\] has a binary solution. The corresponding truth assignment sets \(z_j\) true precisely when \(t_j=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CNF satisfiability is binary covering of every clause by a selected true literal, together with one consistency equation per Boolean variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Satisfiability Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5 Generalized Set Covering: The Satisfiability Problem p. 58

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct CNF encoding using one binary variable per Boolean variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\) represent the truth value of \(z_j\). For clause \(C_i\), let \(P_i\) and \(N_i\) index its positive and negated literals. Then\[C_i\text{ is satisfied}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_{j\in P_i}y_j+\sum_{j\in N_i}(1-y_j)\ge1.\]Thus a CNF formula is satisfiable exactly when all such inequalities have a common binary solution. This is obtained from the two-polarity interface by substituting \(t_j=y_j\) and \(f_j=1-y_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each clause is one covering inequality in the truth variables, with negated literals represented by complements.
assumptions_latex: The CNF formula has finitely many nonempty clauses.
\(y_j\) is binary for every Boolean variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The clause inequalities have a common binary solution exactly when the CNF formula is satisfiable.

notation.meaning: Indices occurring positively in clause i.
Indices occurring negated in clause i.

children.title: Clause–Cover Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between clause satisfaction and coverage requirements.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a CNF formula and \(U\) is its set of clauses.
For every literal \(\ell\), \(S_\ell\subseteq U\) contains exactly the clauses in which \(\ell\) occurs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Truth assignments satisfying \(F\) correspond exactly to consistent selections of literal sets covering \(U\).

notation.meaning: Set of clauses containing literal l.
Indicator that literal l is selected as true.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) contain one element for each clause of \(F\), and define \(S_\ell=\{C\in U:\ell\in C\}\) for every literal \(\ell\). A truth assignment induces a literal-set selection satisfying \[\sum_{\ell:C\in S_\ell}x_\ell\ge1\quad(C\in U),\qquad x_{z_j}+x_{\neg z_j}=1\quad(j=1,\ldots,n).\] Conversely, every binary selection satisfying these constraints defines a truth assignment and covers each clause by a true literal. Dropping the complementary-literal equations leaves an ordinary cover that need not encode any assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clauses form the universe and each literal covers its containing clauses; exact equivalence to SAT additionally requires selecting exactly one polarity per variable.

children.title: Multiplicity-Induced Gaps
children.top_down_role: Relaxation weaknesses arising from generalized coverage multiplicities.

assumptions_latex: Generalized covering requires each clause-row \(C\) to receive multiplicity \(b_C\ge1\).
Literal variables remain constrained by \(x_z+x_{\neg z}=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(b_C>1\), satisfiability need not imply feasibility of the multiplicity-cover system.

notation.meaning: Required number of selected literals covering clause C.

review_flags: explicit boundary example should be checked against source treatment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the SAT correspondence when clause rows require multiple true literals.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Generalized Set Covering: The Satisfiability Problem p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The clause-cover equivalence uses unit requirements. If a clause row is replaced by \(\sum_{\ell\in C}x_\ell\ge b_C\) with \(b_C>1\), feasibility requires at least \(b_C\) true literals in that clause, which is stronger than satisfiability. For example, \(F=(z_1\lor z_2)\) is satisfied by \(z_1=1\) and \(z_2=0\), but its selected-literal vector has \(x_{z_1}+x_{z_2}=1\) and violates the multiplicity-two row \(x_{z_1}+x_{z_2}\ge2\). Hence unit-demand SAT correspondence does not extend unchanged to generalized multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Demanding multiple selected literals per clause is stronger than SAT, so a satisfying assignment may fail the generalized covering constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity-Induced Gaps

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-minimization form of the generalized assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The generalized assignment problem is \[\min\left\{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\ \text{for every }j\in J,\quad \sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}x_{ij}\le b_i\ \text{for every }i\in I,\quad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\ \text{for every }(i,j)\in I\times J\right\}.\] Each job is assigned to exactly one agent, while the assignments made to an agent jointly respect that agent's capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized assignment sends each job to exactly one agent while respecting agent-specific capacity consumption and minimizing total cost.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite set of agents and \(J\) is a finite set of jobs.
For every \((i,j)\in I\times J\), assigning job \(j\) to agent \(i\) uses \(a_{ij}\ge0\) capacity and incurs cost \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\); every agent \(i\in I\) has capacity \(b_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized assignment problem is \(\min\{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\ (j\in J),\ \sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}x_{ij}\le b_i\ (i\in I),\ x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\ ((i,j)\in I\times J)\}\).

notation.meaning: Indicator that job j is assigned to agent i.
Capacity consumed by assigning job j to agent i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pseudopolynomial algorithm for a fixed number of agents and integral capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\) agents with integral capacities, process jobs sequentially and retain the least cost for every attainable used-capacity vector \((t_1,\ldots,t_m)\). A transition assigns the next job to one agent without exceeding its capacity. A full table runs in \(O\!\left(|J|m\prod_{i=1}^m(b_i+1)\right)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed number of agents, generalized assignment has an exact capacity-vector dynamic program that is pseudopolynomial in the capacities.
assumptions_latex: All consumptions and capacities are nonnegative integers.
The number of agents is fixed for the pseudopolynomial interpretation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T=O\!\left(|J|m\prod_{i=1}^m(b_i+1)\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\) is generalized-assignment feasible and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=q(\lambda)\) for some \(\lambda\ge0\), where \(q\) is the capacity Lagrangian bound, then \(x\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible assignment is optimal when its cost matches a valid capacity-Lagrangian lower bound.

\(q(\lambda)\) is evaluated for a nonnegative multiplier vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With binary-encoded integral data, generalized-assignment feasibility is weakly NP-complete already for two agents having equal capacities and job consumptions independent of the chosen agent. Generalized-assignment optimization is therefore NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even the two-agent feasibility problem contains weak NP-complete instances.
assumptions_latex: Consumptions and capacities are nonnegative integers encoded in binary.
Every job must be assigned to exactly one agent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{GAP\mbox{-}FEASIBILITY}\text{ is weakly NP-complete for two agents}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Job-separable lower bound for the minimization formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda_i\ge0\), relaxing the agent capacities gives \[q(\lambda)=-\sum_i\lambda_i b_i+\sum_{j\in J}\min_{i\in I}\{c_{ij}+\lambda_i a_{ij}\}.\] For every \(\lambda\ge0\), \(q(\lambda)\le z^*\), and its evaluation separates by job.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing agent capacities gives a job-separable lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The model is in minimization form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q(\lambda)\le z^*\quad(\lambda\ge0).
knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Lagrangian Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness with a variable number of equal-capacity agents and agent-independent job sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With binary-encoded integral data and a variable number of agents, generalized-assignment feasibility is strongly NP-complete even when \(a_{ij}=a_j\) is independent of the agent and all capacities are equal. Consequently, a pseudopolynomial algorithm for this unrestricted-agent regime would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized-assignment feasibility is strongly NP-complete for a variable number of equal-capacity agents, even with agent-independent job sizes.
assumptions_latex: Every job must be assigned to exactly one agent.
Consumptions and capacities are nonnegative integers encoded in binary.
The number of agents is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{GAP\mbox{-}FEASIBILITY}\text{ is strongly NP-complete}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LP Rounding with Additive Capacity Violation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical bicriteria rounding guarantee for the minimization formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible solution of the standard generalized-assignment LP, there is a polynomial-time rounding to an integral assignment whose cost is no larger than the LP cost and whose load on agent \(i\) is at most \(b_i+\max\{a_{ij}:x_{ij}>0\}\). After pairs with \(a_{ij}>b_i\) are removed, every agent load is therefore at most \(2b_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard LP rounding preserves cost while exceeding each capacity by at most one fractionally incident job size.
assumptions_latex: The standard assignment-capacity LP is feasible.
Pairs with \(a_{ij}>b_i\) are forbidden or removed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^{\mathsf T}\hat x\le c^{\mathsf T}x^{LP},\qquad \sum_j a_{ij}\hat x_{ij}\le b_i+\max_{j:x_{ij}^{LP}>0}a_{ij}\le2b_i.
review_flags: This is a bicriteria guarantee permitting capacity violation, not a strict-capacity approximation theorem.
knowledge_statements.title: LP Rounding with Additive Capacity Violation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost assignment with machine-dependent processing times and a common per-machine processing bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given $n$ jobs, $m$ machines, processing times $p_{ij}$, assignment costs $c_{ij}$, and a bound $T$, the generalized assignment problem is
\[\min \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}\]
subject to
\[\sum_{i=1}^m x_{ij}=1\quad(j=1,\ldots,n),\qquad \sum_{j=1}^n p_{ij}x_{ij}\le T\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign every job to exactly one machine at minimum total cost, while the machine-dependent processing times assigned to each machine sum to at most T.
assumptions_latex: x_{ij}=1\text{ indicates that job }j\text{ is assigned to machine }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{i=1}^m x_{ij}=1\ \forall j,\ \sum_{j=1}^n p_{ij}x_{ij}\le T\ \forall i\right\}

knowledge_statements.title: Facility Location Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated facility location with binary opening and single-source assignment variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be customers and \(J\) candidate facilities. Given opening costs \(f_j\ge 0\) and assignment costs \(c_{ij}\), the uncapacitated facility-location model is
\[
\min_{x,y}\ \sum_{j\in J}f_jy_j+\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\quad(i\in I),\qquad x_{ij}\le y_j\quad(i\in I,j\in J),
\]
with \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) and \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\). Thus assignments may use only opened facilities. Because each assignment row has unit demand, an optimal solution can be chosen with \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize facility-opening and customer-assignment costs while assigning each customer to exactly one opened facility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \min \left\{\sum_{j\in J}f_jy_j+\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1,\ x_{ij}\le y_j,\ x\ge0,\ y\in\{0,1\}^{J}\right\}.\)

children.title: Fixed-Charge Activation
children.top_down_role: Binary activation structures carrying fixed costs for enabled activities.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Charge Activation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic on-off formulation for paying a fixed cost when an activity is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether an activity is activated, let \(z\ge0\) denote its usage, and let \(U>0\) be a valid upper bound on usage. A fixed-charge term is modeled by
\[
\min\ \{fy+cz:0\le z\le Uy,\ y\in\{0,1\}\},
\]
possibly as a component of a larger model. The linking inequality forces \(z=0\) when \(y=0\), whereas \(y=1\) permits any \(z\in[0,U]\). Consequently, every positive usage incurs the fixed cost \(f\), in addition to the variable cost \(cz\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary activation variable triggers a fixed cost and bounds usage by zero when inactive and by a valid capacity when active.
assumptions_latex: \(U>0\) is a valid upper bound for feasible usage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z>0\Longrightarrow y=1\) under \(0\le z\le Uy\) and \(y\in\{0,1\}\).

source_refs.locator: 2.10.1 Facility Location p. 67

source_witnesses.locator: 2.10.1 Facility Location p. 67

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between the one-way activation implication and exact use-triggered activation at an optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The constraints \(0\le z\le Uy\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\), imply \(z>0\Rightarrow y=1\), but not \(z=0\Rightarrow y=0\). In a minimization model, if \(f>0\) and replacing \((y,z)=(1,0)\) by \((0,0)\) preserves every other constraint and objective term, then every optimum satisfies \(y=\mathbf 1[z>0]\). Exact triggering can fail if \(f=0\), \(f<0\), or another model component requires or rewards idle activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The activation link permits an unused active state; a positive fixed cost and neutral feasible deactivation eliminate that state at every optimum.
assumptions_latex: For the exact-trigger conclusion, idle deactivation is feasible and changes no objective term except removing \(f>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z>0\Rightarrow y=1,\qquad f>0\text{ and neutral feasible idle deactivation}\Rightarrow y=\mathbf 1[z>0]\text{ at every optimum}.

notation.meaning: fixed activation cost in a minimization objective

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Use Versus Exact Activation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex hull of one bounded nonnegative activity controlled by one binary activation variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(U>0\), let \(S=\{(0,0)\}\cup(\{1\}\times[0,U])\). Then
\[
\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(y,z):0\le y\le1,\ 0\le z\le Uy\}.
\]
Thus replacing binary \(y\) by \(0\le y\le1\) gives the exact convex hull of the isolated activation set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard bounded activation inequality is ideal for one isolated activity.
assumptions_latex: The local feasible states are exactly \((y,z)=(0,0)\) or \(y=1\), \(0\le z\le U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(y,z):0\le y\le1,\ 0\le z\le Uy\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear linking conditions between facility-opening indicators and assignment or flow variables.

source_refs.locator: 2.10.1 Facility Location p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite index sets \(I\) and \(J\), let \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\) denote whether facility \(j\) is open, and let \(x_{ij}\ge0\) denote service from facility \(j\) to customer \(i\). A disaggregated location-activation coupling is
\[
x_{ij}\le U_{ij}y_j\qquad(i\in I,j\in J),
\]
where \(U_{ij}\ge0\) is a valid bound. An aggregate coupling is
\[
\sum_{i\in I}a_i x_{ij}\le U_jy_j\qquad(j\in J),
\]
where \(U_j\ge0\) is valid and \(a_i>0\) for every linked customer. Either form forces all linked service to vanish when \(y_j=0\). For binary unit assignments, the disaggregated specialization is \(x_{ij}\le y_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linking inequalities prohibit assignment or flow through a closed facility and permit bounded service after activation.
knowledge_statements.title: Location–Activation Couplings

source_witnesses.locator: 2.10.1 Facility Location p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comparison of Disaggregated and Aggregate Links
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relaxation-strength comparison for componentwise service bounds and one aggregate facility bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_i\ge0\), \(0\le y\le1\), \(a_i>0\), and \(U_i,U\ge0\). The disaggregated system \(x_i\le U_i y\) for all \(i\) implies
\[
\sum_i a_i x_i\le\Bigl(\sum_i a_iU_i\Bigr)y.
\]
Conversely, \(\sum_i a_ix_i\le Uy\) implies \(x_i\le(U/a_i)y\) for every \(i\). Hence the disaggregated system implies the aggregate link with coefficient \(U\) when \(U\ge\sum_i a_iU_i\), while the aggregate link implies all stated disaggregated links when \(U\le a_iU_i\) for every \(i\). Outside these relations, neither formulation need dominate the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Componentwise links imply a summed aggregate bound, while an aggregate bound implies component bounds scaled by the aggregation weights; independently chosen bounds can make the systems incomparable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_i\le U_i y\ (\forall i)\Rightarrow\sum_i a_ix_i\le(\sum_i a_iU_i)y,\qquad \sum_i a_ix_i\le Uy\Rightarrow x_i\le(U/a_i)y.
knowledge_statements.title: Comparison of Disaggregated and Aggregate Links

children.title: Capacity-Constrained Location
children.top_down_role: Facility-location regimes with limited service capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Constrained Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated facility location with splittable demand and activation-dependent facility capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let customer \(i\) have demand \(d_i\ge0\), and let facility \(j\) have capacity \(u_j\ge0\). With opened-facility indicators \(y_j\) and shipped quantities \(x_{ij}\), the capacitated location model is
\[
\min_{x,y}\ \sum_{j\in J}f_jy_j+\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=d_i\quad(i\in I),\qquad
\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}\le u_jy_j\quad(j\in J),
\]
with \(x_{ij}\ge0\) and \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\). Hence a closed facility ships nothing, while an open facility cannot exceed its capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Open facilities and route all customer demand without exceeding the capacity of any opened facility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=d_i\) and \(\displaystyle \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}\le u_jy_j\) characterize demand coverage and activated capacity.

source_refs.locator: 2.10.1 Facility Location p. 67

source_witnesses.locator: 2.10.1 Facility Location p. 67

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial shipment optimization after facility openings are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(y\), minimizing \(\sum_{ij}c_{ij}x_{ij}\) subject to demand equalities and activated facility capacities is a transportation, equivalently minimum-cost-flow, problem. It is polynomial-time solvable, and feasibility is decidable by a maximum-flow computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once openings are fixed, optimal splittable routing is a polynomial-time transportation problem.
assumptions_latex: Costs, demands, and capacities are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The fixed-}y\text{ subproblem is polynomial-time solvable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Opening Transportation Subproblem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity of the splittable capacitated model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Capacitated facility location is NP-hard even when every facility capacity is at least total demand, so the capacity rows are ineffective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacitated facility location remains NP-hard when capacities never bind.
assumptions_latex: Input data are rational and finitely encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{CFL}\text{ is NP-hard}.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated-Location NP-Hardness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fixed-opening feasibility test for complete bipartite service with splittable demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\sum_i d_i\). For fixed \(y\), the shipment constraints are feasible if and only if \(\sum_j u_jy_j\ge D\), provided every customer may ship to every facility, demand is splittable, and no additional arc capacities are imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the complete splittable model, fixed openings are feasible exactly when their total capacity covers total demand.
assumptions_latex: There are no additional arc-capacity restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x\text{ feasible for }y\Longleftrightarrow\sum_j u_jy_j\ge\sum_i d_i.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate-Capacity Feasibility Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Customer-specific valid inequalities strengthening aggregate activated capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every feasible solution satisfies \(x_{ij}\le d_i y_j\) for all \(i,j\). Adding these inequalities preserves the integer feasible set and can strengthen the continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Customer-specific shipment-opening links strengthen the aggregate activated-capacity formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(y_j\) is binary in the original formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{ij}\le d_i y_j\quad(i\in I,j\in J)\text{ is valid}.
knowledge_statements.title: Disaggregated Activation Strengthening

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Benders Decomposition for Splittable Capacitated Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite master-subproblem decomposition over facility-opening vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Benders master chooses \(y\) and a shipment-cost lower-bound variable \(\theta\). For each opening vector, solve the fixed-opening transportation subproblem. If feasible, add an optimality cut from an optimal dual solution; if infeasible, add a feasibility cut from a dual ray. With exact master and subproblem solves and valid cuts preventing repetition of an unresolved opening vector, finiteness of \(\{0,1\}^{|J|}\) gives finite termination at a global optimum or a proof of infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Benders decomposition alternates facility-opening decisions with exact transportation solves and adds dual feasibility or optimality cuts.
assumptions_latex: Master and transportation subproblems are solved exactly.
Infeasible subproblems return valid dual-ray feasibility cuts.
Feasible subproblems return valid dual optimality cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The exact Benders procedure terminates finitely with a global optimum or infeasibility}.

notation.meaning: master lower approximation of shipment cost

knowledge_statements.title: Benders Decomposition for Splittable Capacitated Location

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aggregate Capacity Fails with Restricted Service Arcs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary of the aggregate-capacity fixed-opening test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two customers have demands \(d_1=d_2=1\), and let two opened facilities have capacities \(u_1=u_2=1\). If both customers may use only facility 1, total opened capacity equals total demand, yet facility 1 would need to ship two units, so the routing system is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total opened capacity can cover demand while restricted service arcs overload one facility.
assumptions_latex: Demand remains splittable over available arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_j u_jy_j\ge\sum_i d_i\not\Longrightarrow\exists x\text{ feasible}.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Capacity Fails with Restricted Service Arcs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual of the splittable shipment subproblem for a fixed opening vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(y\), the shipment problem has dual \[\max_{\alpha,\beta}\ \sum_i d_i\alpha_i-\sum_j u_jy_j\beta_j\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \alpha_i-\beta_j\le c_{ij},\ \beta_j\ge0,\ \alpha_i\text{ free}.\] Every dual-feasible pair lower-bounds the fixed-opening shipment cost and yields the valid Benders cut \(\theta\ge\sum_i d_i\alpha_i-\sum_j u_j\beta_jy_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed-opening transportation dual supplies shipment-cost lower bounds and Benders optimality cuts.
assumptions_latex: The fixed-opening transportation subproblem is feasible and has finite optimum when equality with its primal optimum is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta\ge\sum_i d_i\alpha_i-\sum_j u_j\beta_jy_j\text{ is valid for every dual-feasible }(\alpha,\beta).
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Opening Transportation Dual
Network-Design Activation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-commodity capacitated network design with binary arc installation and continuous flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph, with arc-design costs \(f_a\), flow costs \(c_a\), capacities \(u_a\ge0\), and node balances \(b_v\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\). A network-design activation model is
\[
\min_{x,y}\ \sum_{a\in A}f_ay_a+\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\quad(v\in V),
\qquad 0\le x_a\le u_ay_a\quad(a\in A),
\]
where \(y_a\in\{0,1\}\). Flow can traverse an arc only when that arc is installed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose arcs and route a balanced commodity flow, paying design costs and respecting activation-dependent arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_a=0\Longrightarrow x_a=0\), while feasible flows satisfy every node-balance equation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial routing and feasibility subproblem after fixing arc-installation decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed design \(\bar y\), the remaining problem is a capacitated single-commodity transshipment problem with capacities \(u_a\bar y_a\). Feasibility can be tested by a feasible-circulation or maximum-flow construction, and a minimum-cost feasible routing can be found by a minimum-cost-flow algorithm.

Directed Steiner network design is contained as a special case by assigning supply at a root, unit demands at required terminals, sufficiently large installed-arc capacities, and fixed arc-design costs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut characterization of routing feasibility for a fixed single-commodity installed-capacity vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\subseteq V\), let \(b(S)=\sum_{v\in S}b_v\). Every feasible activated design satisfies
\[
b(S)\le\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_ay_a,
\qquad
-b(S)\le\sum_{a\in\delta^-(S)}u_ay_a.
\]
For one continuous commodity with no restrictions beyond conservation, nonnegativity, and arc capacities, these inequalities for all \(S\subseteq V\) characterize the existence of a feasible flow for a fixed vector \((u_ay_a)_{a\in A}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every node set needs enough installed outgoing or incoming capacity for its net supply or demand; for one continuous commodity these cut tests characterize routing feasibility.
assumptions_latex: Flow is continuous and subject only to conservation, nonnegativity, and fixed installed capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b(S)\le\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_ay_a,\qquad -b(S)\le\sum_{a\in\delta^-(S)}u_ay_a\quad(S\subseteq V).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Validity and Strength of Arc Activation Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and relaxation-quality boundary for activation-dependent arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inequality \(x_a\le u_ay_a\) preserves the intended integer feasible set only when \(u_a\) is a valid upper bound on attainable flow through arc \(a\). An undersized value can delete intended designs. An unnecessarily large value preserves integer feasibility but can weaken the continuous relaxation by allowing a given flow with a smaller fractional value of \(y_a\), thereby diluting a positive design cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undersized arc bound can invalidate the model, while an oversized bound can weaken its relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(f_a>0\) when considering fractional dilution of design cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u_a\text{ below a valid attainable-flow bound can remove intended solutions; an oversized }u_a\text{ can weaken the LP relaxation}.

children.title: Max-Cut Models
children.top_down_role: Graph partition models maximizing the weight of crossing edges.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry of unconstrained cut labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in\{0,1\}^V\) represents a cut, then \(\bar x=\mathbf1-x\) represents the same unordered bipartition and \(|\bar x_i-\bar x_j|=|x_i-x_j|\) for every edge. Hence, for any prescribed \(r\in V\), imposing \(x_r=0\) preserves the Max-Cut optimum provided no additional constraint distinguishes the shore names.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing every shore label leaves the cut unchanged, so one vertex label may be fixed without loss.
assumptions_latex: No additional constraint distinguishes the two shore names.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For any \(r\in V\), the fixing \(x_r=0\) preserves the optimal value.

notation.meaning: Componentwise complement of the shore vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Shore-Complement Symmetry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact edge-indicator formulation valid for arbitrary real edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every edge \(e=\{i,j\}\), introduce \(d_e\in[0,1]\) and impose\[d_e\ge x_i-x_j,\quad d_e\ge x_j-x_i,\quad d_e\le x_i+x_j,\quad d_e\le2-x_i-x_j.\]For binary \(x_i,x_j\), these inequalities force \(d_e=|x_i-x_j|\). Therefore \(\max\{\sum_{e\in E}w_ed_e:x\in\{0,1\}^V,\ d\in[0,1]^E\}\), with the displayed inequalities, exactly represents weighted Max-Cut for arbitrary \(w_e\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four XOR-hull inequalities give an exact edge-indicator Max-Cut model even when edge weights have either sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation forces \(d_e=|x_i-x_j|\) and exactly represents weighted Max-Cut.

notation.meaning: Binary shore indicator of vertex i.
Indicator that edge e crosses the cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact XOR Linear Formulation
Max-Cut Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary linear and spin representations of weighted maximum cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with weights \(w_{ij}\), let \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) encode the side containing vertex \(i\). Introducing \(z_{ij}\in[0,1]\), weighted Max-Cut has the linear model
\[
\max\ \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}z_{ij}
\]
subject to
\[
z_{ij}\le x_i+x_j,\qquad z_{ij}\le2-x_i-x_j\quad(\{i,j\}\in E).
\]
When \(w_{ij}\ge0\), maximization makes \(z_{ij}=|x_i-x_j|\). Equivalently, with \(s_i=2x_i-1\in\{-1,1\}\), the objective is
\[
\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(1-s_is_j).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition vertices into two sides to maximize the total weight of edges whose endpoints lie on opposite sides.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \max_{s\in\{-1,1\}^{V}}\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(1-s_is_j)\) equals the maximum cut weight.

notation.meaning: binary side indicator for vertex i
indicator that edge ij crosses the cut
spin encoding of the side of vertex i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonnegative-weight linear and spin formulations are mathematically coherent, but the record has no citation or inspectable locator. An authoritative Max-Cut source is required before candidate-review acceptance.

children.top_down_role: Cut models with positive and negative interaction weights.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-linear representation of signed edge disagreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\). For each edge impose\[d_{ij}\ge x_i-x_j,\quad d_{ij}\ge x_j-x_i,\quad d_{ij}\le x_i+x_j,\quad d_{ij}\le2-x_i-x_j,\quad0\le d_{ij}\le1.\]Then \(d_{ij}=|x_i-x_j|\). Under the convention that \(\sigma_{ij}=+1\) prefers equality and \(\sigma_{ij}=-1\) prefers inequality, define\[z_{ij}=\begin{cases}d_{ij},&\sigma_{ij}=+1,\\1-d_{ij},&\sigma_{ij}=-1.\end{cases}\]Minimizing \(\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}z_{ij}\) is therefore an exact mixed-binary linear model of minimum signed disagreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An XOR variable records differing endpoints; frustration equals it on positive edges and its complement on negative edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed system exactly represents each signed-edge frustration indicator.

notation.meaning: Indicator that edge ij is frustrated.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Signed-Disagreement Linearization
Signed-Cut Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted signed-graph partitioning as minimization of edge disagreements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have nonnegative weights \(w_{ij}\) and edge signs \(\sigma_{ij}\in\{-1,1\}\). For spins \(s_i\in\{-1,1\}\), edge \(\{i,j\}\) is frustrated when \(s_is_j\ne\sigma_{ij}\). Its frustration indicator is
\[
z_{ij}=\frac{1-\sigma_{ij}s_is_j}{2}\in\{0,1\}.
\]
The minimum-disagreement signed-cut model is therefore
\[
\min_{s\in\{-1,1\}^{V}}\ \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}\frac{1-\sigma_{ij}s_is_j}{2}.
\]
Positive edges prefer equal endpoint spins, whereas negative edges prefer opposite spins. Maximizing satisfied weight is equivalent after subtracting the displayed objective from \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign two signs to vertices while minimizing the weight of positive edges cut and negative edges left uncut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle z_{ij}=\frac{1-\sigma_{ij}s_is_j}{2}\) exactly indicates whether edge \(\{i,j\}\) is frustrated.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated sign convention and frustration objective are internally consistent, but no source is supplied. Because signed-cut conventions vary, an authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Sign-Switching Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Equivalences induced by switching vertex labels or interaction signs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete switching invariant on a fixed underlying graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\sigma,\rho:E\to\{-1,1\}\) be signings of the same finite undirected graph. There are vertex signs \(\tau_i\in\{-1,1\}\) with \(\rho_{ij}=\tau_i\sigma_{ij}\tau_j\) for every edge if and only if\[\prod_{e\in C}\rho_e=\prod_{e\in C}\sigma_e\]for every cycle \(C\). It suffices to check a cycle basis. In particular, \(\sigma\) is switchable to the all-positive signing exactly when every cycle is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two signings are switching-equivalent exactly when all their cycle-sign products agree; a cycle basis suffices.
assumptions_latex: Both signings have the same finite undirected underlying graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cycle-sign products are a complete invariant of vertex-switching equivalence.

notation.meaning: Two edge-sign functions on the same graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Sign Characterization of Switching Classes

assumptions_latex: \(s_i,\tau_i\in\{-1,1\}\) for every \(i\in V\), and edge weights are unchanged by switching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \min_{s\in\{-1,1\}^{V}}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}\frac{1-\sigma_{ij}s_is_j}{2}=\min_{s'\in\{-1,1\}^{V}}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}\frac{1-\sigma'_{ij}s'_is'_j}{2}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauge equivalence of signed-cut instances under vertex switching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with edge weights \(w_{ij}\ge0\), edge signs \(\sigma_{ij}\in\{-1,1\}\), and spins \(s_i\in\{-1,1\}\). For arbitrary switching signs \(\tau_i\in\{-1,1\}\), define
\[
\sigma'_{ij}=\tau_i\sigma_{ij}\tau_j,
\qquad s'_i=\tau_i s_i.
\]
Then every edge frustration term is invariant:
\[
\sigma'_{ij}s'_is'_j=\sigma_{ij}s_is_j,
\qquad
\frac{1-\sigma'_{ij}s'_is'_j}{2}=\frac{1-\sigma_{ij}s_is_j}{2}.
\]
The mapping \(s\mapsto s'\) is a bijection preserving every weighted signed-cut objective value. Consequently, switching-equivalent signed graphs have identical optimal disagreement values and corresponding optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Switching signs at vertices changes edge labels and spins together but preserves every disagreement and the optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Switching Equivalence

children.title: Frustrated-Cycle Structure
children.top_down_role: Cycle structures created by incompatible signed interactions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive recognition of balanced signed graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In each connected component choose a root with \(t_r=1\) and traverse the graph, assigning \(t_j=\sigma_{ij}t_i\) when \(j\) is first reached from \(i\). If an examined edge violates \(t_j=\sigma_{ij}t_i\), that edge and the traversal-tree path between its endpoints form a negative cycle. If no conflict occurs, \(t_it_j=\sigma_{ij}\) on every edge. With adjacency lists this takes \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph traversal either constructs signs satisfying every edge or returns a negative cycle, in linear time.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected signed graph stored by adjacency lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Balance and nonbalance have constructive certificates obtainable in \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time.

notation.meaning: Traversal sign assigned to vertex i.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Time Balance and Negative-Cycle Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Frustration Index as a Negative-Cycle Transversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion characterization of minimum weighted frustration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have signs \(\sigma_e\in\{-1,1\}\) and weights \(w_e\ge0\). An edge set \(D\subseteq E\) meets every negative cycle if and only if \(G-D\) is balanced. Consequently,\[\min_{s\in\{-1,1\}^V}\sum_{e=ij}w_e\mathbf1[s_is_j\ne\sigma_e]=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in D}w_e:D\cap C\ne\varnothing\text{ for every negative cycle }C\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum weighted frustration equals the minimum weight of an edge set meeting every negative cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected signed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weighted frustration index equals the minimum weight of a negative-cycle edge transversal.

notation.meaning: Deleted edge set or negative-cycle transversal.

knowledge_statements.title: Frustration Index as a Negative-Cycle Transversal

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected signed graph.
\(\sigma_{ij},s_i\in\{-1,1\}\) for every applicable edge and vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every cycle \(C\), \(\sigma(C)=-1\Longrightarrow |F_C|\equiv1\pmod 2\) and \(\sigma(C)=1\Longrightarrow |F_C|\equiv0\pmod 2\); moreover, all edges are simultaneously satisfiable if and only if every cycle is positive.

notation.meaning: product of edge signs around cycle C
set of frustrated edges on cycle C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle parity characterization of unavoidable frustration in signed graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected signed graph with signs \(\sigma_{ij}\in\{-1,1\}\), and let \(s_i\in\{-1,1\}\) be assigned to every vertex. For a cycle \(C\), define
\[
\sigma(C)=\prod_{\{i,j\}\in C}\sigma_{ij},
\qquad
F_C=\bigl\{\{i,j\}\in C:s_is_j\ne\sigma_{ij}\bigr\}.
\]
Then
\[
(-1)^{|F_C|}=\sigma(C).
\]
Thus a negative cycle contains an odd, and hence nonzero, number of frustrated edges under every spin assignment, whereas a positive cycle contains an even number. All edges of \(G\) can be simultaneously satisfied if and only if every cycle is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every negative signed cycle forces an odd number of frustrated edges, and all edges are simultaneously satisfiable exactly when every cycle is positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Frustrated-Cycle Structure
Quadratic Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Koopmans–Beckmann quadratic assignment of facilities bijectively to locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\) facilities and \(n\) locations be given, with facility flows \(a_{ik}\), location distances \(b_{j\ell}\), and optional assignment costs \(c_{ij}\). With \(x_{ij}=1\) exactly when facility \(i\) is assigned to location \(j\), the quadratic assignment problem is
\[
\min_{x}\ \sum_{i,k=1}^{n}\sum_{j,\ell=1}^{n}a_{ik}b_{j\ell}x_{ij}x_{k\ell}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}x_{ij}
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{ij}=1\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{ij}=1\quad(j=1,\ldots,n),
\]
and \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\). Thus feasible solutions are permutation assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign each facility to one distinct location while minimizing pairwise flow-distance costs and optional direct assignment costs.
assumptions_latex: There are equally many facilities and locations.
All coefficient arrays are finite real-valued arrays of compatible dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is a permutation matrix minimizing the stated quadratic interaction objective.

notation.meaning: indicator assigning facility i to location j
flow or interaction between facilities i and k
distance or cost between locations j and l

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a retained product \(x_{ij}x_{k\ell}\), an auxiliary variable \(w_{ij,k\ell}\ge0\) with
\[
w_{ij,k\ell}\le x_{ij},\qquad w_{ij,k\ell}\le x_{k\ell},\qquad w_{ij,k\ell}\ge x_{ij}+x_{k\ell}-1
\]
satisfies \(w_{ij,k\ell}=x_{ij}x_{k\ell}\) whenever the assignment variables are binary.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w_{ij,k\ell}=x_{ij}x_{k\ell}\quad\text{at every integer assignment}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded quadratic assignment formulation between two equally sized sets. The general quadratic model is clear, but the printed coefficient factorization $c_{ijkl}=t_{ik}d_{ji}$ contains no dependence on $l$ and is retained only as an explicitly ambiguous printed specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S$ and $T$ each contain $n$ members, and define $\delta_{ij}=1$ iff member $i\in S$ is assigned to member $j\in T$. The quadratic assignment problem is $\min \sum_{\substack{i,j,k,l=1\\k>i}}^n c_{ijkl}\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}$ subject to $\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{ij}=1$ for every $i$, $\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{ij}=1$ for every $j$, and $\delta_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$. Here $c_{ijkl}$ is the joint cost of assignments $(i,j)$ and $(k,l)$, and $k>i$ prevents counting each assignment pair twice. The extract additionally prints $c_{ijkl}=t_{ik}d_{ji}$, but its intended indexing is ambiguous because $l$ does not occur on the right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quadratic assignment problem constructs a bijection between two n-element sets. Binary variables satisfy exactly one assignment in every row and column, while a quadratic objective charges joint costs for pairs of selected assignments. Restricting the second source index to k greater than i prevents double counting. The extract's printed product formula for the coefficients omits the destination index l, so it should not be silently normalized to a standard factorization.
assumptions_latex: c_{ijkl}\text{ is the cost jointly incurred by assignments }(i,j)\text{ and }(k,l).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\delta}\ \sum_{\substack{i,j,k,l=1\\k>i}}^n c_{ijkl}\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{ij}=1\ (i=1,\ldots,n),\quad \sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{ij}=1\ (j=1,\ldots,n),\quad \delta_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.

children.title: Quadratic Knapsack Models
children.top_down_role: Capacity-constrained binary selection with pairwise objective interactions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity inherited from the zero-interaction specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Setting \(q_{ij}=0\) for every pair reduces quadratic knapsack to classical zero-one knapsack. Consequently, quadratic knapsack is NP-hard under the usual finite binary encoding of rational or integer data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic knapsack is NP-hard because ordinary zero-one knapsack is its zero-interaction special case.
assumptions_latex: The number of items is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q_{ij}=0\ (i<j)\Rightarrow\mathrm{QKP}=\mathrm{0\text{-}1\ KP},\qquad\mathrm{QKP}\text{ is NP-hard}.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Knapsack Contains Binary Knapsack
Quadratic Knapsack Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary quadratic profit maximization under one nonnegative knapsack-capacity constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For items \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(p_i\) be individual profits, \(q_{ij}\) pairwise interaction profits, \(a_i\ge0\) resource consumptions, and \(B\ge0\) capacity. The quadratic knapsack model is
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}p_ix_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}q_{ij}x_ix_j
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_ix_i\le B.
\]
The product \(x_ix_j\) contributes precisely when both items are selected. Coefficients \(q_{ij}\) may represent complementarities when positive or conflicts when negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select items within a capacity while accounting for both individual profits and pairwise gains or penalties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \max\left\{\sum_i p_ix_i+\sum_{i<j}q_{ij}x_ix_j:\sum_i a_ix_i\le B,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\right\}.\)

notation.meaning: indicator that item i is selected
item resource consumption and total capacity

children.title: Quadratic Selection Models
children.top_down_role: Binary selection models with pairwise interactions under general feasibility structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Selection Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General binary selection over a prescribed feasible family with pairwise interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}\) encode admissible selections, and let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). A quadratic selection model has the form
\[
\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\ x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x.
\]
Because \(x_i^2=x_i\) for binary variables, diagonal terms of \(Q\) can be absorbed into \(c\). Moreover, replacing \(Q\) by \((Q+Q^{\mathsf T})/2\) leaves every objective value unchanged. Off-diagonal terms encode pairwise interaction costs between simultaneously selected items.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an admissible subset while optimizing individual costs and costs arising from pairs selected together.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a nonempty subset of \(\{0,1\}^{n}\).
\(Q\) and \(c\) are finite real-valued coefficient arrays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \min_{x\in\mathcal X}x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}x^{\mathsf T}\frac{Q+Q^{\mathsf T}}{2}x+c^{\mathsf T}x.\)

children.title: Capacity-Coupled Interactions
children.top_down_role: Interaction structure shaped by knapsack-style capacity restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Coupled Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite binary quadratic selection with one additive capacity constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{i:x_i=1\}\) satisfy \(\sum_{i\in S}a_i\le b\), and define \(r(S)=b-\sum_{i\in S}a_i\). For every \(k\notin S\), the set \(S\cup\{k\}\) is feasible if and only if \(a_k\le r(S)\), and \[f(\mathbf 1_{S\cup\{k\}})-f(\mathbf 1_S)=c_k+\sum_{\substack{i\in S\\i<k}}q_{ik}+\sum_{\substack{j\in S\\k<j}}q_{kj}.\] Thus feasibility of the prospective selection depends on the residual capacity determined by the entire selected set, while the displayed quadratic coefficients give its explicit pairwise objective interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An item's feasibility depends on the residual capacity left by all selected items, while its marginal objective value includes every pairwise coefficient joining it to a selected item.
assumptions_latex: Items have weights \(a_i>0\), capacity \(b>0\), and decisions \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\).
The objective is \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}q_{ij}x_ix_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a feasible selected set \(S\) and \(k\notin S\), item \(k\) can be added exactly when \(a_k\le b-\sum_{i\in S}a_i\), and its objective increment is \(c_k+\sum_{i\in S,\,i<k}q_{ik}+\sum_{j\in S,\,k<j}q_{kj}\).

notation.meaning: pairwise interaction coefficient defined for i<j

children.title: Selection-Constraint Regimes
children.top_down_role: Quadratic selection regimes distinguished by cardinality, capacity, or system constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact variable-complement equivalence between positive-weight upper-capacity and lower-quota rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\) and set \(z_i=1-x_i\). Then
\[
\sum_i a_ix_i\le b
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sum_i a_iz_i\ge A-b.
\]
Thus complementing every binary selection variable bijectively converts the packing regime into a covering regime. Equality rows similarly transform into \(\sum_i a_iz_i=A-b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing every selection exchanges an upper-capacity constraint with a lower-quota constraint having the complementary right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_{\le}(b)=\{\mathbf 1-z:z\in X_{\ge}(A-b)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Packing–Covering Complementation
Selection-Constraint Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-row packing, exact-selection, covering, and cardinality regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[X_{\le}(b)=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\le b\right\},\quad X_{=}(b)=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i=b\right\},\quad X_{\ge}(b)=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\ge b\right\}.\] These are, respectively, the packing or upper-capacity, exact-selection, and covering or lower-quota regimes. When \(a_i=1\) for every \(i\), they become at-most, exactly, and at-least cardinality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted binary selection row yields packing, exact, or covering regimes; unit weights specialize these to at-most, exact, or at-least cardinality constraints.
assumptions_latex: The index set is \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the weights satisfy \(a_i>0\), and \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\).
The scalar \(b\in\mathbb R\) is the capacity, target, or quota.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three feasible-set regimes are \(X_{\le}(b)\), \(X_{=}(b)\), and \(X_{\ge}(b)\); setting \(a_i=1\) yields the corresponding cardinality regimes.

notation.meaning: packing, exact-selection, and covering feasible sets

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+p}:A x+B y\le d\}\) be the LP relaxation of a formulation whose designated integer variables are \(x\). The formulation is ideal if every vertex \((\bar x,\bar y)\) of \(Q\) satisfies \(\bar x\in\mathbb Z^n\). Auxiliary coordinates \(\bar y\) need not be integral. knowledge_statements.title: Integral Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral integrality in the full formulation space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational polyhedron \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is integral, and a formulation defining it is an integral formulation, when \[Q=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(Q\cap\mathbb Z^d\bigr).\] Equivalently, every nonempty face of \(Q\) contains an integer point. If \(Q\) is bounded, this is equivalent to every vertex of \(Q\) belonging to \(\mathbb Z^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formulation is integral when its polyhedron is the convex hull of all integer points it contains in the full variable space; for a polytope, this is equivalent to integrality of every vertex.
assumptions_latex: Integrality refers to every coordinate of the formulation space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation is integral exactly when \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(Q\cap\mathbb Z^d)\); when \(Q\) is bounded, this is equivalent to every vertex of \(Q\) being integral.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be the intended feasible set and let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) be the LP relaxation of a valid formulation in variables \((x,y)\). Under the projection-based convention, the formulation is perfect if \[\pi_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(X).\] Hence optimizing any linear objective depending only on \(x\) over \(Q\) gives the same value as optimizing it over \(X\). In a formulation without auxiliary variables, perfection reduces to \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formulation is perfect when its LP relaxation projects exactly onto the convex hull of the intended discrete solutions.

children.title: Quality-Class Implications
children.top_down_role: Logical relationships among ideality, integrality, and perfection.

knowledge_statements.title: Quality-Class Implications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded polyhedral hierarchy under full-space integrality, designated-coordinate ideality, and projection-based perfection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) be a nonempty bounded polyhedron in variables \((x,y)\), where \(x\) comprises all designated integer variables, and let \[X=\left\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:\text{there exists }y\in\mathbb R^p\text{ with }(x,y)\in Q\right\}.\] Under the stated quality conventions, \[\text{integral}\;\Longrightarrow\;\text{ideal}\;\Longrightarrow\;\text{perfect}.\] Here perfection means \(\pi_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(X)\). Neither converse holds in general when continuous auxiliary variables and projection-based perfection are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded formulation whose integer-feasible projection is exactly the represented set, full-space integrality implies ideality, and ideality implies exact convex-hull projection. Continuous auxiliaries allow both converses to fail.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) is a nonempty bounded polyhedron in variables \((x,y)\).
The designated integer variables are \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), while \(y\in\mathbb R^p\) is auxiliary.
The represented set is \(X=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^p,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated conventions, \(\text{integral}\Longrightarrow\text{ideal}\Longrightarrow\text{perfect}\), and neither converse holds in general.

notation.meaning: projection onto the original variables x

children.title: Quality-Class Separation Examples
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes distinguishing the three formulation-quality classes.

assumptions_latex: The original coordinate is \(x\), while \(y\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_1\) is ideal but not integral, whereas \(Q_2\) is perfect but not ideal.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two elementary extended polytopes separate the stated quality classes.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{0,1\}\). The polytope \(Q_1=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(1,1/2)\}\) is ideal for designated variable \(x\), since both vertices have integral \(x\), but it is not integral in \((x,y)\). The polytope \(Q_2=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(1,0),(1/2,1)\}\) satisfies \(\pi_x(Q_2)=[0,1]=\operatorname{conv}(X)\), so it is perfect under the projection convention, but its vertex \((1/2,1)\) makes it nonideal. Hence both reverse implications in the quality hierarchy fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One segment is ideal but has a fractional auxiliary vertex; one triangle projects perfectly but has a fractional original-coordinate vertex.

children.title: Formulation Dominance Orders
children.top_down_role: Orderings used to compare binary formulations through their feasible relaxations.

assumptions_latex: \(Q_1\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p_1}\) and \(Q_2\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p_2}\) are valid LP relaxations of the same original feasible set.
Both formulations share original variables \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_1\) dominates \(Q_2\) precisely when \(P_1\subseteq P_2\), where \(P_k=\pi_x(Q_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-containment order for formulations of one feasible set.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\in\{1,2\}\), let \(P_k=\pi_x(Q_k)\) be the relaxation induced in the common original-variable space. Formulation \(Q_1\) dominates, or is at least as strong as, formulation \(Q_2\) when \[P_1\subseteq P_2.\] It strictly dominates \(Q_2\) when the containment is strict. This definition compares feasible regions after projection and is therefore unaffected by different auxiliary-variable spaces. Dominance is reflexive and transitive, and it becomes a partial order after formulations with identical projections are identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One formulation dominates another when its LP relaxation, projected into the common original variables, is contained in the other's projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Formulation Dominance Orders

children.title: Relaxation Strength Measures
children.top_down_role: Geometric measures of relaxation tightness for binary formulations.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty compact sets.
A minimization objective \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relaxation strength may be quantified by \(z_P(c)\), the additive gap \(z_X(c)-z_P(c)\), or a normalized gap when its denominator is positive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-bound and gap measures for minimization over compact relaxations.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty compact relaxation \(P\supseteq X\) and minimization vector \(c\), define \[z_P(c)=\min_{x\in P}c^\top x,\qquad z_X(c)=\min_{x\in X}c^\top x.\] Validity gives \(z_P(c)\le z_X(c)\). The additive relaxation gap is \(g_P(c)=z_X(c)-z_P(c)\ge0\); smaller \(g_P(c)\), equivalently larger \(z_P(c)\), means a stronger bound for that objective. A relative gap may be used only with an explicitly positive normalization, for example \(g_P(c)/\max\{1,|z_X(c)|\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, a stronger relaxation gives a larger LP bound and a smaller nonnegative gap to the discrete optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Strength Measures

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq P\) are nonempty and both displayed minimization values are finite.
The same objective normalization is used and \(0<z_P(c)\le z_X(c)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_P(c)=\frac{z_X(c)}{z_P(c)}\ge1,\qquad \rho_P(c)=1\iff z_P(c)=z_X(c).

notation.meaning: multiplicative integrality gap for objective c

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ratio-based strength measure and its sign and normalization boundaries for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When \(0<z_P(c)\le z_X(c)\), the multiplicative integrality gap is \[\rho_P(c)=\frac{z_X(c)}{z_P(c)}\ge1.\] A smaller ratio is stronger, and \(\rho_P(c)=1\) means objective-value exactness for \(c\). If either relevant value is zero or negative, the ratio is undefined or can reverse the intended ordering. Moreover, adding a common constant to the objective changes the ratio without changing the feasible sets, so multiplicative gaps are comparable only under a fixed objective normalization; otherwise an additive gap or explicitly positive normalization should be used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive minimization values, the multiplicative gap is the integer optimum divided by the relaxation bound; zero, negative values, or inconsistent objective translations invalidate comparisons.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Integrality-Gap Measures

children.title: Dominance–Strength Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which formulation dominance reflects stronger relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance–Strength Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment of compact convex projected relaxations characterized by all linear minimization bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty compact convex sets \(P_1,P_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[P_1\subseteq P_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \min_{x\in P_1}c^\top x\ge\min_{x\in P_2}c^\top x\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb R^n.\] Consequently, formulation dominance is equivalent to uniformly at-least-as-strong linear minimization bounds. If the containment is strict, the bound inequality is strict for at least one linear objective, though not necessarily for every objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty compact convex projected relaxations, containment is equivalent to giving at least as strong a minimization bound for every linear objective; strict containment improves at least one such bound.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1,P_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty compact convex projected relaxations.
The objectives are linear minimization objectives with \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The containment \(P_1\subseteq P_2\) holds if and only if \(\min_{x\in P_1}c^\top x\ge\min_{x\in P_2}c^\top x\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: minimum objective value over the indicated region

children.title: Incomparable Formulation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where competing formulations cannot be ordered uniformly by strength.

assumptions_latex: Both relaxations are taken in \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxations \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are incomparable, and each gives the stronger bound for a different linear objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two triangular relaxations whose objective-bound rankings reverse.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{(0,0),(1,1)\}\), \(P_1=\operatorname{conv}(X\cup\{(0,1)\})\), and \(P_2=\operatorname{conv}(X\cup\{(1,0)\})\). Since \((0,1)\in P_1\setminus P_2\) and \((1,0)\in P_2\setminus P_1\), neither relaxation dominates the other. For \(c=(1,-1)\), the minima over \(P_1,P_2\) are respectively \(-1\) and \(0\), so \(P_2\) is stronger. For \(d=(-1,1)\), the minima are \(0\) and \(-1\), so \(P_1\) is stronger.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two valid triangular relaxations are incomparable: each contains a point excluded by the other, and their bound rankings reverse across objectives.

children.title: Compact Formulations
children.top_down_role: Binary formulations emphasizing limited variable or constraint counts.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding-aware compactness convention for instance-indexed rational formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each instance \(I\) of binary encoding length \(L\), let \(Q_I\) be a finite rational linear or mixed-integer formulation. The family \(\{Q_I\}\) is encoding-compact if some polynomial \(p\) bounds the numbers of variables and constraints of \(Q_I\), and the binary encoding length of every rational coefficient, by \(p(L)\). Equivalently, the complete explicit description has polynomial total encoding length after a polynomial change of the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding-compact formulation family has polynomially many variables and constraints and polynomially encoded rational coefficients.
assumptions_latex: Problem instances have binary encoding length \(L\).
Each \(Q_I\) is an explicitly encoded finite rational formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{Q_I\}\text{ is encoding-compact when its complete explicit encoding length is polynomial in }L.\)

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of the instance

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Compact Formulation Families

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates polynomial encoded size from constructibility, relaxation strength, and optimization complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Encoding-compactness alone asserts only the existence or size of descriptions. It does not imply that \(Q_I\) can be constructed in time polynomial in \(L\), that its continuous relaxation is strong, or that optimization over a mixed-integer \(Q_I\) is polynomial-time solvable. If, however, \(Q_I\) is a rational linear formulation that is constructible in polynomial time and has polynomial encoding length, linear optimization over it is polynomial-time solvable in the standard bit model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial description size alone does not imply uniform construction, a strong relaxation, or easy mixed-integer optimization; a uniformly constructible compact LP is polynomial-time optimizable.
assumptions_latex: Compactness is measured by explicit rational encoding length.
The tractability conclusion applies to linear, not mixed-integer, formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{compact size}\not\Rightarrow\text{uniform construction, strength, or MIP tractability};\quad \text{uniform compact LP}\Rightarrow\text{polynomial-time LP optimization}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness, Uniformity, and Tractability Boundaries

assumptions_latex: Problem instances have binary encoding length \(L\).
The formulation is a finite linear or mixed-integer system whose coefficients have binary encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A formulation family is compact when its variable count, constraint count, and coefficient encoding length are bounded by a polynomial in \(L\).

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of an instance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding-size definition for an instance-indexed formulation family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each encoded instance \(I\) of length \(L\), let \(Q_I\) be a formulation of the corresponding feasible set. The family \(\{Q_I\}\) is compact if there exists a polynomial \(p\) such that \(Q_I\) uses at most \(p(L)\) variables and at most \(p(L)\) constraints, and every rational coefficient has encoding length at most \(p(L)\). The definition concerns representation size; it does not by itself imply that the relaxation is strong, ideal, or polynomial-time constructible unless those properties are separately required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formulation family is compact when variables, constraints, and coefficient encodings all have size polynomial in the input length.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The encoding-aware definition is mathematically coherent and fits the Compact Formulations leaf, but no citation establishes that this precise convention—especially its coefficient-length and constructibility qualifications—is the intended formulation-complexity terminology.

children.title: Extended Formulations
children.top_down_role: Higher-dimensional formulations whose auxiliary structure strengthens representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral extended formulations for a binary-set convex hull or relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron. An extended formulation of \(P\) is a finite linear system \(Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+r}:Ax+By\le d\}\) satisfying \[P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^r,\ Ax+By\le d\}.\] If only \(P\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\) is required, \(Q\) is an extended relaxation. Its size is conventionally the number of inequalities in the displayed system, excluding equations when these are eliminated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended formulation describes a polyhedron as the projection of a linear system containing auxiliary variables; an extended relaxation need only project to a superset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\).

notation.meaning: polyhedron in the original and auxiliary variables

children.title: Projection-Based Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations viewed through projection from an extended space.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Based Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential projection of a higher-dimensional polyhedron onto binary decision variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For matrices \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r}\), and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^m\), define \(Q=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le d\}\). Its projection is \[\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^r,\ Ax+By\le d\}.\] Thus \(Q\) represents a binary feasible set \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) exactly at the polyhedral level when \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(X)\); it represents a relaxation when \(\operatorname{conv}(X)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-dimensional linear system represents a binary set through all original-variable points admitting auxiliary-variable extensions; exactness means that projection equals the binary-set convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a polyhedron defined by finitely many linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(X)\) characterizes exact polyhedral representation.

notation.meaning: convex hull of the binary feasible set

children.title: Lifting-Based Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations built by introducing variables or inequalities in a richer space.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifting-Based Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Higher-dimensional polyhedral representation obtained by adjoining auxiliary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A polyhedron \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+r}\) is a lifting-based representation of \(P\) when every \(x\in P\) has at least one lift \((x,y)\in Q\), every \((x,y)\in Q\) has \(x\in P\), and hence \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^r,\ (x,y)\in Q\}.\] The auxiliary coordinates may encode disjunct selection, products, flows, or other structure, but exactness is determined solely by the displayed projection identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifting-based representation adds coordinates so that feasible original points are exactly those possessing a feasible lift in the enlarged polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\).

notation.meaning: a lifted point with original and auxiliary coordinates

children.title: Size–Strength Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural compromises between formulation size, relaxation quality, and representational complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Size–Strength Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of extended relaxations by inequality count and projected inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) be extended relaxations of \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and set \(R_k=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_k)\). Formulation \(Q_1\) is at least as strong as \(Q_2\) precisely when \[P\subseteq R_1\subseteq R_2.\] If \(s(Q_k)\) counts inequalities, the size–strength profile of \(Q_k\) is \((s(Q_k),R_k)\). Size and strength are distinct criteria: comparison by strength uses projected set inclusion, whereas comparison by size uses \(s(Q_k)\); neither definition identifies the two orderings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended formulations are stronger when their projections are smaller valid relaxations, while size counts inequalities. Formulation quality therefore records both criteria separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_1\) is at least as strong as \(Q_2\) if and only if \(P\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_1)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_2)\).

notation.meaning: projection of the kth extended relaxation
number of inequalities in the kth formulation
