assumptions_latex: The truncation retains every SOS multiplier and Boolean-ideal multiplier whose resulting term has degree at most \(2r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_r\le\rho_{r+1}\le f^*\), and \(\rho_r=f^*\) for all sufficiently large \(r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOS-dual hierarchy for polynomial optimization over a finite Boolean feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_r(g)\) consist of \(\sigma_0+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_jg_j\), where the \(\sigma_j\) are sums of squares and each retained product has degree at most \(2r\). With \(I_{01,2r}\) denoting the correspondingly truncated multiples of \(x_i^2-x_i\), define \[\rho_r=\sup\{\gamma:f-\gamma\in Q_r(g)+I_{01,2r}\}.\] For \(f^*=\min_{x\in K}f(x)\), validity and nesting give \(\rho_r\le\rho_{r+1}\le f^*\). Because the Boolean quotient is a finite function algebra and the inequalities exclude only finitely many cube points, an exact certificate exists at some finite truncation, so \(\rho_r=f^*\) for every sufficiently large \(r\). The required level is not universally \(n\) under arbitrary polynomial degrees and truncation conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Boolean Lasserre hierarchy gives nested SOS lower bounds and reaches the exact optimum at a finite level, but the numerical level depends on degree and truncation conventions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the moment matrix, its truncation, the lifted feasible set, and the projected Lasserre level.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero and unit propagation for coordinates in K_t
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-consistency properties for vectors in the level-t lifted set K_t; the symbol x in the third assertion is retained from the source context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in K_t\). If \(I,J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(|I|,|J|\le t+1\), then \(y_I=0\Rightarrow y_{I\cup J}=0\) and \(y_I=1\Rightarrow y_{I\cup J}=y_J\). If \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(|I|\le 2t+2\), and \(x_i=1\) for every \(i\in I\), then \(y_I=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For y in K_t, a zero coordinate indexed by I forces the union coordinate indexed by I union J to be zero, while a unit coordinate indexed by I makes that union coordinate equal to the coordinate indexed by J, provided I and J each have size at most t+1. For I of size at most 2t+2, if every corresponding x_i equals one, then y_I equals one.

I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad |I|\le 2t+2,\quad x_i=1\ \forall i\in I\quad\text{for the third assertion}

children.title: Moment Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Moment-based representations used to organize semidefinite relaxation levels.

assumptions_latex: \(y\) is feasible for a truncated moment relaxation and satisfies every localizing condition required to place a representing measure in \(K\).
The relevant truncated moment data admit an appropriate flat extension of rank \(q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\text{ has a }q\text{-atomic representing probability measure supported in }K\), permitting atom extraction and an exactness test.

notation.meaning: flat moment matrix or its flat extension
flat rank and number of atoms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flat-extension certificate for finite atomic representation and optimizer recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the feasible truncated sequence has a positive-semidefinite flat extension whose stabilized rank is \(q\), and the required localizing constraints hold through the corresponding degrees, then it has a representing measure \[\mu=\sum_{k=1}^q w_k\delta_{x^{(k)}},\qquad w_k>0,\quad \sum_k w_k=1,\quad x^{(k)}\in K.\] The support points and weights can be recovered from the multiplication operators on the stabilized column space. If the recovered atoms attain the relaxation value, they certify finite-level exactness and supply global optimizers. Positive semidefiniteness without an applicable flat-extension condition does not by itself justify atomic extraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An appropriately flat feasible moment sequence has a finite atomic measure supported on the feasible set; the atoms can be extracted and certify exactness, whereas PSD feasibility alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Flat Moment Extraction

assumptions_latex: The level is high enough for every displayed moment or localizing matrix and Boolean consistency equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_r\le m_{r+1}\le f^*\), and \(m_r=f^*\) for every sufficiently large \(r\).

notation.meaning: localizing matrix for constraint polynomial g_j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal truncated-moment hierarchy for polynomial optimization on a finite Boolean feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d_j=\lceil\deg(g_j)/2\rceil\). At level \(r\), minimize \(L_y(f)\) subject to \[y_0=1,\qquad M_r(y)\succeq0,\qquad M_{r-d_j}(g_jy)\succeq0\quad(j=1,\ldots,m),\] and \(L_y((x_i^2-x_i)x^\alpha)=0\) whenever the product fits the truncation. If the optimum is \(m_r\) and the true minimum is \(f^*\), then nesting and evaluation at feasible points give \(m_r\le m_{r+1}\le f^*\). Since the feasible set lies in a finite Boolean cube, the hierarchy is exact at some finite level. The terminal numerical level depends on degrees and indexing conventions and need not equal \(n\) under an arbitrary unreduced truncation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Boolean moment hierarchy imposes PSD moment and localizing matrices plus Boolean consistency equations; its lower bounds are nested and become exact at a finite, convention-dependent level.
knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Moment Relaxations

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_r\le m_{r+1}\le f^*\), and the hierarchy is exact by level \(n\) after binary reduction.

children.title: Lasserre–Moment Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Equivalence between hierarchy levels and truncated moment representations.

assumptions_latex: The level-\(r\) moment and SOS programs use exactly matched degree truncations and the same Boolean ideal relations.
The resulting programs are a finite-dimensional primal-dual semidefinite pair with finite relevant optimal values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_r\le m_r\), with \(\rho_r=m_r\) under an applicable relative Slater condition.

notation.meaning: linear functional represented by the moment vector y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-level conic duality and regularity boundary for matched Boolean moment and SOS relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At matched truncation, the adjoints of \(M_r(y)\succeq0\) and the localizing constraints produce SOS Gram terms \(\sigma_0\) and \(\sigma_jg_j\), while multipliers of the Boolean moment equalities produce truncated elements of \(I_{01}\). Thus dual feasibility for \(\gamma\) is exactly a certificate \(f-\gamma\in Q_r(g)+I_{01,2r}\), and weak duality gives \(\rho_r\le m_r\). After affine equalities and forced matrix faces are accounted for, relative strict feasibility of the moment side implies equality and attainment of the SOS optimum; relative strict feasibility of the SOS side, with finite moment optimum, implies equality and attainment on the moment side. Without such regularity, equality or attainment is not automatic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At matched degree, the SOS relaxation is the conic dual of the moment relaxation; weak duality is unconditional, while relative Slater regularity yields equal attained bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Matched Moment–SOS Conic Duality

assumptions_latex: The level-\(r\) moment problem and SOS problem use the same degree truncation.
Both formulations include the binary ideal \(I_{01}=\langle x_i^2-x_i\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_r=\rho_r\) whenever the level-\(r\) semidefinite primal and dual satisfy strong duality.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conic duality between moment-matrix constraints and truncated sum-of-squares certificates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the finite-level SDP primal-dual correspondence under strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic dual of the level-\(r\) moment relaxation associates positive-semidefinite Gram matrices with the constraints \(M_r(y)\succeq0\) and \(M_{r-d_j}(g_jy)\succeq0\). Their adjoints produce sums of squares \(\sigma_0\) and \(\sigma_jg_j\); multipliers of the binary moment equalities produce elements of \(I_{01}\). Thus dual feasibility for value \(\gamma\) is exactly \(f-\gamma\in Q_r(g)+I_{01}\). Weak duality gives \(\rho_r\le m_r\); whenever the finite semidefinite pair satisfies strong duality, \[m_r=\rho_r.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each matched degree, the SOS relaxation is the conic dual of the moment relaxation; under strong SDP duality, their optimal bounds coincide.

children.title: Binary Ideal Reduction
children.top_down_role: Specialization of the hierarchy to polynomial identities induced by binary variables.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R[x]/I_{01}\cong\mathbb R^{\{0,1\}^n}\), with squarefree basis \(\{x^S:S\subseteq[n]\}\) and dimension \(2^n\).

notation.meaning: indicator polynomial of binary point a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-form, evaluation, and positivity structure of the full real Boolean quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Reduction by \(x_i^2=x_i\) gives each quotient class a unique multilinear representative \(\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}c_Sx^S\). Evaluation on \(\{0,1\}^n\) induces an algebra isomorphism \[\mathbb R[x]/I_{01}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{\{0,1\}^n}.\] Equivalently, the point polynomials \(\delta_a(x)=\prod_{i:a_i=1}x_i\prod_{i:a_i=0}(1-x_i)\) satisfy \(\delta_a^2=\delta_a\), \(\delta_a\delta_b=0\) for \(a\ne b\), and \(\sum_a\delta_a=1\) modulo \(I_{01}\). Consequently the quotient has dimension \(2^n\), and every polynomial \(h\) nonnegative on the cube satisfies \[h\equiv\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^n}h(a)\delta_a^2\pmod{I_{01}},\] an exact sum-of-squares representation modulo the Boolean ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The real Boolean quotient is the algebra of all functions on the binary cube: every class has a unique squarefree multilinear form, and every nonnegative cube function is a sum of squares modulo the Boolean ideal.
knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Quotient Evaluation

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Every class in }\mathbb R[x]/I_{01}\text{ has a unique squarefree multilinear representative.}\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard quotient-ring normal form for the Boolean ideal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the quotient-ring reduction underlying finite binary moment and SOS hierarchies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), write \(x^S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\). Reduction by \(x_i^2=x_i\) maps every monomial \(x^\alpha\) to \(x^{\{i:\alpha_i>0\}}\). Consequently, every polynomial \(p\in\mathbb R[x]\) has a unique representative \[\operatorname{ml}(p)=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}c_Sx^S\] modulo \(I_{01}\). Moreover, \(p(x)=\operatorname{ml}(p)(x)\) for all \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), and two multilinear polynomials agreeing on the binary cube have identical coefficients. Thus the quotient has dimension \(2^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Modulo the binary equations, every polynomial reduces uniquely to a squarefree multilinear polynomial, so only the 2^n binary monomials are needed.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Ideal Reduction

children.title: Closure-Rank Barriers
children.top_down_role: Limits arising from the number of closure rounds required for convexification.

assumptions_latex: The rank-one pure-integer CG operator is applied iteratively.
Rank is measured against the binary integer hull in the original n-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{P\subseteq[0,1]^n}\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CG}}(P)=\Omega(n^2)\).

notation.meaning: t-fold rank-one CG closure of the nth relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case round lower bound for rank-one CG closure on binary relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There are an absolute constant \(c>0\) and rational polytopes \(P_n\subseteq[0,1]^n\) such that \[\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{CG}}(P_n)\ge cn^2.\] Consequently, for every integer \(t<cn^2\), \[P_n^{(t)}\supsetneq\operatorname{conv}(P_n\cap\{0,1\}^n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Some n-dimensional binary relaxations require quadratically many rank-one Chvatal-Gomory rounds to reach their binary hulls.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Chvátal-Gomory Rank Lower Bound

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a closure operator with \(P_I\subseteq\mathcal C(P)\subseteq P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\mathcal C}(P_n)\ge g(n)\Rightarrow \mathcal C^t(P_n)\ne(P_n)_I\) for every integer \(t<g(n)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: definitional iteration lower bound for closure rank
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes rank barriers independently of any particular closure family or hard instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the closure rank by \[r_{\mathcal C}(P)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_+:\mathcal C^t(P)=P_I\},\] with value \(+\infty\) if equality never occurs. For a family \((P_n)\), a lower bound \(r_{\mathcal C}(P_n)\ge g(n)\) is a round-complexity barrier: every procedure restricted to applying one \(\mathcal C\)-closure per round leaves a point outside \((P_n)_I\) after any integer \(t<g(n)\). In particular, an unbounded rank family rules out any dimension-independent bound on the number of closure rounds needed for exact convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure rank counts rounds needed to reach the integer hull; a growing rank lower bound proves that every smaller number of rounds remains inexact.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Rank Barriers

children.title: Closure-Size Barriers
children.top_down_role: Limits arising from the representation size of closure descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Size Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Original-space inequality complexity of a binary-polytope closure family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_n\subseteq[0,1]^{d_n}\) be rational polyhedra and let \(C(P_n)\) denote a fixed closure. Define \(\operatorname{size}(Q)\) as the minimum number of linear inequalities in any description of \(Q\) in the original variable space. The family has a closure-size barrier at rate \(g(n)\) when \[\operatorname{size}(C(P_n))\ge g(n).\] In particular, if the input descriptions of \(P_n\) have polynomial encoding length while \(g(n)=2^{\Omega(n)}\), explicitly materializing every facet of the closure requires exponentially many inequalities; extended formulations are excluded from this measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closure-size barrier means that every original-space inequality description of the closure has at least the stated, possibly exponential, number of inequalities.
assumptions_latex: The closure operator \(C\) and original-space size measure are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{size}(C(P_n))\ge g(n)\).

notation.meaning: minimum number of original-space inequalities describing Q

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete exponential original-space barrier for the binary integer-hull closure of a compact relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_n\) be the standard McCormick relaxation, with \(O(n^2)\) inequalities, for variables \(x_i\in[0,1]\) and \(y_{ij}\) representing \(x_ix_j\). For the binary integer-hull closure \(C_I(P)=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap(\{0,1\}^n\times\mathbb R^{\binom n2}))\), \[C_I(P_n)=\operatorname{BQP}(n)=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y):x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ y_{ij}=x_ix_j\}.\] The Boolean-quadric polytope has \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) facets. Hence every exact inequality description of this closure in the original \((x,y)\)-space has exponentially many rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-row McCormick relaxation has a binary integer-hull closure requiring exponentially many original-space inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential Original-Space Barrier for the Boolean-Quadric Hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on interpreting an original-space closure-size lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lower bound on the minimum number of inequalities describing a closure controls row count, not the binary length of individual coefficients. Under any ordinary finite row encoding, an exponential lower bound on \(\operatorname{rows}(Q)\) implies exponential total explicit-description length. Conversely, a polynomial bound on \(\operatorname{rows}(Q)\) does not imply a polynomial bound on \(\operatorname{bits}(Q)\) unless coefficient bit lengths are also polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure row count and total coefficient encoding length are distinct size measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Row Count Does Not Measure Coefficient Encoding Size

children.title: Separation Barriers
children.top_down_role: Computational limits on identifying violated inequalities from a closure.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle complexity obstruction for separating over a closure family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational closures \(Q_n=C(P_n)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_n}\), the strong separation problem takes rational \(y\) and either certifies \(y\in Q_n\) or returns rational \((a,\beta)\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) for all \(x\in Q_n\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}y>\beta\). A separation barrier holds when this problem is NP-hard under polynomial-time reductions, measured in the joint encoding length of \(P_n\) and \(y\). Consequently, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no polynomial-time strong separation oracle exists for the closure family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separation barrier is NP-hardness of finding a valid inequality that separates a queried point from the closure, or certifying membership.
assumptions_latex: Inputs and separating inequalities use binary rational encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), strong separation over \(Q_n\) is not polynomial-time solvable.

children.title: Rank–Size Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between closure depth and representational growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank–Size Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bicriteria accounting for closure rounds and accumulated inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a closure operator \(C\) and a relaxation \(P\), and write \(C^0(P)=P\) and \(C^{r+1}(P)=C(C^r(P))\). For a target polyhedron \(Q\subseteq P\), define the rank–size profile \[s_P(r;Q)=\min\{m:Q=C^r(P)\cap H_1\cap\cdots\cap H_m,\ H_k\text{ is a valid halfspace for }Q\},\] with value \(+\infty\) if no such representation exists. The attainable pairs \((r,s_P(r;Q))\) expose the tradeoff between additional closure rounds and the number of separately retained valid inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rank–size profile records the fewest extra valid inequalities needed to obtain a target after a specified number of closure rounds.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) maps relaxations to tighter relaxations containing \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_P(r;Q)\) is the minimum supplementary inequality count after \(r\) closure rounds.

notation.meaning: a closed valid halfspace for Q

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed rank-size profile is mathematically coherent and the representation content kind fits the container, but it is a specific, nonstandard bicriteria definition with no citation. A source is required to validate the equality-based profile and the convention for counting supplementary versus closure-generated inequalities.

children.title: Description–Separation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Regimes where structural descriptions do not yield comparably efficient separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Description–Separation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes explicit facet count from separation-oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_n\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_n}\) be rational polytopes. An exponential-description/polynomial-separation gap occurs when every original-space inequality description of \(Q_n\) has \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) inequalities, yet strong separation over \(Q_n\) is solvable in time polynomial in \(n\) and the query encoding length. Thus a large facet description does not by itself imply hard separation: an oracle may identify a violated member of an exponentially large inequality family without enumerating that family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope may require exponentially many explicit inequalities while still admitting polynomial-time separation over the entire inequality family.
assumptions_latex: Description size is measured in the original space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exponential original-space description complexity is compatible with polynomial-time strong separation.

notation.meaning: polytope family indexed by input scale n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical original-space example separating facet count from separation complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The perfect-matching polytope of \(K_n\) is described in edge space by nonnegativity, degree equations \(x(\delta(v))=1\), and the odd-cut inequalities \(x(\delta(S))\ge1\) for odd \(S\subset V(K_n)\). Exponentially many odd-set inequalities are facet-defining as \(n\) grows, so every irredundant original-space facet description is exponential. Nevertheless, a violated odd-cut inequality can be found, or their satisfaction certified, by polynomial-time minimum odd-cut separation; the remaining displayed constraints are checked directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perfect-matching polytope has exponentially many original-space odd-set facets but polynomial-time separation through a minimum odd-cut algorithm.
knowledge_statements.title: Perfect-Matching Description–Separation Gap

assumptions_latex: \(Q=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\) is supplied as an explicit rational inequality system.
The total binary encoding length of \((A,b)\) and the query \(y\) is the input-size measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Strong separation over }Q\text{ is solvable in polynomial bit complexity.}\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating implicit exponential families from compact explicitly listed systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational query \(y\), evaluate the row residuals \(A_i y-b_i\). If every residual is nonpositive, then \(y\in Q\); otherwise any row with \(A_i y>b_i\) strongly separates \(y\) from \(Q\). Hence a polynomial-total-encoding-length explicit description supplies a polynomial-time strong-separation procedure. An exponential-description/polynomial-separation gap therefore concerns an implicitly handled inequality family rather than separation from a compact list already given in the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-size explicit rational inequality list is strongly separable by scanning its rows; the description–separation gap concerns exponentially large families handled implicitly.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-List Separation Boundary

children.title: Submodular Quadratics

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient test for submodularity of a quadratic pseudo-Boolean function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[f(x)=c+\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}b_{ij}x_ix_j,\qquad x\in\{0,1\}^n.\] Identifying \(x\) with its support, \(f\) is submodular precisely when \(f(u)+f(v)\ge f(u\wedge v)+f(u\vee v)\) for all \(u,v\in\{0,1\}^n\). For a quadratic function this condition is equivalent to \[b_{ij}\le0\qquad\text{for every }i<j.\] Constant and linear coefficients do not affect submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic pseudo-Boolean function is submodular exactly when every pairwise interaction coefficient is nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is submodular}\iff b_{ij}\le0\text{ for all }i<j\).

notation.meaning: quadratic interaction coefficient for variables i and j

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x,y\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\), then \[x\wedge y\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\qquad\text{and}\qquad x\vee y\in\operatorname*{argmin}f.\] Because the Boolean lattice is finite and the minimizer set is nonempty, repeated meet and join yield unique least and greatest minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimizers of a submodular quadratic form a lattice under componentwise minimum and maximum and have unique least and greatest elements.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a supplied representation satisfies \(f(x)=\kappa+\min_z\operatorname{cap}_G(\delta^+(S(x,z)))\) on a directed network with \(N\) vertices, \(M\) arcs, and nonnegative rational capacities. A minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut yields an optimizing assignment from the designated vertex sides, and \[\min_x f(x)=\kappa+\operatorname{mincut}_G(s,t).\] A maximum-flow algorithm computes this value in time polynomial in the encoded network size. A feasible flow and an \(s\)-\(t\) cut of equal value certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a valid nonnegative-capacity graph representation, one minimum-cut computation returns an optimal assignment, and an equal-valued flow and cut certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cut Optimization and Max-Flow Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Under Nonnegative Sums and Unary Terms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure properties under one fixed nonnegative-capacity cut convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) have ordinary nonnegative-capacity cut representations using the same designated-variable side convention and disjoint auxiliary vertices. For \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\ge0\), \(\alpha_1f_1+\alpha_2f_2\) is graph-representable by taking the union of the networks and scaling capacities. Adding a constant or unary term preserves representability through the additive constant and terminal-incident capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a fixed encoding convention, graph-representable functions are closed under nonnegative sums, constants, and unary terms.
assumptions_latex: f_1,f_2\text{ have valid nonnegative-capacity cut representations under one assignment convention}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha_1f_1+\alpha_2f_2+\text{constant and unary terms is graph-representable}
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Under Nonnegative Sums and Unary Terms
Graph-Representable Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation of binary quadratic minimization by an s–t cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic pseudo-Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is graph-representable if there exist a directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), terminals \(s,t\), nonnegative capacities \(c_a\), auxiliary binary variables \(z\), and a constant \(\kappa\) such that, for every \(x\), \[f(x)=\kappa+\min_z\operatorname{cap}_G(\delta^+(S(x,z))),\] where \(s\in S(x,z)\), \(t\notin S(x,z)\), and designated vertex sides encode \((x,z)\). Hence minimizing \(f\\) reduces exactly to a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic is graph-representable when its value equals a constant plus the minimum cut capacity under vertices encoding its binary variables.
assumptions_latex: Designated cut sides encode each assignment consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\min_x f(x)=\kappa+\min\{\operatorname{cap}_G(\delta^+(S)):s\in S,
t\notin S\}\).

notation.meaning: arcs leaving the source side S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition targets the correct graph-representability notion, but no source is supplied for the exact auxiliary-variable convention. In addition, the token \(f\\\) in the final sentence is malformed and must be repaired once the sourced convention is established.

children.title: Submodularity–Representability Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between submodular interaction structure and graph representability.

knowledge_statements.title: Submodularity–Representability Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic pseudo-Boolean, nonnegative-capacity cut representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be quadratic. Then \(f\) admits an exact representation by an \(s\)-\(t\) cut network with nonnegative capacities, allowing auxiliary vertices minimized out, if and only if \(f\) is submodular. Equivalently, in the expansion \(f(x)=c+\sum_i a_i x_i+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}x_ix_j\), graph representability holds exactly when \(b_{ij}\le0\) for every pair. Under these conditions, a minimum cut yields a global minimizer of \(f\) in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For quadratic pseudo-Boolean functions, exact nonnegative-capacity cut representability is equivalent to all pairwise coefficients being nonpositive.
assumptions_latex: Graph representations use nonnegative capacities and may minimize auxiliary vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is graph-representable}\iff f\text{ is submodular}\iff b_{ij}\le0\text{ for all }i<j\).

notation.meaning: pairwise coefficient in the multilinear expansion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the correspondence leaf, and the stated quadratic coefficient criterion is standard. However, the exact equivalence with the chosen nonnegative-capacity network model, especially with auxiliary vertices minimized out, has no cited source and therefore cannot yet be accepted.

children.title: Graph-Representability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Quadratic interaction patterns that obstruct exact graph representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable obstruction to an ordinary nonnegative-capacity cut representation, including minimized auxiliary vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct \(i,j\), fix the other coordinates to \(u\) and define \[\Delta_{ij}f(u)=f(1,1,u)-f(1,0,u)-f(0,1,u)+f(0,0,u).\] If \(\Delta_{ij}f(u)>0\), then \(f\) is not submodular and cannot be obtained by minimizing a nonnegative-capacity cut function over auxiliary binary vertices. For a quadratic multilinear function, \(\Delta_{ij}f(u)=b_{ij}\), independently of \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One positive binary mixed difference certifies failure of ordinary cut representability; for a quadratic it is exactly a positive pair coefficient.
assumptions_latex: \text{ordinary cut representations use nonnegative capacities and minimize auxiliary binary vertices}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta_{ij}f(u)>0\Rightarrow f\text{ has no ordinary cut representation with minimized auxiliaries}

notation.meaning: coefficient of x_i x_j in a quadratic multilinear representation

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Mixed-Difference Obstruction Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smallest quadratic excluded from the ordinary nonnegative-capacity cut model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1x_2\), \[f(1,1)-f(1,0)-f(0,1)+f(0,0)=1>0.\] Hence \(f\) has no exact ordinary nonnegative-capacity cut representation, even with minimized auxiliary binary vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two-variable positive product is the minimal ordinary-cut obstruction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_1x_2\text{ is not representable by the ordinary nonnegative-capacity cut model}
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Positive-Product Obstruction

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut Submodularity and Preservation Under Partial Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural reason the ordinary cut obstruction persists when auxiliary binary vertices are minimized out.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonnegative-capacity directed cut function is submodular in its vertex-side indicators. If \(g:\{0,1\}^{n+r}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular and \(f(x)=\min_{z\in\{0,1\}^r}g(x,z)\), then \(f\) is submodular. Consequently, minimized auxiliary vertices cannot make an ordinary nonnegative-capacity cut model represent a non-submodular function of the designated variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut functions are submodular, and partial minimization preserves submodularity; auxiliaries therefore cannot evade the ordinary cut obstruction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is submodular}
knowledge_statements.title: Cut Submodularity and Preservation Under Partial Minimization
Graph-Representability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of nonnegative-capacity cut representation beyond submodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=c+\sum_i a_i x_i+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}x_ix_j\). If some \(b_{ij}>0\), then \(f\) is not submodular and has no exact representation as a nonnegative-capacity \(s\)-\(t\) cut function. Allowing auxiliary variables does not remove this obstruction when they are minimized out: partial minimization of a submodular function remains submodular. Thus an exact cut reduction requires either a variable complementation making every transformed pair coefficient nonpositive or a representation outside the ordinary nonnegative-capacity cut model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive pair coefficient blocks exact ordinary cut representation unless variable complementation removes all such coefficients or the representation model is enlarged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_{ij}>0\text{ for some }i<j\Rightarrow f\text{ is not exactly graph-representable in the ordinary cut model}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary role fits the terminal container, but the obstruction depends on the exact definition of graph representability. No source is supplied for either that convention or the claim that minimizing out auxiliary variables preserves submodularity.

children.title: Non-Submodular Quadratics
children.top_down_role: Binary quadratic objectives containing interactions outside the submodular class.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Submodular Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient characterization in a fixed binary labeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[f(x)=c+\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}b_{ij}x_ix_j,\] the function is non-submodular in the current binary labeling if and only if at least one pair satisfies \(b_{ij}>0\). Indeed, on the two-dimensional face where all other coordinates are fixed, its discrete mixed difference is \[f_{00}+f_{11}-f_{01}-f_{10}=b_{ij},\] whereas submodularity requires this difference to be nonpositive for every pair and every fixing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic pseudo-Boolean function is non-submodular in its current labeling exactly when at least one interaction coefficient is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is non-submodular}\iff \exists i<j:\ b_{ij}>0\).

notation.meaning: value on a pairwise face with the selected coordinates fixed to p and q

children.title: Signed-Interaction Quadratics
children.top_down_role: Quadratic classes organized by positive and negative interaction patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Interaction Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed interaction graph of a quadratic pseudo-Boolean function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f(x)=c+\sum_i a_i x_i+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}x_ix_j\), its signed interaction graph is \(G_f=(V,E,\sigma)\), where \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(E=\{\{i,j\}:b_{ij}\ne0\}\), and \(\sigma_{ij}=\operatorname{sign}(b_{ij})\). Negative edges are submodular interactions and positive edges are supermodular interactions in the current labeling. The magnitudes \(|b_{ij}|\) determine interaction strengths, while the signed cycle structure determines whether complementing variables can make all interactions submodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signed interaction graph records each nonzero quadratic coefficient as an edge labeled by its sign and weighted by its magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_f=(V,E,\sigma)\text{ records exactly the nonzero pairwise interactions of }f\).

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming
source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 The sparsity graph p. 12

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

A source covering signed interaction graphs and switching is required.

children.title: Interaction-Sign Switching
children.top_down_role: Complementation-based changes to the sign pattern of quadratic interactions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive componentwise test for an all-negative switching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In each connected component, choose a root sign and traverse the graph, assigning across each edge \(ij\) the forced value \[s_j=-\operatorname{sign}(b_{ij})s_i.\] Consistent assignments produce a complementation making every transformed coefficient negative. A conflict returns a cycle certificate of impossibility. The traversal takes \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-time graph traversal either constructs an all-negative switching or returns a conflicting cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All-negative switchability is decidable and a switch constructible in \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Time Switching Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantities preserved by complementation-based interaction switching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(b'_{ij}=s_i s_jb_{ij}\), switching preserves the interaction support and coefficient magnitudes. For every cycle \(C\), \[\prod_{ij\in C}\operatorname{sign}(b'_{ij})=\prod_{ij\in C}\operatorname{sign}(b_{ij}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable complementation preserves the interaction graph, coefficient magnitudes, and every cycle sign product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|b'_{ij}|=|b_{ij}|\), support is unchanged, and every cycle sign product is invariant.
knowledge_statements.title: Switching Invariants
Interaction-Sign Switching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of complementing selected binary variables on interaction signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(t_i\in\{0,1\}\) and substitute \(x_i=y_i\) when \(t_i=0\), while \(x_i=1-y_i\) when \(t_i=1\). Writing \(s_i=(-1)^{t_i}\), the transformed coefficient of \(y_i y_j\) is \[b'_{ij}=s_i s_j b_{ij}.\] Thus complementing exactly one endpoint reverses an interaction sign, while complementing neither or both preserves it. Constant and linear terms change under the substitution but do not affect the transformed pair-sign condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing exactly one endpoint of a quadratic interaction flips its sign; complementing both endpoints or neither preserves it.
assumptions_latex: Each variable is either preserved or complemented.

notation.meaning: indicator that variable i is complemented
switching sign associated with variable i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The switching identity is algebraically precise, all variables are introduced, and the property role fits the container. Nevertheless, the record has no citation, so the identity and its adopted switching convention require a source before acceptance.

children.title: Frustrated Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Signed structures that cannot be transformed globally into a submodular form.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity of minimizing residual frustration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every interaction coefficient is positive and every edge has unit weight, then \[\phi(G)=|E|-\operatorname{MaxCut}(G).\] Consequently, computing the minimum frustration index is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For all-positive interactions, minimizing residual positive edges is the complement of MAX-CUT and is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi(G)=|E|-\operatorname{MaxCut}(G)\), so computing \(\phi\) is NP-hard.

notation.meaning: maximum number of edges crossing a graph cut

knowledge_statements.title: Frustration-Index Hardness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative distance from a signed interaction pattern to global submodular switchability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive edge weights \(w_{ij}\), define \[\phi_w(G_f)=\min_{s\in\{-1,1\}^V}\sum_{ij:\,s_i s_j b_{ij}>0}w_{ij}.\] This equals the minimum total weight of edges whose deletion makes the remaining signed graph switchable to all-negative interactions. Taking \(w_{ij}=1\) gives the unweighted frustration index \(\phi(G_f)\), and \(\phi_w(G_f)=0\) exactly in the unfrustrated regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted frustration index is the minimum weight of positive interactions remaining after switching, equivalently the minimum deletion weight needed for all-negative switchability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_w(G_f)=\min_s\sum_{ij:s_i s_jb_{ij}>0}w_{ij}\), equivalently the minimum deletion weight producing all-negative switchability.
knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Frustration Index
Frustrated Interaction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle obstruction to switching all quadratic interactions to submodular signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_f\) be the signed interaction graph of a quadratic function with nonzero edge coefficients. A switching that makes every transformed coefficient negative exists if and only if every cycle of \(G_f\) contains an even number of positive edges. Indeed, the required vertex signs satisfy \(s_i s_j=-\operatorname{sign}(b_{ij})\) on every edge, and these equations are consistent exactly under that cycle-parity condition. A cycle with an odd number of positive edges is frustrated and forces at least one positive transformed interaction under every complementation pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All interactions can be switched negative exactly when every interaction cycle has an even number of positive edges; an odd-positive cycle is frustrated.
assumptions_latex: Every edge of \(G_f\) corresponds to a nonzero coefficient.
Switching is restricted to complementing original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists s\in\{-1,1\}^V\ \forall\{i,j\}\in E:\ s_i s_j\operatorname{sign}(b_{ij})=-1\iff\text{every cycle has an even number of positive edges}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cycle-parity criterion is internally consistent and the failure_boundary role matches the Frustrated Interaction Regimes leaf. No source is supplied for the signed-cycle switching theorem or for the use of the term frustrated under this sign convention.

children.title: Symmetric Quadratic Classes
children.top_down_role: Binary quadratic objectives invariant under specified variable permutations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=c+a\sum_{i=1}^n x_i+b\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}x_ix_j\) for some \(a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}\).

notation.meaning: Permutation of the coordinates induced by a permutation of the index set
Hamming weight of a binary vector

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation-invariant quadratic pseudo-Boolean functions on the complete variable set.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic pseudo-Boolean function \(f\) is symmetric if \(f(\pi x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and every permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). This holds exactly when all linear coefficients are equal and all pairwise coefficients are equal; equivalently, there exist \(a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[f(x)=c+a|x|+b\binom{|x|}{2}=c+a\sum_{i=1}^n x_i+b\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}x_ix_j.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic binary function is symmetric exactly when every linear coefficient is identical and every pairwise coefficient is identical, so its value is a quadratic function of Hamming weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Quadratic Classes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

children.title: Cardinality-Based Quadratic Classes
children.top_down_role: Quadratic objectives whose structure is governed by selected-set cardinality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=h(|x|)\) exactly when \(h(k)=c+ak+b\binom{k}{2}\) on \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\).

notation.meaning: Hamming weight of the binary vector

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic pseudo-Boolean functions whose values depend only on selected-set cardinality.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic pseudo-Boolean function \(f\) is cardinality-based if there is a function \(h:\{0,\ldots,n\}\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(f(x)=h(|x|)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Such an \(f\) has degree at most two exactly when constants \(a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}\) exist with \[h(k)=c+ak+b\binom{k}{2}\qquad(k=0,\ldots,n).\] Equivalently, the second forward difference \(h(k+2)-2h(k+1)+h(k)\) is constant wherever defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cardinality-based quadratic function has a univariate Hamming-weight profile with constant second finite difference, equivalently a quadratic expression in the weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Based Quadratic Classes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}f(x)=\{x:|x|\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}}h(k)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact unconstrained optimization of a cardinality-based quadratic through its integer weight profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(k)=c+ak+b\binom{k}{2}\). Then \[\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}f(x)=\min_{k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}}h(k),\] and every vector having an optimal weight is optimal. If \(b<0\), an optimal weight is in \(\{0,n\}\). If \(b=0\), the sign of \(a\) selects an endpoint, and every weight is optimal when \(a=0\). If \(b>0\), the optimal weights are the clipped nearest integers to \(\tfrac12-\tfrac{a}{b}\). Thus at most two candidate weights need evaluation once \(a,b,c\) are known.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimization reduces to integer Hamming weight: concave or affine profiles use endpoints, while a convex profile uses clipped nearest integers to its vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Optimization by Hamming Weight

children.title: Bounded-Interaction Quadratic Classes
children.top_down_role: Quadratic objectives with restricted interaction degree, range, or graph structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has bounded interaction \(\Delta\) exactly when \(\max_i|\{j\ne i:a_{\min\{i,j\},\max\{i,j\}}\ne0\}|\le\Delta\).

notation.meaning: Interaction graph with one vertex per variable and edges for nonzero quadratic coefficients
Maximum vertex degree of a graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparsity class defined by uniformly bounded degree of the quadratic interaction graph.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a quadratic pseudo-Boolean function \(f(x)=c+\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}a_{ij}x_ix_j\), its interaction graph is \(G_f=(\{1,\ldots,n\},E_f)\), where \(\{i,j\}\in E_f\) exactly when \(a_{ij}\ne0\). The bounded-interaction class with bound \(\Delta\) consists of all such functions satisfying \[\Delta(G_f)=\max_{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}}|\{j:\{i,j\}\in E_f\}|\le\Delta.\] The linear coefficients and constant term are unrestricted by this interaction bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic binary function has interaction bound Δ when each variable participates in at most Δ nonzero quadratic terms; linear and constant coefficients remain unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Interaction Quadratic Classes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is an unconstrained quadratic pseudo-Boolean objective with rationally encoded coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta(G_f)\le 2\) permits \(O(n)\) arithmetic-operation optimization, whereas minimization remains NP-hard on the class \(\Delta(G_f)\le 3\).

notation.meaning: maximum degree of the interaction graph

review_flags: exact cubic_MAX-CUT hardness locator not supplied
arithmetic-operation bound does not by itself state bit complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp maximum-degree threshold for unconstrained quadratic binary minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Delta(G_f)\le 2\), every connected component of \(G_f\) is an isolated vertex, a path, or a cycle. Dynamic programming with the state of one boundary vertex optimizes each component, giving \(O(n)\) arithmetic operations overall. In contrast, minimization is NP-hard already for \(\Delta(G_f)\le 3\): on a cubic graph, MAX-CUT is equivalent to minimizing \[-\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}|x_i-x_j|=-\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}(x_i+x_j-2x_ix_j).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interaction degree at most two permits linear-size path-and-cycle dynamic programming, while degree three already contains NP-hard cubic MAX-CUT instances.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Degree Complexity Threshold

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|E_f|\le\left\lfloor n\Delta/2\right\rfloor\).

notation.meaning: interaction graph of the quadratic terms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial sparsity implied by a maximum interaction-degree bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The degree sum satisfies \[2|E_f|=\sum_{v\in V(G_f)}\deg(v)\le n\Delta,\] so \(|E_f|\le\lfloor n\Delta/2\rfloor\). A fixed maximum degree alone does not bound component size, diameter, or treewidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum interaction degree Δ permits at most floor(nΔ/2) nonzero pair terms, but does not by itself bound component size, diameter, or treewidth.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Count Consequence of Bounded Interaction

children.title: Structural-Class Intersections
children.top_down_role: Overlap among symmetry, cardinality dependence, and bounded interaction.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a symmetric quadratic pseudo-Boolean function
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=c+a\sum_i x_i\), so its common pairwise coefficient is zero.

notation.meaning: Interaction graph of the quadratic terms of the function
Maximum degree of the interaction graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection of permutation symmetry, cardinality dependence, and bounded interaction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Symmetric and cardinality-based quadratic classes coincide: each member has the form \(f(x)=c+a|x|+b\binom{|x|}{2}\). Its interaction graph is empty when \(b=0\) and is the complete graph \(K_n\) when \(b\ne0\). Consequently, for \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le\Delta<n-1\), the intersection of the symmetric class with the interaction-bound-\(\Delta\) class is exactly \[\left\{x\mapsto c+a\sum_{i=1}^n x_i:a,c\in\mathbb{R}\right\}.\] For \(\Delta\ge n-1\), the interaction bound imposes no further restriction on the symmetric class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric and cardinality-based quadratic classes coincide. Under an interaction bound below n−1, their intersection contains only affine cardinality functions because any nonzero common pair coefficient creates a complete graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Structural-Class Intersections

children.title: Boolean-Quadric Polytope Geometry
children.top_down_role: Faces, vertices, and representations of the Boolean-quadric polytope.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{BQP}(n)=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y):x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ y_{ij}=x_ix_j\}\).

notation.meaning: Boolean-quadric polytope on n binary variables
Lifted coordinate representing the product of variables i and j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete-graph Boolean-quadric polytope with one lifted coordinate per unordered pair.

source_refs.locator: 2.12 The Quadratic Assignment Problem and Fortet's Linearization p. 72

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Boolean-quadric polytope on \(n\) variables is \[\operatorname{BQP}(n)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{(x,y)\in\{0,1\}^{n+\binom n2}:y_{ij}=x_ix_j\text{ for all }1\le i<j\le n\right\}.\] Its vertices are precisely the lifted binary points \((x,(x_ix_j)_{i<j})\). Hence minimizing any quadratic pseudo-Boolean objective \(c+\sum_i a_i x_i+\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}x_ix_j\) is equivalent to minimizing the linear function \(c+\sum_i a_i x_i+\sum_{i<j}a_{ij}y_{ij}\) over \(\operatorname{BQP}(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Boolean-quadric polytope is the convex hull of binary vectors lifted with all pairwise products, converting every unconstrained binary quadratic objective into a linear objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Boolean-Quadric Polytope Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 2.12 The Quadratic Assignment Problem and Fortet's Linearization p. 72

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_{\mathrm{pair}}(n)\supsetneq\operatorname{BQP}(n)

notation.meaning: intersection of all elementary pairwise product envelopes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dimension boundary for insufficiency of independent product envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_{\mathrm{pair}}(n)\) be the intersection of all elementary product inequalities. It equals \(\operatorname{BQP}(n)\) for \(n\le2\), but is strictly larger for every \(n\ge3\). For example, setting \(x_1=x_2=x_3=\tfrac12\), \(y_{12}=y_{13}=y_{23}=0\), and all remaining coordinates to zero satisfies every pairwise envelope but violates the valid inequality \(x_1+x_2+x_3-y_{12}-y_{13}-y_{23}\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent product envelopes describe the Boolean-quadric polytope only through two variables; from three variables onward an explicit half-integral point shows strictness.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The correlation polytope is the convex hull \[\operatorname{COR}(n)=\operatorname{conv}\{xx^{\mathsf T}:x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\] in the space of real symmetric \(n\times n\) matrices. Every generating matrix satisfies \(X_{ii}=x_i\) and \(X_{ij}=x_ix_j\) for \(i<j\). Consequently, deleting the redundant lower-triangular coordinates and identifying \(x_i=X_{ii}\) and \(y_{ij}=X_{ij}\) gives a linear bijection between \(\operatorname{COR}(n)\) and \(\operatorname{BQP}(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The correlation polytope is the convex hull of binary rank-one matrices. Its diagonal and upper-triangular entries are exactly the Boolean-quadric variables and products.

Incidence vector of the cut determined by S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete-graph cut polytope used in the Boolean-quadric correspondence.

source_refs.locator: Matrix relaxations in combinatorial optimization p. 483

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the complete graph \(K_m\) with vertex set \(V=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\), define \(\delta(S)_{ij}=1\) when exactly one of \(i,j\) belongs to \(S\), and \(\delta(S)_{ij}=0\) otherwise. The cut polytope is \[\operatorname{CUT}(m)=\operatorname{conv}\{\delta(S)\in\{0,1\}^{\binom m2}:S\subseteq V\}.\] Since \(\delta(S)=\delta(V\setminus S)\), fixing vertex \(0\) on one side selects a unique representative of every cut and yields \(2^{m-1}\) distinct cut vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cut polytope is the convex hull of complete-graph cut-incidence vectors. Complementary shores define the same vector, giving 2^(m−1) distinct cuts.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vert}(\operatorname{CUT}(m))=\{\delta(S):S\subseteq V\}\) and \(|\operatorname{vert}(\operatorname{CUT}(m))|=2^{m-1}\).

children.title: Affine Polytope Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Affine transformations linking Boolean-quadric, correlation, and cut-polytope representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{BQP}(n)\) and \(\operatorname{CUT}(n+1)\) are affinely isomorphic under the displayed map.

notation.meaning: Cut coordinates on vertices 0 through n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit complete-graph affine equivalence among Boolean-quadric, correlation, and cut coordinates.

source_refs.locator: Matrix relaxations in combinatorial optimization p. 483

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define an affine map from Boolean-quadric coordinates to edge coordinates of \(K_{n+1}\) by \[z_{0i}=x_i,\qquad z_{ij}=x_i+x_j-2y_{ij}\quad(1\le i<j\le n).\] It maps every lifted binary point to the cut separating \(\{i:x_i=1\}\) from the distinguished vertex \(0\), and therefore maps \(\operatorname{BQP}(n)\) onto \(\operatorname{CUT}(n+1)\). Its inverse is \[x_i=z_{0i},\qquad y_{ij}=\frac{z_{0i}+z_{0j}-z_{ij}}{2}.\] Together with \(X_{ii}=x_i\) and \(X_{ij}=y_{ij}\), this also identifies \(\operatorname{COR}(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit affine formulas identify Boolean-quadric, correlation, and one-higher-dimensional complete-graph cut polytopes while preserving their lifted binary vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Polytope Correspondences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\operatorname{BQP}(n)\to\operatorname{CUT}(n+1)\) be the affine bijection from the immutable seed. For every face \(F\) of \(\operatorname{BQP}(n)\), \(T(F)\) is a face of \(\operatorname{CUT}(n+1)\), and this map is an inclusion-preserving bijection of face lattices that preserves dimension. Consequently vertices, edges, and facets correspond, and inverse affine substitution preserves validity, tightness, and facet status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine Boolean-quadric–cut correspondence preserves the entire face lattice and transports valid inequalities and facets in both directions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines linear isomorphism for polytopes and records the source's assertion that the relation is symmetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polytopes \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) are linearly isomorphic if there is a linear map \(f:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^q\) such that \(f(P)=Q\) and, for every \(y\in Q\), there is a unique \(x\in P\) satisfying \(f(x)=y\). This relation is symmetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polytopes P and Q are linearly isomorphic when a linear map sends P onto Q and has exactly one preimage in P for every point of Q. The source also states that this relation is symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\cong_{\mathrm{lin}}Q\iff \exists f\text{ linear}: f(P)=Q\text{ and }(\forall y\in Q)(\exists!x\in P)\,f(x)=y;\qquad P\cong_{\mathrm{lin}}Q\iff Q\cong_{\mathrm{lin}}P.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le y_{ij}\le x_i,\ y_{ij}\le x_j,\ y_{ij}\ge x_i+x_j-1\) gives the convex hull for each isolated product.

notation.meaning: Auxiliary variable for the binary product of variables i and j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fortet-McCormick linearization for all pairwise products of binary variables.

source_refs.locator: 2.12 The Quadratic Assignment Problem and Fortet's Linearization p. 72

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each pair \(1\le i<j\le n\), replace the product \(x_ix_j\) by \(y_{ij}\) and impose \[0\le y_{ij},\qquad y_{ij}\le x_i,\qquad y_{ij}\le x_j,\qquad y_{ij}\ge x_i+x_j-1,\] together with \(0\le x_i\le1\). If \(x_i,x_j\in\{0,1\}\), these inequalities force \(y_{ij}=x_ix_j\). For one isolated pair, they describe exactly the convex hull of \(\{(x_i,x_j,y_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^3:y_{ij}=x_ix_j\}\); imposing them independently for all pairs defines the standard relaxation \(L_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fortet-McCormick inequalities exactly linearize each isolated binary product. Applying them independently to every pair yields the standard Boolean-quadric relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Standard Product Linearization

With four envelope inequalities per pair, it has \(4\binom n2\) product inequalities, in addition to \(n\) unit-bound intervals for \(x\), or \(2n\) written bound inequalities. Its lifted size is \(\Theta(n^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete pairwise product linearization uses one auxiliary and four envelope inequalities per pair and has quadratic lifted size.
assumptions_latex: One auxiliary variable is introduced for every unordered pair
The convention includes \(y_{ij}\ge0\) as one of four pairwise inequalities

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The triangle relaxation \(T_{n+1}\) of \(\operatorname{CUT}(n+1)\) consists of the edge vectors \(z\in\mathbb{R}^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\) satisfying \(0\le z_{ij}\le1\) and, for every unordered triple of distinct vertices \(\{i,j,k\}\), \[z_{ij}\le z_{ik}+z_{jk},\qquad z_{ik}\le z_{ij}+z_{jk},\qquad z_{jk}\le z_{ij}+z_{ik},\qquad z_{ij}+z_{ik}+z_{jk}\le2.\] Every cut vector satisfies these inequalities. Substitution of \(z_{0i}=x_i\) and \(z_{ij}=x_i+x_j-2y_{ij}\) transfers \(T_{n+1}\) to a linear relaxation in Boolean-quadric coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The triangle relaxation is defined by edge bounds together with all three metric inequalities and the perimeter inequality on every triple of complete-graph vertices; affine substitution transfers it to Boolean-quadric coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct membership and separation for the explicit triangle system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Check all edge bounds and, for every one of the \(\binom m3\) vertex triples, its three metric inequalities and perimeter inequality. A violation separates the input from \(T_m\); if none exists, the input belongs to \(T_m\). This takes \(O(m^3)\) arithmetic operations. Under the seed convention the system has \(4\binom m3+2\binom m2\) written inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scanning all triples gives an exact cubic-time membership and separation procedure for the triangle relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The input explicitly stores all \(\binom m2\) edge coordinates
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership in \(T_m\) is decidable in \(O(m^3)\) arithmetic operations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict strengthening caused by triangle inequalities coupling three independently linearized products.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge3\), the triangle relaxation transferred to Boolean-quadric coordinates satisfies \(T_{n+1}\subsetneq L_n\). A point in \(L_n\setminus T_{n+1}\) is given by \[x_1=x_2=x_3=\frac12,\qquad y_{12}=y_{13}=\frac12,\qquad y_{23}=0,\] and, when \(n>3\), by \[x_k=0\quad(4\le k\le n),\qquad y_{ik}=0\quad(1\le i<k\le n,\ k\ge4).\] All independent Fortet-McCormick inequalities hold at this point. Under the affine cut map, \(z_{12}=z_{13}=0\) and \(z_{23}=1\), so the triangle inequality \(z_{23}\le z_{12}+z_{13}\) is violated.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ satisfies all cycle inequalities}\iff d(v^+,v^-)\ge1\text{ for every }v\in V

notation.meaning: two parity copies of vertex v in the doubled graph
shortest-path distance in the doubled graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact polynomial separation of all cycle inequalities by parity shortest paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\bar x\in[0,1]^E\), form a doubled graph with vertices \(v^+,v^-\). For every edge \(uv\), add same-parity links of length \(\bar x_{uv}\) and opposite-parity links of length \(1-\bar x_{uv}\). A cycle inequality is violated exactly when some shortest path from \(v^+\) to \(v^-\) has length less than one; the path recovers an odd-parity closed walk and hence a violated simple-cycle inequality. Running nonnegative shortest paths from each vertex copy gives exact polynomial-time separation, for example in \(O(|V|(|E|+|V|\log |V|))\) time with binary heaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All cycle inequalities can be separated exactly in polynomial time by shortest paths in a doubled parity graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Cycle-Inequality Separation

assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
C\subseteq E\text{ is a simple cycle}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{e\in F}x_e-\sum_{e\in C\setminus F}x_e\le |F|-1\text{ is valid, and it defines a facet iff }C\text{ is chordless}

notation.meaning: convex hull of cut-incidence vectors of G
incidence vector of the cut determined by S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-subset cycle inequalities and their exact chordless-cycle facet boundary in graph cut coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every simple cycle \(C\) of \(G\) and every odd-cardinality \(F\subseteq C\), \[\sum_{e\in F}x_e-\sum_{e\in C\setminus F}x_e\le |F|-1\] is valid for \(\operatorname{CUT}(G)\). Equivalently, \(\sum_{e\in F}(1-x_e)+\sum_{e\in C\setminus F}x_e\ge1\). The odd choices of \(F\) are related by cut switching. The inequality defines a facet of \(\operatorname{CUT}(G)\) exactly when \(C\) is chordless; when \(C\) has a chord, it is implied by cycle inequalities on smaller cycles and is not facet-defining.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every odd edge subset of a cycle gives a valid cut inequality, and the inequality is facet-defining exactly for a chordless cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Inequality Validity and Facet Boundary
Cycle Facet Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle inequalities for graph cut polytopes and their affine binary-quadratic images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(\operatorname{CUT}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\delta(S):S\subseteq V\}\), where \(\delta(S)_e=1\) exactly when edge \(e\) crosses the cut. For every simple cycle \(C\subseteq E\) and every odd-cardinality set \(F\subseteq C\), the cycle inequality is \[\sum_{e\in F}x_e-\sum_{e\in C\setminus F}x_e\le |F|-1.\] It is valid for \(\operatorname{CUT}(G)\). When \(C\) is chordless, the inequality is facet-defining under the standard nondegeneracy convention for the graph cut polytope. Affine cut–Boolean-quadric correspondences transport this family to facets of the corresponding binary quadratic polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every odd edge subset of a cycle yields a valid cycle inequality; chordless cycles generate the standard cycle facets and their binary-quadratic images.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a simple cycle and \(|F|\) is odd.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{e\in F}x_e-\sum_{e\in C\setminus F}x_e\le |F|-1\) is valid, and is facet-defining for chordless \(C\) under the stated convention.

children.title: Hypermetric Facet Families
children.top_down_role: Facet classes arising from hypermetric structures.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{1\le i<j\le n}b_i b_jx_{ij}\le0\quad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{CUT}_n

notation.meaning: cut polytope of the complete graph on n vertices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical sum-one convention for hypermetric inequalities in complete-graph cut coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(b\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(\sum_i b_i=1\), the hypermetric inequality is \[\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}b_i b_jx_{ij}\le0.\] It is valid for \(\operatorname{CUT}_n\). Permuting the entries of \(b\) and the corresponding vertices gives an equivalent family member. Validity alone does not imply facetness: if \(b\) has one entry equal to one and all other entries zero, the resulting inequality is \(0\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every integral coefficient vector summing to one defines a valid hypermetric inequality, although some choices give redundant or trivial nonfacets.
knowledge_statements.title: Hypermetric Validity

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b=(1,1,-1,0,\ldots,0)\text{ and }b=(1,1,1,-1,-1,0,\ldots,0)\text{ yield facets of }\operatorname{CUT}_n
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two canonical facet-defining subclasses within the hypermetric family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Up to permutation, the vector \(b=(1,1,-1,0,\ldots,0)\) gives a triangle facet of \(\operatorname{CUT}_n\) for \(n\ge3\). The vector \(b=(1,1,1,-1,-1,0,\ldots,0)\) gives the classical pentagonal facet for \(n\ge5\). Zero-padding these coefficient vectors gives their standard lifted members on larger complete graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Triangle and pentagonal inequalities are the canonical small-support facet-defining members of the hypermetric family.
knowledge_statements.title: Triangle and Pentagonal Hypermetric Facets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit optimization formulation for separation over the full sum-one hypermetric family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R^{\binom n2}\), exact separation asks whether \[\sup\left\{\sum_{i<j}b_i b_jx_{ij}:b\in\mathbb Z^n,\ \sum_i b_i=1\right\}>0.\] Any feasible \(b\) with positive value supplies a violated hypermetric inequality; if the supremum is nonpositive, \(x\) satisfies every inequality in this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full hypermetric separation searches integral sum-one coefficient vectors for a positive hypermetric violation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists b\in\mathbb Z^n:\ \sum_i b_i=1,\ \sum_{i<j}b_i b_jx_{ij}>0\iff x\text{ violates a sum-one hypermetric inequality}
review_flags: supremum_used_because_the_integer_quadratic search need not attain a finite maximum for arbitrary x
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Hypermetric Separation Problem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality characterization and affine-rank certificate for a specified hypermetric inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\in\mathbb Z^n\) satisfy \(\sum_i b_i=1\), and set \(b(S)=\sum_{i\in S}b_i\). For a cut vector \(\delta(S)\), \[\sum_{i<j}b_i b_j\delta(S)_{ij}=b(S)(1-b(S)).\] Thus \(\delta(S)\) is tight exactly when \(b(S)\in\{0,1\}\). Since \(\operatorname{CUT}_n\) is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^{\binom n2}\), the inequality is facet-defining exactly when its tight cuts include \(\binom n2\) affinely independent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tight cuts are exactly the shores whose coefficient sum is zero or one; full affine rank of those cuts certifies facetness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta(S)\text{ is tight}\iff b(S)\in\{0,1\},\quad\text{and facetness holds iff the tight-cut face has dimension }\binom n2-1

notation.meaning: sum of hypermetric coefficients on shore S

knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Cut Facet Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Restriction and Zero Extension of Hypermetric Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension compatibility for coefficient vectors containing zeros.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\in\mathbb Z^n\) satisfy \(\sum_i b_i=1\), and let \(T=\{i:b_i\ne0\}\). Then \[\sum_{i<j}b_i b_jx_{ij}=\sum_{\substack{i<j\\i,j\in T}}b_i b_jx_{ij}.\] Hence the member indexed by \(b\) is the zero extension of the hypermetric inequality indexed by \(b_T\). Appending zero coefficients preserves validity on larger complete-graph cut polytopes, but this identity alone does not establish preservation of facetness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero coefficients embed a lower-dimensional hypermetric inequality into a larger graph; validity survives, whereas facetness requires separate certification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_b(x)=H_{b_T}(x|_{\binom T2})\le0\quad\text{for }x\in\operatorname{CUT}_n.

notation.meaning: Support of the hypermetric coefficient vector.
Hypermetric left-hand side indexed by b.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Restriction and Zero Extension of Hypermetric Inequalities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral generalized hypermetric inequality without the sum-one normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\in\mathbb Z^n\), put \(\sigma=\sum_i b_i\), and define \(b(S)=\sum_{i\in S}b_i\). Every cut vector satisfies \[\sum_{i<j}b_i b_j\delta(S)_{ij}=b(S)(\sigma-b(S))\le \left\lfloor\frac{\sigma^2}{4}\right\rfloor.\] Consequently, \[\sum_{i<j}b_i b_jx_{ij}\le\left\lfloor\frac{\sigma^2}{4}\right\rfloor\] is valid for \(\operatorname{CUT}_n\). The sum-one hypermetric convention is the case \(\sigma=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every integral coefficient vector yields a generalized hypermetric inequality with right-hand side floor of one quarter of its squared coefficient sum; the sum-one family is a special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i<j}b_i b_jx_{ij}\le\left\lfloor\sigma^2/4\right\rfloor\quad\forall x\in\operatorname{CUT}_n

notation.meaning: Coefficient sum on one shore of a cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Integral Hypermetric Validity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Valid Hypermetric Member Need Not Define a Facet
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal failure boundary between validity and facetness within the sum-one hypermetric indexing convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b=e_1=(1,0,\ldots,0)\). Then \(\sum_i b_i=1\), but every product \(b_i b_j\) with \(i<j\) is zero. The indexed hypermetric inequality is therefore \(0\le0\), so it is valid but does not define a proper face or facet of \(\operatorname{CUT}_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit coefficient vector indexes the trivial inequality, showing that hypermetric validity alone does not imply facetness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_b(x)=0\le0\text{ is valid but not facet-defining}.

notation.meaning: Hypermetric left-hand side indexed by b.

knowledge_statements.title: Valid Hypermetric Member Need Not Define a Facet

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit optimization formulation for separation over the full sum-one hypermetric family; it is not itself a terminating algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R^{\binom n2}\), exact separation asks whether \[\sup\left\{\sum_{i<j}b_i b_jx_{ij}:b\in\mathbb Z^n,\ \sum_i b_i=1\right\}>0.\] Any feasible \(b\) with positive value supplies a violated hypermetric inequality; if the supremum is nonpositive, \(x\) satisfies every inequality in this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full hypermetric separation is represented as an integer quadratic search for a positive sum-one hypermetric violation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists b\in\mathbb Z^n:\ \sum_i b_i=1,\ \sum_{i<j}b_i b_jx_{ij}>0\iff x\text{ violates a sum-one hypermetric inequality}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Hypermetric Separation Interface
Hypermetric Facet Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypermetric inequalities in the cut-semimetric coordinates of binary quadratic polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge 2\), let \(b\in\mathbb Z^n\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i=1\), and use cut coordinates \(x_{ij}\). The associated hypermetric inequality is \[\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}b_i b_j x_{ij}\le 0.\] For a cut vector \(x=\delta(S)\), its left side equals \(t(1-t)\), where \(t=\sum_{i\in S}b_i\in\mathbb Z\), and hence is nonpositive. Thus every such inequality is valid for \(\operatorname{CUT}_n\). A member is facet-defining precisely when its equality cut vectors affinely span a face of dimension \(\dim(\operatorname{CUT}_n)-1\); permutation and switching produce equivalent family members.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every integral vector summing to one defines a valid hypermetric inequality. Facet members are those whose tight cuts affinely span a codimension-one face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i<j}b_i b_jx_{ij}\le0\) is valid for \(\operatorname{CUT}_n\).

notation.meaning: Sum of coefficients indexed by one shore of a cut.
Cut polytope of the complete graph on n vertices.
