children.title: Symmetry-Aware Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching choices adapted to symmetric binary search spaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit-exhaustive branching on whether a symmetric binary orbit contains a one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let O be an orbit of unfixed binary variables under the current node group. The pointwise disjunction (\sum_{i\in O}x_i=0)\vee(\sum_{i\in O}x_i\ge1) is exhaustive and disjoint. In the second case, if search intentionally retains one representative from every solution orbit, it may choose r\in O and replace that case by x_r=1: every feasible assignment having a one at some i\in O has a symmetric feasible image with x_r=1. The resulting two children are orbit-exhaustive, although after this replacement they need not cover every labeled parent assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orbital branching separates the all-zero case from the case containing a one and may canonically place that one at a representative when quotient search is valid.
assumptions_latex: O is an orbit under symmetries preserving the current node and objective.
The search is authorized to retain one representative per feasible-solution orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced children retain at least one representative of every feasible parent orbit.
review_flags: The representative-restricted children are orbit-exhaustive, not pointwise exhaustive.
knowledge_statements.title: Orbital Branching Disjunction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe update of parent symmetries after imposing a child restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If child restriction D is added to node N, every inherited parent symmetry g\in G_N satisfying gD=D remains valid for the child. Thus the inherited child group is \operatorname{Stab}_{G_N}(D)=\{g\in G_N:gD=D\}. Using a parent element outside this stabilizer for child pruning is unsound in general because it may map a child-feasible assignment outside D. The child can have additional accidental symmetries, so the stabilizer need not equal its full symmetry group.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parent symmetries remain usable in a child exactly when they preserve the added child restriction; the child may also acquire other symmetries.
assumptions_latex: G_N is a valid symmetry group for the parent node.
D denotes the complete added child restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Safe inherited child processing uses a subgroup of \operatorname{Stab}_{G_N}(D).

notation.meaning: setwise stabilizer of the child restriction inside the parent group

knowledge_statements.title: Inherited Child-Symmetry Stabilizer
Symmetry-Aware Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit-based branching for a symmetry-invariant binary optimization node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a branch-and-bound node with unfixed binary indices \(U\), and let \(G_N\) be a group of permutations preserving its feasible set, objective, and current domains. Partition \(U\) into \(G_N\)-orbits. Assign each orbit \(O\) an invariant aggregate score \(S(O)\), select an orbit of maximal score, choose a canonical representative \(i\in O\), and create the exhaustive children \(N_0=N\cap\{x_i=0\}\) and \(N_1=N\cap\{x_i=1\}\). At each child replace \(G_N\) by the subgroup preserving the new domain assignment. Stop when no unfixed binary variable remains or the node is fathomed; output the resulting children.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on a canonical representative of a highest-scoring symmetry orbit, then retain only symmetries stabilizing each child’s new domain assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(G_N\) preserves feasibility, objective values, and current domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N=N_0\cup N_1\), and branching-variable selection is independent of the labeling within each \(G_N\)-orbit.

notation.meaning: symmetry group stabilizing the current node

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but no evidence is cited. In addition, choosing a merely canonical representative does not by itself make variable selection independent of labeling; the canonicalization rule must be defined and shown equivariant under relabeling. A source must also support the orbit-scoring and stabilizer-update procedure.

children.title: Score Stability Under Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Regimes where symmetric candidates weaken or distort branching-score discrimination.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-candidate counterexample to label-independent representative selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=\{e,(1\ 2)\} exchange two candidates with s(1)=s(2). The rule 'choose the smallest index' selects label 1. After relabeling by (1\ 2), the rule again selects label 1, whereas equivariance would require the image (1\ 2)1=2. Thus index-order tie-breaking does not commute with relabeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing the smallest numbered member of a symmetric tie is label-dependent.
assumptions_latex: Candidates 1 and 2 are exchanged by a node symmetry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c((1\ 2)O)\ne(1\ 2)c(O) for the smallest-index selector.
knowledge_statements.title: Smallest-Index Tie-Breaking Is Not Equivariant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of within-orbit discrimination forced by symmetry invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If s(gi;N)=s(i;N) for every node symmetry g\in G_N, then s is constant on every G_N-orbit O. If all admissible candidates form one orbit, every candidate maximizes the score. Moreover, a deterministic selector c(O) cannot be G_N-equivariant when the stabilizer of O fixes no member: equivariance would require c(O)=gc(O) for every g\in G_N. A solver must therefore branch on an invariant object, accept symmetry-breaking tie resolution, or use additional symmetry-breaking structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invariant scores tie all members of an orbit, and a nontrivial transitive orbit generally admits no deterministic equivariant representative selector.
assumptions_latex: G_N preserves the node and its candidate set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s|_O is constant; an equivariant deterministic representative exists only if the relevant stabilizer has a fixed candidate.

notation.meaning: deterministically selected representative of orbit O

knowledge_statements.title: Orbitwise Score Degeneracy
Score Stability Under Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariance requirement for binary branching scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary optimization node \(N\), let \(G_N\) act on its unfixed indices and preserve the node formulation. A branching score \(s(i;N)\) is symmetry-stable if \[s(gi;gN)=s(i;N)\qquad\text{for every }g\in G_N.\] Because \(gN=N\) for a node symmetry, symmetry stability implies \(s(gi;N)=s(i;N)\). Hence all indices belonging to the same \(G_N\)-orbit receive equal scores, and any score-based selection rule can be made label-independent by selecting an orbit before selecting a canonical representative within it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetry-stable branching score is constant on every orbit, so relabeling symmetric variables cannot change the selected orbit.
assumptions_latex: \(s(i;N)\) is defined for every unfixed binary index \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(i\) and \(j\) in the same \(G_N\)-orbit imply \(s(i;N)=s(j;N)\).

notation.meaning: branching score of index i at node N
symmetry group of the current node

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind and orbit-constancy implication fit the leaf and are mathematically coherent, but the record has no citation or inspectable locator supporting the symmetry-stability formulation or its branching interpretation.

children.title: Binary Probing
children.top_down_role: Domain inference obtained through temporary binary assignments.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-count bound for probing each selected binary variable once.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p\) variables are selected and each trial invokes one propagation-to-termination call, testing both values uses at most \(2p\) propagation calls. If one call costs at most \(T\), the sweep costs \(O(pT)\) plus state-restoration and implication-recording overhead. Optional re-probing after reductions is not included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One probing sweep makes at most two propagation calls per selected variable.
assumptions_latex: Each selected variable is tested at both binary values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{prop}}\le2p,\qquad\text{propagation time}=O(pT).

notation.meaning: Cost bound for one propagation closure

knowledge_statements.title: Full Binary Probing Sweep Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits inference from a probing branch that survives propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sound propagation ensures that a contradiction under \(x_i=v\) proves that no feasible completion has \(x_i=v\). The converse requires complete propagation: termination without contradiction may occur even when the restricted problem is infeasible. Likewise, failure to derive a literal does not show that the literal is invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A detected contradiction safely eliminates a value, but a surviving propagation state need not have a feasible completion.
assumptions_latex: Propagation is sound but not necessarily complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{contradiction}(x_i=v)\Rightarrow\neg\exists\text{ feasible completion},\quad\text{but the converse need not hold}.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Incompleteness Boundary
Binary Probing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided implication discovery by temporary binary assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a binary optimization state with domains \(D_i\subseteq\{0,1\}\), choose an unfixed variable \(x_i\). For each \(v\in\{0,1\}\), temporarily impose \(x_i=v\), apply sound propagation to a fixed point, and record the resulting domains \(D_j^{(v)}\) or a contradiction. If one branch contradicts, permanently fix \(x_i=1-v\). If both survive, retain every literal or bound implied in both branches; branch-specific implications may also be recorded as \(x_i=v\Rightarrow x_j=w\). Restore the permanent state between trials. Stop after the selected variables are probed or no new reduction occurs, and output the strengthened domains and implications.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Temporarily test both values of a binary variable, fixing the opposite value after contradiction and retaining consequences common to both tests.
assumptions_latex: All propagation steps preserve every feasible completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned domains contain exactly all original feasible solutions, while each recorded implication is valid for every such solution.

notation.meaning: current domain of binary variable i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits binary probing, and the stated reductions are sound under the propagation assumption. No source is supplied for the two-sided probing procedure, common-consequence rule, or implication recording, so the candidate cannot pass source review.

children.title: Variable Fixing
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms that certify fixed values for binary variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes a binary value shared by every optimum from one occurring in at least one optimum, without relying on ambiguous persistency terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F^*=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in F}f(x)\). A value \(v\in\{0,1\}\) is universal for coordinate \(i\) over the optimal set if \(F^*\subseteq\{x:x_i=v\}\), and existential if \(F^*\cap\{x:x_i=v\}\ne\varnothing\). Universal fixing preserves every optimum; existential fixing preserves the optimal value but can remove other optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value common to every optimum can be fixed without losing any optimum. A value occurring in only one optimum can preserve the optimal value while removing other optimal solutions.
assumptions_latex: The minimum of \(f\) over \(F\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^*\subseteq\{x:x_i=v\}\text{ in the universal case, while }F^*\cap\{x:x_i=v\}\ne\varnothing\text{ in the existential case.}

notation.meaning: set of globally optimal feasible solutions

review_flags: Terminology revised to avoid field-dependent meanings of persistent and weakly persistent.
knowledge_statements.title: Universal and Existential Optimal-Value Fixing
Variable Fixing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe fixing criterion based on exclusion of one binary value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be the feasible set of a minimization problem with objective \(f\), and let \(i\) be a binary index. Fixing \(x_i=v\) is feasibility-safe if \(F\subseteq\{x:x_i=v\}\). It is optimality-safe if, for every \(x\in F\) with \(x_i=1-v\), there exists \(y\in F\) with \(y_i=v\) and \(f(y)\le f(x)\). Under either criterion, as applicable, replace \(F\) by \(F_v=F\cap\{x:x_i=v\}\); feasibility-safe fixing preserves all feasible points, while optimality-safe fixing preserves the optimal value whenever an optimum exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary value may be fixed when the other value is infeasible or every solution using it is dominated by one using the retained value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility-safe fixing gives \(F_v=F\); optimality-safe fixing gives \(\min_{x\in F_v}f(x)=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits this safe-fixing criterion. The feasibility-safe and optimality-safe cases are mathematically plausible, but no authoritative source or specific locator is cited for these criteria.

children.title: Dominance Reduction
children.top_down_role: Reductions based on dominance relations among choices or states.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure When a Proposed Dominance Replacement Is Infeasible or Worsening
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that violating either sufficient mapping condition can make deletion unsafe.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proposed replacement map does not justify deletion through the dominance criterion unless its image is retained and feasible and it is non-worsening. For example, if \(F=\{0,1\}\), \(f(0)=0\), \(f(1)=1\), \(R=\{1\}\), and \(T(0)=T(1)=1\), then the worsening replacement of \(0\) changes the optimum from \(0\) to \(1\). A nominal replacement outside \(F\) likewise supplies no retained feasible representative. Thus omission of either mapping requirement can make the reduction invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A worsening or infeasible proposed representative can destroy the optimum, so it cannot certify dominance deletion.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Violation of }T(F)\subseteq R\subseteq F\text{ or }f(Tx)\le f(x)\text{ can make deletion unsafe.}
review_flags: This states sharp failure possibilities, not logical necessity of the mapping criterion for every value-preserving reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure When a Proposed Dominance Replacement Is Infeasible or Worsening

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dominance Preserves an Optimum, Not Necessarily All Optima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact preservation guarantee of objective-based dominance deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under a valid dominance map \(T:F\to R\) with \(f(Tx)\le f(x)\), restriction to \(R\) preserves the optimal value and at least one optimizer. It need not preserve all optimizers: for \(F=\{0,1\}\), \(f(0)=f(1)=0\), \(R=\{0\}\), and \(T(0)=T(1)=0\), the dominance conditions hold although optimizer \(1\) is discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dominance deletion preserves the optimal value and a retained optimum, but may remove other equally good optima.
assumptions_latex: \(T:F\to R\) is a feasible non-worsening dominance map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in R}f(x)=\min_{x\in F}f(x),\quad\text{but }\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in R}f(x)\text{ may be a strict subset.}
knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Preserves an Optimum, Not Necessarily All Optima
Dominance Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality-preserving deletion using a feasible dominance mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{f(x):x\in F\}\) with \(F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), and let \(R\subseteq F\) be a proposed retained set. A dominance reduction is valid if there exists a mapping \(T:F\to R\) such that \(f(Tx)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\), with \(Tx=x\) for every \(x\in R\). Then every discarded solution \(x\in F\setminus R\) has a retained solution no worse than it. Consequently, whenever the minimum is attained, restricting the problem from \(F\) to \(R\) preserves the optimal value and leaves at least one optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard solutions only when a feasible mapping sends each discarded solution to a retained one with no larger objective value.
assumptions_latex: The minimum of \(f\) over \(F\) is attained.
\(T:F\to R\) satisfies the stated dominance inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in R}f(x)=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: dominance mapping into the retained subset

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, and the dominance mapping is sufficient to preserve an attained minimum. The record nevertheless provides no source or locator supporting this formulation of dominance reduction.

children.title: Variable Substitution
children.top_down_role: Elimination or replacement of binary variables through structural relations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies nonconstant affine substitution relations between two genuinely varying binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x_i,x_j\in\{0,1\}\), feasible points occur with both values of \(x_i\), and \(x_j=\alpha+\beta x_i\) holds throughout the feasible set with \(x_j\) nonconstant. Then \((\alpha,\beta)=(0,1)\) or \((1,-1)\); equivalently, \(x_j=x_i\) or \(x_j=1-x_i\). Constant affine cases instead fix \(x_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconstant affine relation between two varying binary variables is necessarily equality or complementation; a constant relation is a fixing.
assumptions_latex: Feasible points occur with \(x_i=0\) and with \(x_i=1\).
\(x_j=\alpha+\beta x_i\) holds throughout the feasible set and \(x_j\) is nonconstant.
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Affine Binary Substitution Classification
Variable Substitution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination of a binary variable linked by equality or complementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) satisfy either \(x_j=x_i\) for every \(x\in F\), or \(x_j=1-x_i\) for every \(x\in F\). Replace every occurrence of \(x_j\) in the constraints and objective by \(x_i\) in the first case and by \(1-x_i\) in the second, then delete \(x_j\). The projection deleting coordinate \(j\) is a bijection between \(F\) and the reduced feasible set; its inverse reconstructs \(x_j\) using the corresponding equality. Thus feasibility and objective values are preserved exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equality or complementation relation permits one binary variable to be eliminated and uniquely reconstructed without changing feasible objective values.
assumptions_latex: The selected relation holds for every \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and substituted formulations have bijective feasible sets with identical corresponding objective values.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits exact elimination by equality or complementation, and the stated bijection is coherent when the reduced set is the substituted formulation. No citation or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Coefficient Reduction
children.top_down_role: Simplification of binary formulations through coefficient tightening or replacement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coefficient capping for nonnegative binary covering and packing inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) and \(a_i,b\ge0\). The covering inequality \(\sum_i a_ix_i\ge b\) is equivalent over the binary domain to \(\sum_i\min\{a_i,b\}x_i\ge b\). If additionally \(a_i,b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), the packing inequality \(\sum_i a_ix_i\le b\) is equivalent over the binary domain to \(\sum_i\min\{a_i,b+1\}x_i\le b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative binary covering coefficients can be capped at the threshold; integral packing coefficients can be capped at one above the threshold.
assumptions_latex: For the packing form, \(a_i\) and \(b\) are integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and capped inequalities define identical subsets of \(\{0,1\}^n\) in their respective cases.

notation.meaning: covering coefficient capped at the threshold
packing coefficient capped one unit above the threshold

knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Saturation of Nonnegative Coefficients
Coefficient Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact greatest-common-divisor reduction of an integral binary inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a\in\mathbb Z^n\), \(b\in\mathbb Z\), and \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). If \(g=\gcd(|a_1|,\ldots,|a_n|)>0\), then \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) is an integer multiple of \(g\). Therefore the inequality has the exact reduced representation \[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\le b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{a_i}{g}x_i\le\left\lfloor\frac{b}{g}\right\rfloor.\] The transformation preserves the represented binary set while replacing all left-hand coefficients by integers with no common divisor greater than one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide integral coefficients by their greatest common divisor and round the right-hand side down; the binary inequality remains equivalent.
assumptions_latex: At least one coefficient \(a_i\) is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and reduced inequalities define the same subset of \(\{0,1\}^n\).

notation.meaning: greatest common divisor of the coefficient magnitudes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the exact gcd normalization. The equivalence is mathematically standard for an integral left-hand side, but the candidate cites no authoritative source or section/page locator.

children.title: Symmetry Reduction
children.top_down_role: Reduction of equivalent binary representations or search states.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp condition for preserving all invariant binary objectives under a symmetry-breaking restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G preserve a finite feasible set F and let B be an added restriction. If B\cap Gx\ne\varnothing for every x\in F, then minimizing any G-invariant objective over F\cap B preserves the optimum over F. Conversely, if B omits a feasible orbit O, the G-invariant objective f(x)=0 for x\in O and f(x)=1 otherwise witnesses loss of the optimum whenever F\cap B\ne\varnothing; if F\cap B=\varnothing, feasibility itself is lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetry-breaking restriction is uniformly safe for invariant objectives exactly when it retains at least one point from every feasible orbit.
assumptions_latex: G acts on and preserves the finite set F.
B is imposed as an additional feasibility restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\cap Gx\ne\varnothing\ (x\in F) is sufficient and, for safety over all G-invariant objectives, necessary.
knowledge_statements.title: Orbit-Coverage Boundary for Symmetry Breaking

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact size of a complete representative set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite group G acting on a finite feasible set F, every complete transversal has |F/G| points, where Burnside's formula gives |F/G|=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{Fix}_F(g)|. Hence complete symmetry reduction changes |F| labeled feasible points into exactly |F/G| representatives; this counting reduction alone gives no guarantee that a compact formulation or efficient separation procedure exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reduced feasible set has one point per orbit, whose number is given by Burnside's formula, but orbit reduction need not have a compact implementation.
assumptions_latex: G is finite and preserves the finite set F.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |R|=|F/G|=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{Fix}_F(g)| for every complete transversal R.
knowledge_statements.title: Orbit Count and Maximum Reduction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical representative set for a permutation group acting on binary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a total lexicographic order \preceq_{\mathrm{lex}} and define L_G=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:x\preceq_{\mathrm{lex}}gx\text{ for every }g\in G\}. Every G-orbit contains exactly one vector in L_G. Thus, for a G-invariant feasible set F and objective f, F\cap L_G is a transversal of the feasible orbits and \min_{x\in F}f(x)=\min_{x\in F\cap L_G}f(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lex-leader restrictions retain the unique lexicographically least vector from each orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |(Gx)\cap L_G|=1 and the invariant optimum is preserved.

notation.meaning: set of lexicographically least orbit representatives

knowledge_statements.title: Lex-Leader Symmetry Breaking
Symmetry Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction to orbit representatives under objective-preserving symmetries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act on \(F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), and suppose \(gF=F\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in F\). Let \(R\subseteq F\) contain exactly one representative from each orbit \(Gx=\{gx:g\in G\}\). Then \[\min_{x\in F} f(x)=\min_{r\in R} f(r).\] Thus adding a complete symmetry-breaking condition whose feasible points are precisely \(R\) removes orbit-equivalent solutions while retaining one solution of every attainable objective value, including an optimum whenever one exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an invariant feasible set and objective, retaining one representative from each symmetry orbit preserves the optimal value.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility and the objective are invariant under \(G\).
\(R\) contains exactly one point from each orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(F)=f(R)\) and, in particular, \(\min_{x\in F}f(x)=\min_{r\in R}f(r)\).

notation.meaning: orbit of x under the group action

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind is appropriate for restriction to orbit representatives, and objective invariance supports the stated preservation claim. No source or specific locator is supplied for the symmetry-reduction statement.

children.title: Reduction Interaction Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Compatibility limits between coefficient simplification and symmetry handling.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Equivalence Does Not Preserve the Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between binary-set-preserving coefficient reduction and continuous-relaxation equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\{0,1\}\), the inequalities \(2x\le1\) and \(x\le0\) are equivalent and both force \(x=0\). Over \(0\le x\le1\), however, the first permits \(0\le x\le\tfrac12\), whereas the second permits only \(x=0\). Thus a coefficient reduction exact on the binary domain can strictly change the continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two inequalities can describe the same binary points but different continuous relaxations; binary equivalence is not relaxation equivalence.
assumptions_latex: The reduction is certified only over the binary domain.

notation.meaning: continuous relaxation of the binary domain

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Equivalence Does Not Preserve the Relaxation
Reduction Interaction Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for composing coefficient, fixing, and symmetry reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sound reductions compose only when each reduction's validity conditions are rechecked on the formulation produced by all preceding reductions. In particular, symmetry need not survive a non-invariant fixing: the binary set \(F=\{x\in\{0,1\}^2:x_1+x_2=1\}\) is invariant under swapping coordinates, but the reduced set \(F\cap\{x_1=0\}=\{(0,1)\}\) is not. Hence the swap cannot be used afterward to delete or identify points unless the current stabilizer is recomputed. Coefficient transformations can likewise invalidate syntactic symmetry tests even when semantic equivalence is preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reductions may destroy assumptions needed by later reductions; after fixing a symmetric variable, only symmetries stabilizing the current formulation remain valid.
assumptions_latex: Each constituent reduction is sound only under its stated preconditions.
Later reductions are applied to the current, not original, formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original symmetry group cannot generally be reused after asymmetric domain reduction; the valid group is the stabilizer of the updated formulation.

notation.meaning: binary feasible set in the counterexample
feasible set after fixing the first variable

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the counterexample correctly shows that the original coordinate swap does not preserve the asymmetrically fixed set. The broader claims about recomputing stabilizers and syntactic symmetry tests lack cited support.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard event-driven implementation of the same unit-propagation closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain two watched literals in each nonunit clause whenever possible. When a watched literal becomes false, search the clause for a replacement literal not currently false. If none exists, the other watched literal being false yields conflict, while it being unassigned yields a unit deduction. Initial unit clauses are queued directly. Processing the queue to exhaustion returns the same unit-propagation closure as exhaustive clause scanning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two watched literals avoid rescanning unaffected clauses while preserving exactly the deductions and conflicts of exhaustive unit propagation.
assumptions_latex: The CNF and initial assignment are finite.
Watch updates and generated unit literals are processed fairly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{UP}_{\mathrm{watch}}(F,\alpha)=\operatorname{UP}(F,\alpha)\text{, including the conflict outcome}.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Watched-Literal Unit Propagation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit Propagation Is Not a Complete Satisfiability Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsatisfiable CNF with no initial unit clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The formula \(F=(x\vee y)\land(x\vee
eg y)\land(
eg x\vee y)\land(
eg x\vee
eg y)\) is unsatisfiable, but under the empty assignment every clause has two unassigned literals. Unit propagation therefore reaches a fixed point without detecting conflict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unsatisfiable formula can contain no unit clause, so unit propagation may stop without discovering infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is unsatisfiable but }\operatorname{UP}(F,\varnothing)\ne\bot.
knowledge_statements.title: Unit Propagation Is Not a Complete Satisfiability Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Confluence and Finite Termination of Unit Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order independence and elementary work bounds for exhaustive unit propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite CNF \(F\) over \(n\) variables and a consistent partial assignment \(\alpha\), every fair sequence of unit-clause deductions either reaches conflict or makes at most \(n-|\operatorname{dom}(\alpha)|\) new assignments. In the nonconflicting case all exhaustive sequences derive the same literals. If \(L\) is the number of literal occurrences, an implementation that fully scans all clauses after every new assignment uses \(O((n-|\operatorname{dom}(\alpha)|+1)L)\) literal inspections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exhaustive unit propagation terminates after at most one deduction per initially unassigned variable, has an order-independent nonconflicting closure, and admits a direct full-scan work bound.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite CNF over \(n\) Boolean variables.
Every generated unit clause is eventually processed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{UP}(F,\alpha)\text{ is a well-defined nonconflicting closure, or conflict is derived}.

notation.meaning: number of literal occurrences in the CNF

knowledge_statements.title: Confluence and Finite Termination of Unit Propagation
Clausal Boolean Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit propagation for clauses over binary literals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given clauses \(C_k=\ell_{k1}\vee\cdots\vee\ell_{km_k}\) and a partial binary assignment, repeatedly inspect every unresolved clause. If all its literals are false, report conflict. If exactly one literal \(\ell\) is unassigned and all others are false, assign \(\ell\) true; equivalently, set \(x_i=1\) when \(\ell=x_i\) and \(x_i=0\) when \(\ell=\neg x_i\). Continue until a conflict occurs or a full scan makes no assignment. Output either the conflict certificate clause or the propagation fixed point. Every produced assignment is entailed by the clauses and the input assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly satisfy the sole unassigned literal of each unit clause; an entirely false clause certifies conflict.
assumptions_latex: Every literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\) with \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\).
The input partial assignment is internally consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns either a falsified clause or a fixed point containing only logically implied assignments.

notation.meaning: a positive or negative binary literal

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits clausal unit propagation, and the conflict and unit rules are stated consistently. No authoritative SAT or constraint-programming source with a specific locator is cited.

children.title: Cardinality Propagation
children.top_down_role: Propagation behavior for general cardinality constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound propagation for a two-sided binary cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L\le\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\le U\), let \(p\) be the number of variables fixed to one and \(q\) the number still unassigned. Report conflict if \(p>U\) or \(p+q<L\). If \(p=U\), fix every unassigned variable to zero. If \(p+q=L\), fix every unassigned variable to one. Recompute \(p,q\) after each assignment and repeat until neither equality applies or conflict occurs. Output the resulting domains. These rules enforce bound consistency for this single cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare fixed and possible ones with the lower and upper cardinality bounds to detect conflict or force all remaining variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, each remaining value has support in the cardinality constraint; otherwise a conflict or forced assignment has been returned.

notation.meaning: number of variables currently fixed to one

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits cardinality propagation. The conflict and forcing rules are coherent and support bound consistency for the single two-sided binary cardinality constraint, but no source or locator is provided.

children.title: At-Most-One Propagation
children.top_down_role: Propagation behavior specialized to at-most-one constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: At-Most-One Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialized propagation for an at-most-one binary constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the constraint \(\sum_{i\in I}x_i\le1\), inspect the current binary assignments. If at least two variables are fixed to one, report conflict and return those two assignments with the constraint. If exactly one variable \(x_j\) is fixed to one, fix every unassigned \(x_i\), where \(i\in I\setminus\{j\}\), to zero. If no variable is fixed to one, make no assignment. Repeat after updates until no domain changes. Output either the conflict or the propagation fixed point; every derived zero is logically implied by the constraint and \(x_j=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an at-most-one constraint, one true variable forces all others false, while two true variables constitute a conflict.
assumptions_latex: Current singleton domains represent fixed assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure detects every conflict and forced value obtainable from the current assignments using the single at-most-one constraint.

notation.meaning: index set of the at-most-one constraint
the unique variable currently fixed to one, when present

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits specialized at-most-one propagation, and the stated conflict and forcing cases are correct for the single constraint. The record has no authoritative citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Cardinality Encoding Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of propagation strength on the chosen cardinality representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Equivalence Does Not Imply Propagation Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit witness that existentially equivalent CNF encodings of one at-most-one constraint can have different unit-propagation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(K(x_1,x_2):x_1+x_2\le1\), let \(E_1=(
eg x_1\vee
eg x_2)\) and \(E_2=(
eg x_1\vee
eg x_2\vee y)\land(
eg x_1\vee
eg x_2\vee
eg y)\). Then \(K\iff E_1\iff\exists y\,E_2\). Under \(x_1=1\), unit propagation on \(E_1\) derives \(
eg x_2\), whereas unit propagation on \(E_2\) derives no original-variable literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Existentially equivalent encodings can differ in propagation: the direct at-most-one clause forces the other variable false, while the auxiliary encoding does not.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_1(x_1=1)\ne P_2(x_1=1)\text{ despite identical projections onto }(x_1,x_2).
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Equivalence Does Not Imply Propagation Equivalence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation completeness of a cardinality encoding relative to its original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A CNF encoding \(E(x,y)\) of \(K(x)\) is propagation complete on the original variables if, for every partial assignment \(\alpha\) of \(x\), unit propagation on \(E\land\alpha\) derives contradiction whenever \(K\land\alpha\) is infeasible and otherwise derives every original-variable literal \(\ell\) such that \(K\land\alpha\models\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cardinality encoding is propagation complete on its original variables when unit propagation detects every inconsistent original assignment and derives every implied original literal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{UP}(E\land\alpha)\text{ recovers every required original-variable consequence or contradiction}.

notation.meaning: CNF encoding with original variables x and auxiliary variables y

knowledge_statements.title: Original-Variable Propagation Completeness
Cardinality Encoding Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of unit propagation to logically equivalent CNF encodings of one cardinality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K(x)\) be a cardinality constraint on \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), and let \(E_1(x,y)\) and \(E_2(x,z)\) be existentially equivalent CNF encodings: \(K(x)\iff\exists y\,E_1(x,y)\iff\exists z\,E_2(x,z)\). For a partial assignment \(\alpha\) of \(x\), let \(P_i(\alpha)\) be the literals on original variables derived by unit propagation in \(E_i\) under \(\alpha\), or \(\bot\) if propagation detects inconsistency. Encoding sensitivity occurs when some \(\alpha\) satisfies \(P_1(\alpha)\ne P_2(\alpha)\), although both encodings have identical feasible projections onto \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent CNF encodings of a cardinality constraint can produce different unit-propagation deductions or detect infeasibility at different partial assignments.
assumptions_latex: Each encoding has the same feasible projection onto the original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\alpha:\ P_1(\alpha)\ne P_2(\alpha)\) characterizes sensitivity to the encoding.

notation.meaning: cardinality constraint on the original binary variables
CNF encoding, possibly using auxiliary variables
unit-propagation closure projected onto original literals

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard distinction between encoding equivalence and propagation equivalence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports the distinction between projection equivalence and propagation equivalence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separate Residual Propagation Is Incomplete for Equalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of treating a weighted equality solely as two independently propagated threshold inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The binary equality \(2x+2y=3\) is infeasible. Its lower side \(2x+2y\ge3\) has residual maximum \(4\), and neither literal is forced because \(4-2\not<3\). Its upper side is equivalently \(2(1-x)+2(1-y)\ge1\), which likewise neither conflicts nor forces a literal under the empty assignment. Hence independently applying the residual rule to the two sides does not detect infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual propagation is domain-consistent for one threshold inequality but can miss infeasibility when a weighted equality is split into two independently propagated inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 2x+2y=3\text{ is infeasible although separate residual propagation reaches a nonconflicting fixed point}.
knowledge_statements.title: Separate Residual Propagation Is Incomplete for Equalities

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalization of Repeated and Complementary Literals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical preprocessing before independent-literal residual propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Collect all occurrences involving each binary variable \(x\). An expression \(Ax+B(1-x)\) equals \(B+(A-B)x\); move \(B\) to the threshold and retain \(|A-B|x\) when \(A\ge B\), or \(|A-B|(1-x)\) when \(A<B\). Repeating this for every variable gives an equivalent inequality with at most one nonnegative-weight literal per variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregate repeated positive and negative occurrences of each variable into one oriented nonnegative literal and adjust the threshold before residual propagation.
assumptions_latex: All weights and the threshold are finite integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_i a_i\ell_i\ge b\iff\sum_k c_km_k\ge b',\quad c_k\ge0,\text{ with at most one }m_k\text{ per variable}.

notation.meaning: total positive- and complemented-literal coefficients for one variable

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization of Repeated and Complementary Literals

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain Consistency of the Residual-Weight Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness of residual propagation for one normalized nonnegative lower-threshold inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\ell_i\ge b\), with \(a_i\ge0\) and at most one literal per underlying variable, let \(R\) be the total weight of literals not fixed false. Then \(R<b\) exactly when no completion satisfies the inequality. If \(R\ge b\), an unassigned value \(\ell_j=0\) has a satisfying completion exactly when \(R-a_j\ge b\), while \(\ell_j=1\) has a satisfying completion. Thus removing every value with \(R-a_j<b\) enforces domain consistency for this single inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For one normalized nonnegative weighted lower threshold, the residual test detects every conflict and every unsupported false value.
assumptions_latex: Each underlying variable contributes at most one literal.
Only this single inequality is considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R<b\iff\text{conflict},\qquad R-a_j<b\iff\ell_j=1\text{ is forced}.

notation.meaning: maximum attainable left-hand side over completions

knowledge_statements.title: Domain Consistency of the Residual-Weight Rule
Weighted Pseudo-Boolean Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slack-based propagation for a nonnegative weighted pseudo-Boolean inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\ell_i\ge b\), where \(a_i\ge0\) and each \(\ell_i\) is a binary literal, maintain a partial assignment \(\alpha\). Define \(R(\alpha)=\sum_{i:\ell_i\text{ is not false under }\alpha}a_i\). If \(R(\alpha)<b\), report conflict. Otherwise, for every unassigned \(\ell_j\), if \(R(\alpha)-a_j<b\), assign \(\ell_j=1\). Repeat after every assignment until no literal is forced or a conflict occurs. The output is the propagation fixpoint or a conflict certificate consisting of the violated residual bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted inequality conflicts when the remaining possible weight is too small and forces a literal when losing its weight would make satisfaction impossible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a sound propagation fixpoint or detects that no completion of \(\alpha\) satisfies the inequality.

notation.meaning: maximum attainable left-hand side among completions of the partial assignment

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard slack rule for pseudo-Boolean propagation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the container and states the standard residual-capacity rule, but it requires a source. It also implicitly requires distinct indexed literals or aggregation of repeated literals; otherwise subtracting only a_j may not represent fixing the underlying literal false.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion of valid real bounds into Boolean values for a binary MIP variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\{0,1\}\) with valid bounds \(l\le x\le u\), let \(D=\{0,1\}\cap[l,u]\). Then \(D=\varnothing\) exactly when \(\max\{0,\lceil l\rceil\}>\min\{1,\lfloor u\rfloor\}\). If \(D\ne\varnothing\), \(l>0\) implies \(x=1\), and \(u<1\) implies \(x=0\). Thus Boolean export need not wait for numerical equality \(l=u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive valid lower bound fixes a nonempty binary domain to one, an upper bound below one fixes it to zero, and incompatible rounded binary bounds certify conflict.
assumptions_latex: \(l,u\) are valid bounds for the current MIP subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D=\varnothing\text{ or }D\text{ yields exactly the stated Boolean fixing}.

notation.meaning: current binary domain after intersecting with the MIP bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Binary Bound-to-Literal Channeling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which a numerical MIP bound may justify a permanent Boolean deduction or learned conflict.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numerical bound may be exported as a permanent Boolean literal only when a valid exact consequence excludes the opposite binary value and an explanation identifies assumptions and valid constraints sufficient for that exclusion. A floating-point comparison made solely against a tolerance, or a bound lacking a valid reason, is not by itself a logical certificate for permanent learning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numerical tolerances and unexplained bounds may guide propagation, but permanent Boolean learning requires a valid exact implication and an explanation.
assumptions_latex: Exported literals or conflicts may be used for permanent logical learning.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Permanent export requires exact validity and a sufficient implication explanation}.
knowledge_statements.title: Explanation and Tolerance Boundary
MIP Domain-Propagation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional exchange between Boolean assignments and MIP variable-bound propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a Boolean assignment \(x_i=0\) or \(x_i=1\) as the bound fixing \(u_i=0\) or \(l_i=1\) for a binary MIP variable \(x_i\). After each Boolean fixing, invoke valid MIP bound propagation on every affected constraint and update \([l_j,u_j]\). If \(l_j>u_j\), return conflict. If propagation yields \(l_j=u_j\in\{0,1\}\), export the corresponding Boolean literal with its explaining constraints. Iterate until neither subsystem produces a new fixing. The interface outputs the common fixpoint or an infeasible bound explanation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boolean fixings enter the MIP engine as bounds; implied integral bounds return as literals, while inconsistent bounds return as an explained conflict.
assumptions_latex: Each imported bound deduction is valid for the current MIP constraints and bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The common fixpoint preserves every feasible binary solution compatible with the initial domains.

notation.meaning: current MIP domain of binary variable \(x_i\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard channeling of Boolean assignments and MIP bounds
solver-interface conventions require a supporting source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm appropriately describes a Boolean–MIP propagation interface, but the validity, explanation, and fixpoint conventions are solver-interface claims requiring a specific supporting source.

children.title: Clause Conflict Learning
children.top_down_role: Conflict learning whose retained consequences are clauses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reverse-Trail Rule for Standard First-UIP Learning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolution-order condition that guarantees the standard first-UIP clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the standard first-UIP procedure, repeatedly select the most recently assigned current-level literal in the working conflict clause that has a reason and resolve with that reason until one current-level literal remains. Other resolution orders can still derive entailed clauses, but arbitrary selection does not guarantee the first-UIP cut or an asserting clause at the intended backjump level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse-trail resolution is the standard selection rule guaranteeing first-UIP learning; arbitrary resolution remains sound but may produce a different clause.
assumptions_latex: Trail order and valid reason clauses are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reverse-trail elimination guarantees the standard first-UIP stopping result; arbitrary elimination does not.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Trail Rule for Standard First-UIP Learning

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Learned clauses represented by cuts separating decisions from conflict.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an implication graph ending at a conflict vertex, a cut separating the decision side from the conflict side induces a boundary clause from the negations of assignments on the reason side that support crossing implications, with duplicate literals removed. Resolving reason clauses for conflict-side propagated vertices derives this clause, which is entailed and falsified by the current trail. The first-UIP cut has exactly one current-level boundary literal at the first unique implication point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Implication-graph cuts correspond to entailed conflict clauses, and the first-UIP cut yields an asserting clause.
assumptions_latex: Every propagated vertex has a valid reason clause.
The conflict is represented by a valid falsified clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The derived cut clause is entailed and excludes the current conflicting trail.

notation.meaning: unique implication point on every current-level path to conflict

knowledge_statements.title: Implication-Graph Cut Clauses

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness of clause-learning resolution steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For C_1=(A\vee p) and C_2=(B\vee\neg p), their resolvent R=A\vee B, after deletion of duplicate literals, satisfies C_1\land C_2\models R. Consequently, every clause obtained by a finite resolution derivation from permanent clauses and previously entailed learned clauses is entailed by the permanent formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolving clauses on complementary literals preserves entailment, so resolution-derived learned clauses are sound.
assumptions_latex: The parent clauses are consequences of the permanent formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_1\land C_2\models R, and finite resolution derivations preserve entailment.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolution Entailment for Learned Clauses
Clause Conflict Learning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-UIP clause learning from a Boolean implication graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a propagation conflict, form the implication graph whose vertices are assigned literals and whose reason edges connect antecedent literals to each propagated literal. Start with the conflicting clause and repeatedly resolve it with the reason clause of a current-decision-level literal until exactly one literal from that level remains. The resulting first-UIP clause \(C\) is entailed by the original and previously learned clauses. Add \(C\), backtrack to the greatest decision level among the other literals of \(C\), and enqueue its unique current-level literal when \(C\) becomes unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolve conflict and reason clauses until a first-UIP clause remains, learn it, backjump to its assertion level, and propagate its asserting literal.
assumptions_latex: Every propagated literal has a valid reason clause.
The conflict is represented by a falsified clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The learned clause is entailed, excludes the conflicting assignment, and is unit after backtracking to its assertion level.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard first-UIP conflict-driven clause-learning procedure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and topic match, but first-UIP learning requires a cited algorithmic source. The resolution step should also specify selection by reverse trail order; resolving an arbitrary current-level literal does not by itself characterize first-UIP learning.

children.title: Pseudo-Boolean Conflict Learning
children.top_down_role: Conflict learning whose retained consequences are pseudo-Boolean constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conflict and forcing tests for one normalized positive-coefficient inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C:\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\ell_i\ge b\), with \(a_i>0\), define \(U(\alpha)\) as the sum of coefficients of literals true or unassigned under \(\alpha\). Then \(C\) conflicts exactly when \(U(\alpha)<b\). If \(U(\alpha)\ge b\), an unassigned literal \(\ell_j\) is forced true by \(C\) exactly when \(U(\alpha)-a_j<b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A row conflicts when its maximum attainable left side misses the threshold; in a nonconflicting state it forces a literal when the threshold is unattainable without that literal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U(\alpha)<b\iff C\text{ conflicts};\qquad U(\alpha)\ge b\land U(\alpha)-a_j<b\iff C\text{ forces }\ell_j.

notation.meaning: maximum attainable left-hand side extending the partial assignment

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Boolean Slack Propagation Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness boundary for coefficient division during pseudo-Boolean derivation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Division of an integer pseudo-Boolean inequality by \(d>1\) is sound only with a specified implication-preserving rounding rule. For positive-coefficient literals, \(\sum_i a_i\ell_i\ge b\) implies \(\sum_i\lceil a_i/d\rceil\ell_i\ge\lceil b/d\rceil\); arbitrary independent rounding of coefficients and right-hand side need not preserve implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudo-Boolean division requires a proved rounding rule; arbitrary rounding can create an invalid learned inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{An unspecified division convention is not a sound inference rule.}
review_flags: Other admissible division and weakening rules depend on the selected proof calculus.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsafe Division Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic inference underlying weighted pseudo-Boolean conflict analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the database entails \(A+q\ell\ge r\) and \(B+q(1-\ell)\ge s\), where \(q\ge0\), then it entails \(A+B\ge r+s-q\). Positive integer multiplication may first equalize unequal coefficients of complementary literals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entailed inequalities with matched coefficients on complementary literals can be added and the complementary pair eliminated soundly.
assumptions_latex: The displayed occurrences are separated from the remaining literal sums \(A,B\).
Both premises are entailed by the active database.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A+q\ell\ge r,\ B+q(1-\ell)\ge s\Longrightarrow A+B\ge r+s-q.
knowledge_statements.title: Sound Complementary-Literal Cancellation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implication-preserving simplifications for normalized positive-coefficient pseudo-Boolean inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C:\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\ell_i\ge b, where a_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}, b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}, and \ell_i\in\{0,1\}. Replacing every a_i by \min\{a_i,b\} yields an inequality equivalent to C. For any k, C implies \sum_{i\ne k}a_i\ell_i\ge b-a_k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coefficients above the threshold may be saturated without changing the binary constraint; deleting a literal is sound when its coefficient is subtracted from the threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\iff\sum_i\min\{a_i,b\}\ell_i\ge b,\qquad C\models\sum_{i\ne k}a_i\ell_i\ge b-a_k.
knowledge_statements.title: Sound Saturation and Weakening Rules

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Line-by-line verification under an explicitly declared pseudo-Boolean inference calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pseudo-Boolean derivation certificate is a finite sequence \(C_1,\ldots,C_t\) in which each line is either an indexed input inequality or is annotated as the result of a fully specified implication-preserving rule applied to earlier lines. A verifier checks premise indices, arithmetic, and every rule's side conditions. If all lines verify, acceptance certifies \(D\models C_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A learned inequality is checkable when every derivation step names a sound, fully specified rule and earlier premises.
assumptions_latex: Every permitted inference rule has a fully specified implication-preserving definition.
All coefficients and indices have finite exact encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Verify}(C_1,\ldots,C_t)=\mathrm{accept}\Longrightarrow D\models C_t.
review_flags: Certificate validity depends on the declared rule set; unspecified division or reduction rules are not verifiable.
knowledge_statements.title: Checkable Pseudo-Boolean Derivation Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of an independently rounded pseudo-Boolean division step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The valid binary inequality \(3x_1+3x_2\ge5\) has the feasible assignment \((x_1,x_2)=(1,1)\). Dividing by \(2\), flooring both coefficients, and ceiling the right-hand side produces \(x_1+x_2\ge3\), which rejects that feasible assignment. Hence this independently rounded division rule is not implication-preserving.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flooring coefficients while ceiling the threshold after division can turn a feasible pseudo-Boolean row into an invalid learned constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 3x_1+3x_2\ge5\centernot\Longrightarrow \lfloor3/2\rfloor x_1+\lfloor3/2\rfloor x_2\ge\lceil5/2\rceil.
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Floor-Coefficient Division

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asserting Pseudo-Boolean Row at a Backtrack Level
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational test for whether a learned positive-coefficient row propagates after backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C:\sum_i a_i\ell_i\ge b\) with \(a_i>0\), and let \(\beta\) be the partial assignment remaining after a proposed backtrack. Put \(U(\beta)=\sum\{a_i:\ell_i\text{ is true or unassigned under }\beta\}\). For an unassigned literal \(\ell_j\), the row forces \(\ell_j=1\) at \(\beta\) exactly when \[U(\beta)\ge b\quad\text{and}\quad U(\beta)-a_j<b.\] If exactly one unassigned literal satisfies this test, the row is uniquely asserting at that state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A learned row asserts after backtracking when it can reach its threshold with a chosen unassigned literal but cannot reach it if that literal is false.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U(\beta)\ge b\land U(\beta)-a_j<b\iff C\text{ forces }\ell_j\text{ under }\beta

notation.meaning: Maximum left-hand side attainable by extensions of the post-backtrack assignment.

review_flags: This condition does not select a cancellation, reduction, division, reason, or backjump policy.
knowledge_statements.title: Asserting Pseudo-Boolean Row at a Backtrack Level

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic definition independent of a particular conflict-analysis policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a pseudo-Boolean database \(D\) and a partial assignment \(\alpha\), a learned conflict constraint is a pseudo-Boolean inequality \(C\) such that \(D\models C\) and every total binary extension of \(\alpha\) violates \(C\). It is asserting at a backtrack state \(\beta\subset\alpha\) when propagation by \(C\) forces an unassigned literal at \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A learned pseudo-Boolean conflict constraint is an entailed inequality excluding every completion of the analyzed assignment; it is asserting when it propagates after backtracking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\models C\quad\land\quad\forall x\supseteq\alpha,\ x\not\models C.
knowledge_statements.title: Learned Pseudo-Boolean Conflict Constraint

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalization Required for Coefficient-Sum Slack Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for propagation and saturation formulas when complementary literals share an underlying variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The formula \(U(\alpha)=\sum\{a_i:\ell_i\text{ is true or unassigned}\}\) is the maximum attainable left-hand side only when the simultaneously counted unassigned literals can all be true, as in a normalized row containing at most one polarity of each variable. For \(x+(1-x)\ge2\) at the empty assignment, the formula gives \(U=2\), although every binary assignment has left-hand side \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coefficient-sum slack tests require a normalized literal representation; complementary unassigned literals cannot both attain their coefficients.

notation.meaning: coefficient-sum upper estimate used by the slack test

review_flags: The prior slack, asserting-row, and saturation records require an explicit normalized-row assumption or a dependence-aware attainable-activity computation.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Required for Coefficient-Sum Slack Tests

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct activity formula after eliminating simultaneous complementary occurrences of an underlying variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C:\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\ell_i\ge b, where a_i>0, and suppose at most one polarity of each underlying variable occurs. For a partial assignment \alpha, define U_C(\alpha)=\sum_{i:\ell_i\text{ is true or unassigned}}a_i. Then U_C(\alpha)=\max_{x\supseteq\alpha}\sum_i a_i\ell_i(x). Consequently, C conflicts exactly when U_C(\alpha)<b, and an unassigned \ell_j is forced exactly when U_C(\alpha)\ge b>U_C(\alpha)-a_j.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a normalized row containing at most one polarity of each variable, coefficient-sum activity is exact and yields the conflict and forcing tests.
assumptions_latex: Each underlying variable occurs in at most one polarity.
\alpha\text{ is a consistent partial binary assignment.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U_C(\alpha)=\max_{x\supseteq\alpha}\sum_i a_i\ell_i(x).

notation.meaning: maximum row activity attainable by an extension of the partial assignment

review_flags: This supplies the normalization assumption missing from the earlier coefficient-sum slack and asserting-row formulations.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized-Row Attainable Activity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elimination of Complementary Literals from a Pseudo-Boolean Row
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact normalization of a positive-coefficient literal row so that each underlying variable occurs in at most one polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a pseudo-Boolean row contain the terms \(a x+b(1-x)\), where \(a,b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). Then \[a x+b(1-x)=\min\{a,b\}+|a-b|\ell,\] where \(\ell=x\) if \(a\ge b\) and \(\ell=1-x\) otherwise. Moving the constant to the threshold replaces the complementary occurrences by at most one positive-coefficient literal without changing the satisfying binary assignments. Repeating this operation for every variable yields an equivalent normalized row.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary occurrences of one binary variable combine exactly into a constant and one positive-coefficient literal, yielding the normalized rows required by coefficient-sum propagation tests.
assumptions_latex: The row is a threshold inequality, with generated constants transferred to its right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a x+b(1-x)=\min\{a,b\}+|a-b|\ell,\quad \ell=x\text{ if }a\ge b\text{ and }\ell=1-x\text{ otherwise}.
knowledge_statements.title: Elimination of Complementary Literals from a Pseudo-Boolean Row
Pseudo-Boolean Conflict Learning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflict analysis by cancellation of weighted pseudo-Boolean reasons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a violated pseudo-Boolean inequality and a propagated current-level literal with a valid pseudo-Boolean reason, multiply the two inequalities by positive integers so that the coefficients of complementary forms of that literal agree, add them, cancel the complementary pair using \(x+(1-x)=1\), and apply sound saturation or division rules. Repeat until the learned inequality has the chosen asserting form, such as exactly one current-level literal whose falsification can consume the available slack. Add the resulting inequality and backtrack to a level where it propagates that literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted conflict learning combines and simplifies a violated inequality with propagation reasons until it obtains an entailed inequality that asserts after backtracking.
assumptions_latex: All coefficients and right-hand sides are integral.
Every propagation reason is valid for all feasible binary assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The learned pseudo-Boolean inequality is entailed by the constraint database and excludes the analyzed conflicting assignment.

notation.meaning: binary complementation identity used for cancellation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard cutting-planes-style pseudo-Boolean conflict analysis
choice of reduction and asserting conditions needs a supporting source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm belongs in this leaf, but its saturation, division, and asserting-condition claims depend on exact pseudo-Boolean inference rules that are not defined or sourced.

children.title: Learned-Constraint Strength Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparative expressiveness, propagation value, and storage cost of learned constraint families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing representation-dependent propagation after projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(x\lor y)\) and \(D=(x\lor y\lor z)\land(x\lor y\lor\neg z)\). After existentially projecting the auxiliary variable \(z\), \(C\) and \(D\) have the same assignments on \((x,y)\). Under the partial assignment \(x=0\), unit propagation on \(C\) forces \(y=1\), whereas unit propagation on \(D\) forces neither \(y\) nor \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two projected-equivalent representations can propagate differently: the direct clause forces y after x is false, while an auxiliary-variable decomposition does not.
assumptions_latex: Only deductions on the original variables \(x,y\) are compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(F_C)=\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(F_D)\quad\text{but}\quad \operatorname{cl}_{UP}(C,x=0)\ne\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}\operatorname{cl}_{UP}(D,x=0).

notation.meaning: complete-assignment feasible sets of the two representations

knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Equivalence Without Propagation Equivalence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expressiveness and direct representation-size comparison without auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary literals \(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m\), the clause \(\ell_1\lor\cdots\lor\ell_m\) is equivalent to \(\sum_{i=1}^m\ell_i\ge1\). Conversely, \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\ge k\) is equivalent to the clauses \(\bigvee_{i\in S}x_i\) for all \(S\subseteq[n]\) with \(|S|=n-k+1\). This direct auxiliary-free CNF contains \(\binom{n}{k-1}\) clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every clause is one pseudo-Boolean inequality, while a cardinality inequality can require binomially many direct clauses without auxiliaries.
assumptions_latex: The CNF representation uses only the original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Clauses are a special case of linear pseudo-Boolean constraints, while direct CNF expansion may be exponential.}
knowledge_statements.title: Clausal Constraints as Pseudo-Boolean Constraints

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pseudo-Boolean Dominance over the Direct Cardinality CNF Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-relaxation strength comparison for equivalent binary cardinality representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in[0,1]^n\), the pseudo-Boolean inequality \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\ge k\] implies every direct cardinality-clause inequality \[\sum_{i\in S}x_i\ge1\qquad(|S|=n-k+1),\] because at most \(k-1\) variables lie outside \(S\). The reverse implication fails whenever \(1<k<n\): the uniform point \(x_i=1/(n-k+1)\) satisfies every clause inequality but obeys \[\sum_i x_i=\frac{n}{n-k+1}<k.\] Thus the single pseudo-Boolean row and the direct CNF are equivalent on binary points, while the pseudo-Boolean LP relaxation is strictly stronger in the nontrivial range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cardinality pseudo-Boolean row strictly dominates the auxiliary-free direct CNF relaxation for intermediate thresholds, despite binary equivalence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x\in[0,1]^n:\sum_i x_i\ge k\}\subsetneq\bigcap_{|S|=n-k+1}\{x:\sum_{i\in S}x_i\ge1\}

notation.meaning: Index set defining one clause in the direct cardinality CNF.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Boolean Dominance over the Direct Cardinality CNF Relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison preorders for learned-constraint representations on a common set of original binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,C_2\) be learned-constraint representations whose complete satisfying assignments project to \(F_1,F_2\subseteq\{0,1\}^V\) on the same original variables \(V\). Define \[C_1\succeq_s C_2\iff F_1\subseteq F_2.\] For specified propagators \(P_1,P_2\), define \((C_1,P_1)\succeq_p(C_2,P_2)\) when, for every partial assignment \(\alpha\) on \(V\), every original-variable literal derived by \(P_2\) is derived by \(P_1\), and every conflict detected by \(P_2\) is detected by \(P_1\). Auxiliary variables are existentially projected for semantic comparison, and only original-variable deductions are compared. Both relations are preorders. Semantic dominance or equivalence alone does not guarantee propagation dominance or equivalence for incomplete propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semantic dominance compares projected satisfying sets; propagation dominance compares all original-variable deductions and conflicts under specified propagators.
assumptions_latex: C_1\text{ and }C_2\text{ share the original-variable set }V
P_1,P_2\text{ have specified deduction and conflict semantics}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_1\succeq_s C_2\iff F_1\subseteq F_2,\quad (C_1,P_1)\succeq_p(C_2,P_2)\iff P_1\text{ reproduces every projected deduction and conflict of }P_2

notation.meaning: Satisfying complete assignments projected onto original variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Semantic and Propagator-Relative Dominance
Learned-Constraint Strength Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic and propagation-strength orders for learned binary constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(C_1,C_2\) on the same binary variables, define semantic dominance by \(C_1\succeq_s C_2\) when every binary assignment satisfying \(C_1\) also satisfies \(C_2\). Fix propagation procedures \(P_1,P_2\). Define propagation dominance by \((C_1,P_1)\succeq_p(C_2,P_2)\) when, for every partial assignment \(\alpha\), every original-variable literal derived by \(P_2\) from \(C_2\) is derived by \(P_1\) from \(C_1\), and every conflict detected by \(P_2\) is detected by \(P_1\). These orders need not coincide because propagation depends on representation and inference rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One learned constraint is semantically stronger by implication, or propagation-stronger when its chosen propagator always derives at least the other's deductions and conflicts.
assumptions_latex: Both constraints are interpreted over the same original binary variables.
Propagation is compared after projection away from auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\succeq_s\) compares feasible sets, whereas \(\succeq_p\) compares inference closures under specified propagators.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: implication and propagation closure provide standard strength comparisons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the comparison leaf and distinguishes semantic from propagation strength coherently, but the proposed orders and their noncoincidence have no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Nonchronological Backtracking Interface
children.top_down_role: Interface concerns for conflict-directed jumps across binary search levels.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact clause condition for propagation immediately after a nonchronological jump.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an entailed learned clause C be falsified by the current trail and let \ell\in C be its unique literal assigned at the current decision level d. Set b=\max\{\operatorname{lev}(q):q\in C\setminus\{\ell\}\}, taking b=0 when the set is empty. After deleting assignments above b, every literal in C\setminus\{\ell\} remains false and \ell is unassigned, so C is unit and propagates \ell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clause with one current-level literal becomes unit after jumping to the greatest level of its remaining falsifying assignments.
assumptions_latex: C is entailed by the active clause database.
C has exactly one literal assigned at the current decision level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Backtracking to b makes C unit with asserting literal \ell.

notation.meaning: decision level of the assignment falsifying q

knowledge_statements.title: Asserting-Clause Backjump Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why validity alone does not justify a clause-style assertion level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Validity of a learned constraint does not imply propagation after a jump. Under clause unit propagation, if C=(a\vee b\vee c) and restoration leaves a and b unassigned while c remains false, then C is not unit. Thus the clause assertion-level formula requires exactly one unassigned clause literal after restoration; pseudo-Boolean or other learned constraints require their own propagation semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid learned constraint need not assert after backtracking; clause formulas require unit-clause semantics.
assumptions_latex: The propagation engine uses ordinary clause unit propagation for C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A generic learned constraint cannot use the clause assertion-level interface without an appropriate asserting condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonasserting Learned-Constraint Boundary
Nonchronological Backtracking Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backjump computation and state restoration after learning an asserting constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a learned asserting constraint contain one literal assigned at the current decision level \(d\). Compute \(b<d\) as the greatest decision level among its remaining falsifying assignments, taking \(b=0\) if none exists. Remove every assignment made above level \(b\), restore all reversible propagation state to its level-\(b\) snapshot, retain globally valid learned constraints, insert the new constraint, and propagate its asserting literal at level \(b\). The interface outputs the restored trail and propagation queue, or a root-level conflict if \(b=0\) is already inconsistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backjump to the highest lower level represented in the learned constraint, restore reversible state, retain valid learning, and enqueue the asserting literal.
assumptions_latex: The learned constraint is entailed by the active permanent constraints.
It has exactly one literal assigned at the current decision level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After restoration to level \(b\), the learned constraint is unit or otherwise asserting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the interface leaf, but the backjump-level formula is stated in clause-like literal terms while allowing a generic learned constraint. A source must establish the intended asserting semantics and restoration protocol.

children.title: Restart Policy Interface
