children.title: Cutting-Plane Proof Systems
children.top_down_role: Proof-system structure based on cutting-plane inference.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a finite system of integer linear inequalities.
The fixed cutting-planes calculus contains Boolean axioms, nonnegative integer aggregation, and a sound integer-rounding rule sufficient for Chvátal-Gomory derivations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\cap\{0,1\}^n=\varnothing\ \Longleftrightarrow\ F\vdash_{CP}0\ge1.

notation.meaning: derivability in the fixed cutting-planes calculus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of finite cutting-planes refutations for infeasible Boolean linear systems; no short-proof claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite integer linear system \(F\) over \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a standard cutting-planes calculus with Boolean axioms, nonnegative integer aggregation, and sufficient sound integer rounding is refutationally complete: \(F\) has no Boolean solution if and only if a finite derivation of \(0\ge1\) exists. This existence statement implies no polynomial bound on line count, coefficient magnitude, or total proof encoding size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard cutting planes is refutationally complete for finite Boolean linear systems, but completeness alone gives no efficient proof-size bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Refutational Completeness on the Boolean Cube
knowledge_statements.title: Refutational Completeness on the Boolean Cube
Cutting-Plane Proof Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic pseudo-Boolean proof system based on deriving integer linear inequalities by sound cutting-plane rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cutting-plane refutation of an unsatisfiable pseudo-Boolean system \\(F\\) is a finite sequence of integer linear inequalities ending in a contradiction such as \\(0\ge1\\). Each line is either an inequality of \\(F\\), a Boolean axiom \\(x_i\ge0\\) or \\(-x_i\ge-1\\), or is derived from earlier lines by sound rules: nonnegative integer linear combination, and division with coefficient and right-hand-side rounding in a direction preserving validity for integer assignments. A cutting-plane proof of an inequality \\(C\\) from \\(F\\) is a refutation of \\(F\\) together with the integer negation of \\(C\\). Proof size is measured by a declared encoding measure, commonly line count or total bit length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutting-plane proof derives integer inequalities from premises and Boolean axioms by sound combination and rounded division, ending in the target consequence or a contradiction.
assumptions_latex: All coefficients and right-hand sides are integers.
The precise division and encoding conventions are fixed for the chosen proof-system variant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every derivable line is valid for all Boolean assignments satisfying the premises; a terminal contradiction certifies unsatisfiability.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the pseudo-Boolean cutting-plane proof-system definition.
Exact division and proof-size conventions vary by proof-system variant.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and cutting-planes proof systems differ in their division rule, negation convention, coefficient normalization, and size measure. A precise proof-system variant with an inspectable definition is required.

children.title: Generalized-Resolution Proof Systems
children.top_down_role: Proof-system structure based on generalized resolution.

assumptions_latex: Every axiom and derived line is an integer linear inequality.
Only nonnegative integer combination, Boolean normalization, and sound integer division with rounding are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every derived inequality is valid for all binary assignments satisfying the axioms; deriving \(0\ge 1\) certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the cutting-planes interpretation of generalized resolution over binary linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized-resolution derivation from integer inequalities \(A x\ge b\) is a finite sequence whose lines are axioms, Boolean bounds \(x_i\ge0\) and \(-x_i\ge-1\), or inequalities obtained from earlier lines by sound rules. A combination rule forms \(\sum_j \lambda_j(a_j^\top x-b_j)\ge0\) with \(\lambda_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). An integer-division rule may replace \(a^\top x\ge b\) by \((a/d)^\top x\ge\lceil b/d\rceil\) when every component of \(a\) is divisible by \(d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), together with permitted Boolean normalization. A refutation ends with \(0\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized-resolution proof derives valid integer inequalities from binary axioms by combination, normalization, and rounded division; the contradiction zero at least one is an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Resolution Proof Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but no citation identifies which generalized-resolution formalism is intended or supports the stated combination, division, and normalization rules. The local inventory does not contain a source on this proof system, so the exact rule set cannot be validated.

children.title: Simulation Strength Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relative simulation power and representation cost across the two proof families.

assumptions_latex: Proof lines may contain explicitly encoded integer coefficients, premise indices, rule parameters, and witnesses.
Polynomial simulation is measured by total binary encoding size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m_P\le\operatorname{poly}(m_Q)\ \not\Longrightarrow\ |\pi_P|\le\operatorname{poly}(|\pi_Q|)\quad\text{without polynomial encoding-growth bounds}.

notation.meaning: line counts in proof systems P and Q
total binary sizes of proofs in P and Q

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-cost boundary for simulations of proof systems with explicit arithmetic data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A translation sending every \(Q\)-proof with \(m\) lines to a \(P\)-proof with \(\operatorname{poly}(m)\) lines need not be a polynomial simulation in the standard bit model. Polynomial simulation additionally requires polynomial bounds on the binary lengths of generated coefficients, premise indices, rule parameters, and witnesses. Line-count and total-bit-size simulation therefore coincide only under an explicit polynomial encoding-growth bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial growth in proof lines does not imply polynomial bit-size simulation unless all generated arithmetic data and witnesses also have polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Line Count Does Not Control Bit-Size Simulation
knowledge_statements.title: Line Count Does Not Control Bit-Size Simulation

assumptions_latex: Proof systems \(P\) and \(Q\) refute the same encoded class of unsatisfiable binary instances.
Proof size counts all symbols, including binary encodings of coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial simulation is transitive; if \(P\) polynomially simulates \(Q\), every polynomial-size \(Q\)-refutation translates into a polynomial-size \(P\)-refutation.

notation.meaning: size of proof pi under the fixed encoding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines polynomial simulation using total bit size rather than line count alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proof system \(P\) polynomially simulates \(Q\) if there is a polynomial \(p\) and a polynomial-time transformation that maps every \(Q\)-refutation \(\pi\) of every encoded instance \(F\) to a \(P\)-refutation \(T(\pi)\) of the same \(F\), with \(|T(\pi)|\le p(|F|+|\pi|)\). The systems are polynomially equivalent when each polynomially simulates the other. A separation of \(Q\) from \(P\) requires an instance family \((F_n)\) having polynomial-size \(Q\)-refutations but requiring superpolynomial-size \(P\)-refutations under the same encoding convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulation compares proof systems by efficient proof translation with polynomial growth; equivalence requires translations both ways, while separation requires a superpolynomial lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulation Strength Comparisons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit simulation-strength comparisons, but the total-bit-size convention and polynomial-time translation requirement need a proof-complexity source with a specific locator. No cited source supports them.

assumptions_latex: The initial conflict inequality is a valid consequence of \(F\).
Every reason inequality used in the derivation has previously been validated as a consequence of \(F\).
Every transformation applied by the derivation is sound over the Boolean domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall j,\ F\models R_j\bigr)\ \land\ \text{sound inference}\ \Longrightarrow\ F\models C,\qquad C(\alpha)=\mathrm{false}\ \not\Longrightarrow\ F\models C.

notation.meaning: reason inequality used in conflict analysis

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates local conflict exclusion from globally valid pseudo-Boolean learning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a conflict derivation starts from an inequality entailed by \(F\), uses reason inequalities \(R_1,\ldots,R_t\) already validated as consequences of \(F\), and applies only sound transformations, then its learned inequality \(C\) satisfies \(F\models C\). The fact that \(C\) is falsified by the current partial assignment \(\alpha\) does not by itself imply \(F\models C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A learned inequality is globally sound only when its initial conflict, reasons, and transformations are certified; merely excluding the current conflict is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Reason-Soundness Boundary for Learned Inequalities

assumptions_latex: Both parent inequalities are valid consequences of the original system.
\(\mu a=\nu b=c\) for positive integer scales \(\mu,\nu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a\ell+A\ge\alpha,\ b\bar\ell+B\ge\beta\ \models\ \mu A+\nu B\ge\mu\alpha+\nu\beta-c.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic cancellation kernel for pseudo-Boolean conflict derivations; weakening, saturation, and division remain separate rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(a\ell+A\ge\alpha\) and \(b ar\ell+B\ge eta\) are valid pseudo-Boolean inequalities, where \(a,b>0\), \( ar\ell=1-\ell\), and neither \(A\) nor \(B\) contains \(\ell\). For \(\mu,
u\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) satisfying \(\mu a=
u b=c\), their scaled sum and the Boolean identity \(\ell+ ar\ell=1\) yield the valid inequality \(\mu A+
u B\ge\mu\alpha+
u eta-c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling two valid inequalities to equal complementary-literal coefficients and adding them eliminates the selected literal while preserving entailment.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementary-Literal Cancellation

assumptions_latex: The original constraints and the current conflict are pseudo-Boolean inequalities over \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\).
Every logged weakening, combination, saturation, or division step is sound for binary assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The learned inequality is entailed by the original constraints and excludes the conflicting partial assignment without excluding any feasible binary solution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract conflict-analysis procedure independent of a particular solver or proof-log syntax.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F\) and a partial assignment \(\alpha\) under which some inequality is falsified, initialize the working inequality with that conflict. Repeatedly select an assigned literal responsible for falsification and combine the working inequality with a logged reason inequality for that assignment, using nonnegative integer scaling; then apply only logged sound weakening, saturation, or integer-division operations. Stop when the resulting inequality \(C\) is falsified by \(\alpha\) and satisfies the chosen learning criterion. Append every inference and \(C\) to the proof log. Output \(C\), which must satisfy \(F\models C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conflict analysis combines a violated inequality with logged reasons until it obtains an entailed pseudo-Boolean inequality excluding the current conflicting assignment.
knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-Derived Pseudo-Boolean Proofs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An algorithm is appropriate for the leaf, but conflict analysis, reason inequalities, saturation, division, and the learning criterion vary across pseudo-Boolean proof systems. Without a specified format and source, the stated procedure and entailment guarantee cannot be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates supporting the absence of feasible binary assignments.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verification complexity for an explicitly represented, locally checkable pseudo-Boolean derivation in a fixed calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi=(L_1,\ldots,L_m)\) have encoded length \(|\pi|\). If checking each axiom, inference, and premise reference takes time polynomial in its encoded input length, then the complete verification time is polynomial in \(|F|+|\pi|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-size derivation with polynomial-time checkable steps is a polynomial-time verifiable infeasibility certificate.
assumptions_latex: The derivation and all premise references are explicitly encoded.
Every admitted local check is polynomial-time in the relevant encoded data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{check}}(F,\pi)=\operatorname{poly}(|F|+|\pi|).

notation.meaning: Total bit length of the encoded derivation

knowledge_statements.title: Refutation Verification Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which an accepted pseudo-Boolean refutation establishes infeasibility of the original binary system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Acceptance of a derivation ending in contradiction certifies infeasibility only when the checked encoding is satisfiability-preserving for the original binary system and every admitted inference is sound over the encoded Boolean domain. Without either condition, checker acceptance need not imply original-system infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A checked contradiction is conclusive only with a faithful encoding and sound inference rules.
assumptions_latex: A purported refutation is checked against an encoding of an original binary constraint system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\text{faithful encoding})\land(\text{sound inferences})\Longrightarrow(\text{accepted refutation}\Rightarrow\text{original-system infeasibility}).
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Soundness Boundary

assumptions_latex: The constraint set \(F\) is encoded as pseudo-Boolean inequalities over \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\).
Each inference in the derivation is locally checkable and preserves semantic consequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid derivation of \(0\ge1\) proves that \(F\) has no binary satisfying assignment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic refutation certificate for infeasible binary constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An infeasibility certificate for \(F\) is a finite derivation \(\pi=(L_1,\ldots,L_m)\) in which each \(L_k\) is either an encoded member of \(F\), a Boolean-domain axiom, or the result of a specified sound inference applied to earlier lines, and the final line is \(L_m:0\ge1\). A checker validates the encoding of every axiom, every inference and its referenced premises, and the final contradiction. Since every binary model of \(F\) would satisfy every line of \(\pi\), acceptance certifies that no such model exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A checkable derivation ending in zero at least one certifies that the encoded pseudo-Boolean constraint set has no binary solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record has the correct certificate role and states a standard soundness pattern, but validity depends on the unspecified inference calculus and encoding. No cited source with an inspectable locator supports the certificate definition.

children.title: Optimization-Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates supporting objective lower bounds or upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direction-reversed threshold-refutation certificate for binary maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z^*=\max\{c^\top x:x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ x\models F\}\). If \(B_U\) exactly encodes \(c^\top x>U\), then a valid refutation of \(F\cup B_U\) certifies \(z^*\le U\). When the objective and \(U\) lie on the integer lattice, the threshold may be encoded as \(c^\top x\ge U+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximization, refuting every feasible solution above U certifies U as an upper bound.
assumptions_latex: The feasible-system and objective-threshold encodings are exact.
The refutation calculus is sound over the encoded binary domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\cup\{c^\top x>U\}\text{ infeasible}\Longrightarrow z^*\le U.
knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bound Threshold Certificate for Maximization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Off-by-one, scaling, and lattice conditions for objective-threshold refutations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The replacement \(c^\top x<L\iff c^\top x\le L-1\) is valid when both attainable objective values and \(L\) lie on the integer lattice. For rational data, coefficients and thresholds must be scaled consistently to a verified integer lattice, or the strict inequality must be encoded exactly. An inexact threshold can exclude too many or too few objective values and does not certify the claimed bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing a strict objective threshold by an adjacent non-strict inequality is sound only on a verified objective lattice.
assumptions_latex: A strict objective threshold is converted into a non-strict pseudo-Boolean inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^\top x,L\in\mathbb Z\Longrightarrow(c^\top x<L\iff c^\top x\le L-1).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Threshold Encoding Boundary

assumptions_latex: The minimization problem is \(z^*=\min\{c^\top x:x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ x\models F\}\).
The strict threshold \(c^\top x<L\) has an exact pseudo-Boolean encoding \(B_L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A refutation of \(F\cup B_L\) certifies the lower bound \(z^*\ge L\).

notation.meaning: encoding of objective values strictly below L

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound certificates for minimization; upper bounds are supplied by feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimization-bound certificate for the claim \(z^*\ge L\) is an infeasibility certificate for the augmented system \(F\cup B_L\), where \(B_L\) exactly expresses \(c^\top x<L\). For integral \(c\) and integral \(L\), one may take \(B_L=\{c^\top x\le L-1\}\). The checker first verifies the threshold encoding and then verifies the refutation of the augmented system. Acceptance proves that no feasible binary point has objective value below \(L\), hence \(z^*\ge L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refuting the feasible region augmented by an objective threshold below L certifies that every feasible binary solution has value at least L.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Bound Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role and minimization direction fit the leaf. However, the exact threshold encoding, its integration with the proof calculus, and the checker obligations require a specialized source; none is cited.

children.title: Optimality-Certificate Composition
children.top_down_role: Composition of feasible solutions with objective-bound certificates for optimality claims.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of a verified feasible binary solution and a certified global lower bound when their values do not coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary minimization problem, let \(\bar x\) be verified feasible with \(U=c^\top\bar x\), and let a valid certificate establish \(z^*\ge L\). Then \(0\le U-z^*\le U-L\). Hence \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) certifies additive \(\varepsilon\)-optimality, while \(U=L\) certifies exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible value U and certified lower bound L certify suboptimality of at most U minus L.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is verified feasible for the encoded binary minimization problem.
\(L\) is a certified global lower bound for the same problem and objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\le c^\top\bar x-z^*\le c^\top\bar x-L.
knowledge_statements.title: Additive Approximate-Optimality Composition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp logical boundary for composing primal and objective-bound evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible witness supplies only \(z^*\le U\), and a certified lower bound supplies only \(z^*\ge L\). If \(L<U\), their composition establishes only \(L\le z^*\le U\), not exact optimality of the witness. The components must also refer to the same feasible system, objective, sense, scaling, and encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and lower-bound evidence proves exact optimality only when the values match and both components concern the same encoded problem.
assumptions_latex: The two certificate components are independently checked for a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L<U\Longrightarrow L\le z^*\le U\text{ without, in general, }z^*=U.
knowledge_statements.title: Compatibility and Nonmatching-Bound Boundary

assumptions_latex: The problem is a finite binary minimization problem with objective \(c^\top x\).
A candidate \(\bar x\) is accompanied by checkable feasibility data.
A lower-bound certificate proves \(z^*\ge c^\top\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composed certificate proves \(z^*=c^\top\bar x\) and that \(\bar x\) is optimal.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of a primal witness with a matching certified lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimality certificate is the pair \((\bar x,\pi_U)\), where the checker verifies \(\bar x\in\{0,1\}^n\), \(\bar x\models F\), and \(U=c^\top\bar x\), while \(\pi_U\) is a valid infeasibility certificate for \(F\cup B_U\) with \(B_U\) encoding \(c^\top x<U\). Feasibility gives \(z^*\le U\), and the refutation gives \(z^*\ge U\). Therefore the independently checkable components compose to certify \(z^*=U\) and the optimality of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible solution gives an upper bound, and a refutation excluding every better solution gives the matching lower bound; together they certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality-Certificate Composition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate content kind fits optimality-certificate composition, and the bound directions are internally consistent. A source is still required for the claimed proof-log composition, feasibility data, and threshold-refutation interface.

assumptions_latex: All variables are binary and all constraints have a canonical pseudo-Boolean encoding.
Every inference rule has a deterministic, locally checkable side condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A proof log is valid exactly when each record parses, references available premises, satisfies its rule predicate, and its declared conclusion matches the recomputed inequality.

notation.meaning: inference rule tag of record k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common abstract representation encompassing multiple pseudo-Boolean proof-log formats.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pseudo-Boolean proof log is an ordered sequence \(\mathcal L=(R_1,\ldots,R_m)\). Each record \(R_k=(r_k,I_k,D_k)\) contains a rule tag \(r_k\), indices \(I_k\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k-1\}\) of premises, and data \(D_k\) sufficient to reconstruct a canonical pseudo-Boolean conclusion. Rule families may include input, Boolean axiom, addition, multiplication by a nonnegative integer, weakening, saturation, division, deletion, and objective-bound declarations. A format determines a family by specifying its grammar, coefficient encoding, rule predicates, conclusion normalization, and accepted terminal records.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudo-Boolean proof-log family fixes record syntax, coefficient encoding, inference tags, local validation rules, and the terminal records accepted as certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Boolean Proof-Log Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is a suitable content kind, but the record blends possible rules and terminal records from multiple proof-log families without naming a format. A format specification or authoritative survey with a precise locator is required.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(\mathcal L\) use a fixed self-delimiting binary format.
Parsing, premise access, canonicalization, and every local inference predicate are polynomial-time in the explicit lengths of their operands.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{check}}(F,\mathcal L)=\operatorname{poly}(|F|+|\mathcal L|).

notation.meaning: combined input and certificate bit length

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional complexity bound for exact replay under a fixed proof-log specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=|F|+|\mathcal L|\). If each record can be parsed, its available premises retrieved, its rule predicate checked, and its conclusion canonicalized in time polynomial in the explicit operand lengths, then sequential independent replay takes time polynomial in \(N\). A polynomial number of records alone is insufficient when coefficients, witnesses, or individual rule checks have superpolynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent replay is polynomial-time in total transcript size when every local rule check is polynomial-time; polynomial line count alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Bit Complexity of Independent Checking

assumptions_latex: The checker receives the original encoded instance \(F\) and a purported log \(\mathcal L\).
The checker implementation shares no unverified solver state with the producer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The checker accepts only if the terminal claim follows through validated local inferences from \(F\) and Boolean axioms.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent replay checking with exact arithmetic and no trust in solver-internal state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On input \((F,\mathcal L)\), parse \(F\) and every coefficient using exact arithmetic. Process records in order: verify input records against \(F\), verify every premise index refers to an available earlier line, recompute each rule conclusion, check all rule side conditions, and compare the result with its canonical logged form. Apply deletion records only to availability, not validity. Finally verify that the designated terminal line is the claimed contradiction or objective bound. Reject at the first failed check; otherwise output acceptance and the terminal claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent checker exactly replays each logged inference from the original instance and accepts only a correctly derived contradiction or optimization bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Certificate Checking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits independent certificate checking, but premise availability, deletion semantics, canonicalization, and accepted terminal claims are format-specific. No checker or proof-format specification is cited.

assumptions_latex: The feasible domain is finite and binary.
Every strict objective threshold used by the optimizer has an exact encoding in the proof language.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Refutational completeness yields complete optimality certificates by combining a feasible optimum with a refutation of every strictly better value; failure of either assumption breaks this implication.

notation.meaning: encoding of solutions with objective below z star

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes existence of optimization proofs from polynomial proof size or efficient discovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\) refutes every unsatisfiable encoded pseudo-Boolean system, then any feasible finite binary minimization problem has a \(P\)-optimality certificate: choose an optimizer \(x^*\), verify its feasibility, and refute \(F\cup B_{z^*}\), which is unsatisfiable. This completeness claim does not imply polynomial proof length or polynomial-time certificate generation. It fails as a general implication when \(P\) is not refutationally complete, when the proof language cannot express the strict threshold \(B_{z^*}\), or outside finite attained problems where no primal optimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refutation completeness plus exact objective-threshold encoding gives optimality certificates on finite binary domains, but says nothing about short proofs or efficient proof generation.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Proof Completeness Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct role, and the statement distinguishes completeness from efficiency. The implication and its listed boundaries nevertheless depend on the precise proof language and threshold encoding, for which no source is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathrm{PHP}_{n+1}^{n}\) is the standard unary CNF encoding with pigeon clauses and pairwise hole-collision clauses.
Proofs, coefficients, and inference data use an explicit binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{size}_{R}(\mathrm{PHP}_{n+1}^{n})=2^{\Omega(n)}\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{size}_{CP}(\mathrm{PHP}_{n+1}^{n})=n^{O(1)}.

notation.meaning: standard pigeonhole-principle contradiction with n+1 pigeons and n holes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard unary pigeonhole CNF; proof size includes explicit coefficient encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathrm{PHP}_{n+1}^{n}\) contain clauses requiring each of \(n+1\) pigeons to occupy one of \(n\) holes and clauses forbidding two pigeons from sharing a hole. Its resolution refutations require size \(2^{\Omega(n)}\), while its clause inequalities have cutting-planes refutations of size polynomial in \(n\). Hence cutting planes is not polynomially simulated by resolution under these common encoding and size conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard pigeonhole contradictions require exponential-size resolution refutations but have polynomial-size cutting-planes refutations.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pigeonhole Separation of Resolution from Cutting Planes
knowledge_statements.title: Pigeonhole Separation of Resolution from Cutting Planes

assumptions_latex: Cutting-planes proofs permit nonnegative integer combination and sound integer rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cutting planes polynomially simulates resolution under the clause-to-inequality encoding.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the robust simulation direction; quantitative separations depend on proof and encoding conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Encode clauses \(C\vee x\) and \(D\vee\neg x\) as \(S_C+x\ge1\) and \(S_D+(1-x)\ge1\), where \(S_C\) and \(S_D\) are sums of their remaining literals. Adding the inequalities gives \(S_C+S_D\ge1\), which implies the inequality encoding of the resolvent after duplicate-literal normalization. Thus every resolution inference has a constant-size cutting-planes simulation, and a resolution refutation \(\pi_R\) translates into a cutting-planes refutation \(\pi_{CP}\) with polynomially related total bit size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standard clause encoding, each resolution step has a constant-size cutting-planes derivation, so cutting planes polynomially simulates resolution.
knowledge_statements.title: Resolution versus Cutting-Planes Strength

children.title: Proof Length Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes measured by proof length.

assumptions_latex: A proof system \(P\), instance encoding, and line encoding are fixed.
The size of an instance \(F\) is its total input bit length \(|F|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomially bounded proof length means that some polynomial \(p\) satisfies \(L_P(F)\le p(|F|)\) for every refutable instance \(F\) in the class.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses total encoded bit length; line-count complexity is a distinct convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a refutable instance \(F\), the proof-length complexity in system \(P\) is \[L_P(F)=\min\{\,|\pi|_{\mathrm{bit}}:\pi\in\mathrm{Ref}_P(F)\,\},\] where \(|\pi|_{\mathrm{bit}}\) counts the complete encoding of rule tags, premise references, variables, coefficients, and constants. For an instance family \((F_n)\), its length complexity is the function \(n\mapsto L_P(F_n)\). If line count is used instead, it must be denoted and analyzed separately because unbounded coefficients can make line count polynomial while bit length is superpolynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof-length complexity is the minimum total bit length of a refutation, including coefficients and references; line count is a separate measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Proof Length Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits proof-length complexity and consistently distinguishes bit length from line count. Its encoding convention and the coefficient-size warning require a proof-complexity source with a specific locator; none is cited.

children.title: Proof Rank Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes measured by proof rank or inference depth.

assumptions_latex: A directed acyclic proof \(\pi\) has axioms as source nodes and inference lines as non-source nodes.
Each derived line has directed edges from all premises used in its inference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Proof rank is the minimum possible maximum inference depth among all refutations of the instance in the fixed proof system.

notation.meaning: inference depth of proof line v
minimum refutation rank for F in P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inference-depth rank for directed acyclic proofs, distinct from system-specific cutting-plane rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign each axiom line \(v\) rank \(r(v)=0\). If a derived line \(v\) uses premises \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\), set \(r(v)=1+\max_i r(u_i)\). The rank of a proof is \(\operatorname{rank}(\pi)=\max_{v\in\pi}r(v)\), equivalently the maximum number of inference edges on an axiom-to-line path. For a refutable instance \(F\), define \[R_P(F)=\min\{\operatorname{rank}(\pi):\pi\in\mathrm{Ref}_P(F)\}.\] This measure captures sequential inference depth and need not be controlled by proof length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof rank is the least possible maximum inference depth of a refutation, measured from axioms through the proof dependency graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Proof Rank Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent, but proof rank is system-dependent and may mean something more specific than generic DAG inference depth, especially for cutting-planes systems. A source is needed to establish that this convention matches the exact leaf context.

children.title: Coefficient Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes measured by coefficient magnitude or encoding burden.

assumptions_latex: A proof line is an integer inequality with coefficients encoded in binary.
The proof system and admissible normalization of inequalities are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coefficient complexity is \(\operatorname{cc}(\pi)\), and a family has polynomial coefficient complexity when \(\operatorname{cc}(\pi_n)\leq \operatorname{poly}(|F_n|)\).

notation.meaning: An integer-inequality refutation of a binary infeasible system
Binary encoding length of an integer
Maximum coefficient encoding length in the proof

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports coefficient complexity for binary proof systems.
standard_field_rationale: coefficient complexity is conventionally measured by the largest coefficient bit length, relative to a fixed proof system and normalization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses maximum coefficient bit length; alternative aggregate-size measures are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\pi=(L_1,\ldots,L_s)\) be a proof whose line \(L_t\) is an integer inequality \(a_{t0}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{tj}x_j\geq 0\). For an integer \(a\), set \(\ell(a)=1+\lceil\log_2(|a|+1)\rceil\). The coefficient complexity of \(\pi\) is
\[
\operatorname{cc}(\pi)=\max_{0\leq t\leq s,\,0\leq j\leq n}\ell(a_{tj}).
\]
For a family \((F_n)\), polynomial coefficient complexity means that each \(F_n\) has a refutation \(\pi_n\) satisfying \(\operatorname{cc}(\pi_n)\leq p(|F_n|)\) for one polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coefficient complexity is the largest binary bit length of any integer coefficient appearing in a normalized proof; a family is polynomially bounded when this maximum is polynomial in input size.
knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The leaf and definition role are compatible, but the maximum ranges over t=0 although only L_1 through L_s and their coefficients are introduced. More importantly, maximum coefficient bit length is only one possible proof-system-dependent coefficient measure, and no inspectable source supports this exact convention or the family-level definition.

children.title: Proof-Measure Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs among proof length, rank, and coefficient complexity.

assumptions_latex: A fixed proof system assigns length, rank, and coefficient complexity to every refutation.
The formula family and input-size encoding are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounds on one proof measure alone do not imply bounds on the others; tradeoffs are expressed by the attainable triples in \(\mathcal T_P(F)\).

notation.meaning: Length, rank, and coefficient complexity of a refutation
Attainable proof-measure region for a formula

review_flags: A proof-system-specific tradeoff theorem and locator are required.
standard_field_rationale: proof tradeoffs are represented by Pareto-minimal attainable measure vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A proof-system-relative Pareto formulation, not a universal separation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an infeasible binary formula \(F\) and proof system \(P\), define
\[
\mathcal T_P(F)=\{(L(\pi),R(\pi),C(\pi)):\pi\text{ is a }P\text{-refutation of }F\}.
\]
A proof-measure tradeoff is a lower bound of the form \(C(\pi)\geq g(L(\pi),R(\pi),|F|)\), or a permutation thereof, valid for every \(P\)-refutation \(\pi\). The relevant optimal profiles are the coordinatewise minimal elements of \(\mathcal T_P(F)\); minimizing one coordinate need not minimize either remaining coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proof tradeoffs are lower bounds relating length, rank, and coefficient size. Their meaningful profiles are Pareto-minimal attainable triples for a fixed formula and proof system.
knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Measure Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The attainable-region formulation fits the tradeoff leaf, but the claim that minimizing one measure need not minimize the others is not a consequence of the definition alone. A proof-system-specific source or explicit separation result is required, and the length, rank, and coefficient measures must be fixed.

children.title: Propagation-Complete Encodings
children.top_down_role: Encoding families classified by propagation completeness.

assumptions_latex: The encoding is a CNF formula over primary variables and auxiliary variables.
Unit propagation is iterated to closure under a partial assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The encoding is propagation-complete exactly when every semantically forced primary literal is derived by unit propagation, with contradiction derived for inconsistent assignments.

notation.meaning: CNF encoding over primary variables X and auxiliary variables Y
Unit-propagation closure of E under a partial assignment alpha

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses propagation-complete CNF encodings.
standard_field_rationale: this is the standard semantic-completeness definition for unit propagation on designated variables.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness is required for consequences on primary variables; auxiliary consequences are not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A CNF encoding \(E(X,Y)\) is propagation-complete on the primary variables \(X\) if, for every partial assignment \(\alpha\) to \(X\): first, if \(E\wedge\alpha\) is unsatisfiable, then unit propagation on \(E\mid\alpha\) derives the empty clause; second, if \(E\wedge\alpha\models \ell\) for a literal \(\ell\) on \(X\), then \(\ell\in\operatorname{UP}(E\mid\alpha)\). Thus unit propagation detects every inconsistent primary assignment and every forced primary literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding is propagation-complete when unit propagation detects every inconsistent partial primary assignment and derives every primary literal semantically forced by such an assignment.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation-Complete Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is internally coherent as propagation completeness restricted to partial assignments and consequences on primary variables. However, propagation-complete encoding terminology varies over whether auxiliary variables and assignments are included, so an authoritative locator is needed to support this exact designated-variable version.

children.title: Proof-Strong Encodings
children.top_down_role: Encoding families designed to support strong proof-system behavior.

assumptions_latex: A proof system P and a class of constraints are fixed.
Encoding size and proof length use fixed polynomially equivalent representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An encoding family is proof-strong when it polynomially simulates the chosen reference proof system for every encoded constraint instance.

notation.meaning: Encoding of a constraint instance I
Reference proof system and encoding-level proof system
Minimum refutation length in proof system P

review_flags: The term proof-strong is not canonical without naming the simulated proof system.
No supplied locator supports this proof-simulation definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength is relative to specified proof systems and an encoding family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix proof systems \(Q\) for constraint instances and \(P\) for their binary encodings. An encoding family \(E\) is \((P,Q)\)-proof-strong if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every infeasible instance \(I\),
\[
L_P(E(I))\leq p(|E(I)|+L_Q(I)).
\]
Equivalently, every \(Q\)-refutation can be transformed into a \(P\)-refutation of the encoding with polynomial overhead. The designation is meaningless unless \(P\), \(Q\), and the size conventions are specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proof-strong encoding polynomially simulates a stated reference proof system. The property is relative to both proof systems and their size conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Strong Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Proof strength is correctly presented as relative to named proof systems, but the minimum-length inequality does not by itself imply an efficient transformation of every Q-refutation; the asserted equivalence needs an additional constructive simulation hypothesis. Because proof-strong is noncanonical and no source fixes the intended definition, the mathematical version remains source-dependent.

children.title: Propagation–Proof Strength Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between propagation completeness, proof strength, and encoding size.

assumptions_latex: Encoding families represent the same constraint class.
Propagation strength and proof strength are compared using fixed preorders.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The frontier consists of the undominated attainable pairs \((u(E),v(E))\).

notation.meaning: Propagation and proof-strength scores of encoding E

review_flags: The path does not specify particular propagation and proof-strength metrics.
No supplied source establishes a canonical frontier theorem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An abstract Pareto frontier; concrete metrics must be fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal E\) be encoding families for one constraint class, and let \(u(E)\) and \(v(E)\) measure propagation strength and proof strength, respectively, with larger values stronger. Define \(E'\succeq E\) when \(u(E')\geq u(E)\) and \(v(E')\geq v(E)\). The propagation-proof strength frontier is
\[
\mathcal F=\{E\in\mathcal E:\nexists E'\in\mathcal E\text{ with }E'\succeq E\text{ and at least one strict inequality}\}.
\]
Its image consists exactly of the undominated attainable strength pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The propagation-proof frontier is the set of encodings whose propagation and proof strengths cannot both be weakly improved, with at least one strict improvement.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation–Proof Strength Frontiers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed set is a valid abstract Pareto frontier once numerical strength scores and their order are fixed, but neither score is defined by the node context and no source establishes this as a propagation-proof frontier notion. Concrete preorders or metrics and a supporting locator are required.

children.title: Encoding Strength Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where compact encodings lose propagation or proof strength.

assumptions_latex: Unit propagation is applied to CNF formulas to closure.
Semantic consequences are evaluated over the displayed variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equisatisfiability does not imply propagation completeness: \(F\models y\), but unit propagation on \(F\) derives no literal from the empty assignment.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed two-clause formula directly verifies the claimed failure boundary.
Content kind corrected to match the exact failure-boundary leaf.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete boundary between semantic equivalence and unit-propagation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=(x\lor y)\land(\neg x\lor y)\). Then \(F\models y\), and the satisfying assignments of \(F\) are exactly those with \(y=1\). Under the empty partial assignment, unit propagation derives no literal and no contradiction. Hence semantic equivalence to the constraint \(y=1\) does not imply propagation completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The formula (x or y) and (not x or y) entails y, yet empty-assignment unit propagation derives nothing. Semantic equivalence therefore does not guarantee propagation completeness.
knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Strength Failure Boundaries

children.title: Canonical Binary Hardness Sources
children.top_down_role: Canonical binary problem families used as sources of hardness.

assumptions_latex: SAT instances are CNF formulas over Boolean variables.
Binary feasibility permits linear inequalities over variables in \(\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The clause-to-inequality map is polynomial and preserves satisfiability, making CNF-SAT a canonical source of binary-feasibility hardness.

notation.meaning: Positive and negative variable indices in clause C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the direct clause-to-binary-linear-feasibility reduction from CNF-SAT.

source_refs.locator: Section 2.6, NP-complete problems, p. 20
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each CNF clause \(C\), let \(P(C)\) index its positive literals and \(N(C)\) its negative literals. Replace \(C\) by
\[
\sum_{i\in P(C)}x_i+\sum_{i\in N(C)}(1-x_i)\geq 1,
\qquad x_i\in\{0,1\}.
\]
A Boolean assignment satisfies \(C\) exactly when its binary vector satisfies this inequality. Applying the replacement to every clause yields, in polynomial time and linear total clause-occurrence size, a binary linear feasibility instance feasible exactly when the CNF formula is satisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CNF-SAT reduces directly to binary linear feasibility by requiring each clause's satisfied-literal indicators to sum to at least one.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Binary Hardness Sources

source_witnesses.locator: Section 2.6, NP-complete problems, p. 20
source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical weakly NP-complete numerical source for binary reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: SUBSET-SUM asks whether \sum_{i=1}^na_ix_i=B has a solution x\in\{0,1\}^n. Under binary encoding it is NP-complete, while a reachable-sum dynamic program runs in O(nB) state transitions for nonnegative data. It is therefore a canonical weakly NP-complete source.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subset sum is NP-complete but has an O(nB) pseudo-polynomial dynamic program, exposing its weak-hardness regime.
assumptions_latex: a_1,\ldots,a_n,B\in\mathbb Z_+\text{ are encoded in binary.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \textsc{Subset-Sum}\text{ is NP-complete and solvable in }O(nB)\text{ pseudo-polynomial state transitions.}
knowledge_statements.title: Subset-Sum Weak Hardness Source

knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-completeness inherited from the direct 3-SAT encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each 3-CNF clause C, impose \sum_{i\in P(C)}x_i-\sum_{i\in N(C)}x_i\ge1-|N(C)|. Binary linear feasibility is NP-complete even when every row has at most three nonzero coefficients in \{-1,1\} and right-hand side in \{-2,-1,0,1\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary linear feasibility remains NP-complete with at most three bounded coefficients per row.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Restricted binary linear feasibility is NP-complete.}

notation.meaning: Positive and negative variable indices in clause C.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Bounded-Coefficient Binary Feasibility Hardness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical graph source for binary linear optimization hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph G=(V,E), the binary system x_u+x_v\le1\ (uv\in E),\ x\in\{0,1\}^V represents exactly the independent sets, with cardinality \sum_{v\in V}x_v. Hence INDEPENDENT-SET reduces in linear graph size to threshold binary linear optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent set is encoded by one binary variable per vertex and one exclusion inequality per edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha(G)\ge k\iff\max\{\sum_vx_v:x_u+x_v\le1\ (uv\in E),\ x\in\{0,1\}^V\}\ge k.

notation.meaning: Indicator that vertex v is selected.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Set Hardness Source

children.title: Binary Reduction Families
children.top_down_role: Reduction families used to transfer hardness among binary problems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision, count-preserving, and oracle reductions over finitely encoded binary instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial many-one reduction from A to B is a polynomial-time map f with x\in A\iff f(x)\in B. For finite witness relations, it is parsimonious when |S_A(x)|=|S_B(f(x))| for every x. A polynomial-time Turing reduction decides A using an adaptive B-oracle computation whose total running time, and hence query count and query lengths, are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The principal families are many-one maps preserving decision truth, parsimonious maps preserving witness counts, and adaptive polynomial-time Turing reductions.
assumptions_latex: S_A(x),S_B(y)\text{ are finite witness sets when parsimoniousness is considered.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\le_m^pB,\quad A\le_{\mathrm{pars}}^pB,\quad\text{and}\quad A\le_T^pB\text{ denote distinct preservation regimes.}

notation.meaning: Witness set of source instance x.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Reduction Families

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates standard count preservation from stronger witness-correspondence requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition |S_A(x)|=|S_B(f(x))| does not itself supply a specified or polynomial-time computable bijection between the two witness sets. Requiring such a correspondence is a stronger solution-preserving reduction notion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parsimonious reductions preserve witness counts; count equality alone does not provide a computable witness bijection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |S_A(x)|=|S_B(f(x))|\centernot\implies\text{an explicitly given polynomial-time witness bijection.}
knowledge_statements.title: Parsimonious Count-Preservation Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transitivity of the principal polynomial reduction families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polynomial many-one and polynomial-time Turing reductions are closed under composition. Parsimonious mapping reductions are also closed under composition because their witness-count equalities compose.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Many-one, polynomial-time Turing, and parsimonious mapping reductions are transitive.
assumptions_latex: A\le_m^pB\text{ and }B\le_m^pC\text{, or the analogous Turing or parsimonious relations, hold.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\le_m^pC,\quad A\le_T^pC,\quad\text{or}\quad A\le_{\mathrm{pars}}^pC\text{ respectively.}
knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Reduction Families

assumptions_latex: Source and target instances use finite binary encodings.
Polynomial time is measured in source encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Many-one, parsimonious, and polynomial-query Turing reductions form distinct binary reduction families with progressively different preservation guarantees.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes mapping, solution-preserving, and oracle reduction families.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6, Complexity and Problem Reductions, p. 95
Chapter 2, Problems, algorithms, and complexity, p. 14
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial many-one reduction maps each instance \(I\) to \(f(I)\) in polynomial time and satisfies \(I\in A\iff f(I)\in B\). It is parsimonious when there is a polynomial-time bijection between \(S(I)\) and \(S(f(I))\). A polynomial-query Turing reduction may instead adaptively query a decision oracle for \(B\), using polynomially many queries of polynomial encoding length. These families preserve, respectively, decision truth, solution counts, and polynomial-time oracle solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary reductions include many-one maps preserving yes-instances, parsimonious maps bijecting solutions, and adaptive Turing reductions using polynomially many decision queries.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Reduction Families

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, Complexity and Problem Reductions, p. 95
Chapter 2, Problems, algorithms, and complexity, p. 14
source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The many-one and Turing clauses are standard, but parsimonious reductions are commonly defined by preservation of solution counts rather than necessarily by a polynomial-time bijection. The cited general complexity chapters do not clearly support this exact three-family taxonomy, and the conclusion's suggestion of progressive preservation guarantees is potentially misleading because Turing reductions preserve less instance structure.

children.title: Structure-Preserving Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions that preserve selected graph, coefficient, or formulation structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonvacuity requirement for a parameter-based structure-preservation notion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(|f(I)|\le p(|I|)\) and every target instance \(J\) satisfies \(\kappa(J)\le |J|^d\) for fixed \(d\). Then \(\kappa(f(I))\le p(|I|)^d\). Thus allowing an arbitrary polynomial dependence on total source length makes the proposed preservation condition automatic for every polynomial-output reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural bound allowing arbitrary polynomial dependence on total source length may be vacuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa(f(I))\le p(|I|)^d,\text{ so unrestricted polynomial dependence on }|I|\text{ does not express preservation.}
knowledge_statements.title: Vacuity of Unrestricted Source-Length Bounds

assumptions_latex: A structural parameter is defined on both source and target instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reduction preserves the selected structure when target size and every designated parameter are polynomially bounded functions of the source size and parameters.
review_flags: The exact structural parameters must be specialized for each reduction application.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A parameterized definition covering sparsity, width, degree, and block or network structure.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6, Complexity and Problem Reductions, p. 95

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) reduce binary instances of \(A\) to binary instances of \(B\), and let \(\kappa_1,\ldots,\kappa_r\) be designated structural parameters, such as incidence width, maximum degree, sparsity, or block count. The reduction is structure-preserving for these parameters if it preserves answer truth and there exist polynomials \(p_0,p_1,\ldots,p_r\) such that
\[
|f(I)|\leq p_0(|I|),\qquad \kappa_j(f(I))\leq p_j(|I|,\kappa_1(I),\ldots,\kappa_r(I))
\]
for every instance \(I\) and every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduction is structure-preserving when it preserves the answer and polynomially bounds target size and each chosen structural parameter in terms of the source.
knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Preserving Reductions

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, Complexity and Problem Reductions, p. 95

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition is coherent but not a standard structure-preserving reduction notion without fixing the parameters and their intended preservation regime. Allowing each target parameter to depend polynomially on the full source length can make the structural condition nearly vacuous, and the cited general reductions chapter does not specifically support this formulation.

children.title: Reduction-Induced Encoding Growth
children.top_down_role: Representation growth caused by reductions between binary problem families.

assumptions_latex: All numerical data are encoded in binary.
The reduction explicitly constructs every target variable, constraint, and coefficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial-time constructibility implies polynomial target bit length, but does not imply linear growth or polynomial bounds on coefficient magnitudes themselves.

notation.meaning: Source and target binary encoding lengths

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates total bit-length growth from numerical coefficient-magnitude growth.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3, Linear algebra and complexity, p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6, Complexity and Problem Reductions, p. 95

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be an explicitly constructive reduction running in time \(T(N)\) on an input of binary length \(N\). Its output length satisfies \(M=|f(I)|\leq T(N)\). Consequently, a polynomial-time reduction has polynomial total encoding growth. If \(C_{\max}(f(I))\) is the largest target coefficient magnitude, then only
\[
\log_2(C_{\max}(f(I))+1)\leq M
\]
is automatic. Thus polynomial bit length permits exponentially large coefficient values and does not by itself guarantee strong polynomiality or linear-size growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constructive polynomial-time reduction has polynomial output bit length, but its numerical coefficients may still have exponentially large magnitudes and its output need not grow linearly.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduction-Induced Encoding Growth

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 3, Linear algebra and complexity, p. 27
source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6, Complexity and Problem Reductions, p. 95

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition law for total output length, distinct from preservation of finer structural parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(|f(I)|\le p(|I|)\) and \(|g(J)|\le q(|J|)\), where \(q\) is nondecreasing, then \(|g(f(I))|\le q(p(|I|))\). Hence polynomial output-length bounds are closed under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Output-length bounds compose, so a composition of polynomial-output reductions still has polynomial output length.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) and \(q\) are output-length bounds, and \(q\) is nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |g(f(I))|\le q(p(|I|));\text{ polynomial }p,q\text{ imply polynomial encoding growth.}
knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Encoding-Growth Bounds

The output is \(\min_{x\in X}c(x)\), and the algorithm uses at most \(\lceil\log_2(U-L+1)\rceil\) oracle calls.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-to-Optimization Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-oracle equivalence for well-described rational polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a class of nonempty, bounded, well-described rational polytopes \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with polynomially bounded facet complexity. Given a polynomial-time strong separation oracle that, for rational \(y\), either confirms \(y\in P\) or returns rational \(a,\beta\) satisfying \(a^\top y>\beta\ge a^\top x\) for every \(x\in P\), the ellipsoid method computes, for every rational \(c\), a point \(x^*\in P\) attaining \(\max\{c^\top x:x\in P\}\) in time polynomial in the encoding lengths of \(P\) and \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For well-described bounded rational polytopes, a polynomial-time strong separation oracle yields polynomial-time exact linear optimization through the ellipsoid method.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is nonempty, bounded, rational, and well described.
The separation oracle returns polynomial-encoding rational separating inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong separation implies exact linear optimization in oracle-polynomial time.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse direction of exact optimization-separation equivalence for well-described rational polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty well-described rational polytope \(P\), exact linear-optimization access for every \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\) permits strong separation: for each \(y\in\mathbb Q^n\), one can either certify \(y\in P\) or return rational \(a,\beta\) satisfying \(a^\top y>\beta\ge a^\top x\) for all \(x\in P\), using polynomially many oracle operations and polynomial-bit arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact linear optimization over a well-described rational polytope yields polynomial-time strong separation.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty well-described rational polytope.
The exact optimization oracle supports rational objectives and polynomially encoded outputs.
The class supplies the standard polynomial encoding bounds required by oracle equivalence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Exact linear optimization implements strong separation with polynomial oracle and bit complexity.}
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-to-Separation Direction

children.title: Oracle-Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Encoding, access, or representation conditions limiting the equivalence relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Equivalence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which separation and optimization are not automatically polynomially equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The separation–optimization equivalence is not an unconditional statement about arbitrary sets or oracle encodings. The standard polynomial reduction requires a rational convex body or polytope with controlled encoding complexity and suitable radius or facet-complexity bounds. It also distinguishes strong exact oracles from weak approximate oracles. If convexity, rational representability, polynomial output length, or the required geometric bounds are absent, a separation response may not support polynomial-time exact optimization; for discrete \(S\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), separation applies naturally to \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\), not merely to membership in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle equivalence needs convexity, controlled encoding, geometric bounds, and compatible exactness; membership in a discrete feasible set is not a separation oracle for its convex hull.
assumptions_latex: The computational cost includes oracle calls and the bit lengths of oracle outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dropping the standard representation or oracle hypotheses invalidates the general polynomial-equivalence guarantee.

notation.meaning: convex hull of the feasible set
