assumptions_latex: Complexity is measured relative to an oracle interface for a rational polytope.
The cost of implementing an oracle and the bit length of its answers are not automatically charged as one unit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polynomial number of oracle calls implies polynomial-time solvability only when every call and returned certificate has polynomial bit complexity. Moreover, polynomial-time separation need not imply polynomial extension complexity; implicit access and compact explicit formulation are distinct resources.

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of the original instance.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: oracle-call complexity must be distinguished from bit complexity and formulation size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes oracle calls, oracle implementation cost, and explicit formulation size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an algorithm accesses \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) only through an oracle and makes \(\operatorname{poly}(L)\) calls, where \(L\) is the instance encoding length. This call bound yields a polynomial-time algorithm only if each oracle call is implementable in \(\operatorname{poly}(L)\) time and every returned rational certificate has \(\operatorname{poly}(L)\) bit length. Treating an arbitrary oracle response as unit cost can conceal exponential computation or encoding. Separately, efficient separation does not force \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\) to be polynomial: implicit algorithmic access and a polynomial-size exact linear extension measure different representational resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Few oracle calls are meaningful only with efficient, polynomial-bit oracle answers, and efficient separation does not guarantee a compact exact extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-Access Complexity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle-call versus bit-complexity warning is precise and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The additional assertion that efficient separation can coexist with superpolynomial extension complexity is nontrivial and needs an authoritative source or a specifically cited example family.

children.title: Binary Symmetry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural symmetry patterns in binary formulations and search spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(R\) are coordinate- and row-permutation matrices, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Px\in X\) and \(c^\top Px=c^\top x\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Permutation matrix acting on binary variables.
Permutation matrix acting on constraint rows.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable sufficient certificate that a coordinate permutation is a symmetry of a binary linear model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\le b\}\) with objective \(c^\top x\). Let \(P\) be a coordinate-permutation matrix. If there is a row-permutation matrix \(R\) such that \(AP=RA\), \(Rb=b\), and \(P^\top c=c\), then \(x\mapsto Px\) preserves \(X\) and the objective value. Hence \(P\) is an instance symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable permutation is certified as a symmetry when it merely permutes the constraint rows, preserves their right-hand sides, and leaves the objective coefficients unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Row-Permutation Certificate for Binary Linear Symmetry
knowledge_statements.title: Row-Permutation Certificate for Binary Linear Symmetry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semantic Symmetry Need Not Admit the Row-Permutation Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of necessity for the syntactic row-permutation certificate when redundant constraints break literal row symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^2:x_1+x_2\le1,\ x_1\le1\}\) and let the objective be zero. The transposition \(P(x_1,x_2)=(x_2,x_1)\) preserves \(X\) and the objective because the second inequality is redundant on the binary domain. For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(b=(1,1)^\top\), however, \(AP=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\ne RA\) for either row-permutation matrix \(R\). Thus the row-permutation certificate is sufficient but not necessary for semantic instance symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A redundant asymmetric row can prevent literal row-permutation symmetry even though swapping the variables preserves the binary feasible set and objective.
assumptions_latex: The binary domain is part of the formulation.
Symmetry is defined semantically by preservation of the feasible set and objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is a semantic symmetry, but no row permutation }R\text{ satisfies }AP=RA\text{ and }Rb=b.

notation.meaning: Permutation interchanging the two binary coordinates.
Permutation matrix acting on the two displayed constraint rows.

knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Symmetry Need Not Admit the Row-Permutation Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic structure of all coordinate permutations preserving a fixed binary feasible set and objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\). Define \[\operatorname{Sym}(X,f)=\{g\in S_n:gX=X\text{ and }f(gx)=f(x)\ \forall x\in X\}.\] Then \(\operatorname{Sym}(X,f)\) is a subgroup of \(S_n\) and is contained in \(\operatorname{Aut}(X)=\{g\in S_n:gX=X\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coordinate permutations preserving both feasibility and objective value form a subgroup of the symmetric group and a subgroup of the feasible-set automorphism group.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Sym}(X,f)\le\operatorname{Aut}(X)\le S_n.

notation.meaning: Coordinate-symmetry group of the optimization instance.
Coordinate permutations preserving the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Group Structure of Coordinate Symmetries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible-Set Automorphism Need Not Preserve the Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict boundary between symmetries of the feasible binary set and symmetries of the full optimization instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{0,1\}^2\) and \(f(x)=x_1\). The coordinate transposition \(g(x_1,x_2)=(x_2,x_1)\) satisfies \(gX=X\), but \(f(g(1,0))=0\ne1=f(1,0)\). Hence \(g\in\operatorname{Aut}(X)\) but \(g\notin\operatorname{Sym}(X,f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate permutation can preserve every feasible binary point while changing the objective, so feasible-set symmetry is weaker than optimization-instance symmetry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\in\operatorname{Aut}(X)\setminus\operatorname{Sym}(X,f).

notation.meaning: Coordinate automorphism group of the feasible set.
Coordinate symmetries preserving feasibility and objective value.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Automorphism Need Not Preserve the Objective

assumptions_latex: A finite group \(G\) acts on \(\{0,1\}^n\) by permutations of coordinates.
The feasible set \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) and objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) are invariant under this action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in X\), the orbit \(Gx=\{g x:g\in G\}\) lies in \(X\), and \(f(y)=f(x)\) for all \(y\in Gx\). Thus optimization may be restricted to one representative per orbit without changing the optimal value.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard group-action definition of optimization symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-permutation symmetries preserving feasibility and objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and let a finite group \(G\) act by permuting coordinates. The instance is in a binary symmetry regime with group \(G\) when \(g x\in X\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(g\in G\). The orbit of \(x\) is \(Gx=\{gx:g\in G\}\), and all of its members are equivalent feasible solutions having the same objective value. Consequently, replacing each orbit by any one representative preserves the set of attainable objective values and hence the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary symmetry regime has a coordinate-permutation group preserving feasibility and objective value, so every orbit consists of equivalent solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Symmetry Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The group action, invariance conditions, orbit notation, and optimization consequence are consistent, and definition fits the Binary Symmetry Regimes leaf. No inspectable authoritative source is supplied for the optimization-symmetry definition and orbit-representative consequence.

children.title: Equivalent-Solution Multiplicity
children.top_down_role: Search redundancy caused by multiple representations of equivalent binary solutions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S/G|=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{Fix}_S(g)|\).

notation.meaning: Set of symmetry orbits in the solution set.
Solutions in S fixed by the group element g.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Count of symmetry-equivalence classes inside a finite invariant feasible or optimal solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act on a finite \(G\)-invariant set \(S\) of binary solutions. For \(g\in G\), let \(\operatorname{Fix}_S(g)=\{x\in S:gx=x\}\). The number of distinct solution orbits is \[|S/G|=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{Fix}_S(g)|.\] If \(S\) is the optimal-solution set of a \(G\)-invariant instance, this is the number of inequivalent optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Burnside's lemma counts inequivalent feasible or optimal solutions by averaging the number fixed by each symmetry.
knowledge_statements.title: Burnside Count of Equivalent-Solution Classes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Large Symmetry Group with Unit Solution Multiplicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp stabilizer boundary showing that group order alone does not determine equivalent-solution multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_n\) act on \(\{0,1\}^n\) by coordinate permutations and take \(x=0^n\). Every permutation fixes \(x\), so \((S_n)_x=S_n\) and \(S_nx=\{x\}\). Hence \(|S_n|=n!\) while the multiplicity contributed by \(x\) is one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The all-zero vector is fixed by every coordinate permutation, so a factorial-size symmetry group can produce an orbit of size one.
assumptions_latex: The selected feasible or optimal solution is \(x=0^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |(S_n)_x|=n!\quad\text{and}\quad |S_nx|=1.

notation.meaning: Symmetric group on the coordinate set.

knowledge_statements.title: Large Symmetry Group with Unit Solution Multiplicity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence-class formulation of symmetry-induced solution multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(G\) act on a \(G\)-invariant set \(S\). Define \(x\sim_G y\) if and only if \(y=gx\) for some \(g\in G\). Then \(\sim_G\) is an equivalence relation, its class at \(x\) is \(Gx\), and \[S=\biguplus_{O\in S/G}O.\] If \(S\) is finite, then \(|S|=\sum_{O\in S/G}|O|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetry equivalence partitions a solution set into disjoint orbits whose sizes sum to the total number of solutions.
assumptions_latex: For the cardinality identity, \(S\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\biguplus_{O\in S/G}O,\qquad |S|=\sum_{O\in S/G}|O|\text{ when }S\text{ is finite}.
knowledge_statements.title: Orbit Equivalence and Solution-Class Partition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: The Number of Equivalent Optima Need Not Be Divisible by the Group Order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary caused by optimal orbits with different stabilizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=S_2\) act on \(\{0,1\}^2\) by interchanging coordinates, and let the optimal-solution set be \(S=\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\}\). Then \(S\) is \(G\)-invariant and decomposes into the orbits \(\{(0,0)\}\) and \(\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\). Consequently \(|S|=3\), which is not divisible by \(|G|=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different optimal solutions can have different stabilizers, so the total number of optima need not be a multiple of the symmetry-group order.

notation.meaning: Set of symmetry orbits in the optimal-solution set.

knowledge_statements.title: The Number of Equivalent Optima Need Not Be Divisible by the Group Order

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Multiplicity under a Free Symmetry Action
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equal equivalent-solution multiplicity when no nonidentity symmetry fixes a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act freely on a finite \(G\)-invariant set \(S\), meaning that \(gx=x\) for \(x\in S\) implies \(g=e\). Then every stabilizer is trivial, every orbit has cardinality \(|G|\), and \(|S|=|G|\,|S/G|\). If \(S\) is the optimal-solution set of a \(G\)-invariant binary instance, every inequivalent optimum represents exactly \(|G|\) distinct optimal binary vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A free symmetry action gives every solution orbit the full group size, so the total number of solutions is the group order times the number of inequivalent solutions.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is a finite }G\text{-invariant solution set}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in S:\ |Gx|=|G|,\qquad |S|=|G|\,|S/G|.

notation.meaning: Set of symmetry-equivalence classes in S.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Multiplicity under a Free Symmetry Action

assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(F\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) and objective \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\) are \(G\)-invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point in an optimal orbit is an equivalent optimal solution, and the multiplicity contributed by \(x\) equals \(|G|/|G_x|\).

notation.meaning: Orbit of a feasible point under the group action

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite symmetry groups acting on binary feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(x\in F\), invariance gives \(Gx\subseteq F\) and \(f(y)=f(x)\) for every \(y\in Gx\). Hence, if \(x\) is optimal, every member of \(Gx\) is an equivalent optimal solution. By orbit-stabilizer counting, \[|Gx|=\frac{|G|}{|G_x|}.\] Thus one optimal representative may correspond to \(|G|/|G_x|\) distinct binary optima; multiplicity is largest when the stabilizer is small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetry orbit of one optimum consists entirely of optima, with multiplicity equal to the group order divided by the stabilizer order.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent-Solution Multiplicity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orbit-invariance and orbit-stabilizer claims are mathematically precise and fit the property container, but no inspectable citation supports them.

children.title: Orbit Growth
children.top_down_role: Growth patterns in symmetry orbits as binary model size increases.

assumptions_latex: \(S_n\) acts on \(\{0,1\}^n\) by all coordinate permutations.
The selected vector has Hamming weight \(k\).
For the asymptotic statement, \(k=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\) with fixed \(0<\alpha<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S_nx|=\binom nk\), and \(\log|S_nx|=nH(\alpha)+O(\log n)\) at fixed positive density; for central weight, \(|S_nx|=\Theta(2^n/\sqrt n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical exponential orbit family generated by coordinate permutations of fixed-density binary vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_n\) act on \(\{0,1\}^n\) by coordinate permutations, and let \(x\) have Hamming weight \(k\). Then \[|S_nx|=\binom{n}{k}.\] If \(k=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\) for fixed \(0<\alpha<1\), then \[\log |S_nx|=nH(\alpha)+O(\log n),\qquad H(\alpha)=-\alpha\log\alpha-(1-\alpha)\log(1-\alpha).\] In particular, for \(k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), \(|S_nx|=\Theta(2^n/\sqrt n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under all coordinate permutations, a weight-k binary vector has binomial orbit size. Fixed positive density gives exponential growth, with central weight producing order 2^n divided by square root n.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Weight Orbit Growth under Full Coordinate Symmetry
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Weight Orbit Growth under Full Coordinate Symmetry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic classification of selected orbit sizes across a family of binary instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For actions \(G_n\curvearrowright F_n\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) and selected points \(x_n\in F_n\), the orbit sequence has polynomial growth when there exist constants \(C>0\), \(k\ge0\), and \(n_0\) such that \(|G_nx_n|\le Cn^k\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). It has superpolynomial growth when for every \(C>0\), \(k\ge0\), and \(n_0\), there exists \(n\ge n_0\) such that \(|G_nx_n|>Cn^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orbit growth is polynomial when one fixed polynomial eventually bounds the selected orbits; it is superpolynomial when no such eventual polynomial bound exists.
assumptions_latex: For each \(n\), a finite group \(G_n\) acts on \(F_n\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\).
A point \(x_n\in F_n\) is selected for each \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Polynomial growth}\iff\exists C,k,n_0\ \forall n\ge n_0:\ |G_nx_n|\le Cn^k.

notation.meaning: Selected orbit at instance size n.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial and Superpolynomial Orbit Growth

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Fixed-Weight Orbits Have Polynomial Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-growth counterpart to fixed-density exponential orbits under full coordinate symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_n\) act on \(\{0,1\}^n\) by coordinate permutations. If \(x_n\) has fixed Hamming weight \(k\), then \[|S_nx_n|=\binom nk=\frac{n^k}{k!}+O(n^{k-1})=\Theta(n^k).\] More generally, if the Hamming weights satisfy \(k_n\le k\) for a fixed \(k\), then \(|S_nx_n|=O(n^k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under full coordinate symmetry, uniformly bounded Hamming weight produces polynomial orbit growth.
assumptions_latex: The selected vectors have uniformly bounded Hamming weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k_n\le k\Longrightarrow |S_nx_n|=\binom n{k_n}=O(n^k),\quad k_n=k\Longrightarrow |S_nx_n|=\Theta(n^k).

notation.meaning: Hamming weight of the selected vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Fixed-Weight Orbits Have Polynomial Growth

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Orbit Growth of an Action Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case orbit-size regime over all feasible points at each instance size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite actions \(G_n\curvearrowright F_n\), define \(M_n=\max_{x\in F_n}|G_nx|\) whenever \(F_n\ne\varnothing\). The family has polynomial maximum-orbit growth when \(M_n\le Cn^k\) eventually for some constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge0\), and exponential maximum-orbit growth when \(M_n\ge c^n\) eventually for some \(c>1\). This worst-case classification differs from the growth of a preselected orbit sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum-orbit growth classifies an action family by its largest feasible orbit at each size rather than by a selected sequence of points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_n=\max_{x\in F_n}|G_nx|\le2^n.

notation.meaning: Largest feasible orbit at size n.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Orbit Growth of an Action Family

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum Orbit under Full Coordinate Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact largest orbit and its asymptotic size for the full symmetric-group action on the binary cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the action of \(S_n\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\) by coordinate permutations, orbit size depends only on Hamming weight: \(|S_nx|=\binom{n}{|x|_1}\). Consequently, \[\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}|S_nx|=\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}=\Theta\!\left(\frac{2^n}{\sqrt n}\right).\] The maximum is attained exactly at weight \(n/2\) when \(n\) is even and at weights \((n-1)/2\) and \((n+1)/2\) when \(n\) is odd.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For full coordinate symmetry, the largest binary orbit is the central Hamming layer and has order 2 to the n divided by square root n.
assumptions_latex: S_n\text{ acts on }\{0,1\}^n\text{ by coordinate permutations}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_x|S_nx|=\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}=\Theta(2^n/\sqrt n).
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Orbit under Full Coordinate Symmetry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intermediate Growth of Sparse Unbounded-Weight Orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit superpolynomial but subexponential orbit family under full coordinate symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_n\) act on \(\{0,1\}^n\) by coordinate permutations, and let \(x_n\) have Hamming weight \(k_n=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\). Then \[|S_nx_n|=\binom{n}{k_n},\qquad \log|S_nx_n|=\Theta(\sqrt n\log n).\] Hence this orbit sequence is superpolynomial and subexponential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weight about square root n gives binomial orbits larger than every polynomial but smaller than every fixed-base exponential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |S_nx_n|=\exp(\Theta(\sqrt n\log n))=n^{\Theta(\sqrt n)}=e^{o(n)}.

notation.meaning: Hamming weight of the selected binary vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate Growth of Sparse Unbounded-Weight Orbits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic boundary between polynomial or intermediate growth and exponential selected-orbit growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite actions \(G_n\curvearrowright F_n\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) and selected \(x_n\in F_n\), the orbit sequence has subexponential growth when \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log |G_nx_n|}{n}=0,\] equivalently when \(|G_nx_n|=e^{o(n)}\). This permits polynomial and superpolynomial growth but excludes every eventual lower bound \(|G_nx_n|\ge c^n\) with fixed \(c>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subexponential orbit growth means logarithmic orbit size is little-o of the binary dimension; it may still be superpolynomial.
assumptions_latex: Each \(G_n\) is finite and acts on \(F_n\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\).
A point \(x_n\in F_n\) is selected for each \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |G_nx_n|=e^{o(n)}\Longleftrightarrow \lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\log|G_nx_n|=0.

notation.meaning: Selected orbit at binary dimension n.

knowledge_statements.title: Subexponential Orbit Growth
Orbit Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic growth of symmetry orbits in binary-instance families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence \(x_n\in F_n\), orbit-stabilizer counting gives \[|G_nx_n|=\frac{|G_n|}{|(G_n)_{x_n}|}.\] The orbit sequence has exponential growth when there exist constants \(c>1\) and \(n_0\) such that \(|G_nx_n|\ge c^n\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). Because \(G_nx_n\subseteq F_n\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), every such orbit also satisfies \(|G_nx_n|\le 2^n\); thus a factorial-size acting group can have only a correspondingly large stabilizer on these binary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orbit size equals the acting-group order divided by the stabilizer order. Binary orbits can grow exponentially but cannot exceed the 2^n points in the binary cube.
assumptions_latex: For every positive integer \(n\), a finite group \(G_n\) acts on a set \(F_n\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\).
For every \(n\), a point \(x_n\in F_n\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(n\), \(|G_nx_n|=|G_n|/|(G_n)_{x_n}|\le 2^n\), with exponential orbit growth characterized by a uniform lower bound \(|G_nx_n|\ge c^n\) for some \(c>1\).

notation.meaning: Orbit of the selected binary feasible point
Stabilizer of the selected binary feasible point

children.title: Symmetry-Induced Search Redundancy
children.top_down_role: Search-tree and neighborhood redundancy caused by large equivalence classes.

assumptions_latex: \(d\) binary variables are interchangeable under coordinate permutations.
The residual subproblem is determined by the Hamming weight of their fixed values.
The procedure materializes every node of the depth-\(d\) frontier without orbit identification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The frontier contains exactly \(2^d-(d+1)\) nodes beyond one representative for each of its \(d+1\) symmetry orbits.

notation.meaning: Number of interchangeable binary branching decisions already fixed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact combinatorial redundancy count for a fully materialized symmetric binary branching frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a complete binary branching frontier after fixing \(d\) interchangeable binary variables. Suppose the residual subproblem depends on their partial assignment only through the number of fixed ones. The frontier has \(2^d\) nodes but exactly \(d+1\) symmetry orbits, indexed by Hamming weights \(0,\ldots,d\). Therefore any procedure that materializes every frontier node without identifying symmetric nodes materializes \[2^d-(d+1)\] nodes beyond one representative per orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When d interchangeable branching decisions matter only through their number of ones, the full frontier has 2^d nodes but only d+1 distinct subproblem types, yielding exponential representational redundancy.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Symmetric-Frontier Redundancy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Representative Pruning of Symmetric Search States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness-preserving duplicate-state pruning under exact canonicalization and equivariant search transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\kappa\) map each complete solver state to a canonical form such that \(\kappa(s)=\kappa(s')\) exactly when \(s\) and \(s'\) are solver-state symmetry equivalent. Maintain the canonical forms of retained representatives. When a state \(s\) is generated, discard it if an equivalent retained representative already exists; otherwise retain and process \(s\). If branching, bounding, pruning, and learning are equivariant and every discarded state's unexplored continuations correspond bijectively to continuations of its retained representative, then the reduced search preserves feasibility detection and the global optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonicalize complete solver states and retain one representative per symmetry class; correctness requires equivariant search operations and coverage of every discarded state's continuations.
assumptions_latex: Canonical forms identify exactly the solver-state equivalence classes.
Branching, bounding, pruning, and learning are equivariant.
Every discarded state's unexplored continuations correspond to those of a retained representative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{At most one retained representative per canonical class is required, without changing feasibility detection or the optimal value.}

notation.meaning: Canonical-form map on complete solver states.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Representative Pruning of Symmetric Search States

knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-aware equivalence required before conclusions from one symmetric search node may be reused at another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two search nodes \(u\) and \(v\) are solver-state symmetry equivalent under a bijection \(g\) when \(g\) maps the node domains and feasible completions of \(u\) bijectively onto those of \(v\), preserves objective values and relaxation bounds, and transports every retained cut, incumbent-dependent restriction, branching datum, and learned object used at \(u\) to a valid corresponding object at \(v\). Only under these conditions may state-dependent conclusions obtained at one node be reused at the other through \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric node domains are informationally interchangeable only when bounds, cuts, branching data, incumbent-dependent restrictions, and learned information are transported consistently.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is a bijection between the node-variable labelings.
Every state component used for pruning or learning is included in the equivalence relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\sim_g v\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{every valid state-dependent conclusion at }u\text{ transports to a valid conclusion at }v.

notation.meaning: Solver-state symmetry equivalence under relabeling g.

knowledge_statements.title: Solver-State Equivalence of Search Nodes

assumptions_latex: A branch-and-bound search contains nodes whose subproblems are transformed into one another by an objective- and feasibility-preserving group action.
No symmetry-breaking rule identifies or eliminates nodes in the same orbit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All but one processed node in each node orbit are symmetry-redundant, totaling \(|\mathcal O|-1\) redundant nodes for an orbit \(\mathcal O\).

notation.meaning: Orbit of mutually symmetric search nodes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundancy measured among symmetry-equivalent branch-and-bound subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\) be an orbit of search nodes under a symmetry action, so every pair of nodes in \(\mathcal O\) has isomorphic feasible completions and the same relaxation bound after relabeling. Processing one representative supplies, up to that relabeling, the information supplied by every other member. Consequently, if all members are processed separately, exactly \(|\mathcal O|-1\) processed nodes are symmetry-redundant. Growing node orbits can therefore translate directly into growing redundant search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without symmetry handling, processing every node in an orbit repeats equivalent subproblems; all but one node per orbit are redundant.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Induced Search Redundancy

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim fits a failure-boundary container, but the assertion that one processed representative supplies all information from every symmetric node depends on the solver's state, learning, and symmetry handling. No source establishes the stated exact redundancy count.

children.title: Degenerate Relaxation Optima
children.top_down_role: Covers relaxation faces with many equivalent optima that obscure variable discrimination.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates primal basic-solution degeneracy from multiplicity of optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear program \(\min\{x_1:x_1+x_2=0,\ x\ge0\}\) has the unique feasible and optimal point \((0,0)\). Its equality matrix has rank \(m=1\), while the optimum has no positive component, so its optimal basic feasible solution is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear relaxation can have a unique optimum that is nevertheless degenerate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{optimal degeneracy}\not\Longrightarrow\text{multiple optimal solutions}.
knowledge_statements.title: Unique Optimum With Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiple Optima Without Degenerate Optimal Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates multiplicity of optimal solutions from primal basic-solution degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear program \(\min\{0:x_1+x_2=1,\ x\ge0\}\) has the entire feasible segment as its optimal set. Its basic feasible solutions \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) each have one positive component, equal to the row rank \(m=1\), and are nondegenerate. Hence it has multiple optima but no degenerate optimal basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear relaxation may have many optimal solutions although all its optimal basic feasible solutions are nondegenerate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{multiple optimal solutions}\not\Longrightarrow\text{a degenerate optimal basic feasible solution}.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Optima Without Degenerate Optimal Bases
Degenerate Relaxation Optima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form linear-relaxation degeneracy at an optimal basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the standard-form relaxation \[\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\] where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\). An optimal basic feasible solution \(x^*\) is degenerate when it has fewer than \(m\) positive components, equivalently when at least one variable in an associated basis has value zero. The relaxation has a degenerate optimum when it admits such an optimal basic feasible solution. This condition is distinct from merely having multiple optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear relaxation has a degenerate optimum when it admits an optimal basic feasible solution with fewer positive components than the number of independent equality constraints; this is different from having multiple optima.
assumptions_latex: The matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), and the relaxation has an optimal basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal basic feasible solution \(x^*\) is degenerate exactly when it has fewer than \(m\) positive components; the relaxation has a degenerate optimum when it admits such a solution.

notation.meaning: Rank and number of independent equality constraints

children.title: Weak Pseudocost Signals
children.top_down_role: Covers unreliable pseudocost information arising from limited or uninformative branching observations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional pseudocost observations for a fractional binary variable at a minimization node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a node with relaxation bound \(z\) and \(\bar x_j\in(0,1)\), let finite child bounds be \(z_j^0\) after imposing \(x_j=0\) and \(z_j^1\) after imposing \(x_j=1\). The directional observations are \[p_j^0=\frac{z_j^0-z}{\bar x_j},\qquad p_j^1=\frac{z_j^1-z}{1-\bar x_j}.\] Historical directional estimates may be formed from such normalized observations, yielding predicted gains \(\widehat p_j^0\bar x_j\) and \(\widehat p_j^1(1-\bar x_j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directional pseudocost observation divides child-bound improvement by the fractional displacement in that branch direction.
assumptions_latex: The parent and child values are valid minimization lower bounds from comparable node relaxations.
\(0<\bar x_j<1\), and the relevant child bounds are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_j^0=(z_j^0-z)/\bar x_j,\qquad p_j^1=(z_j^1-z)/(1-\bar x_j).

notation.meaning: Fractional relaxation value of binary variable j

knowledge_statements.title: Displacement-Normalized Pseudocost Observations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions preventing historical pseudocost estimates from being treated as reliable predictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directional pseudocost estimate with no observations is undefined. Estimates based on few, stale, or highly variable observations have no general deterministic accuracy guarantee at a new node, and degeneracy can produce zero observed bound improvement despite nontrivial child subproblems. Reliability thresholds and strong-branching fallbacks are algorithm-dependent safeguards, not certificates of prediction accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse, variable, stale, or zero-gain pseudocost histories are weak predictive evidence and carry no general accuracy guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Pseudocosts are estimated from historical branching observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{limited, stale, or variable history}\Longrightarrow\text{no general guaranteed accuracy for the next branching-gain prediction}.
knowledge_statements.title: Pseudocost Reliability Boundary

assumptions_latex: For a minimization node with bound \(z\), branching on binary variable \(x_j\) yields child bounds \(z_j^0\) and \(z_j^1\).
The observed bound changes are finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pseudocost signal is weak when both estimated directional gains are small or statistically unreliable relative to the branching tolerance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational condition for weak binary-variable pseudocost information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: From observations \(\Delta_{j,t}^b\) in direction \(b\in\{0,1\}\), let \(\widehat p_j^b\) be their sample mean and \(s_j^b\) their sample standard deviation. For tolerances \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(r>0\), the signal for \(x_j\) is weak if \[\max_{b\in\{0,1\}}\widehat p_j^b\le\varepsilon\quad\text{or}\quad\max_{b\in\{0,1\}}\frac{s_j^b}{\max\{\widehat p_j^b,\varepsilon\}}\ge r.\] The first condition captures negligible improvement; the second captures unreliable variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudocost signal is weak when estimated child-bound gains are negligible or vary too much relative to their estimated size.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Pseudocost Signals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed statistic uses unnormalized child-bound changes, whereas standard pseudocosts normally account for the variable's fractional displacement. The reliability ratio and thresholds are solver-dependent and require a source before this formula can be treated as a pseudocost condition.

children.title: Branching Score Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Covers regimes where candidate variables receive nearly indistinguishable branching scores.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completion of a score-based branching policy when the score maximizer is not unique at the adopted tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When \(|M_\tau|\ge2\), a score-based branching policy requires an additional selection rule. A deterministic total order gives reproducible selection, while randomized tie-breaking specifies a probability distribution over \(M_\tau\). Neither choice strengthens the underlying score evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambiguous branching score requires a deterministic or randomized tie-break, which selects a candidate without resolving the weak information.
assumptions_latex: The ambiguity set contains at least two admissible branching candidates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |M_\tau|\ge2\Longrightarrow\text{an additional rule is required for single-valued selection}.

notation.meaning: Candidates within the adopted tolerance of the best score

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Breaking Requirement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits on conclusions drawn from tied or nearly tied branching scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Candidates within tolerance under a selected score are indistinguishable only under that score, aggregation convention, scale, and tolerance. This does not imply equal child bounds, subtree sizes, or runtimes. Rescaling the scores without rescaling \(\tau\), or changing the aggregation rule, can change \(M_\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A score tie says only that the selected scoring rule does not distinguish the candidates; it does not make their search consequences equal.
assumptions_latex: Candidate scores are compared using a specified aggregation rule, scale, and tolerance \(\tau\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: i,j\in M_\tau\not\Longrightarrow\text{equal child bounds, subtree sizes, or runtimes}.
knowledge_statements.title: Score Ambiguity Is Rule-Relative

assumptions_latex: A finite candidate set \(J\) has branching scores \(S_j\in\mathbb{R}\).
A nonnegative comparison tolerance \(\tau\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Branching is score-ambiguous exactly when at least two candidates lie within \(\tau\) of the best score.

notation.meaning: Set of candidates indistinguishable from the best score at tolerance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based ambiguity for maximized branching scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^*=\max_{j\in J}S_j\) and define \[M_\tau=\{j\in J:S^*-S_j\le\tau\}.\] The branching score is \(\tau\)-ambiguous when \(|M_\tau|\ge2\). At \(\tau=0\), this is an exact tie for the maximum. For \(\tau>0\), it records candidates whose score differences are too small to distinguish under the adopted numerical or statistical tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching decision is ambiguous when two or more candidates tie, or fall within a chosen tolerance of the best score.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching Score Ambiguity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tolerance-based tie condition is internally correct and fits the condition container, but it is a chosen operational definition rather than a source-supported standard notion.

children.title: Search-Tree Consequences
children.top_down_role: Covers tree growth, unstable variable selection, and delayed progress attributable to weak branching guidance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degeneracy Does Not Imply Exponential Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary on attributing large search trees to degeneracy or weak branching guidance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Degeneracy, weak pseudocosts, and tied branching scores do not individually or jointly force a large search tree. A degenerate instance can still be fathomed at the root by infeasibility, integrality, or a matching incumbent bound. Exponential complete-subtree growth requires additional conditions preventing pruning over many branching levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degeneracy and weak branching guidance may contribute to a large tree but do not prove one; persistent failure of pruning is additionally required.
assumptions_latex: The branch-and-bound method uses valid node pruning tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{degeneracy or score ambiguity}\not\Longrightarrow N=2^{\Omega(d)}.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Does Not Imply Exponential Search

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tie-Breaking Can Change the Generated Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of search-tree consequences on the complete branching policy under ambiguous scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When distinct branching candidates are equally preferred by the adopted score, different admissible tie-breaking choices can create different child relaxations and subsequent pruning decisions. Generated tree size and processing order therefore depend on the instance together with the complete branching and node-selection policy, not on the tied score vector alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different tie-breaks among equally scored variables can generate different search trees.
assumptions_latex: At some node, at least two distinct branching candidates are score-maximal.
The candidates induce different branching disjunctions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{equal scores}\not\Longrightarrow\text{identical generated search trees}.
knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Breaking Can Change the Generated Tree

assumptions_latex: A binary branch-and-bound subtree branches twice at each internal node through depth \(d\).
No node at depths \(0,dots,d-1\) is pruned by bounds, infeasibility, integrality, or dominance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subtree contains \(2^{d+1}-1\) processed nodes and \(2^d\) depth-\(d\) leaves.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case node count caused by complete binary branching without pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At depth \(k\), complete binary branching creates \(2^k\) nodes. Therefore the number of processed nodes through depth \(d\) is \[N_d=\sum_{k=0}^{d}2^k=2^{d+1}-1,\] including \(2^d\) leaves at depth \(d\). Thus, whenever degeneracy and uninformative branching prevent all pruning for \(d\) successive levels, the corresponding search effort is exponential in \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If binary branching proceeds for d levels without pruning, the resulting complete subtree has 2^(d+1)-1 nodes.
knowledge_statements.title: Search-Tree Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complete-binary-tree count is mathematically correct and the complexity-bound kind fits the container, but the candidate supplies no citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Dense Conflict Graphs
children.top_down_role: Covers high-density incompatibility structures among binary decisions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflict-graph convention with one vertex for each represented binary literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\{x_i,\neg x_i:1\le i\le n\}\) be the represented literals. The conflict graph \(G_L=(L,E)\) has \(\{\ell_1,\ell_2\}\in E\) exactly when no feasible binary assignment satisfies both literals. For \(q=|L|\ge2\), \(\rho(G_L)=2|E|/[q(q-1)]\). A family is dense when its density is eventually bounded below by a positive constant, equivalently \(|E|=\Omega(q^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the literal-level convention, vertices are signed literals and edges join pairs that cannot simultaneously be true; density means quadratically many conflicts.
assumptions_latex: Conflicts are defined semantically relative to a fixed binary feasible set.
The represented literal set is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E=\{\{\ell_1,\ell_2\}:\nexists x\text{ feasible satisfying both}\},\qquad |E|=\Omega(|L|^2).
knowledge_statements.title: Literal-Level Dense Conflict Graph

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pairwise Conflicts Need Not Characterize Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the information represented by a binary conflict graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conflict graph records infeasible pairs of represented literals but need not record higher-order minimal infeasible sets. For \(x_1+x_2+x_3\le2\), every pair of active literals can hold simultaneously, so the active-literal conflict graph has no edges, although \((1,1,1)\) is infeasible. Graph density therefore measures pairwise incompatibility only.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conflict graphs can miss purely higher-order incompatibilities, so a sparse graph does not imply a weakly coupled feasible set.
assumptions_latex: Edges encode only pairwise simultaneous-literal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{pairwise conflict graph}\not\equiv\text{complete feasibility representation in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Conflicts Need Not Characterize Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementary-Literal Edges Do Not Imply Density
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mandatory conflicts when both polarities of each binary variable are represented.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If both \(x_i\) and \(\neg x_i\) are vertices, then \(\{x_i,\neg x_i\}\in E\) for every \(i\). These \(n\) mandatory edges are only linear in the number of variables and do not by themselves make a literal-level graph family dense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposite literals always conflict, but these linear-many mandatory edges do not create a dense graph.
assumptions_latex: Both polarities of each of \(n\) binary variables are represented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x_i,\neg x_i\}\in E\ \forall i,\qquad n=o((2n)^2).
knowledge_statements.title: Complementary-Literal Edges Do Not Imply Density

assumptions_latex: A binary feasibility system has variables indexed by \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
A pair is declared conflicting when the corresponding two literals cannot simultaneously hold in any feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conflict graph is dense when its edge density stays bounded away from zero as \(n\) grows.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-level conflict graphs for binary assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conflict graph is \(G_c=(V,E_c)\), where \(\{i,j\}\in E_c\) exactly when the designated active literals for variables \(i\) and \(j\) cannot both occur in a feasible binary assignment. Its density is \[\rho(G_c)=\frac{2|E_c|}{n(n-1)}.\] A family \((G_{c,n})\) is dense when some \(\delta>0\) satisfies \(\rho(G_{c,n})\ge\delta\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), equivalently \(|E_{c,n}|=\Omega(n^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conflict graph connects incompatible binary assignments; it is dense when a constant fraction of all variable pairs conflict.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Conflict Graphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The density calculation is correct under the stated variable-level convention, but conflict graphs are commonly literal-level objects. The selected convention and its relation to designated active literals require an authoritative source.

children.title: Dense Variable Interaction Graphs
children.top_down_role: Covers widespread coupling among variables beyond explicit pairwise conflicts.

assumptions_latex: A binary optimization formulation has variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and finitely many constraint or objective terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The variable interaction graph is dense when it has \(\Omega(n^2)\) edges, equivalently density bounded below by a positive constant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal co-occurrence graph induced by a fixed binary formulation.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 The sparsity graph p. 12
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The variable interaction graph \(G_I=(V,E_I)\) has \(\{i,j\}\in E_I\) when variables \(x_i\) and \(x_j\) occur together in at least one formulation term. A family \((G_{I,n})\) is dense if there are \(\delta>0\) and \(n_0\) such that \[\rho(G_{I,n})=\frac{2|E_{I,n}|}{n(n-1)}\ge\delta\] for every \(n\ge n_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable interaction graph links variables appearing in a common formulation term; density means quadratically many such links.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Variable Interaction Graphs

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 The sparsity graph p. 12
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense Interaction Does Not Imply Computational Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of graph density alone to certify difficult binary optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f_n(x)=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}x_ix_j\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), the interaction graph is \(K_n\), yet \(f_n(x)=\binom{\sum_i x_i}{2}\) has minimum value \(0\), attained exactly when \(\sum_i x_i\le1\). An optimizer and the optimal value are obtainable in \(O(n)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete interaction graph can accompany a trivially solvable objective, so density alone is not a hardness certificate.
assumptions_latex: The problem is unconstrained minimization of \(f_n\) over \(\{0,1\}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G_I=K_n\quad\text{and}\quad\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}f_n(x)=0\text{ is computable in }O(n).

notation.meaning: Quadratic binary objective containing every pairwise product.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Interaction Does Not Imply Computational Hardness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-invariance of the primal co-occurrence graph under exact extended reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge2\), the set \(S_n=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\le1\}\) has a one-row formulation whose interaction graph is \(K_n\). It also has the exact extended formulation \(s_0=0\), \(s_i=s_{i-1}+x_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), with \(s_i\in\{0,1\}\). Its extended interaction graph has \(O(n)\) edges and bounded maximum degree. Thus interaction density is not invariant under exact extended reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same binary set can have a dense direct formulation and a sparse exact extended formulation.
assumptions_latex: Edges join variables occurring together in a formulation row or term.
Auxiliary variables are included as vertices of the extended interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_n\text{ admits both a complete direct interaction graph and an exact extended interaction graph with }O(n)\text{ edges}.

notation.meaning: Binary vectors containing at most one selected component.

knowledge_statements.title: Interaction Density Is Formulation-Dependent

children.title: Overlapping Clique Structure
children.top_down_role: Covers heavily intersecting clique regions that complicate graph-based reasoning.

assumptions_latex: A graph \(G=(V,E)\) represents binary conflicts or interactions.
A family of cliques \(\mathcal C=\{C_1,\ldots,C_q\}\) has been selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The clique family is overlapping when distinct cliques intersect, with total overlap measured by repeated vertex incidence.

notation.meaning: Number of selected cliques containing vertex v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overlap within a specified family of graph cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each \(C_k\subseteq V\) is a clique when \(\{u,v\}\in E\) for every distinct \(u,v\in C_k\). The family is overlapping if there exist \(k\ne\ell\) with \(C_k\cap C_\ell\ne\varnothing\). Writing \(m_v=|\{k:v\in C_k\}|\), its total repeated incidence is \[O(\mathcal C)=\sum_{v\in V}\max\{m_v-1,0\}.\] Thus \(O(\mathcal C)>0\) exactly when the family contains an overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clique family overlaps when some vertex belongs to multiple cliques; repeated vertex incidence gives a quantitative overlap measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Overlapping Clique Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intersection condition and repeated-incidence measure are mathematically consistent and fit the condition container, but the particular quantitative measure is introduced without a source.

children.title: Dense-Graph Processing Costs
children.top_down_role: Covers memory, separation, propagation, and presolve burdens induced by dense graph structure.

assumptions_latex: An undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has \(|V|=n\), \(|E|=m\), and constant-time adjacency access.
The processing task explicitly inspects every edge or materializes the full adjacency matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Edge inspection costs \(\Theta(n+m)\), while matrix materialization costs \(\Theta(n^2)\); both are \(\Theta(n^2)\) on dense graph families.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time and storage costs for explicit processing of dense interaction graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An adjacency-list traversal that visits every vertex and edge uses \(\Theta(n+m)\) time and \(\Theta(n+m)\) storage. Constructing or scanning an adjacency matrix uses \(\Theta(n^2)\) time and \(\Theta(n^2)\) storage. If the graph family is dense, so \(m=\Theta(n^2)\), then either explicit edge traversal or matrix processing requires \(\Theta(n^2)\) time, and explicit representation requires quadratic worst-case space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicitly processing a dense graph takes quadratic time; a full adjacency matrix also requires quadratic storage.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Processing Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The adjacency-list and adjacency-matrix bounds are correct for the explicitly limited tasks, and the complexity-bound kind fits the container, but no citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Propagation-Blind Encodings
children.top_down_role: Covers formulations whose encoded structure yields little domain reduction during propagation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Forced Literal Missed by Unit Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete propagation-blind CNF encoding under ordinary unit propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E(a,b)=(a\lor b)\land(\neg a\lor b)\). Every satisfying assignment of \(E\) has \(b=1\), but from the empty partial assignment neither clause is unit, so unit propagation reaches a fixed point without deriving \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-clause CNF logically forces b, although unit propagation from the empty assignment derives nothing.
assumptions_latex: The encoding language is CNF over primary variables \(a,b\).
The propagation operator is ordinary unit propagation from the empty partial assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E\models b\quad\text{but}\quad b\notin P_E(\varnothing).

notation.meaning: Literals derived by unit propagation from the empty assignment.

knowledge_statements.title: A Forced Literal Missed by Unit Propagation

assumptions_latex: An encoding \(E(X,Y)\) represents feasible assignments of primary binary variables \(X\), possibly using auxiliary variables \(Y\).
A sound propagation operator \(P_E\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The encoding is propagation-blind when some logically forced primary literal is not derived by propagation from the corresponding partial assignment.

notation.meaning: Set of feasible completions consistent with partial assignment alpha
Literals derived by the propagation operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding-relative visibility under a specified sound propagation procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partial assignment \(\alpha\) to \(X\), let \(\operatorname{Comp}_E(\alpha)\) contain all satisfying completions of \(E\) consistent with \(\alpha\). The encoding is propagation-blind if there exist \(\alpha\) and a primary literal \(\ell\) such that \(\operatorname{Comp}_E(\alpha)\ne\varnothing\), every completion in \(\operatorname{Comp}_E(\alpha)\) satisfies \(\ell\), but \(\ell\notin P_E(\alpha)\). Thus the encoding preserves feasibility while hiding an implication from the chosen propagation mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding is propagation-blind when feasibility logically forces a primary literal but the specified propagation procedure cannot derive it.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation-Blind Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent once the encoding language and sound propagation operator are fixed, but it introduces the term propagation-blind without a source connecting it to established propagation-completeness terminology.

children.title: Proof-Weak Encodings
children.top_down_role: Covers formulations that provide poor support for concise infeasibility or bound certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Weak Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative definition comparing refutation lengths of two encodings under a fixed proof system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a proof system \(P\) and two polynomial-size encodings \(E_n\) and \(E'_n\) of the same binary feasibility problem. The family \((E_n)\) is proof-weak relative to \((E'_n,P)\) if both encodings have identical feasible projections, but there exists an infinite set \(I\subseteq\mathbb N\) of infeasible instances such that every \(P\)-refutation of \(E_n\) has length \(2^{\Omega(n)}\), whereas some \(P\)-refutation of \(E'_n\) has length bounded by a polynomial in \(n\). Thus semantic equivalence does not imply comparable certification strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding is proof-weak when an equivalent formulation admits polynomial refutations but the encoding requires exponentially long refutations in the chosen proof system.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a fixed, sound, and complete refutation system for the encoded constraints.
\(E_n\) and \(E'_n\) have polynomial description size and identical feasible projections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_P(E_n)=2^{\Omega(n)}\) while \(L_P(E'_n)=n^{O(1)}\) on infinitely many infeasible instances.

notation.meaning: Length of a shortest proof-system P refutation of encoding E.
Semantically equivalent encoding families indexed by instance size.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and terminal container fit, but the proposed relative terminology and exponential-versus-polynomial separation require a source that fixes the proof system, encoding map, instance indexing, size parameter, and refutation-length convention. As written, E_n alternates between denoting an encoding family and an encoding of an individual infeasible instance.

children.title: Structural Visibility Gaps
children.top_down_role: Covers combinatorial relationships hidden from solver inference by the selected representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Visibility Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Visibility is defined relative to a specified polynomial-time inference closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E(x,y)\) encode a binary set \(S=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\exists y\ E(x,y)\}\), and let \(\mathcal C(E)\) denote all inequalities produced from \(E\) by a fixed inference closure. A valid inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) exhibits a structural visibility gap when it is valid for every \(x\in S\), has polynomial encoding length, but neither it nor any inequality implying it belongs to \(\mathcal C(E)\). The gap is representation-dependent: an equivalent extended formulation may expose the same inequality to its corresponding closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural visibility gap occurs when a compact valid consequence of a binary model cannot be recovered by the chosen inference closure from its encoding.
assumptions_latex: \(E(x,y)\) is a finite encoding whose projection onto \(x\) equals \(S\).
\(\mathcal C\) is a fixed, explicitly specified inference closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) is semantically valid for \(S\) but invisible to \(\mathcal C(E)\).

notation.meaning: Consequences obtainable from E by the selected inference rules.
Polynomial-size valid inequality whose visibility is tested.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the failure-boundary container, but its mathematical sense depends on a sourced and instantiated inference closure. The domain over which one inequality implies another is also unspecified, so source uncertainty affects the definition itself.

children.title: Search Certification Burden
children.top_down_role: Covers enlarged search effort and prolonged certification caused by inference-poor encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Search Certification Burden
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching-tree certificate for infeasibility under a fixed node-refutation procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an infeasible binary encoding \(E(x)\), a search certificate is a finite binary tree whose internal nodes branch on an unfixed variable \(x_i\), whose root represents \(\{0,1\}^n\), and whose leaves partition that cube. Every leaf must be declared infeasible by a fixed, independently checkable node procedure \(R\). Its certification burden is \(B_R(E)=\min_T |\operatorname{leaves}(T)|\), where the minimum ranges over valid search certificates. A family has exponential search certification burden when \(B_R(E_n)=2^{\Omega(n)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certification burden is the minimum number of leaves in a complete branching tree whose leaves are all verifiably infeasible under a fixed node procedure.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) soundly certifies infeasibility of every leaf it accepts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid tree certifies infeasibility of \(E\), and \(B_R(E)\) measures the smallest such certificate.

notation.meaning: Minimum leaf count of a valid R-certified branching tree.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the appropriate content kind, but the record needs a source defining the branching proof model and leaf rule. In particular, R must certify infeasibility of E under the leaf's partial assignment, and the size convention and admissible branching rules must be fixed.

children.title: Penalty Coefficient Scaling
children.top_down_role: Covers the magnitude and relative scaling of penalty coefficients in binary formulations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(X=F\), then \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(f(x)+\lambda p(x))=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\); otherwise, the same equality holds whenever \(\lambda\delta>\Delta\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative penalty whose zero set is the feasible set.
Objective range over the finite binary domain.
Smallest positive penalty value on an infeasible point when such points exist.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain exact-penalty threshold for binary minimization, with the all-feasible case handled separately.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Penalty Function Approach p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be nonempty and finite, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(p:X\to\mathbb R_+\), and define \(F=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}\neq\varnothing\) and \(\Delta=\max_{x\in X}f(x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\). If \(X=F\), then the penalized and feasible minimizers coincide for every \(\lambda\ge0\). Otherwise, define \(\delta=\min_{x\in X\setminus F}p(x)>0\). If \(\lambda\delta>\Delta\), then \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(f(x)+\lambda p(x))=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite binary domain, if infeasible points exist and the penalty coefficient times the smallest positive violation exceeds the objective range, the penalized and feasible minimizers coincide. If every point is feasible, they coincide for every nonnegative coefficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalty Coefficient Scaling

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5 Penalty Function Approach p. 37

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), \(p:X\to\mathbb R_+\), and \(F=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}\) is nonempty.
\(X\setminus F\neq\varnothing\), so \(p(x)>0\) for every \(x\in X\setminus F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\lambda\ge0\), \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(f(x)+\lambda p(x))=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\) if and only if \(\lambda>\lambda_{\mathrm{crit}}\). If \(\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{crit}}\ge0\), an infeasible point ties the feasible optimum value.

notation.meaning: Largest infeasible objective advantage per unit penalty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient strict coefficient threshold for exclusion of all infeasible penalized minimizers on a finite domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f^*=\min_{y\in F}f(y)\) and define \[\lambda_{\mathrm{crit}}=\max_{x\in X\setminus F}\frac{f^*-f(x)}{p(x)}.\] For every \(\lambda\ge0\), the penalized minimizers equal the feasible minimizers if and only if \(\lambda>\lambda_{\mathrm{crit}}\). If \(\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{crit}}\ge0\), at least one infeasible point attains the feasible optimum value and hence is also a penalized minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sharp coefficient threshold is the largest objective advantage per unit violation among infeasible points. Strictly exceeding it is necessary and sufficient for the penalized and constrained minimizer sets to coincide; an admissible equality produces an infeasible tie.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Finite-Domain Penalty Threshold

children.title: Underweighted Penalty Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers penalty levels too small to enforce the intended preference or violation cost.

assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in X\setminus F\), \(p(\bar x)>0\), and \(f(\bar x)<f^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(0\le\lambda<(f^*-f(\bar x))/p(\bar x)\), then \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(f(x)+\lambda p(x))\cap F=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Minimum unpenalized objective over feasible points.
Infeasible point exhibiting an insufficient penalty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise threshold at which a specified infeasible binary point ceases to dominate all feasible points.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Penalty Function Approach p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be nonempty and finite, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(p:X\to\mathbb R_+\), define \(F=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}\neq\varnothing\), and put \(f^*=\min_{x\in F}f(x)\). Suppose \(\bar x\in X\setminus F\) satisfies \(p(\bar x)>0\) and \(f(\bar x)<f^*\). If \(0\le\lambda<(f^*-f(\bar x))/p(\bar x)\), then \(f(\bar x)+\lambda p(\bar x)<f^*\), so no global minimizer of \(f+\lambda p\) over \(X\) is feasible. At equality, \(\bar x\) ties the feasible optimum value, although another infeasible point may still have a smaller penalized value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A penalty is underweighted for a specified infeasible point when that point's objective advantage exceeds its weighted violation, forcing all penalized minimizers to be infeasible. Equality makes that point tie the feasible optimum value but need not make it globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Underweighted Penalty Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5 Penalty Function Approach p. 37

children.title: Overweighted Penalty Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers excessively large penalties that distort coefficient balance and solver behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), \(p:X\to\mathbb R_+\), and \(F=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}\) is nonempty.
\(X\setminus F\neq\varnothing\), \(\delta=\min_{x\in X\setminus F}p(x)>0\), and \(\Delta=\max_{x\in X}f(x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\lambda>\Delta/\delta\), \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(f(x)+\lambda p(x))=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: A sufficient exact-penalty threshold on the finite domain.
Penalty coefficient classified as overweighted relative to the sufficient threshold.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic invariance above a sufficient finite-domain exact-penalty threshold.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Penalty Function Approach p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be nonempty and finite, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(p:X\to\mathbb R_+\), and define \(F=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}\neq\varnothing\). Suppose \(X\setminus F\neq\varnothing\), put \(\Delta=\max_{x\in X}f(x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\), and let \(\delta=\min_{x\in X\setminus F}p(x)>0\). For every \(\lambda>\Delta/\delta\), \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(f(x)+\lambda p(x))=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\). Increasing \(\lambda\) further therefore cannot change the exact minimizer set or the ordering of feasible points. For any infeasible \(x\) and feasible \(y\), it increases the signed gap \((f(x)+\lambda p(x))-f(y)\) at rate \(p(x)>0\), although numerical behavior may still change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Above the stated sufficient exact-penalty threshold, larger coefficients do not change the exact minimizers or the ordering of feasible points. They increase each infeasible point's penalized objective relative to every feasible point, while numerical behavior may still change.
knowledge_statements.title: Overweighted Penalty Regimes

children.title: Numerical Instability
children.top_down_role: Covers loss of numerical reliability associated with poorly scaled penalized formulations.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the set of evaluated candidates and \(f,p:X\to\mathbb R\).
\(q_\lambda=f+\lambda p\) is the exact penalized objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A gap greater than \(2\varepsilon\) preserves strict ordering; a gap less than \(2\varepsilon\) can be reversed, and a gap equal to \(2\varepsilon\) can be erased to a tie.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-ordering failure boundary under an explicit uniform absolute evaluation-error model.

source_refs.locator: 5.6 Numerical results p. 66
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a set of evaluated candidates, let \(f,p:X\to\mathbb R\), and define \(q_\lambda(x)=f(x)+\lambda p(x)\). Suppose \(|\widehat q_\lambda(z)-q_\lambda(z)|\le\varepsilon\) for every \(z\in X\), where \(\varepsilon>0\). For \(x,y\in X\) with \(q_\lambda(x)<q_\lambda(y)\), the computed strict ordering is guaranteed when \(q_\lambda(y)-q_\lambda(x)>2\varepsilon\). If the gap is less than \(2\varepsilon\), admissible errors can reverse the ordering; if it equals \(2\varepsilon\), they can erase the strict ordering by producing a tie. If a particular solver's bound \(\varepsilon\) increases with penalty-coefficient magnitude, increasing \(\lambda\) correspondingly enlarges the unresolved-gap regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a uniform absolute evaluation error bound epsilon, a strict objective gap greater than 2 epsilon is reliably ordered. A smaller gap can be reversed, while a gap exactly equal to 2 epsilon can be reduced to a tie. Penalty scaling enlarges this regime only when it increases the solver's error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Instability

children.title: Solver Tolerance Interactions
children.top_down_role: Covers sensitivity of penalized models to feasibility, integrality, and optimality tolerances.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) is nonempty and finite, and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), \(p:X\to\mathbb R_+\).
The solver returns a point whose penalized objective is at most \(\eta\ge0\) above the global penalized optimum and accepts it only if \(p(x)\le\tau_{\mathrm{feas}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted \(\eta\)-optimal return is in \(F\) if \(\tau_{\mathrm{feas}}<\delta\) or \(\lambda\delta>\Delta+\eta\).

notation.meaning: Solver feasibility tolerance applied to the penalty measure.
Smallest positive penalty value on the finite binary domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternative feasibility- and optimality-tolerance safeguards on a finite binary domain.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Penalty Function Approach p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be nonempty and finite, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(p:X\to\mathbb R_+\), and define \(F=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}\neq\varnothing\). Suppose \(X\setminus F\neq\varnothing\), let \(\delta=\min_{x\in X\setminus F}p(x)>0\), and put \(\Delta=\max_{x\in X}f(x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\). Assume the solver returns a point whose value of \(f+\lambda p\) is at most \(\eta\ge0\) above the global penalized optimum and accepts it only if \(p(x)\le\tau_{\mathrm{feas}}\). Every accepted return is truly feasible if either \(\tau_{\mathrm{feas}}<\delta\) or \(\lambda\delta>\Delta+\eta\). If both safeguards fail, these aggregate bounds alone do not guarantee true feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accepted approximately optimal return is guaranteed feasible if either the feasibility tolerance is below the smallest positive violation or the penalty gap exceeds the objective range plus the optimality tolerance. If neither safeguard holds, these bounds alone provide no feasibility guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver Tolerance Interactions

source_witnesses.locator: 2.5 Penalty Function Approach p. 37

assumptions_latex: The solver's optimality tolerance is the absolute additive value \(\eta\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in X\) satisfying \(q_\lambda(x)\le\min_{z\in X}q_\lambda(z)+\eta\) lies in \(F\) if and only if \(\gamma_\lambda>\eta\).

notation.meaning: Gap between the best infeasible penalized value and the feasible optimum.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp feasibility test for every absolute-eta-optimal penalized return on a finite domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_\lambda(x)=f(x)+\lambda p(x)\), let \(f^*=\min_{y\in F}f(y)\), and define \[\gamma_\lambda=\min_{x\in X\setminus F}q_\lambda(x)-f^*.\] Every point \(x\in X\) satisfying \(q_\lambda(x)\le\min_{z\in X}q_\lambda(z)+\eta\) is feasible if and only if \(\gamma_\lambda>\eta\). When \(\gamma_\lambda\le\eta\), an infeasible \(\eta\)-optimal point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every absolute-eta-optimal penalized return is feasible exactly when the best infeasible penalized value exceeds the feasible optimum by more than eta.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Approximate-Optimality Feasibility Margin
